Remember him always filming us doing stupid stuff at uni? Maybe he's found his calling. Speaker_2: He was always more interested in the filming than the actual ‘stupid stuff’ though, wasn’t he? Right, I'm just going to quickly text me nan and tell her the cat is lovely. Again. Speaker_3: Did anyone watch that new series on Netflix? “Dark Horizon” or something? It was… a bit out there. Speaker_4: Nah, I’ve been stuck on “The Crown” again. Proper binge-watching material. Makes me feel slightly guilty knowing how much privilege they had, though. Compared to, like, struggling through essays. Speaker_5: I tried it, but I got to the Diana episodes and it just made me sad. I needed something a bit lighter. Been watching a load of baking shows. Speaker_1: Baking shows? You? I thought you lived off instant noodles and questionable takeaways. Speaker_5: Hey, a man can change! Besides, it's inspiring. Maybe I'll actually attempt a Victoria sponge this weekend. Speaker_2: (Looking at his phone) Oh, right, me nan wants to know if I’m coming round on Sunday. Apparently, she’s made a roast. And a pavlova. Speaker_3: Pavlova? Now *that* sounds good. Speaker_4: You lucky sod. I’m stuck with baked beans on toast, probably. Unless I can convince my mum to send me some leftovers. Speaker_1: You could always attempt your own Victoria Sponge, mate. Join the baking revolution. Speaker_5: Just checked, appointment's still showing as being another 20 minutes. This is a joke. Speaker_3: Maybe we should have brought a deck of cards.

Speaker_1: Right, so, shopping list. Milk’s definitely on there, isn’t it? We’re almost out. Speaker_2: Aye, milk, bread… and get some more of them disinfectant wipes. I swear, this house attracts flies like nobody’s business. I just batted one away from Leo’s head a minute ago. Speaker_3: Mum! You didn’t *bat* it, you tried to swat it with the TV remote! Speaker_2: Well, it were the closest thing, weren’t it? And it nearly worked. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Sounds like a scene from a cartoon. Honestly, the wildlife you get in Bolton… Speaker_1: It's ridiculous. I swear the bins are a beacon. Oh! And loo roll. Definitely need loo roll. And… what about fruit? Apples? Bananas? Speaker_3: Can we get those little oranges, the satsumas? Please? Speaker_1: Yeah, satsumas are good. Right, fruit sorted. Mum, did you put anything on that bite on your arm? It looks awful. Speaker_2: Just some antihistamine cream. Still itching though, the little blighter. I think it might be a mosquito, even though they’re not really around this time of year. Speaker_4: Could be a horsefly. Nasty things. They leave a really nasty reaction. Perhaps some calamine lotion would help? Speaker_2: Oh, good shout. I forgot about calamine. Add that to the list, love. Speaker_1: Done. Calamine. Right, anything else? Oh! Biscuits! Need biscuits. Digestive or… Speaker_3: Chocolate digestives! Definitely chocolate digestives. Speaker_4: (Smiling) Always chocolate digestives with this lot. Speaker_1: Of course. Now, speaking of things being bitten… did you see the game yesterday? United absolutely hammered them. Speaker_3: YES! I told you they would! Rashford was on fire. Speaker_2: Honestly, all that shouting at the telly. You'd think your life depended on it. Speaker_1: It kinda does, doesn't it? It’s the only joy we have sometimes! Speaker_4: (Laughing) A bit dramatic, perhaps. Though, I have to admit, it was a good match. I saw the highlights. Speaker_3: Highlights? You have to *watch* the whole thing! You miss all the best bits. Speaker_1: He's right, Dad. You miss the dodgy tackles and the angry managers. It's crucial viewing. Speaker_2: Alright, alright. Don't you two gang up on me. Just get me that calamine lotion on the list, will you? And maybe a fly swatter that isn’t a TV remote. Speaker_1: Consider it done. Calamine, fly swatter, milk, bread, loo roll, satsumas, chocolate digestives... Anything else before I finalise this masterpiece? Speaker_3: Can we get those Monster Munch crisps? The Pickled Onion flavour? Speaker_1: Leo! Seriously? We just had crisps yesterday! Speaker_3: But… Pickled Onion! Please? Speaker_4: (Winking at Speaker_1) A small treat wouldn’t hurt. Speaker_1: (Sighs) Fine. Monster Munch. Pickled Onion. You're spoiling him, honestly. Speaker_2: It’s a bit of a bribe, I reckon. Keeping him quiet about the remote incident. Speaker_1: Maybe. Probably. Right, list is officially complete. Let’s get this sorted.

Speaker_1: Ugh, P.E. was *awful* today. Miss Davies made us do shuttle runs. Shuttle runs! Like, seriously? Speaker_2: No way! Shuttle runs are the worst. I thought she liked us? I mean, we're in her form. Speaker_1: Apparently not enough to spare us the torture. My legs are still burning. And then Ben kept trying to… well, you know… show off. Speaker_2: Ben? Showing off? Groundbreaking. What was he doing this time? Trying to do like, a flip or something? Speaker_1: Worse. He was trying to run the shuttle runs sideways. Sideways! Miss Davies just stared at him. It was glorious. Speaker_2: Oh my god, I wish I’d seen that. Speaking of glorious, have you seen what Holly’s posted on Instagram? It’s just…filters. So many filters. She looks completely different. Speaker_1: Ugh, Holly. She's obsessed. I saw a TikTok about how everyone on Instagram looks the same now because of those filters. It’s kind of scary, actually. Speaker_2: Totally. Remember when people used to just…post normal pictures? Before everyone wanted to look like a cartoon version of themselves? Speaker_1: Yeah. It’s all about the aesthetic now, isn’t it? It's exhausting. Did you finish the science homework? The one on… what was it, osmosis? Speaker_2: Almost. I’m stuck on question three. It doesn't make any sense. Something about potatoes and salt? Speaker_1: Oh, that one! It's a trick question. You have to remember what happens to the water inside the potato cells. It's all to do with… Wait, let me try and explain. Imagine the potato cells are like balloons… Speaker_2: Okay, balloons… go on. Speaker_1: And the skin of the potato is like the balloon's surface. If you put it in salty water, the water *leaves* the cells, so they shrivel up. It's like the balloons are deflating. Speaker_2: Oh! Okay, okay, I think I get it now. You're a lifesaver. Seriously. Mr. Henderson would have my hide if I didn't understand osmosis. He’s so intense about science. Speaker_1: I know! He's the kind of teacher who gets genuinely excited about chemical reactions. It’s a bit…much. Have you seen that new YouTuber, ‘Science Sam’? She explains things really clearly. Speaker_2: Science Sam? No, I haven't. I’ll check her out. I need all the help I can get. Oh! And did you hear what happened with Chloe and Mr. Peterson? Speaker_1: Ooh, spill! What? Speaker_2: Apparently, she accidentally called him ‘Dad’ in the middle of history. A full-on, loud ‘Yes, Dad!’ She went bright red. Everyone was trying not to laugh. Speaker_1: *No way!* That’s amazing. Mr. Peterson’s face must have been a picture. She is so clumsy. Speaker_1: I feel like we're always talking about school stuff. We need a life. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. But honestly, what *else* is there to talk about in Linton? It’s not exactly brimming with excitement. Except Ben trying to run sideways, obviously. Speaker_1: True, true. Well, at least P.E. is over for the week. Speaker_2: Amen to that.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I feel like death warmed up. My throat is absolutely killing me. Speaker_2: Oh, no! That’s awful. Still? You said you were feeling a bit rough yesterday, but I thought you'd bounced back. Speaker_1: Bounced back? Ha! More like face-planted into a duvet and stayed there. It’s proper bad, like the kind of cold where you can *feel* your eyeballs aching. Speaker_2: Ugh, those are the worst. Have you taken anything? Lemsip? Paracetamol? I’ve got loads if you need. Speaker_1: Yeah, downed a load of Lemsip earlier. Doesn't seem to be doing much good, to be honest. It feels like one of those ones that settles in your chest. I’m worried about getting proper ill right before Christmas. Speaker_2: You and everyone else, I suspect. Hospitals are already rammed, even before the winter really hits. Remember when I had that, uh, *incident* with the dodgy prawns last summer? Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t remind me. You were practically green! And the noises… Speaker_2: (grimaces) Let’s not dwell. But seriously, A&E was absolute chaos. All this talk about strain on the NHS, it’s true. And you’ve had your flu jab, haven’t you? Speaker_1: Yeah, ages ago. Honestly, I'm starting to wonder if these jabs even *work*. All my colleagues have been dropping like flies, vaccinated or not. Speaker_2: It's never a guarantee, is it? It just reduces the severity, hopefully. Speaking of feeling rubbish, I was watching that old "MasterChef" episode last night with Lloyd Grossman… Speaker_1: Oh, bless him. A national treasure. Speaker_2: Seriously! And he was talking about how he always used to get food poisoning on set, because he was constantly tasting everything. Proper dedication, that. Makes my little cold seem a bit pathetic. Speaker_1: Don't say that! It's a proper vile cold and I need sympathy. Besides, Lloyd Grossman probably had a team of doctors on speed dial. Speaker_2: True. It's just… it makes you think. He was always so cheerful, even when no doubt feeling absolutely dreadful. You know, I was reading an article the other day about how they're developing AI that can read body language accurately. Speaker_1: Really? Like, tell if someone's lying? Speaker_2: That's part of it. But also detect subtle cues about how someone is *feeling* - pain, discomfort, even just mild annoyance. Imagine the implications for TV interviews, or even just everyday conversations. It's a bit creepy, actually. Speaker_1: Totally creepy. I’m trying not to show anyone how miserable I am, just in case the AI finds out and starts sending me targeted ads for tissues. Though, to be fair, I could probably do with some. And maybe a hot water bottle. And a lifetime supply of Lemsip. Speaker_2: I'll raid the medicine cabinet. You just focus on feeling…slightly less awful. Speaker_1: You’re a lifesaver. I owe you one. Speaker_2: Just get better soon, that's all. Nobody wants a sickly friend over Christmas. Speaker_1: Deal. Now, put the kettle on, yeah? And maybe find something awful to watch on TV – a distraction is desperately needed. Speaker_2: Consider it done. Though, fair warning, I’m on a 90s sitcom binge at the moment. Speaker_1: Bring it on. Anything is better than contemplating my impending demise from a simple cold.

Speaker_1: Right, my turn. Hmm… Let’s see. I’m going to play ‘quixotic’ across the double word score. That’s… oh, a hefty 38 points! Sorry, David. Speaker_2: Ouch! Quixotic, eh? Showing off a bit now, aren’t you, Margaret? I was saving up for a good one myself, but you’ve rather scuppered my plans. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) You two are at it again. Just like your father and I used to be, always trying to one-up each other at Scrabble. Though, *he* always accused *me* of having a dictionary hidden up my sleeve. Speaker_4: (A dry cough) A likely story, Moira. You always had a knack for words. Remember that time you corrected the Bishop’s grammar during the village fete? Caused quite a stir, that did. Speaker_1: Oh, Grandad, you always have a story! It’s lovely. Though, I think that story might be slightly embellished. Anyway, David, you’re looking a bit glum. Don’t worry, there are plenty of tiles left. Speaker_2: Just a bit frustrated. I was hoping to use that ‘x’ for something spectacular. Speaking of spectacular, did you see the gridlock at the Trafford Centre today? Absolute chaos. I spent forty minutes just trying to find a parking space. Speaker_3: Oh, dear. That sounds dreadful. I’m glad I stayed in and finished that recipe I saw in that new cooking magazine. It was for a Moroccan tagine, absolutely delicious. You must try it, Margaret. I could send you the recipe. Speaker_1: Oh, yes please! I’ve been meaning to try more Moroccan food. We had that lovely tagine in Marrakech a few years ago, remember? Speaker_4: Marrakech… splendid city. Though, rather noisy. I prefer quieter holidays, myself. More conducive to reading. I’ve been re-reading my old copies of ‘The Gramophone’. Found a fascinating article on early jazz recordings. Speaker_2: (Smiling) You and your jazz, Dad. You live and breathe it. I saw Michael posting on Facebook about his new band’s gig next week. He’s getting quite good, actually. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s wonderful! I must send him a message of encouragement. He’s so shy about performing. Speaker_3: It’s good he has a creative outlet. Keeps him stimulated. Though, I do worry about him. He works so hard. Reminds me of you, David, always burning the candle at both ends. Speaker_2: (Raises his hands in mock surrender) I’m trying to take it easy, honestly! Although… I did promise to pick up some sausages from Mr. Henderson’s butcher shop tomorrow. Apparently, the queue stretches down the street on a Saturday morning. Speaker_1: Oh, the queue at Henderson’s is legendary! You’ll need to take a book, or perhaps listen to some jazz, to keep yourself entertained. Speaker_4: A very good suggestion, Margaret. A good book, and a fine sausage… what more could a man want? Although… a winning Scrabble score would be nice, too. Speaker_2: Don’t even think about it, Dad. My turn now. And I *think* I’ve found a word that might just put me back in the game… Does this fit what you were looking for? I can continue the conversation if you'd like, or adjust it to better suit the context. Speaker_2: Don’t even think about it, Dad. My turn now. And I *think* I’ve found a word that might just put me back in the game…

Speaker_1: Goodness, this queue is moving slowly, isn’t it? Though I suppose it’s to be expected on a day like this. Lovely sunshine, everyone wanting to get out and about. Speaker_2: It is rather. I’m just trying to sort out my ticket for the steam train. Been meaning to do this for ages. Used to come to these sorts of things with my father when I was a boy. Though, admittedly, they weren’t quite as…well, organised. Speaker_1: Oh, you’re going on the steam train? How lovely! I’m just volunteering today, helping with the TME – the Taunton Model Engineers, you know. I dabble in a bit of miniature painting myself, so it seemed a fitting way to spend a Saturday. Speaker_2: Miniature painting, you say? Interesting. I spent my working life surrounded by rather larger machinery, you see. Printing machinery, specifically. Speaker_1: Oh really? That sounds…technical. Speaker_2: It was. I spent a good thirty years inventing and marketing printing systems. Mostly offset lithography, though we dabbled in flexography too. Kept me busy, it did. Had a little company, built it up from nothing. Speaker_1: Goodness me! That sounds incredibly demanding. I was always more of an…artistic type. Antiques, mostly. Had a gallery for a while, down in Devon. Trying to convince people that slightly chipped porcelain was ‘characterful’. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) I can imagine. A different skill set entirely, that's for sure. My biggest challenge wasn’t convincing people of character, but convincing them of efficiency! We did a lot of work in Germany, you know. Exhibitions in Frankfurt and Düsseldorf. The Germans are very keen on precision engineering. Speaker_1: Oh, Germany! I’ve been a few times. To art fairs, mostly. Quite different from Somerset, wouldn’t you say? Always felt very…efficient, as you say. Speaker_2: Very. And demanding customers. They weren’t afraid to tell you if something didn’t work. But it kept you on your toes. We developed a system for colour separation that was rather innovative at the time. Made life a lot easier for commercial printers. I’d spend weeks at those exhibitions, demonstrating the systems, explaining the intricacies…sometimes felt like I lived in a hotel room. Speaker_1: I can imagine. Though I suspect explaining the subtleties of a Ming vase is a slightly different beast. It’s all about the narrative, you know? The provenance, the history…making people *feel* something. Speaker_2: A narrative, yes. I suppose there *is* a narrative to a well-engineered machine. The story of its creation, the problems overcome…though, admittedly, a slightly less romantic one than a centuries-old piece of porcelain. Still, it’s satisfying to see something you designed working smoothly. Speaker_1: I’m sure it is. It’s funny, isn’t it? How very different our lives have been, yet here we are, queuing for train tickets on a lovely Saturday afternoon. Speaker_2: Indeed. A small world, isn’t it? Ah, looks like it’s finally our turn.

Speaker_2: Right, nearly at the M5 then, eh? Feels like we’ve been driving for days already. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. My legs are all cramped. Are we stopping at Gloucester Services? They do the best pasties. Speaker_2: Gloucester Services it is, then. Though I maintain, they’re a bit pricey for a pasty. Still, better than those motorway ones that look like they’ve been sat under a heat lamp since 1972. Speaker_1: True. Speaking of things that look ancient, did you realise how weird English is when you think about it? Like, all the exceptions to the rules. Mrs. Davies was going on about it in English today. Speaker_2: Oh? What's she been drilling into you now? She was a stickler for proper grammar, your Mrs. Davies. Speaker_1: She was saying how there's no logical reason why 'though' is spelled with a 'gh' when it's pronounced 'tho'. And 'knight' has a 'k' but 'know' doesn't. It’s madness. Speaker_2: It's evolution, love. Language changes. Words get borrowed, spellings get muddled up over the centuries. ‘Knight’ comes from Old English, originally pronounced with a hard ‘k’ sound. ‘Know’… well, that’s a whole different story. It’s practically a different language now than it was back then. Speaker_1: It's just… frustrating when you’re trying to remember all the rules for the A-Level. Especially the etymology bits. Honestly, tracing words back to Old English and Latin feels like detective work. Speaker_2: It *is* detective work, in a way. That’s the fascinating part. And it helps you understand *why* things are the way they are. You thinking about what you want to study at Uni still? Speaker_1: Yeah. Still torn between English Lit and Philosophy. Philosophy's just… so abstract. Like, we were talking about free will today and my brain just short-circuited. Speaker_2: Philosophy’s got a habit of doing that. It's good to challenge you though, isn’t it? Makes you think about things differently. Your Mum always said you were a deep thinker. Speaker_1: Mum says I overthink everything. Speaker_2: She’s right! But it’s a good quality. Right, approaching the services now. Do you fancy a browse in the farm shop? They usually have some decent local stuff. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! Actually, I saw on Instagram they had a farmer’s market in Padstow on Saturday. We should go. Speaker_2: Padstow, eh? Sounds good. Always a good place to get fresh seafood. They had a proper bike race going on there last year. Remember? All those lycra-clad people zooming around. Speaker_1: Vaguely. I was probably complaining about being bored. Speaking of food… are you okay with quinoa? The cafe at the services does a quinoa salad. Speaker_2: Quinoa? That… stuff? No, not really. Looks like birdseed. Give me a proper sandwich any day. Ham and pickle, please. Speaker_1: You are so predictable. Okay, ham and pickle for you. I might get the quinoa. It's… healthy. Speaker_2: You can be healthy when we get to Cornwall. For now, it’s holiday time. And a large slice of cake, if they have one. Did you see the storm warnings for down there? Apparently, lots of lightning. Speaker_1: I did. Dad was saying something about needing to unplug all the electronics. Speaker_2: Definitely. Don't want to risk a power surge. Makes you think, doesn't it? All that energy, just… flashing across the sky. Reminds you how small we are. Like that bit about organ donation we were talking about last week. It feels like a really big decision, but in the grand scheme of things… Speaker_1: Yeah, it does.

Speaker_1: Right, so I reckon if we chuck all this into the pot, it’ll be grand. It's just a posh shepherd’s pie, innit? My Nana used to make it all the time. Speaker_2: Posh shepherd’s pie? Sounds fancy for a Tuesday night, doesn't it? My mum just used to throw mince at potatoes. Same result, though, I suppose. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Your mum sounds a woman after my own heart. No point in fussing, is there? Just get it on the table. Though, a bit of gravy never hurt anyone. Speaker_1: Nana always said the secret was a splash of red wine. And loads of Worcestershire sauce. Gives it a little…oomph. Speaker_2: Red wine, eh? Alright, sounds alright. I’m on spud-mashing duty, then. Can I at least have butter in ‘em? Don’t want them being dry as a bone. Speaker_1: Absolutely! Loads of butter. And a good dollop of cream cheese, if you're feeling particularly naughty. Speaker_3: Cream cheese in mash? Now there’s a thing. Sounds a bit modern for me, that. I stick to a good knob of butter and a bit of milk. Simple. Speaker_1: Oh, you’re old school, aren’t you, Geoff? You wouldn’t know a flavour explosion if it hit you in the face. Speaker_3: (Smiling) I know what I like, lass. And I like things that taste like they’re supposed to. Speaking of liking things… how’s your sister, the one who went travelling? Still gallivanting around Thailand? Speaker_1: Yeah, she’s still out there. Just sent me another load of pictures of beaches and monkeys. Makes me properly jealous, honestly. Says she’s thinking of going to Vietnam next. Speaker_2: Vietnam, proper? That's a bit…out there, isn't it? Sounds mental. Is she going on her own still? Speaker_1: Mostly. She met a bloke in Bali, apparently. Some Australian surfer dude. Mum's a bit worried, naturally. Wants her to come home and get a “proper job”. Speaker_3: Mothers, eh? Always wanting their chicks to settle down. My Elsie was the same. Wanted me to take over the shop, but I weren’t having any of it. Too much work, that. Speaker_2: Speaking of work, this job’s killing me, honestly. Been on that building site all week, shifting bricks in the rain. My back is screaming. Speaker_1: Aw, that sounds awful! You deserve a proper break. Maybe we could all go out for a pub lunch on Sunday? To celebrate the posh shepherd’s pie? Speaker_2: Yeah, I’m in. Need a pint and a proper sit-down, that’s for sure. And Geoff can tell us all about the good old days. Speaker_3: (Laughing) The good old days? There weren’t that good, you know. Just different. Though I will say, things were simpler back then. Didn’t have all this… avocado on toast and cream cheese in mashed potatoes. Speaker_1: Simpler, maybe. But definitely less tasty. Right, I’m gonna get this sauce bubbling. Someone keep an eye on the spuds, will you? Don't want them turning into concrete! Speaker_2: Aye aye, Captain! Spud-watch is a go. Speaker_3: Just remember, a good mash needs a good beating. Show 'em who's boss, lad.

Speaker_1: Right, so this is… significantly busier than I expected it to be for a Tuesday morning. Thought I could just grab a quick coffee and a scone before my shift. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I was hoping to get a bit of marking done, but there’s barely a spare seat. I should have known, it’s right next to the swimming pool, all the parents dropping kids off and grabbing a coffee. Speaker_1: You a teacher then? I guessed something academic with the marking and all. Speaker_2: Yeah, languages actually. French and Spanish. Secondary school. It's… rewarding, most of the time. What about you? You look a bit too young to be retired already. Speaker_1: (Laughs) No, thankfully. I’m a bartender down at The Flute. It's alright, keeps me busy. Just finished my degree last year in History, but jobs weren’t exactly flooding in. Speaker_2: History, that’s interesting! I always loved history at school. It's just, trying to make a career out of it… yeah, I can see why you ended up behind a bar. It's a good source of stories though, right? You must hear some good ones. Speaker_1: Oh, you have no idea. Though most of them are probably best left unsaid. It's less ‘historical accounts’ and more ‘people making questionable life choices’. What age group do you teach? Speaker_2: Year 7 mostly, so eleven and twelve-year-olds. It’s… a lot. It's amazing how much energy they have. Speaking of energy, are you doing anything sporty to keep fit? You mentioned a shift, is it a busy one? Speaker_1: Nah, I’m pretty useless at sports. Tried football for a bit, was spectacularly bad. Keep meaning to join a gym, but… well, you know how it is. The shift is usually alright. Weekends are mental, obviously. Tonight's pretty standard, though. Speaker_2: I know the feeling. I keep saying I'll take up swimming again, got a membership here, haven't been in three months. Just… life gets in the way. Have you been driving long? I saw you pull up in a pretty… compact car. Speaker_1: (Grimaces) Oh, Betsy. That’s her name. It's a Fiat 500. It was cheap. And small, which is essential for parking in Birmingham. I’ve had my license about five years, so yeah, fairly new to it all. Still get nervous on the motorways. Speaker_2: I remember that feeling! I passed on my fourth attempt. My instructor nearly had a breakdown. Just take it slow, and don't let other people rush you. It’s amazing how many people think they’re Lewis Hamilton. Speaker_1: Good advice. Are you settled here in Birmingham then? Or just visiting? You’ve got a bit of a different accent… Hertfordshire way, right? Speaker_2: Hertfordshire born and bred, but I moved here about three years ago for a job. I'm still figuring it out, to be honest. It’s… different. Not necessarily bad, just different. It’s a good city, though. Got a real vibe to it. Speaker_1: Yeah, it's got its moments. You get used to the chaos eventually. Are you seeing anyone at the moment? Or is teaching taking up all your time? Speaker_2: Oh, don't even get me started! Dating in this day and age is… exhausting. I had a disastrous Tinder date last week involving a man who spent the entire evening talking about his collection of garden gnomes. I think I’m taking a break. How about you? Anyone keeping you out of trouble?

Speaker_2: Oh, honestly, time's flown. I meant to have a proper coffee break ages ago. Are you wanting one, Arthur? Speaker_1: Please, Doreen. And yes, a cuppa would be lovely. Though it'll have to be instant, I reckon. Don't want to keep David waiting while you get the cafetière out. Speaker_3: Don't worry about me delaying things. I'm perfectly happy hovering. Though, I did notice the hydrangea looks a bit peaky. Needs watering, doesn't it? Speaker_2: Oh, you're right, David. I meant to do that this morning. Honestly, I’m all over the place. I keep forgetting things. It’s probably age, isn't it? Speaker_1: Probably. Or maybe you're just thinking about that trip to the Gambia. You were saying it was hot, wasn't it? Blisteringly hot? Speaker_2: Oh, it was! Beautiful, though. And the people were so friendly. I was reading something the other day about a woman there... or maybe it was in Africa somewhere… who pretended to be ill to get attention. Apparently, it’s called Munchausen Syndrome. Dreadful, really. Deliberately making yourself sick. Speaker_3: A fascinating, disturbing condition. I read a case study once about a mother doing it *to* her child. Utterly appalling. Speaker_1: Sounds it. Anyway, Doreen, about those banners for the bell ringing… do you think we should keep them simple? Just ‘Bell Ringing – Open Day’ or something? Speaker_2: Simple is good, Arthur. Less is more, as they say. Though we could maybe add a picture of the bells, couldn’t we? I’ve got that digital camera, I could take a photo. Speaker_3: I can design something on the computer, if you'd like. Make it look proper and professional. I used to do a bit of graphic design for the old firm. Speaker_1: That would be brilliant, David. You're a star. While you're at it, perhaps something for the donation box too? We need a new one for the village hall roof fund. Speaker_2: Oh, yes. A nice little sign saying ‘Help Restore Our Village Hall Roof!' Something like that. And a little slot, of course. Speaker_3: Easily done. Though have you two thought about how you’re getting the banners and the donation box to the hall? Arthur, you were saying your car's playing up again? Speaker_1: That's the truth. It’s hesitating again. I think it might need a new fuel filter. Though I’m loath to take it to a garage, they charge an arm and a leg these days. I might just give it a go myself. Speaker_2: Oh, Arthur, be careful! You shouldn’t be crawling around under cars at your age. Let a professional do it. Speaker_1: Nonsense. I’ve been tinkering with cars since I was a boy. It’s in my blood. Besides, I don’t fancy relying on buses, honestly. The timetable is a joke. Speaker_3: I could give you a lift, if you like. I'm going past the hall on Tuesday. Speaker_1: Would you, David? That would be very kind of you. Perhaps you could help me load everything up too. It’ll be a bit of a palaver. Speaker_2: See? Problem solved. Now, Arthur, about that coffee... I really must make it. And then we need to finalize that list for the plant sale. Are we doing tomatoes this year, do you think?

Speaker_1: Honestly, this pasta is amazing, Chloe. Did you make the sauce from scratch? Speaker_2: Yeah, pretty much. Just chucked a load of stuff in really. Tomatoes, garlic, a bit of chilli… didn’t measure anything. Speaker_3: It’s so good! Way better than anything I could manage. My cooking skills peak at beans on toast, and even that’s a disaster half the time. Speaker_4: Speaking of disasters, have you guys seen that new app, “FailFeed”? It’s just compilations of people’s cooking fails, DIY blunders…it's hilarious. Speaker_1: Ooh, no, I haven't. I’m currently obsessed with “PlantSnap”. It identifies plants from a photo. I was walking in the park yesterday and finally figured out what that weird purple flower was! Speaker_2: That sounds…surprisingly useful. I'm still stuck on TikTok, endlessly scrolling. It's a black hole. Speaker_3: TikTok is dangerous. You lose hours. I was just saying to Liam the other day - we *need* to plan a holiday. We've been talking about Greece for ages. Speaker_4: Oh, Greece! Yes! I went to Santorini with my family years ago, it was stunning. Ridiculously expensive, but stunning. Speaker_1: Santorini's on my list. I'm leaning towards Italy, though. More affordable, and pizza. Honestly, pizza is a life goal. Speaker_2: Pizza is *always* a good idea. Did anyone catch that new horror film, “The Hollow”? Everyone's been raving about how terrifying it is. Speaker_3: Oh god, I heard! Apparently, there’s this one scene with… never mind, I don’t want to ruin it. I’m such a scaredy-cat. I can’t even watch trailers. Speaker_4: I love a good scare! I’ll probably watch it this weekend. Although, I'm still recovering from “Hereditary”. That one messed me up for weeks. Speaker_1: Oh, "Hereditary" is genuinely disturbing. It’s not just jump scares, it’s… unsettling. Anyway, changing the subject slightly – how’s Ben? I haven’t seen him out with you lately, Leo. Speaker_2: Oh, Ben’s… good. We're taking a bit of a break, actually. It’s complicated. Speaker_3: Oh no, Leo, I’m sorry to hear that. Everything alright? You can tell us, you know. Speaker_4: Yeah, we’re all ears. Speaker_2: It’s just… we want different things right now, I guess. He’s really focused on his music, trying to get a band together. And I just… need someone a little more settled. It's stupid, I know. Speaker_1: It doesn’t sound stupid at all. It’s really hard when you’re not on the same page. Speaker_3: Exactly. You deserve to be happy. And you're brilliant, you'll find someone amazing. Speaker_4: Speaking of amazing, have you guys heard from Sarah? I haven’t seen her post anything on Instagram in ages. Speaker_1: She messaged me last week. She's volunteering at a wildlife sanctuary in Costa Rica! Apparently, she's rescuing sloths. Speaker_2: No way! That's so Sarah. Always doing something amazing. Good on her. Speaker_3: Sloths! That’s adorable! Maybe we should all go volunteering somewhere. Escape the horrors of…well, everything. Speaker_4: I’m in. Providing there’s good food. And zero scary spiders.

Speaker_1: Right well that was a nice little visit wasn’t it. Bit chilly walking back from the bus stop though. Speaker_2: It is. Still, good to see Maureen. Haven’t seen her properly since… well, ages. Speaker_3: It was lovely. She’s looking well, considering. Still on about that new electric car she’s thinking of getting, though. Speaker_1: Oh, is she? What sort of range does she need, really? She doesn’t do a lot of miles. Speaker_2: Exactly. I said to her, Maureen, you mostly potter around Norwich, you don’t need something that’ll get you to John O’Groats on a single charge! Speaker_3: She said it’s the principles of it, you know? Doing her bit for the environment. Speaker_1: Principles don't keep you warm on the A11 when the battery runs out, that’s what I say. Though, I suppose, they’re getting better, aren’t they? The range. Speaker_2: That’s what they say. But the price! You'd need to win the lottery. And where do you even *charge* the blasted things around here? Speaker_3: There’s a couple of those charging points at the Long John Hill car park now. Speaker_1: Oh, are there? Didn’t notice them. They’re probably always full. Full of Teslas, no doubt. Speaker_2: Exactly! All these fancy cars. I’m perfectly happy with my old Fiesta. It gets me from A to B, and doesn’t cost a fortune to run. Speaker_1: It's reliable, that's the main thing. I’m starting to worry about my Mondeo though. It’s getting on a bit, and the exhaust’s started rattling again. Speaker_3: Oh dear. Don’t tell me you're thinking of getting a new one? Speaker_1: No, no. Not a *new* one. Just…a newer one. Something a bit more sensible. Something that won’t bankrupt me every time I take it for an MOT. Speaker_2: You wouldn't get away with a newer one. Doreen would have your hide. She likes a bit of comfort, doesn't she? Speaker_1: She does. It’d have to have leather seats, at least. And heated ones. It’s getting cold enough these days! Speaker_3: You’ll have to be careful driving home this evening, though. They said on the news there’s going to be icy patches. Speaker_2: Icy patches? Oh, brilliant. Just what we need. I hate driving in the ice. Makes my hands shake. Speaker_1: We could have got the bus. Speaker_3: Oh, don’t be silly. You’ll be fine, Clive. Just take it slow. And don’t try any sudden stops. Speaker_2: And watch out for those cyclists. They seem to think they own the road. Speaker_1: They do, apparently. According to the council. They're putting in cycle lanes everywhere. Narrowing the roads for the rest of us. Speaker_3: It's all change, isn't it? Nothing stays the same. Speaker_2: That's the truth. Still, at least we have a warm house to come back to. And a nice cup of tea. That’s the important thing. Speaker_1: That it is. Right, shall we get the kettle on then? And watch a bit of telly?

Speaker_1: Honestly, the M6 is just relentless, isn't it? Always something. Though, I suppose it’s a luxury to be complaining about traffic when we’re actually *going* somewhere. Manchester, here we come! Speaker_2: It is a bit of a slog. Still, better than being stuck packing boxes, I suppose. How are you holding up with all that, by the way? It must be exhausting. Speaker_3: She’s coping. She’s always coping. It’s just…the sheer volume of *stuff* people accumulate. It’s terrifying. I’m mostly supervising and occasionally lifting things that look deceptively light. My back is reminding me I’m not twenty anymore. Speaker_1: Oh, don't start, Arthur! You were lifting all those boxes of books yesterday. I told you to let the removal men do it! It’s just…thirty years in one house. You don’t realise how much you’ve got until you have to sort through it. And half of it is things I haven't touched since…well, since the kids were little. Speaker_2: It's the sentimental stuff that's the hardest, isn't it? Speaker_1: Thanks, Mum. Speaker_2: You’re very welcome, darling. Always. Speaker_1: You’re very welcome, darling. Always. Speaker_2: You’re welcome. Now let's get you some chocolate. Speaker_2: You’re welcome. Now let's get you some chocolate. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Thank you. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Thank you. Speaker_2: You’re very welcome. Speaker_2: You’re very welcome.

Speaker_1: Right, okay, so I think I’m going to try and get from Plymouth to… oh, hang on. Bristol. Yes! Bristol. Speaker_2: Bold move. That’s a long way with those little train bits. Take *that*, Rhys! Speaker_3: (Laughing) You fiend! You’ve cut me off! Speaker_1: Okay, I’m officially abandoning the Bristol route. I'm going for… Aberdeen! Yes, Aberdeen. Lots of blue. Much more peaceful. Speaker_2: Good luck with that. That’s a seriously long haul. You'll need more than just strategery for that one. You’ll need a miracle. Speaker_4: Although, the journey to Aberdeen by train is quite scenic… especially the bit through the highlands. It reminds me of a trip I took way back when… Speaker_5: Oh don’t start a story, Dad. We’re trying to win here! Speaker_4: Ah, alright, alright. Just making conversation. But the highlands… Speaker_1: Highlands later. Lemon drizzle now. Anyone fancy another slice?

Speaker_1: Right, your go. Honestly, this game is taking *ages*. I feel like we've been building this railway for hours. Speaker_2: It is a bit of a marathon, isn’t it? Speaker_1: Honestly, this lasagne is divine, Kerrie. You’ve outdone yourself. Speaker_2: It is really good. What's the secret? More cheese? Always more cheese, right? Apparently, the pay is amazing, but she's worried about being so far from everyone. She’s a good girl, Sarah. Always thinking of others. Speaker_2: She is. Well, let’s hope she makes the right decision. More lasagne, anyone? This is seriously good.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this traffic is mental. Like, what’s even *happening* up ahead? It's barely moving. Speaker_2: It’s always like this heading towards Finchley, isn't it? Especially around this time. People trying to get the kids, I suppose. Though honestly, it’s a bit early for the school rush, isn't it? Speaker_1: Yeah, you’d think so. It’s not even half past four. Seriously though, I’m starting to regret offering to drive. Speaker_2: Don’t be silly. You're a good lad for offering. And frankly, I’d rather not attempt a manoeuvre in this mess. You’re much more…composed behind the wheel. Unlike your father. Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh god, Dad. Road rage incarnate. Remember that time in France? The horn, the shouting… Speaker_2: Oh, don’t remind me. The poor French driver looked absolutely terrified. He didn’t understand a word your father was saying, of course, but the *tone* was quite sufficient. It was horrifying *and* hilarious. Speaker_1: It was a disaster. He insists he was perfectly reasonable. Speaker_2: Reasonable? He was practically apoplectic! Anyway, how are things going with the dissertation? Still on the… what was it? The post-structuralist deconstruction of online fan fiction? Speaker_1: (groans) Don’t remind me. It’s…progressing. Slowly. I’m starting to think I’ve bitten off more than I can chew. It feels so… niche. Speaker_2: Nonsense. It sounds fascinating. And rather contemporary, which is good. Though I must admit, I find it hard to keep up with all this digital stuff. I still firmly believe there’s nothing quite like holding a book in your hands. Speaker_1: You and everyone at the TLS, Mum. Still battling the good fight against ebooks, I see. Speaker_2: Of course! Although, even *we’re* having to acknowledge the shift. Circulation’s still good, thankfully, but it’s… different. More focus on online content, reviews streamed through podcasts… it’s all changing so quickly. Speaker_1: It’s inevitable, isn’t it? It’s just… sad, in a way. Feels like something’s being lost. Speaker_2: Perhaps. Though new things are gained, too. It just requires adaptation, that’s all. Speaking of gaining, have you thought any more about what you want for your birthday? Your aunt Susan asked. Speaker_1: Ugh, Aunt Susan. Always asking. Honestly, I don’t need anything. Just…a quiet evening, maybe. Speaker_2: She’ll insist. She always does. You know what she got your cousin last year? A hand-knitted tea cosy. A *hand-knitted tea cosy*. Speaker_1: (bursts out laughing) No way! Classic Aunt Susan. Speaker_2: I kid you not. She’s very proud of her knitting. Perhaps you could suggest something practical? A new driving instructor? Just joking, darling! Though, honestly, seeing you navigate this traffic is giving me palpitations. Speaker_1: Very funny. We’re moving now! Progress! Maybe we'll be at Aunt Carol's before closing time. And honestly… a quiet evening *does* sound good. Maybe after all this. Speaker_2: That sounds lovely. Good, and maybe we can grab a quick bite before heading back. It’s been an age since we properly caught up.

Speaker_1: Right, so then the seagull – and I swear it was *massive*, like a proper, prehistoric-looking thing – swoops down and just *snatches* the chips right out of little Timmy’s hand. Speaker_2: No way! Little Timmy? Proper bawling, was he? Speaker_1: Bawling is an understatement! Full meltdown. Screaming, kicking, the lot. His mum was mortified, trying to explain it was just a bird. Like Timmy gives a toss it's “just a bird” when his chips are gone! Speaker_3: Serves him right for being a show-off with his massive portion. You know he was bragging about how much ketchup he’d gotten? Speaker_4: (Laughing) Oh, classic Timmy. Always gotta one-up everyone. Reminds me of when we were kids, trying to build the biggest sandcastle… Speaker_5: And Liam always had to make his the tallest, even if it meant risking collapse. Remember the tide coming in and washing it away just as he was adding the final turret? Speaker_2: Ha! He was fuming. Absolutely fuming. Head went down, stomped off like a little moody teenager. Speaker_3: It's the best though, isn’t it? Like, intentionally awful. You *expect* it to be a bit rubbish but you still have a laugh. Speaker_4: Totally. I think my highlight was the donkey rides. They looked so miserable. Like they were actively plotting their revenge. Speaker_5: (Chuckles) They probably were. I saw one trying to bite a kid. Gently, but still. A warning. Speaker_2: Don’t get me started on the arcade games. Spent about twenty quid trying to win a fluffy unicorn for my little cousin and came away with a plastic ring and a sense of utter failure. Speaker_1: Oh, the claw machines are rigged. Absolute con. They just *taunt* you. Like, “Oh, you almost got it! Try again! Lose more money!” Speaker_3: My mum is convinced she's a master of the claw machine. She'll spend ages studying the technique, trying to calculate the perfect angle...and still come away empty-handed. Speaker_4: She’s dedicated, though! You gotta admire the commitment. He was sweating, struggling, trying not to drop a slice. It was a spectacle. Honestly, I think he regretted it halfway through. Speaker_2: Sounds like a proper scene. Blackpool, eh? You can't beat it for a bit of madness. Anyone fancy going back next year? Speaker_1: I’m in, if only to witness the seagull attacks again. Speaker_3: Definitely. It's tradition now, isn’t it? Speaker_5: Yeah, let's do it. Speaker_4: Count me in. But I'm bringing earplugs. And a hat. And possibly a shield. Just in case of rogue seagulls or determined pizza-eaters. Speaker_2: Sensible lass. Alright, another round then? To Blackpool – a place where dreams are crushed, chips are stolen, and donkeys look perpetually judgy! All (in unison): To Blackpool!

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the silence. You wouldn’t believe the silence. Not a mechanical hum, not a car engine, not a distant lawnmower. Just…nothing. Except the wind, of course. That’s always *something* in the Highlands in January. Speaker_2: Sounds… intense. I mean, I enjoy a bit of peace and quiet as much as the next person, but completely cut off? Doesn’t it get a bit… lonely? Speaker_3: It’s a different kind of lonely, Mum. It’s not the lonely you get sitting in your flat on a Saturday night. It’s a sort of… expansive loneliness. You feel incredibly small, in the best possible way. Connected to something much bigger. Speaker_1: Exactly, Hamish. It recalibrates you. Everything feels… unnecessary. All the worries and the to-do lists just sort of fade away when you’re battling hypothermia and trying to get a fire going. Puts things in perspective, doesn’t it? Speaker_2: Hypothermia? Good heavens, George! That sounds actively dangerous. Is it even *legal* to just… camp anywhere in the winter? Speaker_1: Legal, yes. Sensible, debatable. Scotland has fantastic access rights, you know. “Right to Roam.” As long as you’re responsible - leave no trace, respect the land - you can camp pretty much anywhere. Speaker_3: We’ve got a pretty robust system for responsible wild camping, aye. It’s ingrained in the culture. But Dad’s downplaying the challenge a bit. It's not just battling hypothermia, it’s the sheer planning involved. Gear selection is crucial. You need a tent that can withstand seventy-mile-an-hour winds, a sleeping bag rated to -20, and enough food to fuel a small army. Speaker_2: Seventy mile an hour winds! My goodness. And you *enjoy* this? What’s the appeal? Besides proving you’re tougher than everyone else, George? Speaker_1: It’s not about toughness, Elsie. It’s about simplicity. Stripping everything back to the basics. It's about being self-reliant. Relying on your skills, your knowledge, your equipment… and a good head for navigation. And it’s stunningly beautiful. The winter landscape up there is breathtaking. The snow-covered mountains, the frozen lochs… It’s a different world. Speaker_3: And there's something deeply meditative about it. It forces you to be present. You’re completely focused on the task at hand – staying warm, finding water, making camp. There’s no room for multitasking or dwelling on things you can't control. Speaker_2: I suppose I can see that. It sounds… therapeutic. A bit like a very extreme form of mindfulness. Though I think I’ll stick to my walking groups in the Pentlands, thank you very much. A warm pub at the end is a definite requirement for me. Speaker_1: Fair enough. But you should try it sometime, Elsie. Just once. It’ll change your perspective on things. And Hamish here is an excellent guide, if you’re brave enough to entrust your life to him. Speaker_3: (Laughing) I am fairly competent, Mum. Though I wouldn’t necessarily recommend starting with a January expedition. Perhaps a slightly milder April… or May. Speaker_2: Don't push it, Hamish. Don’t even *think* about it. I'm quite happy with my central heating, thank you very much. Speaker_1: Alright, alright. More tea, anyone? I think I’ve sufficiently terrified you both with tales of my winter exploits.
