Speaker_1: In a good way, though. Doesn't it? Speaker_2: Yeah. In a good way. Definitely.

Speaker_1: Oh, honestly, look at what she’s wearing. That dress is… a choice. Speaker_2: You’re being harsh! It’s a bit… bold, maybe, but it’s clearly intentional. It’s got that whole, like, maximalist vibe going on. Speaker_3: I think it’s a bit much for daytime TV. It looks like she’s off to a premiere, not discussing gardening. Speaker_1: Exactly! Who dresses like that to talk about begonias? And those shoes! They look like they’re made of plastic. Speaker_2: They *are* plastic, I think. It’s that designer, Melissas, isn't it? They do all those quirky plastic shoes. They're surprisingly comfy, actually. I had a pair of red ones once. Speaker_1: Comfy or not, they just look… cheap. I don’t get the appeal. Give me a good leather boot any day. Speaker_3: I’m a sandal girl, myself. Though I’m definitely feeling a boot vibe for autumn. I saw these really nice Chelsea boots in John Lewis last week. A lovely dark burgundy. Speaker_1: Ooh, burgundy’s good. Classy. I’ve been after a good trench coat for ages. Everything’s either too expensive or looks like something my grandma would wear. Speaker_2: Oh, I know the feeling. I was looking for one last year, and it’s a nightmare. Everything’s either too short, too oversized, or the wrong colour. Have you tried vintage shops? You can sometimes find a really good one. Speaker_1: I have, actually! No luck so far. I keep finding ones that are amazing material but the fit is all wrong. It’s like they were designed for someone completely different. Speaker_3: That’s the problem with vintage, isn’t it? Sizing is all over the place. I’m thinking of just biting the bullet and getting a new one, even if it’s a bit pricey. Speaker_2: Totally. Sometimes you just have to. You get what you pay for, right? Speaking of pricey, did you see that Dior show? The dresses were insane. Speaker_1: Oh my god, yes! Absolutely stunning, but…completely impractical. Like, where are you even *wearing* those? To a gala? A fashion show? Speaker_3: They’re art, aren't they? Pure escapism. I love seeing the creativity, even if I’d never actually wear anything like that. Speaker_1: Me too. It's good for a bit of inspiration, though. I saw a really nice tailored blazer in a similar colour to one they used, I might try and find something similar on the high street. Speaker_2: Good plan! We should hit the shops next weekend. We haven’t had a proper shopping trip in ages. Speaker_3: I’m in! Maybe after brunch on Saturday? We could go to the market first, then head into town. Speaker_1: Perfect! That sounds like a plan. I'm definitely in need of some retail therapy. And maybe a new trench coat…and a pair of burgundy boots.

Speaker_2: So, how was college today? Anything interesting happen? You’ve been a bit quiet since you got in. Speaker_1: It was… okay. We started a new photography project, which is good. Black and white landscapes. I’m thinking of going down to the beach at Camber Sands. It looks really dramatic on a grey day, you know? Speaker_2: Lovely! That’s a brilliant idea. You always had an eye for that sort of thing. Remember when you were tiny and insisted on taking pictures of every single pebble on the beach? Drove your father mad. Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh god, yeah! I thought they were all special. I still kind of do. It’s just… there’s this boy in my class, Leo, and he’s *really* good. Like, properly amazing. And he was looking at my ideas and just… sort of dismissed them. Said they were “a bit cliché.” Speaker_2: Oh, Leo. Sounds delightful. Honestly, darling, don’t let him get to you. People are just threatened by talent, or maybe he's just a bit of a know-it-all. You’ve got a fantastic eye, and your pictures are always so… evocative. Don’t let some boy crush that. Speaker_1: I know, I know. It’s just… it made me doubt myself. It’s stupid, isn’t it? I get so anxious about people judging my work. Speaker_2: It’s not stupid, sweetie. It's perfectly normal. Everyone feels that way sometimes. I get terrified before presentations at work. You wouldn't believe the amount of deep breathing I have to do! Apparently, Mrs. Henderson in accounts thinks I’m meditating. Speaker_1: (smiling) Oh, bless her. How was your day at the reception? Any interesting callers? Speaker_2: Usual chaos. Old Mr. Davies called again, convinced someone had stolen his parking space. Turned out he’d just forgotten where he’d parked. Honestly, the things I put up with. It’s not exactly challenging, but it pays the bills. And the office gossip is surprisingly good. Speaker_1: Have you read anything good lately? I need a new book. I finished that thriller last week, the one you recommended, and it was brilliant. Really kept me guessing. Speaker_2: Oh, I’m so glad you enjoyed it! I've just started a biography of Joan Rivers. She’s fascinating, completely fearless. Although, her life was quite… tumultuous. I saw a documentary about her recently. She was absolutely hilarious, but also incredibly vulnerable. Speaker_1: I love Joan Rivers! She’s amazing. So cutting. I wish more comedians were like that now. Everything feels so… safe. Speaker_2: I agree. It’s all a bit sanitized, isn’t it? Where’s the risk? Anyway, don’t dwell on Leo. Go and take those pictures. And remember, even if he doesn't like them, *I* will. You’ve got talent, darling. Don't you forget that. Speaker_1: Thanks, Mum. That actually makes me feel a lot better. Maybe I’ll go down to the beach tomorrow morning, before it gets too crowded. Speaker_2: Good idea. And I'll make you a proper packed lunch. Sandwiches, fruit, maybe even a little cake. Fuel for the artistic soul! Speaker_1: You're the best. Speaker_2: I know. Now, tell me, is there anyone *else* at college you’re… you know… talking to? Besides Leo, the critic.

Speaker_1: Right, well, that's the blooming application form finished. Took me long enough. All those boxes… honestly. Speaker_2: Oh, good for you, Arthur. What application, dear? The one for the… the assistance with the heating? Speaker_1: That's the one. Says I need to declare every single penny I've ever had. Feels a bit intrusive, doesn’t it? Speaker_3: You’d think they’d have enough information on you already, considering. It's the modern world, isn’t it? All data, all the time. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. And then there was a question about 'dependants'. I put you down, Margaret, naturally. Speaker_2: Oh, Arthur, that’s sweet. Although, I manage perfectly well, thank you very much. Still, it's the thought that counts. Speaking of managing, young Timmy from next door… a dreadful child. Absolutely dreadful. Speaker_3: Oh? Still causing havoc? I thought his parents were finally getting a grip. Speaker_2: Grip? They’re letting him run wild! Yesterday, he was throwing stones at the bird’s nest in the apple tree. Poor little things. I had to go out there and give him a piece of my mind. Speaker_1: Stones at birds? Disgraceful. That cockerel of ours wouldn’t take kindly to that, would he? Gives *me* a right telling off if I get too close to his hens. Speaker_3: He’s a feisty one, that bird. Nearly took my ear off last time I was round. Speaker_2: He does have a personality, I’ll give him that. It's his crowing at five in the morning that’s the problem. Honestly, it’s enough to drive a person mad. And I haven't had a decent night’s sleep in weeks. Speaker_1: You and me both, Margaret. Tossin’ and turnin’ all night. It’s this house, I reckon. It’s getting colder and draftier with every passing year. Speaker_3: You two really should consider moving, you know. A nice bungalow, somewhere manageable. Speaker_2: Manageable… it’s the finances, dear. Things aren't exactly flush. And frankly, the workmanship these days is appalling. Remember old Mr. Henderson? He could build a house with his eyes closed. Now, everyone just rushes things and cuts corners. Speaker_1: Aye, shoddy work. We had a bloke come round to look at the guttering. Said it needed replacing. Quoted me a ridiculous price. I ended up fixing it myself with a bit of sealant and a prayer. Speaker_3: Sounds about right. Speaking of fixing things… I’ve been getting into 3D printing. Trying to make a replacement knob for the shed door. It’s surprisingly addictive. Speaker_2: 3D printing? Good heavens! Is that one of those computer things? Sounds rather complicated. Speaker_3: It is a bit, but it’s good fun. And it's useful. Though, the whole process takes ages, honestly. How’s your daughter by the way? Is she still planning a big birthday bash for her fortieth? Speaker_1: She is. Wants to rent out the village hall. Says she's inviting everyone she's ever met. Sounds… exhausting just thinking about it. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Well, at least it'll be a good party. Though, knowing her crowd, there’ll be a lot of loud music and questionable dancing. Speaker_3: That sounds like a typical family gathering. Well, I really should be heading off. Got some marking to do. And a shed door knob to finish printing. Speaker_1: Alright, then. Good to see you, lad. Speaker_2: Yes, do give our love to your wife, dear. And mind you don’t stay up too late printing things!

Speaker_1: So, she’s actually looking at flats now, can you believe it? After all this time talking about it, it’s… happening. Speaker_2: That’s wonderful, Margaret. Truly. It must be a relief, for both of you. Though, you always did seem fairly resolute about it, didn’t you? I remember you saying years ago, once she’d finished university, you wanted her closer. Speaker_1: Well, resolute and terrified are two sides of the same coin, aren't they? It's a huge upheaval. For *her*, more than anyone. Leaving everything she knows in Barcelona. Her friends, her job… even the sunshine. She's a Mediterranean girl at heart, you know. Speaker_2: She adapted well when she first went, though. She’s always been a resourceful one, your daughter. Remember when she was little and lost her favourite teddy bear at the pier? She organised a full-scale search party! Speaker_1: (chuckles) Oh, God, yes. A tiny dictator, demanding ice cream as payment for information. She gets that from her father, I suspect. But this is…different. It’s not a lost teddy bear. It’s a life. I keep asking myself if I’m doing the right thing, encouraging this. Is it selfish? Am I just craving having her near? Speaker_2: Don’t be silly, Margaret. It’s not selfish at all. You're a mother. It’s natural to want your children close. And she’s an adult. She’s made this decision. You're just supporting her. Speaker_1: I know, I know. It's just…the practicalities are starting to sink in. Finding a flat she can afford in Brighton. The housing market is ridiculous. And helping her with visas, and finding a job… oh, it's a list as long as my arm. Speaker_2: Have you spoken to David about it? He's good with paperwork, isn't he? He might be able to help with the visa side of things. Speaker_1: David's being brilliantly supportive, of course. He's already started researching solicitor's who specialize in immigration. He’s said he'll help with the deposit, too. Honestly, I don’t know what I'd do without him. He’s the practical one. I'm the worrier. Speaker_2: Well, you balance each other out, don’t you? That’s what makes a good partnership. And, truly, Brighton is a lovely place for her to settle. It's vibrant, there's a good arts scene… she’ll love it. Speaker_1: She's a bit worried about the weather, naturally. She keeps sending me links to average rainfall figures. I tried to reassure her it’s not *always* raining, but… well, it often is, isn’t it? Speaker_2: (laughs) It has its moments. But you can't have roses without a little rain, dear. She'll get used to it. And think of the benefits! She'll be able to come round for Sunday lunch whenever she likes. We’ll have a proper family again. That’s worth a bit of drizzle, wouldn't you say? Speaker_1: (smiles faintly) You're right. It is. It really is. And honestly… just knowing she'll be *here*. It makes it all seem a little less frightening. Speaker_2: Good. That's good. Now, are you sure you’ve had enough tea? I can put the kettle on again. And I’ve got those biscuits you like… the ginger ones.

Speaker_1: So, did you catch any of the Scottish referendum coverage last night? Absolute nail-biter, wasn’t it? Speaker_2: Just bits and pieces, to be honest. I was helping my daughter move some furniture. Turns out a three-piece suite is a lot heavier than it looks. Back’s been complaining ever since. No, but seriously, it's a relief, isn't it? Though I suspect it’ll open a whole new can of worms with devolution and things. Speaker_1: Absolutely. A lot of unanswered questions still. Feels like everyone’s holding their breath a little. Still, good on Scotland for having a proper debate about it, you know? Unlike some of the… shall we say, less nuanced discussions we have here. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You’re not wrong. Speaking of nuanced discussions, did you hear back about that job interview at King’s? The one in London? Speaker_1: Oh, that. Yeah, I did. Didn’t get it. Speaker_2: Oh, damn. Sorry to hear that. What did they say? Speaker_1: The usual. “Highly competitive field,” “strong candidates,” “we’ve decided to go with someone whose profile more closely matched the requirements.” You know the script. Speaker_2: The infuriating script. They all sound the same. Was it someone internal, do you think? Speaker_1: Probably. Heard through the grapevine that Professor Davies' son was also applying. Bit of a nepotism situation, I reckon. Speaker_2: Ugh, that’s just… frustrating. Well, you're far too good to let that get you down. There'll be something else. Plenty of opportunities. And honestly, London’s a bit of a hassle anyway. Brighton suits you. Speaker_1: That’s what I keep telling myself. And you’re right about Brighton. I just… I was hoping for a bit of a change, you know? Something a little more… prestigious, perhaps. Stupid, I know. Speaker_2: Not stupid. It’s perfectly natural to want to advance your career. But don’t undervalue what you have here. You're well-respected, you’re good at what you do. And you're close enough to London to pop up for conferences and whatnot. Speaker_1: True. How’s work been for you? Anything exciting happening with the sixth formers? Speaker_2: It’s…the usual teenage drama, really. One’s convinced he's going to be the next Shakespeare, another is currently going through a particularly angst-ridden breakup. Thankfully, I’ve seen it all before. I’m mostly focused on getting them prepped for their mocks at the moment. Dreadful time of year, honestly. Feels like constant pressure. Speaker_1: I can imagine. It’s been a bit calmer over in my department, thankfully. Although, old Mr. Henderson keeps trying to corner me in the staff room to discuss his stamp collection. It’s… a lot. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh dear. He’s a character, that one. You just have to nod and smile, I find. Speaker_1: That's my strategy. So, listen, are you free next week? I was thinking of catching that new sci-fi film, ‘Nebula Drift’? Speaker_2: Oh, I've heard good things! Next week sounds good. Tuesday maybe? My daughter’s got a pottery class on Wednesday. Speaker_1: Tuesday works perfectly. We could grab a bite afterwards, maybe that new Thai place on St. James’ Street? Speaker_2: Sounds lovely. It's a date then. It's good to talk, actually. Gets my mind off furniture and angst-ridden teenagers.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this mousetrap game is going to be the death of me. Where *does* this little arm go? It’s like advanced engineering. Speaker_2: Let me have a look. You’re trying to attach it to the… the flipper bit, aren’t you? It goes underneath, see? There’s a little slot. Speaker_3: It’s remarkably satisfying when it actually works, though, isn’t it? That little chain reaction. Speaker_4: It's like Rube Goldberg machines. We did one in physics. It was epic. Speaker_5: Speaking of epic, remember that time David went to work in America? That was a bit of a Rube Goldberg situation in itself, trying to sort out his visa. Speaker_2: Don’t remind me. The paperwork was… soul-destroying. And the questions! "Have you ever been a communist?" Seriously? Speaker_1: Oh, the Americans and their assumptions! I remember when we visited your sister, Sarah, in Boston. The kids were fascinated by how…loud American children were. Speaker_3: Loud? Speaker_1: Yes! So much more vocal. And confident. Not in a bad way, just… assertive. They’d just come up and *tell* you what they were thinking. No British politeness. Speaker_4: Sounds good, actually. Speaker_2: They’re direct, that's for sure. I think it's a cultural thing. Everything is bigger in America, including the volume. Speaker_5: And the portions! My goodness, the portions. I swear everything came with a side of butter and a gallon of sugar. Speaker_3: I've heard that. I’m thinking of doing a year abroad next year, maybe somewhere in the States. Just to experience it. Speaker_1: That sounds lovely, dear. But be prepared for a shock. It’s very different from here. The healthcare system, for a start… Speaker_2: Don’t even get me started on the healthcare system. It's terrifyingly expensive. You need travel insurance that covers absolutely everything. And don't get sick. Speaker_4: Is it like, if you break your leg, you're bankrupt? Speaker_5: Not necessarily bankrupt, but a broken leg could certainly lead to significant debt. It's a very different approach to social welfare. Speaker_1: Oh, look! The mousetrap is actually… working! Oh, praise be! Finally. Now, who wants to set it up again? Speaker_3: I'll give it a go. Maybe we can make it even more complicated this time. Add some dominoes. Speaker_2: Just promise you won't add anything involving springs. I've had enough of springs for one evening. My head’s spinning. Speaker_4: Can we at least booby-trap it with some of Mum’s knitting? Speaker_1: Absolutely not! My hand-knitted scarves are sacred. And stay away from the mousetrap with the knitting! Honestly, you lot...

Speaker_1: Right, okay, so… operation wardrobe expansion has commenced. Speaker_2: Oh really? Already? Didn’t think you’d be hitting the shops so soon after getting back. Jet lag and all that. Speaker_1: Jet lag is a lie. A conspiracy created by shopkeepers to prevent people from buying things. No, honestly, I needed a distraction. And… well, there was a sale. A *very* good sale. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) A very good sale. That's always dangerous. Let me guess, Taobao? Speaker_1: You know me too well. It was irresistible. I got… a few things. Speaker_2: A few? That sounds ominous. How many is 'a few'? Is it the 'a few' that resulted in the delivery guy looking at our apartment with suspicion? Speaker_1: It’s… manageable. Okay, it’s four dresses, a jumpsuit, and a pair of boots. Speaker_2: Four dresses? Alright. What kind of dresses? Don’t tell me you went full floral again. Remember what happened last time? You couldn't walk down the street without looking like a walking garden. Speaker_1: No, no florals! I learned my lesson. Two are sort of… midi-length, quite simple, dark colours. Good for lectures, you know, professional-ish. Then one is a really lovely silk slip dress, emerald green. Speaker_2: Emerald green? That sounds… you. Very elegant. And the fourth? Speaker_1: The fourth is a bit more… ambitious. It’s a bright orange, patterned thing. Very 70s. I saw it and just thought, “I *need* this in my life.” It might be terrible. Speaker_2: Bright orange? Right. That’s a bold choice. Are you planning on teaching a seminar on psychedelic fashion? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Maybe! No, I just thought it would be fun. It's a change. Everything I own is navy, grey, or black. I need a bit of… zest. Speaker_2: Fair enough. Zest is good. What about the jumpsuit? Speaker_1: Oh, it’s amazing! Wide-legged, navy blue, very comfortable. I can definitely see myself wearing that for evenings out. And the boots… they’re ankle boots, leather, a sort of burgundy colour. Very autumn-y. Speaker_2: Burgundy boots, sounds good. Sensible, practical, yet stylish. You’re covering all the bases. When is all this arriving? Speaker_1: Apparently, tomorrow. And the day after. And possibly the day after that. They’re splitting the delivery into three parcels. Speaker_2: Three parcels! You really did go wild, didn’t you? We’re going to be tripping over boxes for a week. Speaker_1: It’ll be worth it. Trust me. You’ll see. And you can help me decide what to wear! Speaker_2: Oh, excellent. Just what I need. To be your personal stylist in a mountain of cardboard. I look forward to it. Speaker_1: Okay, Okay, I have accepted my fate. Speaker_2: Good. We can start clearing space in the wardrobe now. Speaker_1: Good idea. Speaker_2: After dinner? Speaker_1: Sounds like a plan. Speaker_2: Excellent. Speaker_1: Just dont say I did'nt warn you. Speaker_2: When did you ever warn me, never. Speaker_1: When I bought the dog. Speaker_2: Right you have told me about that alot.

Speaker_1: Jaysus, that was a match alright. Absolutely brutal towards the end. Thought for a minute they’d blown it there. Speaker_2: Yeah, it was tense! Mr. Davies was going mental in history. He kept shouting ‘Come on Ireland!’ and then the teacher had to tell him off. Speaker_3: Oh, typical Mr. Davies! He's a bit of a wildcard. Still, nice to see the lads pull through. Did you enjoy it, Gran? Speaker_4: Oh, I did indeed. Though I confess, I get more excited about the camaraderie than the actual rugby nowadays. All that running about… my knees ache just watching it! Speaker_1: Ah now, you're a hard woman. Sure you used to run rings around those wee bairns in primary school. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) That was a long time ago, Liam. A very long time ago. Though, I did have a particularly competitive netball team. Speaker_2: Netball? Is that like basketball? Speaker_3: A bit, darling. But you can’t bounce the ball, and it’s played with a different ball… Speaker_1: It’s a bit… less rough and tumble, shall we say? Now, speaking of rough and tumble, Oisin’s birthday is fast approaching. We need to get the cards sorted. I’ve got one here, but it needs signing. Speaker_3: Oh, good point. I’ve got mine too. We could all write something special tonight? It’s not every day he's turning eight. Speaker_2: Eight! That’s a proper age. Are we still doing the pirate theme? Speaker_1: Aye, he’s obsessed. Wants a full pirate ship cake. I’m hoping your mother is up to the challenge, love. Speaker_3: Mum’s already on it. She’s been muttering about marzipan sails and edible treasure chests for weeks. She's in her element. Speaker_4: Sounds wonderful. You know, when I was a teacher, we always did stargazing parties for birthdays. A little telescope and a talk about constellations. Wonderful memories. Speaker_2: Stargazing? Cool! Can we do that? I’m learning about space at school. We did the planets this week. Speaker_1: If the clouds cooperate, maybe. It's supposed to be clear tonight. But first, young man, you need to be thinking about bed. It’s a school night. Speaker_2: Aw, but I wanna stay up! Speaker_3: Maybe just one more chapter of your book, then straight to bed? Speaker_2: Okay… deal. Speaker_1: Good lad. Right, so, after Oisin’s tucked in, are we sticking with the plan for Saturday? Trip to Kinsale? Speaker_3: Yep. I’ve booked a table at that seafood restaurant you liked. Fishy Fishy, was it? Speaker_1: That’s the one. They do a mean chowder. Gran, are you feeling up to a day out? Don't want to push you too hard. Speaker_4: Oh, I'm perfectly capable of a bit of Kinsale, thank you very much. A good walk around the harbor and a nice cup of tea… sounds delightful. And who knows, perhaps I’ll even find a rogue seashell or two. Speaker_1: Excellent. Well, let’s finish up this dinner then, and get a move on. Can't have the wee man staying up all night. Speaker_3: Sounds like a plan. More potatoes, anyone?

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to feel like all anyone talks about is babies these days. Chloe announced *another* one this morning. Three kids under five! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Chloe. She always did like a challenge. It's a bit of a baby boom in our friend group, isn’t it? Makes me feel… surprisingly detached. Speaker_1: I know, right? I think it’s because it feels so far off for me. And then when people ask, and I say “not yet” it feels like I’m giving a really long explanation about my PhD and needing to finish that first. It's exhausting. Speaker_2: You don’t need to explain yourself to anyone! It's perfectly valid to want to focus on your career. Speaking of big life changes, how’s the house hunt going? Did you view that one in Grantchester? Speaker_1: Oh, Grantchester was… nice. Very quaint. A bit *too* quaint, if that makes sense? All roses and thatched roofs. It felt like a film set. And honestly, the garden was tiny. We need space for the dog, you know? Speaker_2: Absolutely. A dog needs room to zoom! Have you seen anything else you like then? Speaker_1: A couple. There’s one in Milton, which is a bit further out, but it has a huge garden and a decent kitchen. It needs a bit of work, but it's got potential. It’s also… incredibly beige inside. Speaker_2: Beige is a blank canvas! It just needs your touch. You have such good taste. You could totally transform it. I could help, if you wanted. I’m secretly obsessed with interior design. Speaker_1: Oh, that would be amazing, actually! I’m hopeless at visualizing things. You’re the creative one. Also, practical. I’d probably just end up buying everything in shades of grey. Speaker_2: (Smiling) You *do* have a thing for grey. Hey, on a completely different note, remember that blue dress I wore to Sarah’s birthday? The silk one? Speaker_1: Vaguely? Was that the one you said you regretted buying because it was dry clean only? Speaker_2: That’s the one! I’ve worn it, like, twice. It’s just sitting in my wardrobe. You could totally rock that. You have way better accessorizing skills than me. Do you want to borrow it? Speaker_1: Really? That’s so kind of you! I’d love to. I’ve been trying to be better about not just living in jeans and jumpers. It’s a good excuse to dress up. Speaker_2: Of course! It's practically a wardrobe share agreement then. Although, be warned, I’m also trying to learn Italian and currently relying on Duolingo. It’s… going slowly. Speaker_1: Italian! That’s ambitious. I tried learning Spanish a few years ago and gave up after realizing I couldn’t roll my ‘r’s. Which is essential, apparently. Speaker_2: Oh, it’s the ‘r’s that get me too. But I’m determined! I want to be able to order a proper espresso without sounding like a complete idiot. And maybe understand those incredibly dramatic Italian hand gestures. Speaker_1: A noble goal. Well, good luck with that. And let me know if you need a Duolingo partner. I might be able to offer moral support, even if I can’t pronounce a single word of Italian. Speaker_2: Deal. Now, are you going to finish that sandwich, or can I have a bite?

Speaker_1: Honestly, hearing you two talk… it’s weird, innit? Like, you’re both from Bedford but sound totally different. You've got that proper Bedford twang, Ben, almost… posh. Speaker_2: Posh? Mate, I just… speak normally. You're the one sounding like you've swallowed a gravel pit, Liam. All that East Anglian drawl. It’s proper rural. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Proper rural is putting it mildly. Sounds like he's trying to charm a sheep. Speaker_1: Charming sheep is a perfectly valid skill! Especially if you’re a gardener, Kai. You need to be able to negotiate with livestock. Speaker_3: Negotiate? They just eat everything in sight. My nan used to say… actually, never mind. It’s a bit grim. Speaker_2: Go on, spill. Grim stories are the best. Speaker_3: She used to say old Man Hemmings, down the lane, used to ‘dispose’ of sick sheep by just… leaving them in the woods. Said foxes took care of the rest. Speaker_1: Brutal. Absolutely brutal. You don’t get that in town, do you? That’s proper countryside stuff. Speaking of brutal, anyone see that MMA fight last night? McGregor’s back, apparently. Speaker_2: Saw a few highlights. Proper showboating, as usual. Honestly, I prefer linguistics. Much less… blood. Although, dissecting grammar can feel pretty violent sometimes. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Violent grammar? You're a weirdo, Ben. Speaking of weird, I think my mum’s trying to sell her old guitar online again. She keeps buying them and then deciding she ‘doesn’t have the fingers for it’ anymore. Speaker_3: What kind is it? Maybe I could take a look. I’ve been meaning to get something to mess around with. Always fancied learning. Speaker_1: Some acoustic thing. She thinks it’s a Martin, but knowing her, it’s probably a knock-off from Argos. She keeps saying she’s going to travel the world with it, become a folk singer… It’s a bit sad, actually. Speaker_2: It’s the dream, though, isn’t it? Ditching the nine to five, wandering around with a guitar. Though I'd settle for just finishing marking this batch of essays. Seriously, the grammar… it's a massacre. Speaker_3: Honestly, you guys have proper jobs. I spend all day wrestling with weeds and being judged by snails. Though, someone tried to buy a patch of land off me yesterday. Apparently, they want to build a block of flats. Speaker_1: Really? Where? Near your allotment? Speaker_3: Yeah. Said it was a ‘good investment.’ I told him it was my grandad’s land, been in the family for ages. He just shrugged. People are ruthless. You gotta know how to protect yourself, y’know? Speaker_2: You should get a dog. A proper big one. That’ll scare off developers. Speaker_1: Yeah, and teach it to bite anyone who offers you a dodgy deal. I’m kidding! Mostly. Anyone fancy a game of Monopoly later? Mum dug it out of the attic. Speaker_3: Oh god, no. Monopoly always ends in arguments. And someone always flipping the board. Speaker_2: It does, doesn't it? I'm in. I'll be the hat. And I'm bringing snacks. Though, I'm trying to cut down on biscuits. Doctor says my cholesterol is creeping up. Speaker_1: Doctor says everything is creeping up these days. Oh, and Mum’s on about quitting smoking again. She's been rolling her own tonight, smells like a bonfire in here. Speaker_3: Tell her to switch to vaping. Less smelly. Plus, you get to look like a stormtrooper.

Speaker_1: Right, so onions are going on… you’re being awfully quiet over there, are you alright? Just mentally calculating spreadsheets again? Speaker_2: Nah, just… thinking about the car, actually. It’s due a service next month, and I’m dreading it. The quote they gave me last time was ridiculous. Speaker_1: Oh, no. How much? Speaker_2: Nearly four hundred quid. Four hundred! For an oil change, a filter, and them poking around for ten minutes. It’s daylight robbery. I swear they inflate the prices knowing people rely on their cars. Speaker_1: It *is* mental. I’m so glad I cycle to work. Saves a fortune, even with the rain sometimes. Although, honestly, the state of the roads after all this wet weather… it’s terrifying. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I splashed through a pothole yesterday that felt like driving over a small mountain. I’m worried about the suspension, to be honest. That’s probably another few hundred quid just waiting to happen. Speaker_1: You really need to get it checked out then. Before it’s something *major*. Saves more in the long run, even if it stings now. Speaker_2: I know, I know. It’s just… trying to save for a deposit on a house, and then the car needs constant attention. It feels like all my money just disappears. Speaker_1: It does, doesn't it? Everyone says owning a car is expensive, but you don’t really *feel* it until you’re staring down the barrel of a huge bill. Have you looked into getting quotes from other garages? Maybe a smaller independent one? Speaker_2: I had a quick look a while ago. The main dealers are always the most expensive, obviously. Found a couple of independents, but the reviews were a bit…mixed. Some said they were brilliant, cheap, honest. Others said they’d been ripped off. It’s always a gamble, isn’t it? Speaker_1: It is. Honestly, sometimes I think it would be cheaper to just get the bus. Speaker_2: (laughs) If the bus went anywhere near my work, maybe! It’s a good hour and a half each way on public transport. I’d never get anything done. It’s the commute that kills you, really. All that wasted time. Speaker_1: True. Although, you could read, listen to podcasts… make it productive? Speaker_2: In theory, yes. In practice, I just end up scrolling through TikTok like a zombie. It’s terrible. Speaker_1: We’ve all been there. Right, garlic’s in. Do you want me to start on the rice? Maybe we should start a separate ‘car repair’ savings pot? It might feel less… overwhelming. Speaker_2: That’s actually a really good idea. A dedicated ‘car doom’ fund. I like it. We could set up a direct debit, even if it’s just a fiver a week. It adds up. Speaker_1: Exactly! Every little helps. And we can both contribute, since you’re the one actually driving the thing. Speaker_2: Fair enough. Deal. You’re a lifesaver. And a brilliant chef, by the way. This smells amazing already. Speaker_1: Oh, stop it. It’s just a simple curry. But thanks. Now, about that 'car doom' fund… let's get it set up while the rice is cooking. Speaker_2: Sounds good to me! Let's tackle this automotive financial disaster together.

Speaker_1: Right, now then, love, you’ve had a good brew, haven’t you? And a biscuit. Grandad, more tea? You look like you could do with another one. Speaker_4: Aye, lass, I wouldn't say no. A bit weak, mind, last time. Like dishwater. Speaker_1: Oh, don't start, Harold! It wasn’t weak, you just like to complain. I made it exactly how you usually have it. Two sugars, a splash of milk… Speaker_3: Leave him be, Dorothy. He's just enjoying himself being grumpy. It’s a Yorkshire tradition, you know. Now, this cake’s lovely. Did you bake it yourself? Speaker_1: I did, Nana. Victoria sponge. Thought it’d be a nice treat for your visit. Liam, have you thanked your grandparents for the chocolate biscuits? Speaker_2: Yeah, ages ago. They're good. Better than the ones at school. Speaker_1: That’s good to hear. Now, Liam, your room’s looking a bit of a state. You promised you'd tidy it up before they came. Speaker_2: I will, I will. Just… after playing this level. It’s really hard. Speaker_4: Level? What’s this level? Something to do with that… glowing box you’re always staring at? Speaker_2: It's a game, Grandad. It's a spaceship one. Speaker_3: Spaceships! In my day, we had skipping ropes and hopscotch. Much healthier, if you ask me. You wouldn't get a sore bottom from hopscotch. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) That's true, Nana. Although I distinctly remember *you* falling over during hopscotch once and scraping your knee. Speaker_3: Oh, don’t bring that up! That was years ago, and it was a particularly slippery pavement! Blame the council, I say. They never grit properly. Speaker_4: Aye, the council. Always been useless. Remember when they tried to put a roundabout on Hessle Road? Caused chaos, that did. Absolute chaos. Speaker_1: Goodness me, I'd forgotten about that. It was a disaster, wasn’t it? They had to take it out again after a week. Speaker_2: What's a roundabout? Speaker_1: Oh, it's… it's a circle of road, Liam, where everyone drives around in a circle and gives way to the people already on it. Speaker_4: Sounds complicated. Reckon they should just stick to traffic lights. Less confusing. Speaker_3: Oh, Harold, you’d complain if they gave you a free cup of tea. Now, Dorothy, are you taking us to Bridlington next week like you promised? I want to smell the sea air. Speaker_1: Yes, of course, Nana. I’ve booked the car, and the little tea room you like is still open. We can go on Tuesday, if that suits? Speaker_3: Tuesday's perfect. Though I do wish they still sold proper rock. The stuff they sell now is all artificial flavouring. Speaker_4: Aye, and not enough letters in it. Remember the ones you could get your name in? Speaker_1: I do. They were the best. Right, well, I'm going to put some washing on. Liam, please, just a quick tidy up, eh? And Grandad, I'll get you that fresh tea. Just try not to tell me it's too weak! Speaker_2: Okay, okay. Spaceships can wait. Speaker_3: Poor lad. All this modern technology. It’ll rot his brain. Speaker_4: Nonsense, woman. It’s just a bit of fun. Though I still don't understand it.

Speaker_1: Right, so pirates tomorrow then? Everyone excited for pirate day at school? Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Yes! I’m wearing my sparkly eye patch and a stripy top! And I'm bringing my hook! Speaker_3: (Muttering) I wanna be a pirate too… a scary pirate! With a big sword! Speaker_1: You can be a scary pirate, darling. I think we’ve got a cardboard sword somewhere, haven’t we? We’ll find it in the morning. Now, eat your beans. You need pirate strength! Speaker_2: But they’re… beany. Speaker_1: They are beany, but they’re good for you. And pirates need good food to sail the seas! Speaking of good food, did you two remember to tell me what you wanted for dinner tonight? Speaker_3: Pizza! With pepperoni! Speaker_2: And chips! And… and a little bit of broccoli, maybe. Speaker_1: Right, pizza, chips, and a tiny bit of broccoli. Deal. Now, after pirate day, next week is Shakespeare week at school, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Yes! We’re learning about *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*! Speaker_3: What’s that? Is it about fairies? Speaker_1: It is! It's a play with fairies and magic and lots of silly stuff. We might even try and go to Stratford-upon-Avon if the weather’s nice. It’s where Shakespeare was born, you know. Speaker_2: Wow! Can we see his house? Speaker_1: We can try! It might be a bit busy, but we can definitely visit Shakespeare’s Birthplace. And maybe see a performance. Speaker_3: I want to be in a play! Speaker_1: You might get your chance! Now, remember last week when we talked about the circus workshop? The one in a *real* circus? Speaker_2: (Gasps) Oh yes! It’s on Saturday! I’m going to learn how to juggle! Speaker_3: And I'm going to learn how to walk on a tightrope! Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Very ambitious! It’ll be fun, though. They said it's a proper circus tent, and you'll be learning from real circus performers. Speaker_2: Can we take pictures? Speaker_1: Of course! Speaking of pictures, did you two finish looking at the Easter egg hunt photos? The ones Grandma sent? Speaker_3: Yes! I found the most eggs! Speaker_1: That’s what Grandma said! She said you were a very clever Easter bunny hunter. And… oh! I almost forgot. I signed you both up for that little stop-motion animation workshop next month. Speaker_2: Stop-motion… what? Speaker_1: It’s where you make little films using toys and taking lots of pictures. Like Wallace and Gromit! Speaker_3: Oh! Cool! Can we make a pirate movie? With a scary pirate? Speaker_1: We absolutely can. Now, finish your beans. Pirates, Shakespeare, circuses and movies – it’s going to be a busy few weeks! Speaker_2: Mum? Can pirates do magic? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Well, they *could* if they wanted to, couldn't they? Pirates are pretty good at getting away with things, and that's a kind of magic, isn't it? Now, eat up! Speaker_3: Me too! I want to be a magic pirate!

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the whole thing was utterly ridiculous. I mean, *arrested*! For trying to sail to Cyprus. Speaker_2: From Jeddah? Good Lord, Margaret! That’s… ambitious. And illegal, clearly. Speaker_3: Ambitious is one word for it. Foolhardy springs to mind, if I’m being blunt. What possessed you? Speaker_1: Well, you have to understand, it was the early 80s. I was teaching English in Jeddah – a rather… isolated experience, let me tell you. And I’d met this chap, a Norwegian, absolutely brimming with confidence. He’d sailed all over, apparently. Said it was a perfectly feasible trip. Speaker_4: Feasible, perhaps, for a seasoned sailor with a proper vessel. Not, one imagines, a converted fishing boat and a vague idea of navigation. Speaker_1: It wasn't *vague*! We had charts. And the boat… well, it *had* been a fishing boat. But we’d fitted it out! Sort of. It wasn’t exactly luxurious, I’ll grant you. Anyway, we set off, convinced we’d be sipping ouzo in Cyprus within a week. Speaker_2: And the authorities didn’t take kindly to your unscheduled departure? Speaker_1: Didn’t even let us get past the harbor. We were barely a mile out when this patrol boat came roaring alongside. Honestly, it was terrifying. They hauled us aboard, questioned us for hours - mostly because we couldn’t explain anything in Arabic, naturally. It turned out you need quite a lot of permits to leave Saudi Arabia by sea. Speaker_3: I can imagine. A rather closed society, even now. Were you concerned about… the availability of, shall we say, refreshments along the way? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, absolutely. That was a major factor in the Norwegian’s enthusiasm. Alcohol is, needless to say, strictly forbidden. We’d stocked up, shall we say, rather liberally. That’s likely what raised suspicions in the first place. A boat suspiciously full of tinned peaches and… other things. Speaker_4: Tinned peaches! A classic smuggling disguise. Ingenious, really. Though I suspect they weren’t fooled for a moment. Speaker_2: So, what happened then? Did they confiscate the peaches? Speaker_1: They confiscated everything! The boat, the "supplies", even my passport. We spent three days in a rather grim jail, then were eventually deported. I had to explain to the college principal why I’d abandoned my teaching post and ended up in international incident. Speaker_3: Goodness me. You’ve lived a life, Margaret. Speaker_4: Indeed. Speaking of boats, reminds me of a story… back when I was a young dental student, I decided I needed a sailing dinghy. Completely impractical, of course. No time to use it. But I bought this little thing, and fitted it out with… well, with waterproof covers made from old dental magazines. Speaker_2: *Dental magazines*? Speaker_4: Brilliant for keeping the rain off, you know. Stiff, glossy, and surprisingly durable. Until, that is, I sailed it into a particularly nasty squall off the Isle of Wight. All the covers ripped, and the sea was strewn with pictures of perfectly aligned teeth. Looked like a shark attack. Speaker_1: (Roaring with laughter) Oh, Harold, you are incorrigible! Dental debris floating in the English Channel! That’s… that’s just wonderful! Speaker_3: Perhaps that's why the sharks stayed away. Couldn’t bear to look.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of that bathroom this morning… I don’t know what goes on in there. It looked like a bomb had hit it. Speaker_2: Oh, tell me about it. Boys, eh? It’s like living with a herd of… well, I won’t say what. Just messy. Absolutely messy. Is Leo still sulking about not being allowed to go to Millie’s party? Speaker_1: You know he is. Dramatic sighs, slamming doors, the whole nine yards. I tried to explain, “Leo, it’s a 13th birthday, it's girls only, it’s not a personal rejection.” He just rolled his eyes. Speaker_3: (muttering from another room) It *is* a personal rejection. Speaker_2: Did he say that? Honestly! He's got the world at his feet, that boy. Opportunities galore. Have you seen the work experience placements the school are offering this year? Speaker_1: A bit. There’s that engineering one, isn’t there? Matthew’s mum was saying how good it is. Leo wouldn’t be interested in engineering, though. He’s still obsessed with those explorers, you know, Bear Grylls and all that. Wants to live in a tent in the Amazon. Speaker_3: (louder) I would! It’d be awesome! Speaker_2: Well, maybe not the Amazon. Bit too many spiders for my liking. But he needs to think about his future. He's got good GCSE results coming up, he needs to use them. It wouldn't hurt him to earn a bit of pocket money either. I'm looking for someone to babysit for Mrs. Henderson next week, Thursdays and Fridays. Could he be persuaded? Speaker_1: Hmm. He’d hate it. Too “uncool.” He’d rather spend all day on that computer playing… whatever it is he plays. Though, actually, maybe if it was used to fund a more realistic adventure? Like, say, a camping trip with his mates? Speaker_3: (appearing in the doorway) A proper one? With a campfire and everything? Speaker_2: Maybe. If you promised to clean the bathroom for a month afterwards. And maybe a little babysitting to *earn* the funds. Speaker_3: No way! Babysitting is torture. Speaker_1: Come on, Leo. It’s a few hours of your time. It’s good money, and you can save up. Plus, you’d be doing Mrs. Henderson a favour. She’s really sweet. Actually, she mentioned her grandson's football team needs a referee. Speaker_3: Refereeing? Seriously? I play football! I can’t be refereeing! Everyone will think I'm a traitor. Speaker_2: Well, you won’t be playing *and* refereeing, will you? It’s good experience, builds character. Speaker_1: And, you know, it's earning money. We're going to need to start thinking seriously about a proper holiday this year. Somewhere a bit different... Maybe not a tent in the Amazon, but… somewhere. Speaker_3: Can we at least go somewhere with Wi-Fi? And a swimming pool? And not too many little kids. Speaker_2: We'll see, we'll see. It depends on how willing you are to contribute to the holiday fund, young man. And maybe, just maybe, keep the bathroom looking a little less like a disaster zone. Speaking of which, has anyone seen my good scissors? I swear, things just disappear in this house… Speaker_1: Check Leo’s room! He's probably 'borrowed' them for some extremely important expedition planning.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this bread is amazing. Like, genuinely amazing. I could eat a whole loaf myself. Speaker_2: It is lovely, isn’t it? They do a fantastic job with the local ingredients here. You wouldn’t get bread like this in Tesco's, would you? Speaker_3: No way. Tesco’s bread is… sad. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Sad is a good description. Though, I will say, they do a reasonable sourdough these days. It’s improved. Speaker_1: Still not Croatian sourdough though, is it? Speaking of ingredients, did you see the price of truffles in that little shop in Rovinj? Astronomical! Speaker_2: Oh, don’t even get me started. A tiny jar for the price of a new pair of shoes. And everyone’s obsessed with them. I had a patient last week who was convinced truffle oil would cure her heartburn. Speaker_3: Seriously? Speaker_2: Honestly. People will believe anything. She’d been watching some chef on the telly, apparently. All these celebrity chefs, they’re all the same, aren't they? Shouting and waving knives. Speaker_4: A bit dramatic, perhaps. But they do inspire people to cook, which is a good thing. Remember that Jamie Oliver phase? Everyone was making proper meals. Speaker_1: Yeah, but Jamie Oliver’s practically off-grid now, isn’t he? Living on a farm, raising pigs. I saw an article. Speaker_3: He’s gone full country bumpkin. Speaker_4: Well, he always had a bit of that about him. Still, the food here is wonderful. Remember when we were in America last year? It was… underwhelming. Everything was huge and covered in cheese. Speaker_1: Oh, God, yes. And the portions! I felt ill after every meal. And everyone smokes. Even when it’s clearly not allowed. Speaker_2: It’s a different culture. Still doesn’t make it right, though. Especially considering all the research on stem cells and lung cancer. Speaking of which, I was reading an interesting article about advances in regenerative medicine… Speaker_4: Oh, here we go. A medical lecture on a family holiday. Speaker_2: (Laughing) I can't help it! It's fascinating. They're growing organs in labs now! Imagine the possibilities. Speaker_3: That’s a bit scary actually. Like, Frankenstein’s monster. Speaker_1: It *is* a bit dodgy. What about education, though? I’m stressing about uni applications. It feels like everyone’s got a plan and I’m just…winging it. Speaker_4: Don't worry about having a plan at 18. It’s perfectly acceptable to change your mind. I thought I wanted to be an accountant, ended up a management consultant. Life takes you in unexpected directions. Speaker_2: Your dad’s right. Just focus on enjoying yourself now, and do your best. Oh, and could someone remind me to pack more painkillers? My back is killing me from all this driving. Speaker_3: Can we put the football on when we get to the apartment? Liverpool are playing. Speaker_1: Of course! But you’re doing the washing up afterwards. Speaker_4: And I’m driving again tomorrow. Someone needs to appreciate my excellent navigating skills. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh, we all appreciate your navigating, dear. Just try not to get us lost in the Croatian backroads.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…an experience. I think that’s supposed to be pasta bake? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) It’s…beige. Very beige. Though, to be fair, it's a step up from yesterday's 'mystery meat' situation. I’m pretty sure it involved a lot of offal. Speaker_3: You’re braver than me. I just stuck to the salad. It’s mostly lettuce, but at least I *know* what it is. Plus, I needed something green after staring at spreadsheets all morning. Speaker_1: Spreadsheets, the bane of modern existence. I’m drowning in transcripts at the moment. Seriously, people say the *strangest* things when they think a recorder isn’t really picking up all the nuance. Speaker_2: Oh, tell me about it. I'm trying to A/B test tagline variations for a new book series and the click-through rates are… perplexing. Apparently, “Medieval Mayhem!” doesn’t resonate with the target audience as much as we thought. Speaker_3: Medieval Mayhem *should* resonate! That's… pretty good. What were the alternatives? Speaker_2: “Historical Intrigue” and “A Tale of Two Kingdoms.” Apparently, sophisticated is the way to go? Teens these days. Speaker_1: Maybe they're tired of the alliteration? Or maybe ‘mayhem’ feels a bit… immature. It's fascinating, isn’t it? How much subconscious stuff goes into even the simplest choices. It's practically what my entire research project is based on. Speaker_3: That's cool. What are you researching, exactly? If you don't mind me asking. I always feel a bit weird asking. Speaker_1: No, not at all! I'm looking at how linguistic markers of uncertainty – like ‘sort of’ and ‘kind of’ – are used differently across various age groups and social contexts. It’s surprisingly complex. Speaker_2: Sounds intense. Digital marketing is all about certainty. Trying to *create* certainty. "Buy this! You need this! It will change your life!" It's exhausting. Speaker_1: The pressure to create that manufactured certainty must be huge. We just try to observe what actually *is*. Although, even observing feels… subjective, you know? Speaker_3: Definitely. Especially when people are aware they’re being observed. It changes the data. I had to do a user experience test last week and everyone was behaving so perfectly, it was useless. Speaker_2: (Laughing) The Hawthorne effect in action! It’s the classic research pitfall. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s constantly making me question everything. I spent three hours yesterday debating whether a slightly prolonged pause actually *means* anything, or if the speaker was just thinking. Speaker_3: Sounds tiring. Honestly, I'm looking forward to just...a quiet evening. Maybe binge-watch something ridiculously mindless. What are you guys up to this weekend? Speaker_2: I think I’m attempting a DIY project. Against my better judgement. A shelf. It could end badly. Speaker_1: Oh no. Shelves are treacherous. I’ll bring the first aid kit. I'm aiming for a long walk and maybe finally tackling that pile of books I've been meaning to read… if the weather cooperates. Speaker_3: Sounds good. Maybe we could grab a drink sometime next week, after work? Steam needs a bit of a release valve after all this… beige. Speaker_2: I’m in! Definitely. Speaker_1: Count me in too! This is way more interesting than dissecting ‘sort of’ and ‘kind of’ for another afternoon.

Speaker_2: Right, so are we definitely heading straight to Kasia’s then? No last-minute detour to find pierogi? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Tempting, very tempting, but no. We promised Kasia we’d be there for tea. She’s making that apple cake, remember? The one with the… what is it, the poppy seeds? Speaker_2: Oh, yes! That *is* a good cake. Worth resisting pierogi for, almost. Are you sure you’ve got everything? Passport, wallet, the little tin of biscuits you insisted on bringing? Speaker_1: Everything’s here, darling. I’ve checked three times. Honestly, you’d think I was attempting an expedition to the Antarctic, not a two-hour drive. Though, navigating Tarnow’s one-way system *can* feel that challenging. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You’re not wrong there! Kasia tried to explain it to me on video call, and my brain just short-circuited. It’s like someone designed it purely to confuse outsiders. Speaker_1: She's a saint, trying. And she’s been so kind, putting us up for the week. Honestly, I feel a bit bad, dumping ourselves on her like this. Speaker_2: Don’t be silly. She practically begged us to come! And think of all the sightseeing we can do. We can finally see that medieval castle she was raving about. Speaker_1: Oh, yes! The one with the… dragons? Or was that just Kasia being Kasia? Speaker_2: (Grinning) A bit of both, probably. She does enjoy a good story. Speaking of which, are you still planning on attempting to speak Polish? Remember that phrasebook you bought? Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even ask. It’s mostly just verbs conjugated in a way that makes absolutely no sense to me. I’ll stick to “dziekuje” and hoping for the best, I think. Speaker_2: Sounds sensible. I’ve brushed up on a few basics, but I’m terrified of accidentally saying something incredibly rude. The tones are so different, aren't they? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Although, I suspect Kasia will be lenient with us. She speaks perfect English, bless her. She's just keen for us to experience a bit of Poland. Speaker_2: Which is lovely. And honestly, it’s good to get away, isn’t it? Even if it’s just for a week. It's good to have something to look forward to. Speaker_1: It is. It really is. And this campervan is surprisingly comfortable, isn’t it? I was dreading the drive, but it’s actually rather… relaxing. Speaker_2: It is! It’s like being in a little mobile living room. Though, I might need to claim the passenger seat for a nap later. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Go for it, darling. You've earned it. Just wake me up before we drive into a river, alright? Speaker_2: Deal. Although, knowing Kasia, she'll probably have a detailed itinerary planned for us by the time we arrive, leaving no room for accidental aquatic adventures. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Probably. She does like to be organized. And honestly? After everything… I appreciate that. Speaker_2: Me too. Right, I think I can see the turn-off for Tarnow up ahead. Prepare for one-way system chaos! Speaker_1: (Taking a deep breath) Here we go… Wish me luck. And pass me another biscuit, would you?

Speaker_1: Honestly, that Adidas sponsorship with Man U is just…lazy. It’s the same template every year. Just change the colour and slap a different logo on. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s lacking imagination, isn’t it? Remember when Umbro were doing their stuff with them? Proper designs, a bit different. More…flair. Speaker_1: Flair! Exactly. And I’m not even a Man U fan, but even I notice. It feels like they’re just cashing in on the name at this point. It’s the same with loads of sponsorships, though, isn’t it? Just a financial transaction. Speaker_2: Totally. It's all about visibility now, not necessarily a genuine connection to the sport. Although, I do think some sponsorships work well. The Premier League and Barclays, for example. Seems to fit. Speaker_1: Yeah, that one feels…natural. Though even that’s just down to the money, isn’t it? Speaking of which, have you seen the new Leicester kit? That purple one? Speaker_2: Oh god, yeah. Bold choice. A bit…much, even for me. It's like someone spilled grape juice all over it. Speaker_1: Seriously! It’s like they were intentionally trying to make something divisive. And they succeeded. My brother reckons it’s amazing, naturally. He's a die-hard. Speaker_2: Brothers, eh? Always on the opposite end of the spectrum. Mine thinks anything remotely stylish is “pretentious”. Speaker_1: (laughs) Sounds familiar. Honestly, sometimes I just want everything to go back to the classic designs. Simple stripes, solid colours. Remember when Sheffield Wednesday had that striped one with the little owl on the chest? Iconic. Speaker_2: Now *that* was a kit. Proper retro vibes. Although, I’m getting hungry now. All this football talk is making me crave…something bad. Speaker_1: Oh no, don’t tell me you’re thinking about… Speaker_2: McDonalds. I’m thinking about McDonalds. A Quarter Pounder meal, large fries, the works. Speaker_1: You’re a lost cause. We literally had a really nice meal an hour ago. Speaker_2: A *healthy* meal. There's a difference. And watching this muted football is strangely triggering a need for processed goodness. Speaker_1: It's a psychological phenomenon, I'm telling you! Football and fast food – a dangerous combination. Although… those curly fries *do* look good on Instagram… Speaker_2: See? You're weakening. We could walk there. It’s not *that* far. Speaker_1: Don't tempt me. Let's just finish this cuppa and then *maybe* we'll discuss the merits of a McFlurry. Maybe. Speaker_2: Deal. And I’m ordering extra barbecue sauce. Just saying. Speaker_1: (sighs) Of course you are. Speaker_2: What can I say? Some things never change. Speaker_1: No, they really don't. Speaker_2: Okay…are you going to turn the volume up on the telly or…? Speaker_1: Oh! Sorry. Got lost in the kit chat. Yeah, let's see who's losing…or winning. Speaker_2: Brilliant. And then McDonalds after. Definitely. Speaker_1: We’ll see. Speaker_2: You say that now… Speaker_1: I’m a strong woman! Resist the call of the golden arches! Speaker_2: (laughing) We’ll see about that.

Speaker_2: Honestly, it’s just… draining. Every single day. Speaker_1: What is, babe? Still the Job Centre? Speaker_2: Yeah, well that too. But mainly it’s just… people. Old mates from school getting all… smug. Posting pictures of their new kitchens, holidays, you know. Like they’ve won the lottery or something. Speaker_1: Oh, massively. It’s the Instagram effect. Everyone’s living their best life online. Speaker_2: It's more than that though. It’s Colin, right? Colin from school. His nan left him a fortune. A *fortune*. Apparently, she was secretly a property tycoon. And he’s just… flaunting it. New car, all that. He didn’t even *work* for it. Speaker_1: Ugh, that's so annoying. It feels… unfair, doesn’t it? What about relationships with the existing hospices? We don't want to be seen as competition. Speaker_2: I’ve spoken to St. Julians in Hastings. They’re very supportive, actually. Happy to share best practice, offer advice on staffing models. They see the benefit of expanding access to hospice care in the region. And of course, we’ll need to forge a strong link with the local Macmillan nurses. Speaker_1: Excellent. And what about the actual building? Have you any ideas… brick, timber… modern or traditional? I’m leaning towards something warm and inviting. Nothing too clinical. Speaker_2: Definitely not clinical. I was thinking… Cotswold stone, perhaps? A bit of a nod to the surrounding area. Large windows, overlooking gardens. A central courtyard, maybe. Somewhere that feels… safe. Somewhere where patients – and their families – can find comfort in their final days. It’s the nursing, though, isn’t it? Getting the right team… specialists in pain management, psychological support… it’s crucial. Speaker_1: Absolutely. And ensuring they have access to ongoing training, bereavement counselling… we need to support *them*, too. It’s emotionally draining work. Speaker_2: You’re right. It is. Right. Shall we schedule a meeting with the architects next week? Get some preliminary sketches done, based on this discussion? And I’ll commission a proper analysis of

Speaker_1: Oh, look at this one! Us at Sarah’s wedding. God, we were young. And look at her hair! What *was* that all about? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) The early nineties. Big hair was mandatory. She thought she looked like Kylie Minogue. We all did, probably. Remember how uncomfortable those dresses were? Speaker_3: (Stirring a pot on the stove) Seriously. Corsets and layers of netting. Speaker_1: I think so. It's a bit of a splurge, but it's fun. You should come with me, darling. Speaker_2: Me? In a hat? I think I’ll leave the glamour to you two. I’d probably just end up looking like a beetroot. Speaker_3: (Laughing) You’d rock a fedora, Dad. Embrace the unconventional. Speaker_1: Speaking of unconventional, I saw Chloe Matthews at the supermarket today. Remember her? From school. She looked… different. Lots of tattoos, very brightly coloured hair. Should be here tomorrow. I got you that floral one you were looking at. And a pop socket, because you keep dropping your phone. Speaker_1: You’re the best. Honestly. I'm such a klutz. The people seemed nice, the job itself sounds interesting enough, but I just felt a bit… off. Like it wasn't quite the right fit. Speaker_2: Don’t worry about it, love. You'll find something perfect. You’re incredibly talented. And you're a brilliant copywriter, don't undersell yourself. Speaker_1: Exactly. And even if it’s not perfect, it’s good experience, isn't it? More practice for the next one. Now, are these potatoes nearly ready? I’m starving.

Speaker_1: Don’t laugh! It was terrifying! And it wasn’t just the telly, it was the… the way she *moved*. All jerky and creepy. God. And those seven days… Speaker_2: Okay, okay, point taken. ‘The Ring’ is horrific. But ‘The Descent’ is different, isn't it? It's claustrophobic. It's cave monsters. It's… realistic. That’s what makes it scary. People actually get lost in caves. Speaker_1: That's exactly what makes it scary! People *do* get lost in caves! And then they get eaten by… whatever those things are. I don't even want to think about what they are. They aren’t even properly explained, are they? Speaker_2: I think it's deliberately ambiguous. They're just… creatures born of the darkness. It adds to the atmosphere. Speaker_1: It adds to the nightmares! Honestly, I’m already regretting this. I should’ve stuck with ‘Bridesmaids’ or something. Much safer. Speaker_2: Come on, don't be such a scaredy cat! We’ve got snacks, we’ve got blankets, we’ve got each other to hide behind. It’ll be fine. It’ll be *fun*. Speaker_1: Hide *behind* you? You're about five foot nothing! That's not much protection against subterranean monsters! Speaker_2: It’s the principle of the thing! We can scream together! Misery loves company. Speaker_1: Fine. But if I have another nightmare about shadowy figures crawling out of holes, I'm blaming you. And you’re making me a cuppa. A *strong* cuppa. Speaker_2: Deal. Now, are we dimming the lights or going full blackout? Full blackout is more authentic, you know, for the cave experience. Speaker_1: No way! Dim the lights. I need to be able to *see* the blanket I’m hiding under. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Alright, alright. Dim lights it is. Prepare to be terrified. Speaker_1: I already am. Speaker_2: Good! Let’s go then! Speaker_1: Right, well, I'm just going to put the kettle on one last time. You sure you don't want a biscuit with your cocoa? Speaker_2: No dear, thank you. Cocoa's quite enough. Speaker_1: You’d think so! Look, I'll just have a quick search for the iPad again. It’s probably under a cushion or something. I’m going to rearrange the living room furniture tomorrow, actually. Speaker_1: I will. I promise. It's just feeling a bit… cluttered. Right, no iPad. I’ll check upstairs. What time are you heading to bed, Grandad? It's getting late. Speaker_2: Oh, not long now. Speaker_1: I can take a look at it in the morning if you like. I'm pretty good with things like that... when I can find the iPad to look up instructions! I'll leave your cocoa to cool a bit. Don’t want you burning your tongue. Speaker_2: Thank you, dear. You're a good girl. Now, off you pop and find that machine of yours. And don’t worry about the furniture. It’s all just things, isn’t it? Just things. Speaker_1: You're right. Just things. Okay, night night. Speaker_2: Night, night. Sleep well. Speaker_1: You too.

Speaker_1: Aye, honestly, the sheer scale of it, ye ken? I’d read about Patagonia, seen the photos, but nothing prepares ye for actually bein’ *there*. The mountains just… rise up out of the steppe. Did ye ever get around to reading that Hilary Mantel novel I lent ye? *Wolf Hall*? Speaker_2: Oh, aye! Just finished it last week. Brilliant. Absolute brilliant. Speaker_2: I've been daydreaming about Morocco. The colours, the smells, the souks… and the Sahara Desert. That's a whole different kind of landscape to grapple with, eh? And plenty of water. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Definitely a good hat. And maybe a camel. And a very patient guide.

Speaker_1: So, I sent off the application for the Bartlett summer school. Speaker_2: Oh, lovely! That’s good, darling. Which one was it, the design one? Speaker_1: So, you remember old man Hemmings down the lane? Sold his house last week, apparently. For a tidy sum, they say. Speaker_2: Hemmings? Oh, aye. Lived there donkey's years, didn't he? My granddaughter, Emily, she's saving up for a deposit, too. She works hard, but it’s a losing battle. Speaker_1: They should build more council houses, that's what they should do. Like they used to. Proper houses, built to last. Not these flimsy things they put up now. Remember when everything was built to last? My dad’s Ford Anglia, he had that for twenty years. Never a day’s trouble with it. Speaker_2: Ah, the Anglias. Solid little cars. I had a Cortina, back in the sixties. Teal blue. Now *that* was a car. You didn’t need a computer to drive it! Just a steering wheel and a bit of common sense. These new cars with all the gadgets… it’s just showing off. Speaker_3: It’s all about image these days, isn't it? And the politicians… don’t even mention them. Promises, promises, and not a single one kept. Remember when they said Brexit would free up money for the NHS? Lies, all lies. Speaker_1: Don't I just. They're all the same. Looking after themselves. It's a sorry state of affairs, I tell you. Still, at least we've got our health, eh? Relatively speaking, of course. Speaker_2: Aye, that’s true. Can’t complain too much. Though the knees are starting to give way. And my eyesight’s not what it used to be. I had to get new glasses fitted just last month. Speaker_3: Oh, I know the feeling. I need a new pair myself. But it’s the cost of everything now. Even a simple pair of glasses is a fortune. How is young Thomas getting on, by the way? I haven’t seen him in ages. Speaker_1: Right, so I was chatting with Old Man Hemmings from the community garden this morning, and he's really keen on running some sort of bird-watching workshop in the converted space. A few plants, maybe some nicer artwork than the ‘Protect Our Planet’ posters we’ve had since day one. Speaker_1: Agreed. I was thinking about approaching that art student from Lambeth College. Amelia's off for two weeks in August, and I’m trying to juggle things so we don't have a complete meltdown. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Trying to get anyone to cover facilities management is a nightmare. Everyone thinks it’s just tidying up and changing lightbulbs. They don’t realise the sheer volume of paperwork involved. Speaker_1: You’re preaching to the choir! And then there’s the new booking for the Saturday community brunch… they’ve requested gluten-free options, dairy-free options, vegan options, nut-free options… it’s a minefield. Speaker_2: Right, well, good luck with that. I’m going to go and check on the boiler. It’s making a worrying rattling noise, and I don’t want it to conk out mid-yoga session. Speaker_1: Good plan. And remind me to get Mrs. Davies about those newsletters. Before they take over the entire office. Speaker_2: Will do. And maybe a bird deterrent for the window while you're at it. Just in case Old Man Hemmings encourages a full-scale avian invasion.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this is incredible, Rhys. This roast chicken is… phenomenal. Seriously. Speaker_3: (Grinning) Glad you think so. Bit of a secret marinade, that. Speaker_1: …and then she just went full circle, started talking about her auntie Brenda again. Honestly, you'd think Auntie Brenda single-handedly invented the microwave, the way she goes on. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Sounds about right. Family gatherings, eh? A minefield of anecdotes and questionable opinions. Speaker_1: Exactly! Always seemed a bit…far. Is it good for food? I’m always on the lookout for decent food places. Speaker_2: Yeah, really good. Loads of independent restaurants. I had this amazing Korean fried chicken. And there’s a whole harbour area, really lively. Apparently, Banksy’s from there originally - still has stuff dotted around the city, you can go on a 'Banksy tour'. Speaker_1: Oh really? I didn't know that! We should go sometime. Maybe next year? After…you know. After the caravan debacle. Speaker_2: (Smiling) We absolutely should. Although, admittedly, I’m still slightly traumatized by the thought of navigating those country lanes in that monstrosity. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! Honestly, I’ve never driven anything so wide in my life. I felt like I was piloting a small boat. And the advert for it? "Effortless touring!" It was *anything* but. Speaker_2: "Effortless touring," my foot. They should rename it “Stressful Steering”. Did you see that new advert for the electric car, though? The one with the sheep? Speaker_1: Oh! The one where they’re all just...staring at it? Really weird. I don’t get it. It’s like they’re saying “sheep approve of sustainable transport”. Speaker_2: Exactly! It's baffling.
