I’ll probably vote Labour, out of habit. Though I wouldn’t trust any of ‘em as far as I could throw ‘em. Now, about this cruise… you should definitely go. Get yourselves some sunshine. And don’t forget the factor 50! My skin’s like parchment these days. Burns if I look at a lightbulb. Speaker_1: We will definitely remember the factor 50! It sounds lovely doesn't it? Speaker_2: It does, a real adventure. Maybe we can look at some brochures tonight? And get a quote for the insurance… brace ourselves for the worst, hope for the best! Speaker_3: Good plan. Now, who wants a biscuit? I think I saw a tin of digestives in the cupboard…

Speaker_1: Honestly though, Dad, you and Mum navigating Belgium with a sat nav… I was picturing utter chaos. Speaker_2: Chaos is a strong word, darling. A little… spirited, perhaps. Your mother insisted on reading the paper map *as well*. Just in case, she said. Like the sat nav was going to suddenly sprout legs and wander off. Speaker_3: It was helpful, actually. Just to have something to cross-reference. Though, admittedly, it did lead to a few… disagreements. Especially when the sat nav tried to take us down a pedestrian zone in Bruges. Speaker_1: Oh, no! Did you get told off? Speaker_2: A very stern-looking gentleman in a beret certainly made his feelings known. Lots of waving of arms and rapid-fire Flemish. I understood precisely none of it, but the tone was quite clear. Speaker_3: He thought we were completely mad, trying to drive a car down there. And the roads! So narrow. You’ve barely got room to breathe. Speaker_1: Sounds horrifying! Was the food good, though? You said you were excited about the chocolate and waffles. Speaker_2: Oh, the food was *excellent*. The chocolate, as expected, was divine. And the waffles… well, they were a religious experience. Though I did make the mistake of ordering a waffle with everything on it. Everything. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Everything? What does ‘everything’ even *mean* on a Belgian waffle? Speaker_3: Strawberries, bananas, whipped cream, chocolate sauce, speculoos crumbs… it was a mountain of sugar. Your father barely touched his afterwards. It was a bit much, even for him. Speaker_2: It was… a learning experience. I’ve learned my limits when it comes to waffle toppings. But the markets were wonderful, darling. Bruges has a beautiful market square. We got some lovely cheeses and little trinkets. Speaker_1: Oh, nice! Did you cycle at all? I know Mum was keen to hire bikes. Speaker_3: We did! Just along the canals in Ghent. It was lovely, very flat and easy cycling. Though your father nearly ran over a small child. Speaker_2: (Grumbling) I did *not* nearly run over a small child! I braked in plenty of time. It was the child who ran into my path. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Right. Of course. Speaker_3: Anyway, I’ve just gotten a new mobile phone. A fancy one. One of those with the really good camera. I’m still trying to figure out how it all works. Speaker_1: Oh, nice! What did you get? Speaker_3: A Samsung. Apparently, it’s very good for taking pictures of the cats. Speaker_1: Essential, obviously. I’m thinking of upgrading mine, but I keep putting it off. It’s such a faff transferring everything over. Speaker_2: It is a bit of a pain. But worth it in the end. Though, driving abroad, that’s a faff on a whole other level. All the different rules and regulations… it’s exhausting. I swear, they have a different speed limit on every single road. Speaker_1: Absolutely. I'm going to make a note to ask you lots about driving in Europe when I finally decide to go. Do you think you can do next weekend? We could go for Sunday lunch. It would be good to catch up properly. Speaker_3: That would be lovely, dear. Sunday is perfect. Speaker_2: Sounds good to me. I’ll bring some of the cheese we got from Belgium. Unless, of course, it’s all been eaten by then.

Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve got the chicken marinating, that needs at least an hour, ideally two. Do you want me to start on the roast potatoes then? Speaker_2: Sounds good. Though honestly, the smell of that marinade is already making my mouth water. What did you put in it, again? Speaker_1: Oh, the usual. Lemon juice, garlic, a bit of rosemary, paprika… and a sneaky dash of chili flakes. Don’t tell the kids. Speaker_2: (chuckles) My lips are sealed. You’re getting very clever with your marinades, you know. Remember when we just used…soy sauce and a bit of ginger? Speaker_1: Don’t remind me! Those were the dark days of culinary experimentation. Speaking of experiments, have you seen what Sarah’s done with her hair? On Facebook, I mean. It’s… bright purple. Speaker_2: Oh, Sarah. Always one for a statement. Is it a good purple? Or one of those shades that makes you question reality? Speaker_1: Somewhere in between, I think. A kind of… lavender meets electric plum. I commented, said it looked ‘bold’. Tactful, I thought. Speaker_2: Very diplomatic. She’ll take that as a compliment. Right, potatoes it is then. Are you going to get the fireplace going tonight? It’s a bit chilly, even with the heating on. Speaker_1: I was thinking about it. I’ll need to get some logs down from the shed, though. It’s a bit of a trek. You wouldn’t fancy braving the garden, would you? Speaker_2: Not particularly, no. I’m quite happy stirring these beans. Though I did notice old Mrs. Higgins was putting out her winter bedding plants this morning. Impressive dedication. Speaker_1: She’s always ahead of the game, isn't she? She’s got the most beautiful roses, too. I wish I had her touch with flowers. Everything I plant looks…sad. Speaker_2: You’re being modest. Your hydrangeas were lovely this summer. Though, to be fair, everything looks good next to her garden. It's like something out of a magazine. Speaker_1: Perhaps I should just buy cut flowers. Less effort. Speaking of less effort, did you remember to order that new perfume I mentioned? The one with the…bergamot? Speaker_2: Almost. It’s in my online basket, ready to go. I was just checking the reviews. Apparently, it smells amazing, but fades really quickly. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s annoying. I hate perfumes that disappear after five minutes. It’s such a waste of money. I quite like the one Auntie Maureen wears, though, even if it does smell slightly… mothball-ish. Speaker_2: (grimaces) Ah, yes. Maureen’s signature scent. A classic, in its own way. You know, I was talking to David at work today, he’s moved back up to Edinburgh, and he still speaks with such a strong accent. You wouldn't believe. Speaker_1: Oh really? It must be nice to hear a proper Scottish accent after all this time down south. Everyone sounds the same here, a sort of… bland English. Speaker_2: Exactly! It's… diluted, isn’t it? You lose all the character. Right, potatoes are peeling. You concentrating on the chicken, then? Speaker_1: Yep, chicken is my domain. And keeping an eye on Facebook. Just in case Sarah changes her hair color again. Hopefully, this conversation meets your requirements. Let me know if you’d like any adjustments.

Speaker_1: So you were in Queensland, you said? Lovely part of the world, I hear. Never been myself. Speaker_2: Aye, Queensland. Spent a good six months out there, back in ‘87. Business trip, mostly. Though I did manage to sneak in a bit of fishing. Beautiful coastline. Different world, really. Speaker_3: Six months! That's a decent stretch. I only ever had a short holiday in Sydney. Beautiful, of course, but felt…remote. Did you find the business culture very different? Speaker_2: Oh, vastly. Much more relaxed. Less…sharp elbows, if you know what I mean? Though the suits were still sharp enough, mind. A lot of lightweight linen, thankfully. Couldn’t imagine those heavy worsteds in that heat. Back home, every businessman looks like he’s going to a funeral. Speaker_1: You’re not wrong there! My husband always said they looked terribly uncomfortable. All that stiffness. Did you find it easy, adjusting to the pace of things? Speaker_2: Took a bit of getting used to. I’m a Northern lad, born and bred in Manchester. We’re used to getting straight to the point. Australians, they like a bit of chat first. A lot of “G’day” and “No worries”. Had to learn to slow down. Needed a bit of a bank loan to fund the trip. It was a good earner, but expensive. Speaker_3: Bank loans are always a pain. I had to get one for my house, years ago. Still paying it off! Speaking of accents, I was once mistaken for an Australian in America. Apparently, my Yorkshire dialect bears a surprising resemblance to some of their regional twangs. Speaker_1: Oh really? That’s fascinating! I’m from Bristol, and people often struggle with our accent, even other Brits. We have a bit of a…melody to our speech, apparently. A sort of West Country lilt. Some people think we sound a bit like pirates! Speaker_2: Now, I’ve heard about the Bristol accent. Apparently, you folks drop your ‘h’s like they’re going out of fashion. Speaker_1: (Laughs) We do have a tendency! It’s just…how we speak. I taught English as a foreign language for years, and I had students from all over the world. They’d often ask me to say things slowly, and try to decipher what I was saying. It was always amusing. Speaker_3: Teaching’s a noble profession. I’m a lecturer myself, at the university. Though I'm nearing retirement now. It’s changed so much over the years. The students are…different. Speaker_2: Different how? More entitled? That’s what I found with the younger staff at the company, back then. Speaker_3: A little bit, perhaps. More focused on assessment grades, less on the actual learning. It’s a long story. I suspect we’re digressing. We were talking about Australia...and how polite the business folk were. Speaker_1: It’s lovely chatting with you both. I should probably be heading off. It's getting late. Speaker_2: Aye, best be getting on. It’s been a pleasant hour. Although I'd rather be sat in a pub, frankly. Speaker_3: Absolutely. It was nice to meet you both. Perhaps we'll cross paths again. Speaker_1: Yes, indeed. Goodbye then. Speaker_2: Ta-ra. Speaker_3: Farewell. Goodbye. Certainly, let me know if you’d like me to expand on any part of this!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this pierogi is amazing. I didn't realise vegan pierogi could even *exist*, let alone be this good. Rzeszow is a surprisingly good shout for vegan food, isn’t it? Speaker_2: It really is! I did a bit of research before I came, and there were loads of options. Much better than some places in England, actually. So, how are you finding Poland in general? Properly settled in now? Speaker_1: Settled is…a strong word. Let's say I’m acclimatising. The language is still a hurdle, obviously. I'm trying Duolingo, but it’s slow going. And the sheer number of consonants! It’s brutal. More importantly, I’m utterly addicted to Polish social media now. Speaker_2: Oh really? What platforms are you using? Instagram? TikTok? Speaker_1: TikTok mostly, surprisingly. It’s a rabbit hole. I keep finding these incredibly bizarre, niche accounts. Like, one guy who just films himself meticulously cleaning rusty tools. And he has, like, half a million followers. It’s fascinating. Speaker_2: (Laughing) That *is* bizarre. I get sucked into the language learning side of TikTok. So many people giving tips and tricks. It’s a lot more helpful than my old university textbooks. Though, I did get sucked into a whole drama about a British influencer who went to Bali and tried to open a ‘spiritual retreat’…it was…messy. Speaker_1: Oh, those are the worst. The ‘digital nomad’ dramas are always so cringe. I’ve been trying to wean myself off Instagram, actually. It’s just…noise. I've started listening to podcasts instead. Speaker_2: Oh, what kind? Any recommendations? I’m always looking for new ones. I’m currently obsessed with this true crime podcast, “Root of Evil”. It's about this incredibly complex family history and a series of murders. Speaker_1: Ooh, that sounds intense. I’ve gone a bit more…whimsical. I found one called “Off Menu” – it’s two comedians interviewing people about their dream meal. Utterly ridiculous, but it’s perfect background noise while I’m attempting to decipher Polish grammar. Speaker_2: That sounds lovely! I need something a bit lighter. I’ve been watching a bit too much bleak Scandi-noir on Netflix lately. It's good, but it’s draining. Are you watching anything good on TV? Honestly, British TV feels so…tired at the moment. Speaker_1: I'm not really watching much TV, surprisingly. Partly because I don’t have a proper aerial setup here, but mostly because I'm so easily distracted by my phone. Although, I did binge-watch “Ghosts” recently. Have you seen that? Speaker_2: “Ghosts”? The one with the haunted house? Yes! It’s hilarious. Proper feel-good telly. Though, I think I’ve seen every episode now. I need something new. Maybe I’ll give that podcast a listen. “Off Menu”, was it? Speaker_1: Yes! Definitely. It’s the perfect antidote to the existential dread of…well, everything. And another pierogi? I think I can manage another. This is the life. Speaker_2: Definitely another pierogi. And yes, existential dread is a mood. It's good to escape into silly podcasts and wonderful vegan food, though. Cheers to that! Speaker_1: Cheers! To pierogi, podcasts, and polite escapes. Speaker_2: And to finding rusty tool cleaning accounts on TikTok.

Speaker_1: Right, so swimming tomorrow morning, then… what about Pippy? Are you two excited to see Pippy? Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Yessss! She said she’d bring her juggling balls! Speaker_3: And her sparkly dress! She promised! Speaker_1: That’s lovely. She's a good babysitter, isn’t she? I feel much happier leaving you two when she's here. Speaker_2: She lets us build really big dens! Speaker_3: And she told us a story about a travelling circus. Speaker_1: Oh really? Did she? What was it about? Speaker_2: It had a lion and a clown and… and people flying through the air! Speaker_3: And a strongman! He could lift a car! Speaker_1: Wow! Sounds amazing. You know, Pippy’s trying to get a Blue Peter badge. Speaker_2: A Blue Peter badge?! What for? Speaker_1: She sent in a picture of the amazing things she can do with juggling. But they need a photograph *of* her, for the badge. And she’s a bit shy about being photographed. Speaker_3: We could take a picture of her! Speaker_1: That’s a brilliant idea! We could ask her nicely, and then she'd have a photo for Blue Peter. But we need to make sure it’s a good one, a really special one. Speaker_2: Can we decorate her with glitter? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Hmm, maybe not *too* much glitter. We don't want her looking like a disco ball! Speaker_3: What about when we go on holiday? Do we need passports? Speaker_1: Good question! Yes, we do. I need to dig them out. They’re probably tucked away somewhere safe… which means I’ll never find them. Speaker_2: How old is Pippy? Speaker_1: Oh, she's… a grown-up. Older than me! She’s… twenty-something. Speaker_3: Why does she like juggling? Speaker_1: She told me she used to watch her grandpa juggle when she was little. He was a really good juggler too. It's a family thing, I think. Oh, you won’t believe what she told me… Speaker_2: What? Speaker_1: Apparently, in some parts of China, they eat eggs that are… really, really old. Like, months old! Speaker_3: Ewwww! Speaker_2: Yucky! Do they smell? Speaker_1: She said they smell *very* strong. And they turn a funny colour. She said it's a delicacy, but I don’t think I’d try one! Speaker_3: I wouldn't either. Speaker_1: Right, back to more exciting things. Maybe after swimming, we can practise our own circus skills? We could build a little stage in the garden. Speaker_2: Yes! Can we be the strong people? Speaker_3: I want to be the lion! Roar! Speaker_1: (Smiling) We’ll have to see. Now, who wants some juice? The circus performers need to keep their energy up! Speaker_2 & Speaker_3: Me! Me! speaker_1: Ok, Ok. One each then. And be careful. I don't want a circus disaster on my kitchen floor!

Speaker_1: Right, so then she was goin’ on about how her lad, like, never seems bothered, y’know? Speaker_2: Oh, god. That sounds… awkward. Speaker_1: Awkward is an understatement! She was proper stressed. Said he’s lost all interest, and she’s worried somethin’s up with ‘im. Speaker_2: Well, I mean, life *is* stressful. Could be anything, right? Work, uni… just general life stuff. Speaker_1: Aye, she said that, but she kept goin’ on about… well, about it bein’ somethin’ physical. Like, she was whisperin’ about erectile dysfunction. Speaker_2: Woah. That’s… a lot. She just straight up said that to you? Speaker_1: Not straight up, not at first. It was all hints and worried looks, then eventually she just blurted it out. Said she’d been readin’ online and, well, you can imagine. Speaker_2: Ugh, the internet is the worst. Self-diagnosing is a nightmare. Honestly, it's probably just a phase. Happens to everyone sometimes. Stress can do a lot. Speaker_1: She was convinced it was more than that. She was talkin’ about tablets and doctors and all sorts. It sounded right scary, honestly. Poor lass. Speaker_2: I can see why she’d be worried. But, like, there are so many reasons it could happen. And it’s not exactly something people talk about, is it? Must be awful feelin’ like you can’t even discuss it. Speaker_1: Exactly! She was mortified even talkin’ to *me* about it. Said she couldn’t tell anyone else. Speaker_2: God, that’s rough. It’s such a taboo subject. Makes it even harder to deal with, doesn't it? Maybe she should push him to see a doctor, just to rule things out. Speaker_1: She said she’d tried, but he’s stubborn as an old mule. Wouldn't even entertain the idea. Said he's just “tired”. Speaker_2: “Tired” is a convenient excuse. Honestly, men can be so… obtuse sometimes. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. She’s feelin’ really rejected, as well. She said he doesn’t seem to want her anymore. It’s not just the physical thing; it’s the emotional side of it too. Speaker_2: That’s what’s really heartbreaking, isn’t it? It's not about performance; it’s about feeling desired. Speaker_1: Absolutely. It's like, she understands there can be issues, but the lack of communication is killin’ her. It’s the silence, she said. The lack of affection. Speaker_2: That’s brutal. She’s in a really tough spot. I don't even know what to say to her, really. Just listen, I guess? Offer a shoulder to cry on? Speaker_1: That’s what I did. Just let her vent, really. She just needed to get it off her chest. I feel awful for her, though. It's such a private thing to be goin’ through. Speaker_2: It is. It really is. I mean, we barely talk about *having* sex, let alone… well, you know. Speaker_1: Exactly. It's a miracle anyone manages to have a healthy sex life, honestly. I have tried to reflect the dialects as requested within the bounds of natural conversation.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, for tonight, we could do the chilli with the rice, but like, *really* load up on the speed vegetables in it, yeah? So we get, like, three of our five a day just in the chilli. Speaker_2: Ooh, good shout. Chilli sounds good. And we’ve got loads of that frozen mixed pepper stuff, haven’t we? That counts, right? Like, properly counts towards your five a day? Speaker_1: It does, yeah! It definitely does. And I was thinking, if we do the rice as a Healthy Extra ‘b’… because I’ve been properly good today. Only had fruit for breakfast, and then that massive salad at lunch. Speaker_2: Proud of you! I’ve been a bit… shaky. Had a biscuit with my tea, which is never a good sign. It just happened. It called to me. Speaker_1: Oh, those biscuits are dangerous. They really are. Speaking of tea, fancy a peppermint? I found a new one, it's got proper mint leaves in, not just flavouring. Speaker_2: Oh yes, please! Anything involving actual mint is a win. I’m so over artificial sweeteners and flavourings. Seriously, what *is* in those 0 calorie syrups? It just tastes… wrong. Speaker_1: I know! It’s creepy, isn’t it? And it makes you want more. Like, your brain doesn't register it as sweet properly, so you just keep adding more and more. Anyway, chilli it is. I’ll get the mince browning. Oh, and I found that spice mix in the cupboard – the one with the smoky paprika? That would be perfect. Speaker_2: Perfect! Oh, and did you see they’ve got double peas in the freezer now? Double peas! Like, seriously? Who needs that much pea? Speaker_1: Haha, I know! It’s excessive. But good for us, I suppose. We can freeze half and save it for another time. It’s cheaper than buying two bags, right? Always gotta be thinking about saving money, especially with tax coming up. Speaker_2: Ugh, don't even *mention* tax. It's the bane of my existence as a freelance illustrator. So many forms, so little actual money going in. You’re lucky with your fixed pay as a pharmacy dispenser. Speaker_1: Yeah, it’s… stable, at least. Though they’re always changing our targets now, which is irritating. ‘Dispense ten more prescriptions an hour!’ Like, I'm not a robot! Speaker_2: Seriously! People need things dispensed *correctly* and safely, not just quickly. Anyway, back to the food. We’re agreed chilli, then? And don’t forget we’ve got ‘treat day’ on Saturday! I’m thinking proper homemade chips with a burger. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! But promise me we’ll make cauliflower cheese with the roast on Sunday? I've been craving it *all* week. Speaker_2: Done! Though my scales are being incredibly unreliable at the moment. They either tell me I've lost a pound or gained five, depending on their mood. It's very stressful. Speaker_1: Scales are evil. I've stopped weighing myself so often. Just go by how my clothes fit, you know? Oh, and I’ve been trying to do a little bit of exercise. Just a walk around the park each day, but it’s something. Speaker_2: Good for you. I should probably do that too. Maybe after dinner? I was planning to spend the evening illustrating, but I could probably squeeze in a walk. I feel like I should also mention, I think Sainsbury's has the best Quorn range, honestly. Better than anywhere else. Speaker_1: Ooh, interesting. I usually go to Tesco. Although, we should probably think about getting a veg box delivery again? It forces us to eat more vegetables and it’s usually cheaper. Speaker_2:

Speaker_1: So, have you actually *looked* at villas in Italy, or are you still just… vaguely dreaming of Tuscany? Speaker_2: I’ve looked, alright? It's just… intimidating. So much choice. And everything looks amazing in the pictures, doesn’t it? Then you read the reviews and it’s all, “Thin walls, aggressive wasps, local cats using the pool as a toilet.” Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh, don't start with the cat toilet situation. Honestly. We need a pool, though. That’s non-negotiable. Otherwise, what’s the point? Speaker_2: Agreed. Pool is essential. And a decent kitchen. I want to actually *cook* when we’re away, not just survive on panini and gelato. Although, a lot of gelato is definitely part of the plan. Speaker_1: You and your cooking. Honestly, you make a mean carbonara, but I suspect the main aim is to find a suitably large wine selection to pair with it. Speaker_2: That’s just good planning! Speaking of plans… I was thinking, after Italy, maybe we finally tackle Scotland? I’ve always wanted to do the North Coast 500. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds… bracing. Lots of driving. And midges. I’ve heard terrifying things about the midges. I’d rather get a tattoo, honestly. Speaker_2: (chuckles) You and your threats of tattoos. You've been saying you'll get one for years. What would you even get? A miniature version of Buster? Speaker_1: Very funny. No. I was thinking… maybe some wildflowers. Around my wrist. Relatively small. Not a full sleeve, you know. I don’t want to scare the neighbours. Speaker_2: You wouldn’t scare the neighbours. They’re more worried about Mrs. Henderson’s increasingly elaborate garden gnomes. Though, wildflowers are lovely. A bit… bohemian for you, though, aren’t they? Speaker_1: Oh, stop. I have hidden depths. What about… if we won the lottery? What’s the first thing *you'd* do? Besides buying a lifetime supply of single malt. Speaker_2: Hmm. Good question. I’d probably pay off the mortgage, obviously. Then I’d set up a trust fund for the kids. After that… I’d build a proper home office. This spare bedroom is driving me mad. Too cramped. And the Wi-Fi is terrible. Speaker_1: (rolling her eyes) Of course you would. Always practical. I'd buy a small cottage by the sea. Somewhere ridiculously picturesque. And I’d spend my days writing. Speaker_2: Still on that novel, then? Speaker_1: Always. It’s slow progress. I’m stuck on chapter twelve. The protagonist is facing a moral dilemma, and I just can’t decide which way she should go. Honestly, it's more stressful than dealing with Mr. Davies at work. Speaker_2: Just write the most dramatic thing possible. That’s what I always do when I’m debugging code. Throw everything at it and hope for the best. Speaker_1: That’s… not helpful. But I suppose it's a philosophy. You know what my perfect day would be? No work. No chores. Just you, me, a good book, a glass of wine, and maybe Buster snoring at our feet. And absolutely no wasps. Speaker_2: That actually sounds… perfect, actually. Though, knowing our luck, the cat would still use the pool. Speaker_1: Don’t even!

Speaker_1: Right, so, the 18th is definitely free then? For the… well, for *a* celebration, at least. Speaker_2: Aye, the 18th is good. Though I still think a proper knees-up needs to wait 'til after Sarah's back from Spain. She’d be proper miffed missing her own… well, approaching the big five-oh. Speaker_1: She wouldn't miss it, she'd just… grumble about the timing. And honestly, leaving it another three weeks feels like an age. I’ve already ordered the cake. A rather splendid chocolate one, actually, with… miniature historical figures on top. Speaker_2: Historical figures? You and your little hobbies. What figures? Romans? Tudors? Is there a tiny Oliver Cromwell glaring at the icing? Speaker_1: (chuckles) Mostly Victorians. A little nod to the era. Though there *is* a rather determined-looking Boudicca. I thought it was fitting. Anyway, back to the 18th. We should probably ring Mrs. Higgins and see if she’s still up for doing the catering. She’s brilliant with canapés. Speaker_2: Good shout. I’ll give her a bell tomorrow. Speaking of ringing people, did you get that postcard I sent from Skye? The one with the Old Man of Storr? Speaker_1: Ah, yes! It arrived. Very dramatic. Though the postmark was… smudged. Made it look like it had been wrestled from a particularly grumpy postman. It was a lovely trip, though, wasn’t it? Very bracing. Speaker_2: Aye, bracing is one word for it. I nearly blew away twice. Still, the scenery’s worth it. Saw a golden eagle, did you know? Majestic creature. Speaker_1: Remarkable. And you managed all that walking despite your knee? Speaker_2: Managed. With a considerable amount of grumbling and a walking stick that’s now practically an extension of my arm. Though it got me thinking… all this talk of independence up there… it's a proper mess, isn't it? Speaker_1: It is rather… complicated. I was reading an article in the *Times* about it this morning. Apparently the latest polls suggest… Speaker_2: Polls suggest all sorts. They were saying Labour were going to win in ‘97, weren’t they? And look what happened. The whole thing is fuelled by emotion, I reckon. A lot of ancient grievances. Speaker_1: There is a historical element to it, certainly. Though the economic arguments are equally potent, it seems. And the young people… they seem quite keen on the idea. Speaker_2: Aye, they do. They haven't lived through a lifetime of… well, of being British, I suppose. It’s easy to romanticise independence when you haven't seen the practical realities. Speaker_1: Perhaps. Though romanticism has its place, doesn’t it? It’s what drives historical research, after all. Right. Back to the practicalities. We need to sort drinks for the 18th. Do we have enough Prosecco? Speaker_2: Always a good question. I think we’re a bit low. I can pop to the off-license tomorrow morning. And maybe get a nice bottle of single malt for yourself… a little something to celebrate your… Victorian figures. Speaker_1: (smiling) Very thoughtful of you. And perhaps a little something for Sarah, too, to preempt any grumbling about the imminent arrival of the big five-oh. Speaker_2: Definitely. Can't risk a sulk on her special day.

Speaker_1: Right, so we’re drawing pictures for the Syrian refugees, aren’t we? And Mrs. Davies said they’re sending them to a charity that distributes them to families who’ve had to leave their homes. Speaker_2: (Excitedly) I’m drawing a princess! She’s going to give them a sparkly crown! Speaker_3: (Concentrating intensely, scribbling) I’m making a…a super-robot! He’s going to protect them from monsters. Speaker_1: (Smiling) That’s lovely. Both of you. It's very thoughtful. I was thinking… maybe we could draw them pictures of comfy chairs? Speaker_2: Chairs? Why chairs? Speaker_1: Well, imagine having to leave everything behind. Everything! Your bed, your toys, your favourite chair… it must be so hard not having a comfortable place to sit. So a picture of a nice comfy chair might remind them of home. Speaker_3: Like my beanbag? Speaker_1: Exactly like your beanbag! Or the armchair in here. What kind of chair would you draw? Speaker_2: A pink one with fluffy cushions! And a little table for my dolls. Speaker_1: That sounds wonderful! What about you, Leo? Speaker_3: A racing car chair! With fire coming out the back! It’s a super-chair! Speaker_1: (Chuckling) A super-chair! That's brilliant. You know, there are all sorts of chairs, aren't there? Rocking chairs, office chairs… even those really hard wooden chairs they have at school. Speaker_2: I hate the school chairs! They make my bottom hurt! Speaker_1: (Smiling) They’re not very comfortable, are they? That’s why it’s nice to have a comfy chair at home. It’s somewhere safe and cosy. Like a hug. Speaker_3: I like the chair with the arms. I can build a fort around it. Speaker_1: See? Chairs can be lots of things. And for people who don’t *have* a chair right now, even a picture of one can be a happy thing. Speaker_2: Will they like my princess? Speaker_1: I’m sure they will! A sparkly crown is a brilliant idea. And Leo, a super-robot protector is exactly what everyone needs sometimes. I bet they'll have the pictures on their walls. Speaker_3: Are we having tests at school next week? Miss Jones said something about tests. Speaker_1: (Sighs lightly) Yes, dear. You've got your spelling test on Tuesday, and a maths one on Friday. Speaker_2: I’m good at spelling! I know all the tricky words. Speaker_3: I don’t like maths tests. They’re hard. Speaker_1: I know they can be tricky, but you’re both very clever. And remember, it's not about getting everything right, it's about trying your best. Just like you're trying your best with these lovely pictures for the Syrian refugees. Now, back to the chairs! Let's fill the page with comfy, colourful chairs. Speaker_2: (Returns to drawing with renewed energy) Okay! A rainbow chair! Speaker_3: (Also back to drawing) And mine will fly! It's a flying super-chair! Speaker_1: (Watching them, a soft expression on her face) Perfect. Absolutely perfect. Speaker_1: (Watching them, a soft expression on her face) Perfect. Absolutely perfect. Speaker_2: Okay! A rainbow chair! Speaker_3: (Also back to drawing) And mine will fly! It's a flying super-chair! Speaker_1: (Watching them, a soft expression on her face) Perfect. Absolutely perfect.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m still reeling from Sarah’s announcement. A second one? So soon? Speaker_2: I know, right? It was a bit of a shock. Though, knowing Sarah, she probably started planning it the minute Leo turned six months old. She’s always wanted a big family. Speaker_1: She is, isn't she? It's lovely, genuinely. But massively overwhelming when you think about it. Two under two... I don't know how she’ll cope. Remember how stressed she was with just Leo and the return to work? Speaker_2: Vaguely. I think I was deep in marking hell at that point. But yes, she did seem perpetually exhausted. Though she hides it well. She always puts on a brave face. Speaker_1: She does. And she’ll probably insist on homemade everything again. Organic purees, cloth nappies, the whole nine yards. Bless her. I admire the dedication, truly. Speaker_2: It's a lot of work. A *lot*. Makes my marking deadlines seem rather trivial, doesn’t it? Still, I’m glad for her. And for Mark. He seemed genuinely thrilled when she told him, even if his face did briefly betray a flicker of absolute terror. Speaker_1: Oh, Mark. He’ll be brilliant. He’s so patient. He’ll be the one doing the night feeds while Sarah perfects miniature knitted outfits. Speaker_2: Probably! Though, with both of us being lecturers, we should be sympathetic to the sleep deprivation. We know what it’s like to function on minimal hours! Just… different reasons. Speaker_1: Ha! True. Though I suspect a crying baby is a slightly more pressing concern than a looming essay deadline. Speaking of which, did you manage to get through all of Miller’s papers? He sent a ridiculously long reading list. Speaker_2: Nearly. I skimmed a couple. Don't tell anyone. I’m hoping I can get away with it in the seminar. He’s so easily distracted by tangents anyway. Speaker_1: You rogue! You’re braver than I am. I read every single page, and I still feel like I haven’t absorbed a thing. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if I’m actually cut out for this lecturing business. Speaker_2: Don’t be silly. You're amazing with the students. They adore you. And you have a knack for explaining things clearly, even the really complicated stuff. Remember how flustered poor Emily was about post-structuralism? You sorted her out in five minutes flat. Speaker_1: She was a sweet girl. And yes, that *was* a satisfying five minutes. Still… babies. It's making me think about things. About the future. Speaker_2: Don’t start! We agreed we’d revisit that conversation after Christmas. Let’s just bask in Sarah’s baby news for now and avoid existential dread. Speaker_1: You're right. You're absolutely right. More tea? I made a fresh pot. Speaker_2: Yes, please. And maybe a biscuit? I feel like I deserve one after discussing Miller’s impenetrable prose. Speaker_1: Coming right up. You deserve the whole tin. Speaker_2: Don't tempt me. Speaker_1: (laughing) Okay, okay. One biscuit. For now. Speaker_2: Excellent. One biscuit and then back to pretending we haven’t noticed our friends having babies and fundamentally altering the landscape of our social lives. Speaker_1: Precisely. A perfectly reasonable strategy, I think. Speaker_2: I concur.

Speaker_1: Honestly, that was the worst comedian I’ve ever seen. Absolutely dreadful. All those jokes about mothers-in-law…so predictable. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Harsh, Lottie, harsh. He wasn’t *that* bad. Just…beige. Like a biscuit. Speaker_1: Beige and offensively reliant on tired tropes! You know, my grandmother, she always said you could tell a bad omen if a comedian told a joke about a wife being a bad driver. Utterly superstitious, she was. Speaker_2: Your grandmother and her omens. Did she have one for encountering policemen in the countryside? Because we’ve seen a surprising number today. Speaker_1: Probably involving bad harvests and disgruntled fairies. No, actually, she was quite fond of policemen. She’d bake them cakes. Said they deserved a bit of kindness. Remember that time old Mr. Henderson – the village bobby – got stuck in the duck pond trying to retrieve a rogue football? Speaker_2: (Laughing) How could I forget? He was absolutely furious, but your grandmother just kept offering him tea and biscuits. He looked like he wanted the earth to swallow him whole. Speaker_1: Exactly! She was brilliant. Though, thinking about publicity…that whole incident got in the local paper. "Policeman Rescued From Pond by Cake-Wielding Widow!" The headline was glorious. Speaker_2: Glorious and probably the reason he transferred to a different beat. Speaking of publicity, I’m still slightly mortified about that interview I did for the university website. They made me sound like some sort of eccentric genius. Speaker_1: You *are* an eccentric genius! Just a modest one. Seriously, though, they completely misquoted you about the semiotics of garden gnomes. Speaker_2: They said I believed garden gnomes were “powerful symbols of post-modern alienation.” I just said they were a bit kitsch! Honestly, the things they do. It’s all about boosting student numbers, isn’t it? Speaker_1: Pretty much. It’s all branding. Makes you think about how we spend our holidays, though. Remember that remote cottage in Cornwall? No phone signal, no internet…pure bliss. No chance of being misquoted there. Speaker_2: Blissful isolation. Although, I do vaguely recall you spending half the week trying to build a signal booster out of tin foil and coat hangers. Speaker_1: (Slightly defensively) It was a legitimate scientific experiment! And it almost worked! This countryside is lovely, though. It's good to get away from all that…academic noise. Speaker_2: It really is. And much easier on the feet than those cobbled streets in Norwich. Though I do miss a decent curry. Speaker_1: We'll get a decent curry, I promise. First, we finish this walk. And then, maybe, silence. No comedians, no semiotics, no rogue policemen. Just…silence. Speaker_2: Sounds perfect. Speaker_1: It does, doesn’t it? Until you start analysing the *meaning* of the silence, of course. Speaker_2: (Groans) Don't even start. Speaker_1: (Laughs) I wouldn’t dream of it. For now. Speaker_2: Good. Let's just enjoy the view. Speaker_1: Agreed. It's beautiful. Speaker_2: Absolutely. Speaker_1: Look, a kestrel. Speaker_2: Stunning. Speaker_1: And, no sign of Mr. Henderson, thankfully. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Not yet, anyway.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Dad, you wouldn’t *believe* the signal in my room. It's like living in a black hole. I tried to FaceTime Grandma yesterday, and it just kept cutting out. Speaker_2: Ah, that mobile reception's always been dodgy around the back. They promised to put a mast up years ago, down by the old orchard, but never did. Waste of time, those promises. As long as it doesn’t use all my data. That bill’s enough as it is, even though I don’t use the thing much. Mostly just for the grandkids ringing. Speaker_1: It won't, promise! We'll keep it brief. Speaking of things needing moving, are you still planning on having a clearout of the shed? I might be able to help this weekend. Speaker_2: That shed’s a disaster zone, love. Speaker_2: Good memories, eh? But it’s just sitting there, rotting. I might hire a van to take everything to the tip. Do you know anyone? Speaker_1: I think Mark’s mate, Dave, does van hire. I can ask him for a quote. How much stuff are we talking about? A whole shed full? Speaker_2: Pretty much. And then there's the attic... don’t even get me started on the attic. Thinking of having a bit of a sort through up there too. Maybe find some of those old antiques your grandmother collected. Speaker_1: Oh! Really? I didn’t know she collected antiques. That could be fun! Have you been to the Great Dorset Steam Fair this year? Speaker_2: Not yet, no. Been meaning to, but the weather's been awful. Your Auntie Carol keeps going on about it, though. She loves all that old machinery. We might go next weekend, if it's dry. It'd be a good chance to see your cousins. Speaker_1: Oh, that would be nice. It feels like ages since we all got together. I was thinking of trying to organise something for Christmas, maybe a big dinner at your place? Speaker_2: Hmm, sounds good. But don’t expect me to do all the cooking! My back's playing up again. Speaker_1: Of course not! We can all help. I’ve been getting quite good at making roast potatoes, actually. Oh, and I downloaded a new game on my phone, it’s really addictive. You wouldn’t be interested, would you? Speaker_2: (Scoffs) Computer games? Not for me, thank you very much. I’d rather watch the lottery draw. Though, truth be told, I never win anything. It’s a waste of money really. Still, you never know, do you? Speaker_1: Never say never, Dad. Maybe you’ll have a lucky streak! Now, about that hotspot…

Speaker_1: Honestly, the thought of them actually demolishing the library…it just feels wrong, doesn’t it? It’s been there forever. Speaker_2: It does. And apparently, the council’s justification is…what was it? “Underutilised community space”? I saw Mrs. Henderson down at the shops, and she was absolutely fuming. She uses it every week for the reading group. Speaker_1: Underutilised! It’s always busy! At least, when I’ve popped in. And it’s not just books, is it? They do those computer classes for older people. My aunt went to one last year, said it was brilliant. Where are they supposed to go then? Speaker_2: Exactly. They’ve suggested moving everything into the community centre, but that’s miles away and hardly accessible for those without a car. Plus, it's always booked up with other things. It’s a proper short-sighted decision. Speaker_1: Typical council, though, isn’t it? Always looking at the short-term cost, never the long-term benefit to the community. I saw an article online, a petition's started. I signed it, of course. Speaker_2: Good. I'll have a look. Speaking of online… I spent ages last night looking at fabrics for the armchair. It’s surprisingly difficult to choose! Speaker_1: Oh yes? Trying to match something to the curtains? Speaker_2: A bit, but it’s more… getting a feel for what will actually *work*. Everything looks different on a screen. I thought I wanted something floral, but when I looked at the swatches, it was just too much. Speaker_1: I know what you mean. I ordered paint samples that looked completely different in real life. Ended up going for something totally unexpected. Have you seen those textured weaves? They look quite nice and hardwearing. Speaker_2: I have, but I’m worried they’ll show every bit of fluff and cat hair. And Winston does love to shed. Speaker_1: Good point. He's a fluffy one. Did you read that article in the paper about the old Victorian building they’re restoring down on Elm Street? They're keeping the original facade but doing everything else up. Speaker_2: I did skim it. It's a shame they’re not preserving the whole thing. It's beautiful architecture. It's expensive though, isn’t it, maintaining those old buildings? Speaker_1: That’s what they said. Apparently, it's cheaper to knock them down and build something new. Which is just ridiculous. It’s losing all our history. It’s like they want everything to look the same. Speaker_2: It is. It's all a bit depressing, actually. Although, I did find some very reasonably priced linen blends online. Might be worth a look. They said they’d send samples, and they’re free. Speaker_1: Oh, perfect! You could get Winston to test them for fluff-attracting qualities. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Excellent idea. He's a professional shedder, after all. Maybe we should just leave everything as it is and not bother with the armchair at all. It’s less stressful. Speaker_1: Don't say that! A new armchair will be lovely. And fighting the council over the library is worth it. We just need to keep the pressure on. Speaker_2: You’re right. One battle at a time, I suppose. Now, where’s that biscuit tin…? Speaker_1: On the top shelf, next to the kettle. And I think I saw the paper with the petition details on the kitchen table.

Speaker_1: Right, so are we all agreed? No more eighties power ballads on this trip? Seriously, last time it was non-stop Bon Jovi. Speaker_2: Oh, come *on*! Bon Jovi's classic! And it was only for like, an hour. Speaker_3: An hour that felt like an eternity, honestly. I think my eardrums are still recovering. Can we at least agree on a playlist everyone contributes to? Speaker_4: That sounds sensible. A bit of variety is good. I’m happy to put some stuff on. I’ve been listening to a lot of that new Phoebe Bridgers album, actually. Speaker_1: Phoebe Bridgers? Is that…sad girl music? Speaker_3: (Laughing) A little bit, yeah. But it’s really good. Very atmospheric. I can add some to the playlist. Speaker_2: Ooh, can we have some Dua Lipa? I’ve been properly obsessed with her new single. Speaker_1: Dua Lipa is acceptable. As long as it's not *too* upbeat. My blood pressure thanks you in advance. What about presents? Have you two managed to get anything for Aunt Carol? Speaker_4: I got her one of those… what are they called? Those paint-by-numbers kits? Floral ones. She’s always going on about wanting to get back into painting. Speaker_1: Good thinking. She’ll love that. I got her a ridiculously expensive hand cream. She’s obsessed with hand cream. Speaker_2: Oh, nice! I was stuck. I couldn’t think of anything. She already *has* everything. I ended up getting her a fancy tea towel. Speaker_3: A tea towel is perfectly lovely! Don’t underestimate a good tea towel. What are you doing this weekend, by the way, Mark? Aside from subjecting us to your questionable musical tastes. Speaker_1: Trying to finish building that bloody model railway. It's a disaster. I keep losing tiny little pieces. Honestly, it’s infuriating. I thought it would be relaxing. Speaker_4: You and your hobbies. Always ambitious. I'm attempting to finally tidy the garden shed. It’s been a disaster zone since last summer. Speaker_2: Oh god, sheds. They are magnets for junk. My dad’s shed is full of…well, I don’t even know *what* it's full of. Probably spiders. Speaker_3: Speaking of disaster zones, have you guys been watching that new show, ‘Hoarders: Next Generation’? It's absolutely horrifying. Speaker_1: ‘Hoarders’? No. I can’t cope with that sort of thing. Too stressful. I prefer something a bit lighter. Like…garden makeover shows. Speaker_4: Garden makeover shows are the worst! They always over-design everything. Give someone a tiny patch of grass and suddenly they’ve installed a koi pond and a Japanese zen garden. Speaker_2: True! And all those perfectly manicured lawns…who has time for that? I’d rather be at the salon, honestly. Give me glitter and hairspray any day. Speaker_3: Fair enough! So, playlist order of business? Who’s starting it? I'm happy to build a Spotify one if people send me links. Speaker_1: Good plan. And…maybe just a *small* dose of Bon Jovi, for old times’ sake? Speaker_2: (Grinning) We’ll see. Don't push your luck. Certainly, let me know if you’d like me to continue the conversation or perhaps change the dynamics in any way!

Speaker_1: Right, so you’re seriously thinking about getting a car then? At sixteen? Speaker_2: Yeah, well, a lot of lads at school are starting to learn, and Ben’s already passed. It’d be good to be able to get to football practice without relying on Dad all the time. Speaker_1: It’s a big responsibility, lad. A very big responsibility. Not just the driving, but everything that comes with it. Have you even started to think about the cost? Speaker_2: Sort of. Ben was saying his Dad got him a little Fiat, something cheap. Speaker_1: A Fiat? Good start, I suppose. Though even a little Fiat needs insuring. And that, my love, is where the real pain begins. Speaker_2: How much is insurance? Speaker_1: Oh, don't even ask. It depends on so many things. Your age, your driving experience – which you haven’t got much of, let’s be honest – the car itself, where you live… Malton isn’t the worst, but it's not exactly rural, you see. More chance of accidents. Speaker_2: So, it’s loads then? Speaker_1: Loads is an understatement. Because you're a new driver, and a young one at that, you’re statistically the most likely to crash. Insurance companies *love* that. They practically print money off young drivers. Speaker_2: But Ben said his insurance was only… like, eight hundred quid. Speaker_1: Eight hundred? Bless him. Either his Dad’s paying a hefty premium under his name, or he’s been very lucky. Or, and this is often the case, he’s not telling you the full story. Is that including black box insurance? Speaker_2: What’s a black box? Speaker_1: It’s a telematics device. They fit a little box in the car that monitors everything you do – your speed, your braking, the time of day you drive. If you drive safely, your premium can come down. But if you speed, or drive aggressively… it goes *up*. Speaker_2: That sounds… annoying. Like Big Brother’s watching you. Speaker_1: It is a bit, but it can save you money. It’s something to consider. We’d need to get quotes, of course. Lots and lots of quotes. And compare them. And remember, it’s not just the insurance. It’s the road tax, the MOT, the petrol, maintenance… cars are money pits, honestly. Speaker_2: Right. Okay. So, it’s not as simple as just getting a car, then. Speaker_1: Not at all. It’s a serious financial commitment, and something you need to think carefully about. We’ll do some research, get some quotes, and see what it’s looking like. But don’t get your hopes up too high just yet, eh? It might be a while before you’re cruising around in a Fiat. Speaker_2: Right. Thanks. Speaker_1: You’re welcome. Now, have you finished your homework? Don’t think you can distract me with talk of cars to get out of it! Speaker_2: Nearly. Just the maths. Speaker_1: Ah. Well, seeing as I mark GCSE maths papers for a living, perhaps I can cast an eye over it later. But not until *after* you’ve given it a good try yourself. Speaker_2: Okay, deal. Speaker_1: Good lad. Speaker_2: Perhaps cars will have to wait another year then. Speaker_1: Possibly. Perhaps.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the week… the week was something else. They’re talking about restructuring again, you know? Another “efficiency drive.” It’s just code for making everyone do the work of two people. Speaker_2: Ugh, sounds awful. Like when they made Mr. Henderson teach both Year 9 Maths *and* Science when Mr. Davies left? He was so stressed, kept losing his pen. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Poor Mr. Henderson. It’s terrible though, isn’t it? That pressure. I was reading something about measuring stress levels – apparently, they can tell how stressed you are by looking at the frequency of certain words you use in everyday conversation. Speaker_1: You’re having me on. What, like if I say “deadline” a lot, they know I’m about to have a coronary? Speaker_3: Apparently! And things like "should" and "must." Lots of obligation words. They feed it into a computer and it spits out a stress score. Creepy, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Seriously creepy. Like Big Brother. Are you being recorded at work then? Speaker_1: Not consciously, but who knows what they’re doing with the network traffic. They're always "monitoring performance" or whatever. Speaking of which, did you lot see that Ireland’s finally getting around to… well, I’m sure you know what I mean about allowing young ‘uns to get a present at a certain age? Speaker_3: Oh, the age of consent thing? It’s absolutely ridiculous it’s taken this long. It's a mess, honestly. And everything with the equality vote back then… I remember how tense everything was. Speaker_1: It was a huge deal. It felt like the whole country was holding its breath. (A beat of silence falls over the table) Speaker_2: So… anyone fancy Chinese tonight? I'm starving. Speaker_3: That sounds lovely. Though, honestly, the chicken in their curry has gone downhill. It's all gristle these days. Speaker_1: You’re not wrong. They’re scrimping on everything. It's the same with everything, isn’t it? They'll cut corners anywhere they can. I was listening to a podcast about that – how companies try to manipulate language to make things sound better than they are. Speaker_3: Oh, the power of spin! It’s amazing how they can reframe something awful into a “positive opportunity for growth.” Speaker_1: Exactly. And the importance of how you *say* things. Actually, I was trying to explain the concept of a windpipe to young Saoirse earlier. It’s a tricky one for a four-year-old. Speaker_2: A windpipe? Eww. Sounds… medical. Speaker_1: It is! And the pronunciation. You try explaining that to someone with a Bristol accent, and it gets… interesting. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, don’t start on accents! You’ll have everyone at each other. Speaker_1: I’m just saying. It's fascinating how people use words, and how their faces do… well, they do things. Speaker_2: Like when Mr. Peterson pretends to be angry? His face goes all red, but you know he's secretly enjoying it. It's… weird. Speaker_1: That's acting. Awful acting, mind you. You know what *wasn’t* awful? *Suicide Squad*. The new one. Margot Robbie was brilliant, even though it was a bit… much. Speaker_3: Oh, I haven’t seen that. Is it worth it? Speaker_1: (Pauses, thinking) It depends. If you like loud explosions and ridiculously attractive people. If I were to google the frequency of the word “explosions” in reviews, I reckon it'd be quite high. Speaker_2: (Grinning) You’re terrible. Honestly, you and your awful jokes. But yeah, Chinese sounds really good right now. Can we get extra

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, you wouldn't *believe* the traffic getting out of town. It was backed up all the way to Westhoughton. Speaker_2: Oh, aye? Probably someone having a nosey at the birds again down at the reservoirs. You know folk round here, they get obsessed. Him and his binoculars. More interested in watching the buzzards than the lorries, I reckon. Speaker_3: Buzzards are cool. They just hang in the air. Did you see that plane earlier? It was massive! Speaker_4: That’ll have been coming from Manchester. Probably headed to somewhere in Europe. Shame about Brexit, really. Made things a bit more complicated for travel, didn’t it? Though, I suppose we always managed before the EU, didn’t we? Speaker_1: It's just a faff, isn’t it? All the extra forms. And Dad keeps going on about needing a vignette for Italy again. Speaker_2: He loves driving, your dad. Always has. Says it’s the only way to see the real countryside. That’s why he fancies those hilltop villages in Tuscany. Me, I'm happy on a beach with a good book. Speaker_3: Can we go to Italy this summer? Can we? Please? Speaker_4: We’ll see, son. We’ll see. Depends on a lot of things. Like whether your sister finishes her law conversion course alright. Speaking of which, how’s that going, love? Stressful, I imagine? Speaker_1: It’s… a lot. Honestly, it’s just endless reading and trying to remember case law. It's a different way of thinking than I'm used to. Plus, converting to Scots law is a nightmare. Everything’s slightly different. Speaker_2: You’ll be fine, pet. You always were a bright spark. You just need to remember everything's in kilograms over there, not stones and pounds. And multiply everything by 1.6 to get the kilometers from miles. Honestly, it’s a nightmare trying to follow all that! Speaker_3: Kilograms? That's loads. Why can't everything be in grams? Speaker_4: Because grams are tiny, son! You wouldn't measure a car in grams, would you? It’s all about scale. Which reminds me… remember that time we were arguing about the weight of those bags at the airport? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, don’t even start, Arthur! Honestly, you were convinced you could smuggle a whole wardrobe through security. Thought you were Bear Grylls or something! Speaker_1: Dad's always got a plan. It usually involves bending the rules slightly. Speaker_4: I just like to be prepared! Speaking of prepared, anyone fancy stopping for a coffee? I noticed a nice little café just off the motorway a couple of miles back. Reminded me a bit of Terry Wogan’s little haunts. Always a good cuppa. Speaker_3: Yeah! Coffee and biscuits! Can we listen to music then? Speaker_2: We'll see. Don't start moaning if I put on something you don’t like. Although honestly, I’m more worried about your dad starting on politics again. Last time he started talking about the EU referendum, it went on for the entire journey to Blackpool. Speaker_1: Oh god, please no. Not the referendum again. Speaker_4: Now, now, it’s a perfectly valid topic for discussion. Good to be informed, you know. Speaker_2: That’s what he said last time, and we ended up arguing about Shakespeare and religion. Honestly, it was exhausting. Speaker_3: Can we talk about cars instead? I saw a really shiny red one today. Speaker_4: Now there's a sensible topic. What make was it? Speaker_1: Please let him talk about cars. Anything is better than politics. Speaker_2: It's always cars, isn't it? Or parking. He gets so worked up about finding a good parking spot.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this lentil shepherd’s pie is hitting the spot. I was craving something proper comforting. Speaker_2: It *is* good. Though, I still think you could’ve used a bit more smoked paprika. Just to give it a little…oomph. Speaker_3: She's right, a little paprika would've been good. But it's great either way. It’s just…weird still thinking about where meat *comes* from. Even when it’s, like, lentils pretending to be mince. Speaker_1: Exactly! That’s why I’m so fascinated by the whole ‘cultured meat’ thing. Like, growing actual meat in a lab. No animal suffering, less environmental impact…it sounds perfect. Speaker_2: It does sound a bit…dystopian though, doesn’t it? “Shmeat” as they call it. Like something out of a sci-fi film. Speaker_3: I don't know, I’m kinda with El on this. If it means animals don’t have to go through…well, everything. I’m in. Abattoirs are horrific. I saw a documentary once…I had to turn it off. Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t even. I avoid those documentaries like the plague. It’s just too upsetting. And people are like, “But hunting is natural!” Natural doesn’t equal ethical. It’s just a different kind of suffering. Speaker_1: Right, so I was explaining to Mrs. Higgins today about different metals, because we were talking about armour in history. Speaker_3: Or netherite! Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Perhaps. Perhaps we will. Speaker_2: Can we take snacks? Speaker_1: Always. Always take snacks. Speaker_3: And my diamond pickaxe! Speaker_1: Right, okay, my turn. Ugh, this is awful. “Philosophical.” No describing, no saying ‘thinking’… oh brilliant. Speaker_2: Go on, give it a go. You’ve got a minute! This is impossible!

Speaker_1: Right, okay, so I’m going to lay down… Seven of hearts. And… discard a four of clubs. Someone’s got to take that four, it’s practically begging to be taken. Speaker_2: Absolutely scandalous! Rhys was only eight! I think that’s when Mum implemented the “Bryn-proof Monopoly rules”. No bribery, no trading until you're ten. Speaker_3: Speaking of rules… are we still adhering to the ‘no complaining about your hand’ rule? Because honestly, this is bordering on cruel and unusual punishment. Lay down an eight of hearts...discarding a… oh, this could be interesting. A jack of diamonds. Let the diamond chaos continue! Anyone brave enough? Speaker_2: (Sighs dramatically) Here we go again. I'll risk it, throw down a ten of diamonds. Discard... a nine of hearts. Bring on the pain! Speaker_3: Oh, dear. I’m sensing a theme here… Speaker_4: (Eyes twinkling) Oh, this is going to be *good*. speaker_1: Ooh, it looks like we're gonna be here a while! Anyone fancy a refill on their tea? Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m still recovering from finishing those applications. UCAS is a *nightmare*. It's just… endless personal statements. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I remember when I applied. I've been locked away in a lab with sophisticated equipment, so I'm immune to all the peasant diseases. (He winks) Speaker_2: Oh, be quiet! You’re just lucky you’re not dealing with the public. Honestly, the things people say… Last week someone tried to return a used face mask. A *used* face mask! Speaker_1: No way! Speaker_3: People are wild. Honestly. Trying to make bath bombs, but they just keep crumbling. Speaker_4: I can offer to cover the ingredients, if you like. My salary is slightly more generous these days. Speaker_5: Oh, really? That would be amazing, thank you! Speaker_2: That’s really kind of you, Sam. I was thinking of getting my mum a new scarf. She’s always cold. And Dad… I have no idea. He's impossible to buy for. No stress about applications or work or dying of a cold. Just Christmas and friends. Speaker_3: Cheers to that! Speaker_4: Cheers! Speaker_2: Right. More mince pies, anyone?

Speaker_1: Honestly, this programme is dreadful. Absolute rubbish. I don’t know why we bother sometimes. Speaker_2: It’s alright, Nan. A bit slow, yeah, but it’s easy watching. Good for after dinner. No, it's still leaning against the shed. Honestly, I'm hopeless with anything mechanical. I keep meaning to ask Mr. Henderson next door, but I always forget. He was a menace on two wheels. Speaker_3: I remember. Near broke his neck once trying to jump that ramp at the recreation ground. Speaker_1: Honestly! It gave me palpitations just watching him. Rain or shine. “Good for the constitution,” she used to say. Speaker_1: It is! And it's free. Although, I do miss driving to the coast sometimes. That sea air… Speaker_2: We could all go to Brighton next weekend? Train’s easy, and we don’t have to worry about parking. Speaker_3: That sounds nice. Though it’ll be rammed, won’t it? Full of stag dos and screaming kids. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t be such a grump, dear. A bit of atmosphere never hurt anyone. And I do fancy some fish and chips by the sea. We could walk along the promenade…provided it’s not too windy. I hate it when the wind whips the sand into your face. Speaker_2: We can check the weather forecast. It's a plan then? Brighton next weekend? Speaker_3: If you’re both sure. I’m happy enough. As long as I can bring a book. And maybe a flask of tea. Speaker_1: Of course, dear. Whatever you like. Now, can someone turn this television off? I can’t take another minute of this nonsense.

Speaker_1: Oh, this is a lovely space, isn’t it? I don’t think I’ve been in the Law Faculty since… well, since graduating, actually. Feels very different seeing it like this, all set up for alumni. Speaker_2: It is nice. I work here now, so I’m used to it, but even I think it looks a bit special today. Are you from around Cambridge originally? I’m working as a Language Research Coordinator now. Fascinating stuff, though quite different from tort law! And you? Speaker_2: Lincoln, originally. I stayed on after graduating, working as a Research Administrator here. It’s… steady. Keeps me busy. What kind of language research? Speaker_1: Mostly sociolinguistics, looking at language variation and change. At the moment, I’m focused on dialectal differences across the UK, but a previous project involved looking at language contact in Spain. Have you been? Speaker_3: (Joining the conversation) Spain, you say? Wonderful country. Spent a summer cycling through the Basque country years ago. Absolutely stunning. Though the language… now *that’s* a challenge. Nothing like anything I’ve ever encountered. Speaker_2: Oh, really? I’ve always wanted to go to the Basque country. I’ve done a bit of Spanish, but nothing beyond the basics. Speaker_3: Basque is completely isolated, you see. No relation to any other European language. It's a linguistic puzzle. Reminds me a bit of trying to understand the intricacies of Mandarin, actually. Spent a few weeks in China with the university a while back. Utterly bewildering. Speaker_1: That’s incredible. I’ve done a little bit of Mandarin, just for fun, but I can barely string a sentence together. It’s so tonal. It feels a world away from Indo-European languages. Speaker_2: I tried learning Japanese once, got as far as the Hiragana and Katakana scripts, then just… gave up. Too much! I think I prefer sticking with languages a bit closer to home. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Sensible girl. Though you miss out on some truly fascinating linguistic complexities. Tell me, what brought you both back to Cambridge today? Just reminiscing? Speaker_1: A bit of both. It’s good to see what everyone’s been up to. Plus, there was a talk scheduled about funding opportunities for research. Always useful. Speaker_2: I was hoping to catch up with a few of my old professors. And maybe see if anyone’s hiring in the Faculty’s library. Always good to keep an eye out. Speaker_3: Ah, networking. Very important. Used to go down to London a lot for conferences. Found the rugby clubs there quite… spirited. Enjoyed a good match. Though I'm more of a Shropshire lad at heart, you know. Rest of the family still down Oswestry way. Beautiful scenery; you should visit Wales sometime, it's close enough. Speaker_1: Wales sounds lovely. I’ve been meaning to visit for ages. Although, I'm not a huge sports fan, to be honest. I follow a bit of football, but I don't really understand the offside rule. Speaker_2: I agree. I can appreciate the athleticism, but I'm not really one for the strategic side of things. Give me a good book any day. Though I did watch the Women’s World Cup this summer, that was pretty inspiring.

Speaker_1: Honestly, two years! It feels like ages since we all last properly sat down like this. How’s work, Sarah? Still wrestling with spreadsheets at the dentist? Speaker_2: You know it. Though Mr. Henderson decided he wanted a new filing system last week. Apparently, alphabetical wasn't 'dynamic' enough. Dynamic filing! Honestly, the things people come up with. It took me three days to re-sort everything. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, Mr. Henderson. He sounds…special. I had a candidate today who genuinely asked if our office had a nap room. A nap room! For a recruitment agency. Speaker_1: No way! What did you say? Speaker_3: I tried to keep a straight face and explained the concept of commission. She wasn’t impressed. It’s exhausting, honestly. People's expectations are just… wild. Did anyone see Aunt Carol posted another one of those vaguely political things on Facebook? Speaker_2: Oh, don't even. I had to mute her again. Last week it was something about the price of tomatoes. This week it’s… I honestly didn’t even read it. Too much effort. Remember when everyone was doing the ice bucket challenge? That was a simpler time. Speaker_1: Ha! Simpler indeed. I think I still have ice shivers thinking about it. I’m surprised Mum didn’t make us all do it for charity. She was always keen on a good cause. Speaker_3: She’s got a good heart, Mum does. Though that bake sale she organised for the animal shelter… half the cakes were burnt. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Don't remind me. Remember little Tommy Jenkins trying to sneak a second slice of the charcoal cake? Poor kid. Speaking of kids, how’s little Leo doing, Sophie? He must be getting so big. Speaker_3: He’s a whirlwind. Just turned four. He’s started asking about where babies come from, which is…fun. We’re trying to keep it age-appropriate, but he’s a bright spark. It's a whole different level of exhaustion than recruitment. Speaker_1: Oh, the questions! It’ll be worth it, though. Hey, has anyone heard anything from Uncle David lately? It's been ages since he called. Speaker_2: He mentioned something about a cruise with Brenda. Somewhere in the Mediterranean, I think. He keeps promising to teach me Italian, but he always gets distracted by… well, Brenda. Honestly, they're like teenagers. Speaker_3: They've always been a bit of a whirlwind. Remember when he proposed to Brenda for the *third* time on that rollercoaster? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh my god, yes! She nearly had a heart attack! Poor Brenda. It’s just… they’re them. Have either of you been filling in those online forms for the council tax? It’s a nightmare. Every single question feels like a trap. Speaker_2: Don’t even get me started. They asked me for my grandmother’s maiden name! What on Earth does that have to do with council tax? It's ludicrous. Speaker_3: It's a data-gathering exercise, plain and simple. They want to know everything about you. Reminds me of some of the background checks I have to do for work. Though at least mine are legally justifiable. Speaker_1: Mum said something about Auntie Maureen wanting to talk to me about my… career path. Again. I swear, she thinks lecturing abroad is a waste of a good degree. Speaker_2: Oh, Maureen. Bless her. She still thinks you should have gone to university to study law. She's still stuck in the '80s. Speaker_3: Honestly, it's exhausting trying to explain that being happy is more important than earning potential. Although, let's be real, the earning potential *is* a bit terrifying sometimes.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this coffee machine is driving me mad. It makes a perfectly good cup, when it *deigns* to make one, but half the time it just gurgles and spits and then says ‘descale’. Descale! It’s all so… pragmatic now. No fire. No ideals. It's depressing. I remember when people actually believed in changing the world. Speaker_2: It’s hard to hold onto those ideals, isn’t it? Especially when you're facing things like… removal costs. I finally got a quote back for storing some of the furniture. It’s eye-watering. Speaker_3: Ouch. Seriously? What are they charging? We paid half that when we moved things to storage after your father… well, you know. Speaker_3: Everything is up. Everything. It’s scandalous. And the council tax here… I’m still reeling. Speaker_3: Don’t even joke about that. We've come too far. Speaker_2: I'll take a look at the filter while you do that. Maybe a bit of elbow grease will sort it. Speaker_1: You’re a lifesaver, dear. Honestly, I don't know what I'd do without you two. Speaker_3: We feel the same. Now, about this water… I told you, it’s the water.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the thought of Christmas already fills me with dread. Not the actual day, but *getting* to the actual day. It's the sheer logistical nightmare. I'm thinking of doing a TEFL course specialising in business English. That might open up some better-paid opportunities. I saw one advertised online the other day, fully remote. Speaker_2: Well, that sounds sensible. And potentially lucrative. That’s a good idea. But you can’t live your life glued to a screen, can you? You need… social interaction. Are you still seeing that nice Mark? Speaker_1: (Sighs) We're “seeing each other.” It’s very casual. He’s a musician, so his schedule is… erratic. He's playing a gig in Brighton Boxing Day, wants me to come. But I said I'd tentatively offer to help Sarah with her Christmas decorations. Speaker_2: Sarah? Oh, Sarah from your book club? Is she still with that dreadful man? I always thought he was a bit shifty. Speaker_1: They broke up, actually. It was messy. Hence the decoration help. She's feeling a bit lost, apparently. Actually, she mentioned wanting to come to Totnes for New Year. She’s always admired the area. Speaker_2: Oh, how lovely! We could definitely have her. She seems like a nice girl. We could go to the New Year’s Eve ceilidh at the Guildhall. Remember that last year? Old Mr. Henderson nearly took out Mrs. Gable with a particularly enthusiastic swing! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, I remember! It was brilliant. Right, okay. So, tentative plans: Christmas possibly in Devon, but depending on Dad's turkey ambitions, Brighton Boxing Day maybe, and Sarah potentially for New Year. It’s all wonderfully vague. And we haven’t even started on what I'm doing for Christmas this year… Auntie Mair’s threatening to arrive with her prize-winning goose again! Speaker_1: (Groans) Oh, no. Not the goose.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I thought Nan was gonna kill him last night. The snoring! Speaker_2: Oh, *god*. Was he at it again? Proper saw-milling, was he? Speaker_3: It wasn’t just snoring, it was… a symphony of snorts and wheezes. I genuinely thought something was wrong. Speaker_4: (Laughing) A symphony! That’s brilliant. Though I can imagine why Nan was fuming. She needs her sleep. Speaker_5: He said he had a cold, but I reckon it’s just his default setting. He's always been a snorer. Remember when we went camping and he kept everyone awake? Speaker_1: Don’t even *mention* that camping trip. I was practically catnapping standing up all weekend. It was awful. Anyway, did you lot get yourselves sorted with bread for the week? Waterfields was rammed this morning. Speaker_2: Managed to get a loaf of their white farmhouse, thankfully. Nearly didn't though. Right, they’ve got a corner. This could be interesting. Speaker_2: Depends if they can actually deliver a decent ball. Their crossing’s been… optimistic, to say the least.
