You mean *Escape to Victory*? Speaker_1: That's the one! Honestly, it’s a bit cheesy but still brilliant. Especially the bit with the helicopter… Speaker_2: Ah, a classic. Though their football skills looked a *lot* better than what we're seeing on screen right now. Speaker_1: A low bar, admittedly. Oh! Good header! But the keeper saved it. Of course he did. Speaker_2: He had no chance, actually. Right on the line. Speaker_1: Still, should’ve been more accurate. Speaking of accuracy, have you thought about what we’re doing for Easter? My mum’s already asking. Speaker_2: Easter? Is it already that time? Feels like Christmas was yesterday. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. She wants to know if we’re coming home. And if we bring chocolate. Specifically, Cadbury’s Creme Eggs. It’s a non-negotiable requirement. Speaker_2: Creme Eggs, huh? A worthy demand. I’m happy to acquire a substantial quantity for the mission. Plus, you know your mum’s roast dinner is legendary. Speaker_1: It is. It really is. Though she does make me help peel the potatoes. Traitorous potatoes. Speaker_2: A small price to pay for culinary brilliance. Although, I'm not sure my digestive system can handle a *full* roast dinner these days. PhD life has been kind to my waistline… said no one ever. Speaker_1: You’ve been living off instant noodles and despair, haven't you? Speaker_2: (Smiling) A slight exaggeration. But mostly true. Look! A shot! Speaker_1: Oh… wide. By a mile. I'm starting to think I should just stick to watching karate. At least that’s short and sweet. Speaker_2: Don't give up on football just yet. There's still plenty of time for a dramatic turn around. And think of the snacks… Speaker_1: Oh, snacks are always worth it. Speaker_2:Absolutely. Speaker_1: Can I get you another drink? Speaker_2:Please! Speaker_1: Right! Coming right up

Speaker_1: Ah, look at this one! Little Leo, absolutely covered in chocolate. Must have been… what, four years old? At that funfair in Tralee. Speaker_2: (Peering at the photo) Whoa! He *is* a mess. Did he fall into a chocolate fountain or something? Speaker_3: No, he won a game. One of those where you try to knock down the milk bottles with a ball. And the prize was a huge chocolate bar. He just… demolished it. Right there and then. Face, hands, clothes – everything. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Boys will be boys! Reminds me of your Uncle Hamish. At the Glasgow fair, he managed to get stuck on one of those rotating teacups. Couldn’t stop laughing! Eventually, a strong man had to lift him out. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, Hamish. Always a character. You know, looking at these pictures… it feels like yesterday he was a tiny babbling thing. And now he’s almost taller than me. Speaker_2: He’s growing so fast. He’s already talking about wanting to run the London Marathon one day. Says he wants to raise money for… penguins? Speaker_3: Penguins! Bless him. He’s got a good heart. Though I do worry about him already setting such ambitious goals. He’s only twelve. Speaker_4: Let him dream, dear. It's good for him. Being ambitious isn’t a bad thing. Though I must say, all this talk of marathons… reminds me of that trip we took to Iceland. Speaker_1: Iceland? Oh, the glaciers! And the Blue Lagoon. That was a magical trip. And freezing! Remember how we had to wrap up in about five layers just to walk to the car? Speaker_3: And the Northern Lights! That was truly breathtaking. Though Leo was more interested in finding a volcano. He was obsessed with volcanoes at that age. Speaker_2: I think he still is, actually. He’s building a model one for his science project. It's…messy. Lots of paper mache and red paint. Speaker_1: Sounds about right. He always did like getting his hands dirty. Remember that time he tried to recreate the eruption of Vesuvius in the kitchen? Speaker_3: (Groans) Don’t remind me! The bicarbonate of soda and vinegar everywhere…It took days to clean up. Speaker_4: It’s good to have memories like this. Keeps us grounded. Speaking of which, is anyone up for going to the cinema later? They're showing that new historical drama. Speaker_2: Ooh, yeah! That sounds good. Can I choose the snacks? Speaker_1: As long as it doesn't involve a chocolate fountain, you can choose anything you like. Speaker_3: And after the cinema, we should think about getting a cake sorted for your birthday next week, Mum. You turning seventy-nine, can you believe it? Speaker_4: (Laughing) Seventy-nine and still going strong! Honestly, where does the time go? It feels like only yesterday I was teaching little ones their ABCs…and now I'm watching my grandson nearly outgrow his father! Speaker_1: It really does. It really does. Speaker_2: Can we look at the pictures from Auntie Carol's wedding again? I love that one of us all trying to do the conga! Speaker_3: Oh dear. That was a sight, wasn't it? Speaker_4: A sight indeed! Now, come on, let's get this cake planned before Leo tries to build another volcano.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this shepherd’s pie is amazing, Mum. You’ve really outdone yourself. It tastes just like…well, like being about ten again. Speaker_2: It *is* lovely, isn’t it? I always remember your mum making this when we came round after school. It was a treat. Though, I’m pretty sure she used to sneak a load of extra veg in, hoping we wouldn’t notice. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Oh, I did. Gotta get those five-a-day in somehow, even if they *are* disguised in mashed potato. Your father refused to eat anything green, you know. Said it was ‘rabbit food’. Speaker_1: Dad and his rabbit food. Honestly. He'd happily polish off a sausage roll, but a pea was the enemy. Speaking of things he wouldn’t eat…do you remember that time he tried black pudding in Whitby? Speaker_2: Oh, goodness! How could I forget? He went absolutely puce. Said it tasted like rusty nails. He was moaning for a good hour. Speaker_3: He *did* have a sensitive stomach, your father. Though he’d never admit it. Always thought showing any weakness was a terrible thing. Remember when he tried to fix the garden shed roof himself? Speaker_1: And ended up needing a trip to A&E? Yes, vividly. He was so determined, though. “I can do it myself!” he’d say. Stubborn as a mule, that man. Speaker_2: He was, wasn’t he? But underneath it all, a big softie. Oh, this reminds me - did I tell you I’ve started learning to crochet? Apparently, it’s very therapeutic. Speaker_1: Crochet? That’s…unexpected! You always struck me as more of a speed-reading, multi-tasking kind of person. Speaker_2: Well, I’m trying to slow down a little! My friend, Carol, does it, and she convinced me. I’ve made a rather wonky scarf so far. It looks…rustic. Speaker_3: I used to knit. Years ago. Used to make cardigans for you girls. Though I haven't picked up the needles in ages. My eyesight isn't what it used to be. I do read, though. I’ve got one of those Kindle things. It's marvellous. Speaker_1: They are brilliant, aren’t they? I’ve got a few eBooks, but I still prefer the feel of a real book. The smell, you know? Speaker_2: Oh, absolutely. There’s nothing like curling up with a good book. Though, the convenience of an eBook is hard to beat, especially when travelling. Speaker_3: You know, the world is a funny place. It really is. I was at the doctor’s the other day, and the nurse was originally from…where was it now?…oh, Australia! And she knew someone who’d gone to school with a distant cousin of mine. Honestly, it’s a small world. Speaker_1: Isn't it? It really is. You hear those stories all the time. It makes you wonder how many connections we all have without even realizing it. Speaker_2: It's amazing, isn’t it? Makes you think about those old toys we used to have… I still have my Sindy doll, tucked away in the attic. Do you remember those? Speaker_1: Oh my goodness, yes! And the little houses! I spent hours rearranging the furniture in my Sindy house. It was a whole world in miniature. Speaker_3: And marbles! Remember marbles? We used to spend hours playing marbles in the playground. Aggies and steelies, all sorts. A proper game of skill, that was. Not like this…this computer game nonsense they have these days.

Speaker_1: Lovely bit of bread this, isn’t it? Proper crusty. Speaker_2: It is nice. From that little bakery down the road, wasn’t it? The one near the post office? Speaker_1: That’s the one. Old Mrs. Higgins still makes a good loaf, despite her age. More than I can say for some youngsters, eh? All fancy sourdough and whatnot. Give me a white bloomer any day. Speaker_2: Well, you like what you’re used to, don’t you? I do like a bit of granary myself. Bit more… substantial. Speaker_1: Substantial? It’s just full of bits! Seeds and husks and who knows what else. Makes yer teeth feel like they’re scrubbing the floor. Speaker_2: Oh, don’t be like that. It’s good for you. Fibre and all that. Doctor says… well, *used* to say, I should eat more fibre. Speaker_1: Doctors always say that. They’d have us living on bran flakes and sprouts. Not much enjoyment in that, is there? Speaker_2: No, I suppose not. Though a little sprout now and then doesn’t hurt. Want another cup of tea? I just made a fresh pot. Speaker_1: Don’t mind if I do. Lovely. Though it’s gone a bit lukewarm, hasn’t it? Always happens. Should’ve put a cosy on it, I suppose. Speaker_2: I did! It's right there… oh, you're right. It's slipped off. Silly me. Old age, creeping in, you know? Speaker_1: Don’t talk like that. You’re not *old*. Just… experienced. And slightly forgetful. Like me. Speaker_2: (chuckles) That’s kind of you to say. Though I do forget things more than I used to. Where I put my glasses, what I went into the kitchen for… Speaker_1: I went upstairs earlier to get my slippers, and completely forgot why I was going upstairs. Stood there for a good minute, just… blank. Speaker_2: Happens to the best of us. It’s just… life, I suppose. Slowing down a bit. Speaker_1: Slowing down? I feel like I’m grinding to a halt sometimes! Still, better than the alternative, eh? Speaker_2: Definitely. So, did you hear from young David today? How was his driving lesson? Speaker_1: He rang. Said it went alright, but the instructor kept shouting. Apparently, he nearly stalled in the middle of a roundabout. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Roundabouts are tricky. So many things to think about. Speaker_1: He says he’s getting the hang of it though. Wants to pass his test before his eighteenth birthday. Expensive business, learning to drive. Speaker_2: It is. Still, it gives him his freedom, doesn’t it? And then you won’t have to take him everywhere. Speaker_1: That’s the idea. Though I rather enjoy the trips out with him, to be honest. Good company. Speaker_2: Mmm. They grow up so fast though, don't they? Seems like only yesterday he was a little boy, building Lego towers in the living room… Speaker_1: It does. Time flies when you're… well, when you’re getting old, I suppose. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Don't start that again! Another sandwich then? Speaker_1: If you insist. Lovely bit of bread, this…

Speaker_1: Honestly, the kids were *wild* today. Year twos are just… a different breed, aren’t they? One of them tried to convince me that a badger lives in the staff room. A badger, Chloe! Speaker_2: Oh my god, seriously? That’s amazing. Mine were arguing over who gets to be the unicorn in their role play. It escalated. Full-on glitter and tears. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Sounds about right. Kids and glitter - a dangerous combination. Speaking of dangerous, you will *not* believe the day I’ve had. My car decided it didn’t want to be a car anymore. Just… died on the A2. Speaker_1: No way! You just got that car, didn't you? Speaker_3: I did! Six months. Apparently, it's something to do with the fuel pump. The AA guy was lovely, but it’s just… typical, isn’t it? Right when I was actually, you know, trying to be a functioning adult. Speaker_2: Oh, that's awful, Liv. So frustrating. Is it going to be expensive to fix? Speaker_3: Potentially. He said it could be a couple of hundred, but honestly, who knows? Everything is expensive these days. It’s cheaper to fly to Spain than it is to get a car fixed here. Speaker_1: You’re not wrong. Have you booked that holiday yet, by the way? You were talking about going to Portugal? Speaker_3: I have! Finally. We're going to the Algarve in September. Just a week, but it’ll be nice to get some sun. I desperately need it after this week. What about you two? Any holiday plans? Speaker_2: Not yet. We’re thinking maybe Cornwall? Somewhere fairly low-key. Just a bit of sea air and pasties. Speaker_1: Ooh, Cornwall is lovely! We went last year. You have to try the Cornish ice cream. It’s a religious experience. Speaker_3: I’ve heard! Okay, officially adding that to the itinerary. Speaking of itineraries, have you guys got any ideas for Sarah’s birthday present yet? It's next month. Speaker_1: I’ve been racking my brain! She's so hard to buy for. She always says she doesn't want anything. Speaker_2: She said she was thinking of doing a pottery class, maybe we could get her a voucher for that? Speaker_3: Ooh, good shout! She’d love that. She's always going on about wanting to be more creative. Speaker_1: Yeah, that's a brilliant idea. I'm in. What about Ben? Heard anything more from him? Speaker_2: They broke up, didn’t they? Properly finished? Speaker_3: Yeah, apparently. She seemed pretty upset about it when I saw her last week. Said he wanted “space to find himself” – the classic line. Speaker_1: Honestly, men. They just *say* that when they meet someone else, don’t they? Speaker_2: Probably. Although, he always seemed a bit… lost, even before he met Sarah. Speaker_3: True. He did have that obsession with collecting vintage teacups, which was… a choice. Anyway, let's not dwell on Ben. He's a drama llama. Oh! And guess what? My cat, Winston, tried to eat my houseplant *again*. Speaker_1: (Laughing) That cat is a menace! He's got a death wish for greenery. Speaker_2: He’s just trying to add some flavour to your interior design. It’s an artistic statement. Speaker_3: Right? A very expensive artistic statement, considering how much those plants cost. Honestly, sometimes I think he just does it to wind me up. He looks me straight in the eye while he’s doing it. It’s pure evil.

Speaker_1: Right, so Old Man Hemmings’ daughter’s finally moved out, eh? About time, she was drivin’ everyone mad with the music. Bass thumpin’ ‘til all hours. Speaker_2: Aye, good riddance to her, honestly. Though you’d think he’d be delighted, finally havin’ the house to himself. He just seems… worse, somehow. More grumpy. Speaker_3: Maybe he’s missin’ the noise? Sounds daft, doesn’t it? But some folk get used to a certain level of chaos. Speaker_4: Is he the one who always complains about footballs in his garden? Speaker_1: That’s him. Proper stickler. Says it’ll damage his prize-winning roses. Though, let’s be honest, they look a bit sad, those roses. Speaker_2: You know, remember Mrs. O’Malley? She was sayin’ her grandson’s joined the army. Poor lad, goin’ off to… well, you know. It’s horrifying, what’s happenin’ over there with ISIS and everything. Speaker_3: It’s terrifying. I saw something on Instagram, a news report… you can’t escape it, even online. Makes you feel helpless. Speaker_1: It does. And it’s not just them, is it? The world feels… brittle, lately. Like anything could snap. I was talkin’ to Dieter – my brother, you know, in Germany – and he’s sayin’ they’re worried about things escalating there too. It’s a strange time. Speaker_4: Can we talk about Harry Potter instead? I finished the fourth book last night! It was brilliant! Speaker_2: Oh, lovely! Which bit was your favourite? Speaker_4: When Hermione uses the time-turner! It’s so cool she can go back and do loads of lessons. I wish we had those at school! Speaker_3: I was obsessed with that book when I first read it. Still am, a bit, if I'm honest. I’ve started re-reading the series. It’s just… comforting, you know? A bit of escapism. Speaker_1: Aye, escapism’s good. Actually, speaking of escapism, I’m startin’ to think I need a new project. This house… it’s lovely, don’t get me wrong. But it needs *so* much work. The damp’s comin’ back in the cellar. Speaker_2: Oh, not again! Thought you’d finally got that sorted. That damp’s a nightmare. Always smells like old pennies down there. Speaker_1: It's a constant battle. And with the price of everything goin’ up, it’s getting harder and harder to afford the repairs. I been lookin’ at a couple of places over towards Aigburth, near the park. Speaker_3: Aigburth's nice. More space, isn't it? And the houses are a bit more modern. Speaker_2: Reliable. Aigburth. Though, you'd need to get the buses now wouldn't you? It’s a fair walk from here. How’s your mum doin’, by the way? I haven’t seen her in ages. Speaker_1: She’s… okay. A bit achy, you know. Her arthritis is playin’ up again. She’s not keen on goin’ out much these days, says it’s too cold. And she’s got that cough she can’t seem to shake off. I keep tellin’ her to see the doctor, but she’s stubborn as an old mule. Speaker_4: Is she a fan of Harry Potter? Maybe I could lend her my books! Speaker_1: (chuckles) She’d probably say it’s ‘rubbish’, but she secretly enjoys things like that. She still reads the paper front to back every day. A bit of a news hound, she is. And she loves a good gossip, like the

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork has increased tenfold with this new free school meals system. It's not just ticking a box anymore, is it? We have to know *everything* – every allergy, every dietary requirement, gluten-free, dairy-free… It’s a minefield. Speaker_2: Oh, you’re telling me! Little Timmy can’t have anything green, apparently. Anything. Green. A perfectly good pea is off limits. Honestly, you’d think we were dealing with royalty, not seven-year-olds. Speaker_3: It's the parents, isn’t it? Overprotective, some of them. Though, I suppose it’s better than the old days, when it was just a soggy biscuit and a glass of milk. Remember those? Speaker_1: Just about. My mother used to talk about wartime food, of course. Nothing wasted, everything rationed. She used to make these… well, approximations of sausages. Mostly breadcrumbs and whatever scraps of meat she could get hold of. Speaker_2: Goodness me. My mother-in-law, now *she* had a story. Escaped Siberia as a child, unbelievable journey all the way to Africa. Came here after the war, of course. Always said the food was the biggest shock – so much choice! She’d lived on practically nothing for years. Speaker_3: Incredible. My grandmother practically lived on potatoes and carrots. She’d boast about making a meal out of nothing. I remember her making a sort of ‘mock apple pie’ with biscuits and spices… tasted nothing like apple but we all pretended it did! Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh, that’s clever! Speaking of food, have you been to the Farm Shop lately? They’ve got some lovely gluten-free bread now. Sarah – you know, with the allergies? - she’d be thrilled. Speaker_2: I popped in yesterday. It's getting awfully expensive, though. The Village Shop is cheaper for basics, but the Farm Shop has such lovely produce. Though, honestly, I still prefer a proper butcher for my sausages. You just can’t beat a good pork sausage. Speaker_3: You're right about the sausages. Though I’m trying to cut down on red meat… it’s all this talk of Iron Man, really. My daughter's training for it, you know. Speaker_1: Oh, wow! That’s serious dedication. She's always been sporty, hasn't she? Speaker_3: Always. Keeps me on my toes, just watching her. She's been cycling all over the place. Actually, the Tour of Britain is coming through our village next week. It’s going to be chaos! Speaker_2: Isn’t that wonderful? Such a spectacle. Do you think we should try and get a good spot? It'll be packed, I imagine. Speaker_1: Probably. I’m more excited about Nepal, though. Are you still planning on going next year? Speaker_2: Definitely. I’ve been doing some research, trying to get my head around the logistics. It’s a long way. And I'm worried about the altitude. Speaker_3: I went to Peru a few years ago, and the altitude was a killer. Took me days to adjust. Loads of coca tea, apparently. Helped a bit. Speaker_1: Oh, good tip! I’ll have to remember that. I’m also dreading the flights. I used to be a perfectly calm flyer, but now… I just get anxious thinking about it. Speaker_2: It’s the lack of control, isn't it? I always try to distract myself with a good book. Or a very large coffee. Speaker_3: My husband, bless him, is in charge of snacks for the trip. He’s a whiz in the kitchen, you know. Makes a fabulous lasagna. And he insists on doing all the packing. Says I’m hopeless at it. Speaker_1: Men! Always wanting to fix things. Still, a good lasagna sounds excellent. You’ll need it after

Speaker_1: Right, honestly, this week at work’s been a proper shambles. You wouldn't *believe* the drama. Speaker_2: Oh god, lay it on me. I need a bit of a vent after today. Production’s been a nightmare – everything’s running behind, suppliers are late… the usual. Speaker_3: Sounds stressful. Mine’s been…well, mine’s been beige. Just admin, admin, admin. Spreadsheet central. At least it’s not *actively* awful, you know? Speaker_1: Beige sounds amazing right now. Mine’s been a delegate who decided mid-conference they’d booked the wrong one, demanding a full refund. Then another one who lost their luggage *and* their phone. And then, the icing on the cake, a speaker cancelled five minutes before they were due on stage. Five minutes! Speaker_2: Oof. That’s…a lot. Did you manage to salvage it? Speaker_1: Eventually, yeah. Found someone to fill in, but it involved a frantic search through the attendee list for anyone with vaguely relevant expertise. Turns out a marketing manager from a tech firm was a closet expert on sustainable energy. Who knew? Speaker_3: That's lucky! Seriously. You’re a magician, you are. Speaker_1: Not a magician, just stressed. It just makes you wonder, doesn't it? Like, people just don't *think* before they book things, or pack properly, or…anything. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. It's like people assume everything just magically happens. They don't see all the behind-the-scenes stuff to make it work. I had someone complain *to my manager* that their reports weren't automatically being updated. Like, hello? I literally send you a spreadsheet template and instructions every month! Speaker_3: It’s the entitlement, isn't it? Like everything’s just *owed* to them. Speaking of owed, I need to chase up Sarah about that money she borrowed for the weekend trip to Brighton. It's been… a while. Speaker_1: Oh, good luck with that. Sarah’s legendary for “forgetting” to pay people back. Remember when she ‘forgot’ to chip in for the birthday meal last year? Speaker_2: Oh no, don’t remind me! It took three months and a very pointed email to get that sorted. It's just…awkward, isn't it? Ruining a friendship over twenty quid? Speaker_3: Exactly! But it’s the principle of the thing. I'm skint as it is. And I need to book train tickets for visiting my parents next month. Speaker_1: You should just be straight with her. A simple “Hey, just wondering about the money for Brighton” works wonders. Honestly. Speaker_2: Yeah, don't beat around the bush. Otherwise, it’ll just fester. Anyway, enough work and awkward financial situations. What are we doing this weekend? We haven’t properly hung out in ages. Speaker_1: I'm free Saturday. I was thinking we could go to that new board game café that opened up? Or maybe a movie? Speaker_3: Ooh, the board game café sounds fun! I'm in. We could try and get a table early though, I heard it gets really busy. Speaker_2: Perfect. I’m in too. Book it, [Speaker_1’s name]! Consider it a mission, a strategic logistical operation worthy of your conference planning skills. It’ll be good practice for dealing with difficult delegates. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Right. Operation Board Game Café is a go. Consider it booked. Now, back to complaining about work…

Speaker_1: Honestly, the council are just… unbelievable. Demolishing the library? It’s the heart of the community! Speaker_2: I know, it’s a disgrace. They’re saying it's structurally unsound, but I heard Old Man Hemmings – you remember him, used to volunteer there? – saying it just needs some repairs. They want to build another block of flats, of course. Speaker_1: Of *course* they do. That’s all they ever want to do. Right, I’ve started drafting a petition. I’ve got a basic outline on my laptop, but I’m really rubbish at the wording. It needs to sound… urgent, but not hysterical, you know? Speaker_2: I’m happy to look it over. I’m fairly good at that sort of thing, being an administrator and all. Endless reports to proofread. Though honestly, sometimes I think the people *writing* the reports deliberately try to make them incomprehensible. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. My transcription work is similar. People rambling, awful audio quality... it’s a nightmare. Anyway, petition first. I was thinking something about the library being a vital resource for education and community engagement… too cliché? Speaker_2: Maybe. How about focusing on what *specifically* will be lost? The children’s story time, the access to computers for people without internet at home, the local history collection? Make it tangible. Speaker_1: Good point, good point. I’ll add that. I was also thinking about getting flyers printed and putting them up in local shops. Speaker_2: Definitely. And social media. Everyone’s on Facebook these days, even the pensioners. I can share it on the Plumstead Community Group. Gets a lot of traffic. Speaker_1: Brilliant. You’re a lifesaver. Honestly, if we don’t fight this, what’s next? They’ll be closing the park, then the community centre… Speaker_2: Don't even go there. It’s all part of their plan, isn’t it? Slowly eroding everything that makes Plumstead, Plumstead. Speaking of eroding things, I'm on late shifts all next week. Dreadful. Seven till three. Speaker_1: Oh, no! That’s awful. You’ll be exhausted. Speaker_2: I know. And I always get stuck with the enquiries about parking permits. People are so aggressive about those things. It’s like I personally denied them the right to park outside their house. Speaker_1: People are awful. I heard Doreen's been trying to learn mnemonics to help her remember things. Apparently, her memory's not what it used to be. Speaker_2: Doreen? Really? What kind of mnemonics? Speaker_1: She said she's trying to use the method of loci, or something like that. Imagining things in a familiar place. She was telling me her shopping list is now a tour of her living room. Speaker_2: (laughs) That's brilliant! I’ve been doing those brain training apps on my phone. Supposedly helps keep your mind sharp. Mostly it just makes me feel stressed when I can’t remember where the hidden objects are. Speaker_1: It's a bit like that, isn't it? A bit of mental gymnastics. Anyway, back to the library. I’m thinking… “Save Our Stories, Save Our Space: Protect Plumstead Library!” How does that sound? Speaker_2: That's much better! Catchy. And it highlights the two key things. Definitely use that. Right, I'm starving. This noodle soup is looking very good.

Speaker_1: …and then young Derek, bless ‘im, he comes round with those Jehovah’s Witnesses leaflets again. Honestly, you’d think after ten years he’d realise we’re not interested. Polite as pie, mind you, can’t fault him for that. Just persistent. Speaker_2: They’re a dedicated bunch, alright. Remember old Mrs. Hedges, down the lane? She got right involved with them, years ago. Changed her completely. Stopped going to the Women’s Institute, wouldn’t have a gin and tonic at Christmas. Speaker_3: Goodness me. That's a bit drastic, isn’t it? Though I suppose if it gives people comfort… Still, a gin and tonic at Christmas is a tradition! Speaking of which, are we still on for The Crown next Friday? I fancy a nice bit of fish and chips, and a glass of something bubbly. Speaker_1: Sounds lovely, Mary. Though I’m still grumbling about the price of everything these days. Fifteen pound for fish and chips! Back in my day… Speaker_2: Don’t start on that, Arthur. Everything’s gone up. Even the blooming tax. I swear, they just invent new ways to take our money. I still don’t understand half of it, even after all these years. Speaker_3: They certainly do. It’s a nightmare. Though I’m glad they’re finally doing something about potholes. Did you see the state of the road going into Dereham? It’s like driving over the moon. Speaker_1: Potholes are the least of our worries. Have you seen the parking situation at Cromer these days? Absolute chaos. Tried to take Millie and George last week, and spent half an hour driving around in circles, looking for a spot. In the end, we parked miles away and walked. Speaker_2: That’s nothing new. Always been a nightmare at the coast, especially in summer. Used to be worse though, before they built that new car park near the pier. Speaker_3: Still not enough, though, is it? And all those people just abandoning cars on double yellows. You get some right characters. Speaking of characters, did you hear about old Mr. Peterson and his pigeons? Speaker_1: Oh, don’t get me started on Peterson! That man could talk to those birds for hours. Says they tell him things. Speaker_2: He’s a bit…eccentric. Though harmless enough. He’s been feeding them in the square for years. It’s just a bit messy, all the droppings and feathers. Speaker_3: It is a bit of a mess. Makes you think, though. He’s got his little routine, his little life. Keeps him going. Reminds me a bit of your hoarding, Arthur. Speaker_1: (Grumbling) It’s not hoarding, Mary. It’s…collecting. And everything has a purpose! Speaker_2: (Chuckling) Of course it does, Arthur. Everything has a purpose. Like that collection of bottle caps you’ve had since 1972. Speaker_1: They’re vintage! They'll be worth something one day. Although… my tooth is playing up again. I really should call the dentist. Absolutely dreadful service these days. Can’t get an appointment to save my life. Speaker_3: Oh, I know. It’s the same everywhere. You have to book six months in advance just to get a cleaning. Fancy another slice of cake? I made a lemon drizzle, it’s rather good. Speaker_2: Go on then, Mary. A small slice. Can’t refuse a good lemon drizzle. And Arthur, really, about those bottle caps…

Speaker_1: Honestly, the amount of logs we’ve got stacked up now is ridiculous. I thought we’d be burning through them faster with the weather being so… well, still quite chilly for June. Speaker_2: We didn’t really use the log burner much in May, did we? Too mild. Good job you got a good deal on them, though. Though, stacking them was *your* penance for buying so many, remember? Speaker_1: (Sighs) Don’t remind me. My back still hasn’t forgiven me. Mum, you were admiring the new upholstery on the chairs earlier, weren’t you? Did you think I’d done a good job? Speaker_3: It’s lovely, dear. Really brightens up the room. Though I do still maintain a more traditional fabric would have suited the style of the house better. But that's just my opinion. It looks very comfortable, at least. Speaker_4: Comfortable is the key, isn't it? Style follows function. Though I must say, I still prefer a good wingback chair. A proper wingback. They don’t *make* them like they used to. Speaker_2: Dad, you say that about *everything*. Remember when we were talking about the new Japanese restaurant in town? You said they didn’t make sushi like they used to in… well, I’m not even sure where you were imagining sushi was better! Speaker_4: Honestly, the stories I’ve heard about travelling from Tokyo… the hustle and bustle. It’s not for me, not anymore. Give me a quiet evening by the fire any day. Speaking of which, are we having mashed potato tonight? I do enjoy your mashed potato, dear. Speaker_1: Yes, Dad, mashed potato. And yes, Mum, I know you prefer a more muted colour scheme. It’s my house, though! Speaker_3: Don’t be impertinent, darling. I was merely observing. Honestly, the price of potatoes these days! Have you seen the budget? It’s scandalous. How are young families supposed to manage? Speaker_2: It's frightening. Everything's going up. I was talking to Sarah at work – they're seriously considering outsourcing more of our admin to India just to cut costs. Apparently, it's cheaper to have someone doing the work halfway around the world. Speaker_1: That’s awful. Where does that leave everyone here? The quality of work will suffer too, surely. They’re turning everything into academies now, aren’t they? It’s all about efficiency and cutting corners. Mrs. Henderson next door was saying… Speaker_3: Oh, Mrs. Henderson! Always has something to say. She’s convinced they’re going to build flats on old man Peabody’s field. Though I wouldn't put it past them. They're always looking for land. Speaker_4: Peabody’s field? Used to play cricket there as a boy. Good heavens, time flies. Did anyone see that antique shop opened up on the high street? I might wander down there tomorrow. Perhaps find a nice little… something. Though I’m trying to resist, you know. The house is getting full. Speaker_2: You said that last week and still bought a miniature ship in a bottle! Speaker_4: Well, it was a *very* good ship in a bottle! And it reminded me of my time at sea… oh dear, I’m rambling again, aren’t I? Speaker_1: Not at all, Dad. It’s nice to hear your stories. How are the cats behaving themselves? And have you seen Millie’s new puppy? It's a little terror. Speaker_3: The cats are fine, thank you. Mostly asleep, as usual. And Millie’s puppy *is* rather energetic. A handful, I imagine. Still, good for her. Keeps her active. We must send a little something to Emily and the children, mustn’t we? Have they settled into the new school yet?

Speaker_1: Honestly, the council tax this year… it’s gone up again. I swear, they just pluck figures out of thin air. Do you two feel the same? Speaker_2: Oh, you’re telling me. Mine’s crept up too. Thought being on a fixed pension would offer *some* protection, but no. It’s all going up, isn’t it? Everything. Speaker_3: It’s criminal, absolutely criminal. They say it’s for services, but what services? The roads are full of potholes, the bins get collected when they feel like it… and don't even get me started on the state of the library. Speaker_1: They’re building that new estate out by Old Catton, aren’t they? That’ll be more demand on everything. More people, more taxes, but will anything actually *improve*? I doubt it. Remember when they promised that new roundabout would solve the congestion on the A47? Still a nightmare. Speaker_2: Roundabouts. Don't talk to me about roundabouts! Tried to drive to Cromer last week, Sat Nav sent me round three of ‘em, going backwards half the time. Thing’s got a mind of its own, that Sat Nav. Nearly ended up in a field! Speaker_3: Oh, technology. I tried to record something the other day on the telly, a documentary about remote Scottish islands, fascinating place. Spent half an hour trying to figure out the new remote, ended up missing the whole thing. Honestly, it's designed to confuse us. Speaker_1: Remote places… that's a thought. I was reading about someone who bought a cottage in the Outer Hebrides. No phone signal, no internet, just… peace and quiet. Seems appealing, doesn’t it? After all the fuss and bustle. Speaker_2: Sounds a bit too isolated for my liking. I’d go stir-crazy. I need my telly, and a shop within reasonable distance for a paper. Though, I did see a nice little bungalow for sale in Attleborough. Not exactly the Hebrides, but… Speaker_3: Attleborough? Oh, it's nice enough, but a bit… bland. They’re building houses everywhere around there though. It's losing it’s character. Remember when it was just a little market town? Speaker_1: That’s the problem with progress, isn’t it? Everything changes. Still, a new house might be nice. Lower energy bills, less maintenance. This old place is starting to feel its age, and so am I, come to that. Though, the garden's lovely in the summer. Speaker_2: Speaking of bills, did you see that article about the changes to the state pension? They're tinkering with it again, aren't they? Something to do with triple locking and inflation… makes my head spin. Speaker_3: It's all a mess, a complete mess. They promise you one thing, then change it when it suits them. You work your whole life, pay your taxes, and then they take it away with one hand while offering a pittance with the other. Honestly. Speaker_1: I've been trying to sort out my recycling too. Honestly, it's a nightmare. What goes in what bin? It's constantly changing. They send out leaflets, but they're all contradictory. It's just designed to catch people out. And have you noticed how much less they collect now? Speaker_2: They’ve stopped taking glass, haven't they? Said it's too expensive to process. Makes you wonder what the point of it all is. Just chuck it all in landfill, I suppose. Speaker_3: It’s scandalous. We're supposed to be saving the planet, but they don't make it easy, do they? It’s just… frustrating, that’s what it is. Absolutely frustrating. Now, anyone fancy another cup of tea? I think I need one after all this.

Speaker_1: Right, so the motherboard's definitely gone. Completely fried. I’ve tested everything else, power supply’s good, RAM’s good, even tried a different graphics card just to be sure. Nothing. Speaker_2: So you can't fix it? Is it proper broken broken? Speaker_1: Absolutely proper broken. It’s beyond repair, lad. We’re talking replacement. Speaker_3: Oh dear. That’s not good. Was it still under warranty? Speaker_1: That’s the frustrating part. It *was*, but it expired last month. One month! I swear, these warranties are designed to run out the second something goes wrong. Speaker_2: So we have to *buy* a new one? A whole new computer? Speaker_1: Not necessarily a whole new computer. We can just replace the motherboard. But they’re not cheap, especially a decent one. I’ll have a look tonight, see what's available. Speaker_4: (Mumbling from his highchair) Sauce! Fajita sauce! Speaker_3: Alright, darling, just a minute. We're talking about computers. Honestly, you'd think he could sense we were discussing something expensive. Speaker_1: He's a smart one, that one. He understands more than we give him credit for. Speaking of, did you confirm with Liam’s Dad about the rugby on Saturday? Speaker_3: Yes, everything's sorted. Pick up at nine, drop off after training. He's really excited. Apparently, they're practicing tackling this week. Speaker_2: Cool. I’m hoping I get to play scrum-half. Mrs. O’Malley says I’m quick enough. Speaker_1: You are a quick lad, alright. Now, back to this computer… I really should have renewed that warranty. I was putting it off, thinking it was a waste of money. Famous last words. Speaker_3: Well, you couldn’t have known. And honestly, you’ve spent hours trying to fix it. You’re a wizard with these things. Speaker_1: I appreciate that. It's just annoying. Okay, after I look at motherboards tonight, maybe we could all go swimming? I think we all need a good swim. Speaker_2: Yeah! Swimming would be great! Can I take my goggles? Speaker_1: Of course, you can. Speaker_3: That sounds lovely. Though, I might just stay here with… this little sauce monster. (Gestures playfully at Speaker_4) Someone's clearly lobbying for more fajitas. Speaker_4: (Squealing) More sauce! Sticky ears! Speaker_2: What did he say about his ears? Speaker_3: He keeps poking them and saying they’re "sticky out ears.” It’s adorable, but slightly worrying. Speaker_1: All the better to hear you with, my boy. Right, let’s finish dinner then. I’ll tackle the motherboard research later. And maybe, just maybe, I can find a decent deal. Speaker_3: And for the record, I'm blaming the computer for the lack of fajita sauce. It's all its fault. Speaker_1: (Chuckling) Always a scapegoat, aren’t you? Speaker_2: I'm helping the scapegoat! More sauce! Speaker_4: (Clapping) Sauce! Speaker_1: Ok everyone lets finish up dinner. I think we should get a plan for the evening once the dishes are done. Speaker_3: Sound good, I will get everything cleaned up.

Speaker_1: Right, pizza’s almost ready! Who wants extra pepperoni? Speaker_2: Me! Me! Lots and lots! Like, a whole pizza of pepperoni! Speaker_3: No fair! I want pepperoni too! But not *all* of it. Just… six pieces. Speaker_1: Six pieces, okay. We’ll see. Now, remember what we talked about? No shouting, okay? We use our inside voices. It’s much nicer to listen to inside voices. Speaker_2: But if I shout, you *hear* me better! Speaker_1: That's not always true, sweetheart. Sometimes, shouting just makes it hard to understand what you’re saying. It’s like when you’re trying to tell me about your amazing handstand, but you’re tumbling around yelling at the same time. I miss the important bits! Speaker_3: I did a handstand for *ten* seconds today! Speaker_1: Wow! Ten seconds is fantastic! That’s a really long time. You’re getting so strong. Did you tell your teacher about that? Speaker_3: No. She was busy talking about…about… Nessie! Speaker_1: Nessie? The Loch Ness Monster? What about her? Speaker_2: Nessie! Is she real? Does she eat pizza? Speaker_1: (chuckles) That's a good question! Some people think she’s real, some people don't. It’s a big mystery. And I highly doubt she eats pepperoni pizza – probably more fish, I imagine. It wouldn't be very polite to throw pizza in the loch, would it? Speaker_3: No! It would pollute the water! Speaker_1: Exactly! Good thinking. Right. Pizza’s ready. Now, are you both excited for Lily’s birthday party on Saturday? Have you decided what you’re wearing? Speaker_2: I want to wear my sparkly dress! The one with the unicorns! Speaker_3: But I want to wear my superhero cape! Speaker_1: Hmm… well, perhaps we can think about that later. We need to talk about being good guests, okay? Using our manners, saying thank you… and not shouting over everyone when Lily's opening her presents. Remember? Inside voices. Speaker_2: Inside voices… and lots of cake? Speaker_1: (laughing) And lots of cake! Now, who can tell me – if I have three slices of pizza, and you have two, how many slices do we have altogether? Speaker_3: Five! Speaker_1: Fantastic! You’re brilliant. Okay, pizza time! And after, we can start planning that fairy garden we talked about. We can use all the pretty stones we collected last weekend. Speaker_2: Ooh! And we can make a little pizza for the fairies! Speaker_3: With one pepperoni! Speaker_1: One pepperoni for the fairies. Perfect. Now, dig in! Speaker_2: This IS good pizza! Speaker_3: Even *without* six pepperonis! Speaker_1: (Smiling) That's good to hear. Speaker_2: Mommy, do you think Nessie likes fairy gardens? Speaker_1: Oh, I bet she does! I bet she has a beautiful fairy garden under the water. With seaweed instead of grass! Speaker_3: And little fish fairies! Speaker_1: Exactly! Now let's eat. Speaker_2: Wait! I almost forgot! I told Grandma about the Loch Ness monster, and she told me a joke! Speaker_1: Oh really? What was it? Speaker_2: Why don’t scientists trust atoms? Speaker_3: I don’t know! Why? Speaker_2: Because they make up everything! (Speaker_3 giggles hysterically.) Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Oh, that's a good one! Your Grandma is a clever lady.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this Peka is incredible. I’ve never tasted anything quite like it. It's just… falling apart. Speaker_2: Isn’t it lovely? It's proper slow cooking, isn’t it? They bury it in embers for hours. You won't get that in Bolton, love. Though, mind you, Mrs. Higginbottom did make a pretty decent slow-cooked beef when I was on the ward… she always said the secret was a splash of Worcestershire sauce. Speaker_3: Worcestershire sauce? Sounds grim. This is much better. Can I have another potato? Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Grim? It's a classic! Though, I must say, the potatoes *are* rather good. Not the waxy kind, are they? More of a… floury, Maris Piper sort. Speaker_1: Definitely floury. You can tell they’ve been grown properly. This whole region is just… beautiful. Rovinj was lovely, wasn't it? Though *packed* with tourists. Speaker_2: Rovinj was gorgeous, but yes, a bit of a scrum. Pula was better, more spacious. I preferred the Roman amphitheatre to anything back home, even though I've delivered hundreds of babies in the maternity unit at the Royal Bolton… you’d think I’d be used to grand structures! Speaker_3: Mum! You always bring it back to babies. Speaker_2: Well, someone's got to! And it's a fascinating world, you know. Though these Croatian doctors… apparently, they're very keen on natural births. Very different approach than some of the London hospitals, I heard from a colleague who visited. Speaker_4: (Sipping wine) It's amazing how much healthcare varies. The wife and I were talking about it on the flight – the level of scrutiny you get from immigration officers these days is just… intense. They grilled me about my consultancy work for twenty minutes! Speaker_1: Oh, tell me about it. They gave me the side-eye because I was a student and travelling alone. Like I was planning a marijuana farm or something. Which, admittedly, would be pretty lucrative here, considering… Speaker_3: (Eyes widening) Marijuana farm?! Speaker_2: Olivia! Don’t fill his head with nonsense. Honestly. Speaker_1: I’m just saying! It's legal-ish here. I read an article about it... anyway. Where were we? Oh, the food. It just reminds me, Ben, your food tech class. Are you still making those weird edible spheres? Speaker_3: They're not weird! It’s molecular gastronomy! Mr. Davies says I’m a natural. He said I could be the next Heston Blumenthal. Speaker_4: Heston Blumenthal… now *there's* an innovator. Similar vein to Steve Jobs, really. Completely disrupted an industry. Speaker_2: Speaking of disrupting things, this swimming pool back at the villa is a lifesaver. I was starting to get a tic from the heat, honestly. Restless legs, you know? Speaker_1: A tic? Oh no! You should get that checked, Mum. Speaker_2: Oh, it’s nothing. Probably just dehydration. I'm fine. Besides, I’m more concerned about what country we're going to next year. Japan? You always wanted to go to Japan, didn’t you, Richard? Speaker_4: Japan is on the list. Though I’m rather fancying Iceland. All those volcanoes… and the Northern Lights. That would make for some stunning photography. I’ve been meaning to upgrade my lens, you know. Speaker_3: Can we go somewhere with waterslides? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Maybe after Iceland, Ben. Somewhere with waterslides. Honestly, this is what holidays are for, isn't it? This food, this sun… and the endless debates.

Speaker_1: Right then, finished that up, didn’t we? Good bit of ham, that was. Though I say, this new bread… a bit dry, isn’t it? Not like what Mrs. Higgins used to bake down the lane. Speaker_2: Oh, you always say that, Arthur! It’s perfectly good bread. You're just stuck in the past, you are. Still, it’s nice to have everyone together again for lunch, isn't it? Speaker_3: Indeed. It's a rare treat these days. Though young David did mention something about debt collectors knocking on doors in his street… Apparently, a rather aggressive lot. Speaker_4: Oh, don’t get me started on those. They’re the scourge of the earth. PPI claims, mostly. Preying on people who barely understand what they’re signing up for. I was reading an article about it in *The Week* – absolutely scandalous. Speaker_1: PPI? Fancy that. Always thought it was something for fancy city folk. Never bothered me none. Though I did get a letter once, said I was owed a few quid. Filled it in, never heard a thing back. Speaker_2: They’re very good at taking, aren't they? And not so good at giving back. Speaking of taking… are we still planning on having that little party next month, for Emily’s birthday? Speaker_4: Yes, we booked the hall down by the church, remember? Small one, but perfectly adequate. I’m thinking maybe a bit of a sing-song afterwards? Emily always loved a good croon. Speaker_3: A sing-song in the church hall? Bit ambitious, isn’t it? Though I suppose as long as we don't disturb the Abbey… They’re quite sensitive about noise over there. Remember old Mr. Peterson complaining about the carol singers? Speaker_1: Oh, I remember that! He was a right grumpy old thing. Always moaning about something. But I used to enjoy singing in the choir, back in the day. Though my voice isn’t what it used to be… sounds more like a rusty gate these days. Speaker_2: Don't be silly, Arthur. You still have a lovely voice. Although perhaps we should leave the solos to Emily. She’s the talented one. Speaker_4: Absolutely. Speaking of talents, have you started your seeds yet, Arthur? I know you were talking about growing tomatoes this year. Speaker_1: Not yet, no. Been meaning to, but then I got distracted trying to figure out this computer. That David gave me. It's a devilish machine, I tell you. All flashing lights and strange noises. Spend more time wrestling with it than actually using it. Speaker_3: I offered to set it up for you, Arthur, you know. Speaker_1: Oh, I know, I know. But you’re always so busy. Didn’t want to impose. Besides, I like a challenge. Though I'm starting to think this computer is winning. Speaker_2: You and that computer! It’s a love-hate relationship, isn’t it? Perhaps I could give you a hand? I’m not as tech-savvy as David, but I can manage the basics. Speaker_4: I'm going to nip out and do a bit of driving. Need to pick up a few bits for the party. Anyone need anything? Speaker_3: Just make sure you don’t get stuck in traffic, old boy. It's a nightmare around here, especially on a Sunday. Speaker_1: Just bring back a nice bit of cake if you can, William! That’ll do nicely. And be careful now, don’t want you ending up in a ditch.

Speaker_1: Right, another day done. Honestly, the stories you hear… Speaker_2: Tell me about it, dear. You get used to it, but it never stops being… sobering. Though today was mostly benefit fraud, thankfully. Less drama than the shoplifting cases. Speaker_1: Benefit fraud is… frustrating, isn’t it? Especially when you hear the justifications. I had one woman today, claiming hardship, but she was talking about a holiday to Tenerife next month. Speaker_2: Oh, the cheek of it! You wouldn’t believe some of the excuses people come up with. Though, I suppose everyone's got a story, haven't they? Doesn’t make it right, though. It's just… difficult sometimes, seeing people in such difficult situations. And then others just taking the mickey. Speaker_1: Absolutely. It's a real mixed bag. Makes you think about the whole justice system, really. Is it fair? Is it effective? Do people actually *learn* from it? Speaker_2: A question for the ages, that is. I’ve been doing this nearly ten years now, and I still don't know the answer. Seems to me like it’s more about ticking boxes than actually rehabilitating anyone. They go round and round, don't they? Speaker_1: They do. And the funding cuts… it’s impacting everything. Schools, the NHS, the courts… it all feels a bit precarious. Speaker_2: Precarious is a good word for it. My grandson, little Jamie, he's trying to get extra tutoring for his GCSEs, but it's just so expensive. Everything is so expensive these days, isn't it? Used to be able to put a bit aside, now… it all goes on bills. Speaker_1: It’s awful, isn’t it? I’m a language teacher, and even *I’m* struggling. Private tuition is booming, but it’s mostly for kids whose parents can afford it. Creates such a disparity. Speaker_2: It does. It really does. Makes you wonder what the world’s coming to. Speaking of coming to… did you see the weather forecast? More rain. It’s like Scotland here, honestly! Speaker_1: I did! Honestly, it's relentless. I was hoping to get a weekend trip to the coast, but I think that's out the window. Perhaps a train trip somewhere instead? Though the train fares are… well, you know. Speaker_2: Don't even start me on the trains! Daylight robbery, that's what it is. I went up to see my sister in Aberdeen last month, and it cost me a fortune. I’m starting to think a good book and a cup of tea is the best travel you can get these days. Speaker_1: You might be right! It's a shame, though. I used to love exploring. My parents used to take me all over Europe when I was a kid, those were the days. Speaker_2: Ah, good times. Family is everything, isn’t it? My sister’s alright, but we don't see each other often enough. She’s got a big family, you see, always busy. Speaker_1: It’s hard to keep up. Well, I’d better get going. Got a pile of marking waiting for me. Speaker_2: You too dear. Stay dry on your way home. And don't let those teenagers bring you down! Speaker_1: I'll try my best! You have a good evening, too. Speaker_2: You too dear, you too.

Speaker_1: Right, so we were talking about what makes people happy, weren’t we? What makes *you* happy, Lily? Speaker_2: Um… ponies! And chocolate! And… and when you read me stories! Speaker_1: Lovely! Those are all brilliant things. And what about you, Leo? What makes *you* feel happy? Speaker_3: Dinosaurs! Roar! And building really tall towers. And… and when I beat you at Connect Four! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, you *do* love beating me at Connect Four, don’t you? It’s good to have things that make you smile. It doesn’t always need to be something big or expensive, does it? Speaker_2: Does it mean you need lots of money to be happy? Speaker_1: That’s a really good question, Lily. Not at all, sweetie. Not at all. Lots of people *think* money will make them happy, but it doesn’t always work like that. Speaker_3: If I had lots of money, I’d buy a *massive* dinosaur! A really, really BIG one! Speaker_1: You would, wouldn’t you? But even if you didn’t have lots of money, you could still imagine a massive dinosaur, couldn’t you? You could draw one, or build one out of blocks… Speaker_2: And I could pretend to ride a pony! Even if it’s just a pretend pony! Speaker_1: Exactly! See? It's about using your imagination and enjoying the little things. Like sunshine, or having a cuddle, or… hmm… can you think of a rhyme for 'happy'? Speaker_3: Snappy! Like a crocodile! Speaker_1: (Smiling) That’s a good start! But maybe something that *sounds* a bit more like 'happy'? Speaker_2: Pappy! Like… Grandpa! Speaker_1: Clever girl! Pappy rhymes with happy. And you know what makes *me* happy? Seeing you two having fun and being kind to each other. That makes me the happiest person in the world. Speaker_3: I like being kind! I shared my stickers with Lily today. Speaker_2: And I let Leo have a turn with the red car! Speaker_1: See? That’s wonderful. That’s *much* more important than having lots of money or lots of toys. That’s what true happiness is all about. Speaker_3: Can we build a tower now? A really, really tall one? Speaker_2: Yes! And then we can pretend it's a castle for the pony and the dinosaur! Speaker_1: Sounds like a fantastic plan! Let’s go build the tallest tower Comberton has ever seen! Speaker_1: Right, what did you say rhymes with happy? Speaker_2: Pappy! Speaker_1: That’s right, pappy! Now, what rhymes with blue? Speaker_3: Shoe! Speaker_1: Perfect! You guys are brilliant at rhyming! Speaker_1: I also think making other people feel good, makes you feel good. Speaker_2: So it's like a circle? Speaker_1: It is, a very good circle. Speaker_3: If I had all the money in the world I still wouldn’t give up building forts. Speaker_1: That is a very wise thing to say, Leo. Speaker_2: I'd still want to read books with you even if I had lots of money! Speaker_1: Oh you sweet girl, that makes my heart sing.

Speaker_1: Seriously though, have you thought about what you’re doing after sixth form? Like, *really* thought about it? Everyone else seems to have a five-year plan already. Speaker_2: Five-year plan? Mate, I’m struggling to plan what I’m having for dinner tonight. Uni’s the vague idea, yeah, but beyond that… nothing. What about you, Mr. Future CEO? Speaker_1: I’m thinking of trying to patent something. Seriously. I had this idea for a self-cleaning dog bowl. Like, automatic scraper and water filter. People would buy it. Dogs are messy. Speaker_2: A self-cleaning dog bowl? That’s… niche. But actually, not terrible. You'd need loads of funding though, right? Patents aren’t cheap. Speaker_1: Exactly! And that's where it gets tricky. I was reading about this guy who invented a better mousetrap, patented it, but then couldn’t afford to *market* it. Sat on the invention for years. Speaker_2: Harsh. That’s rubbish. So, what, you’d need investors? Like… Dragons’ Den stuff? Speaker_1: Possibly. Or maybe crowdfunding. But then you have to give away equity, and what if it’s a massive success? You want to keep the bulk of the profit. I’ve been looking into investment, actually. Trying to understand it. Speaker_2: Investment? You’re going deep, aren’t you? I barely understand my pocket money, let alone shares and stocks. Speaker_1: It’s not *that* hard. It’s all about risk, and potential return. Like, China's growing so fast, right? Investing in Chinese tech companies now could be huge in ten years. Speaker_2: China, eh? My dad said something about that. Said they’re basically taking over the world. Everything’s made in China. Speaker_1: Not taking over, but definitely becoming a superpower. And that means economic opportunities. You could, like, put a little bit of money into a tech fund, and just… watch it grow. It's like planting a seed. Speaker_2: Sounds… boring. I’d rather just spend the money on a new graphics card for my computer. Speaker_1: That’s a valid use of funds. But think bigger! This is about future financial security. Becoming independent. Not having to work nine-to-five for someone else. Speaker_2: Okay, okay, you’ve convinced me to… think about it. But I'm not promising anything. My priorities are currently beating level seven on *Elden Ring*. And then maybe finally finishing that history coursework. Speaker_1: Fair enough. But seriously, keep it in the back of your mind. This whole investment thing. It could be big. We could be rich! Rich enough to buy all the graphics cards we want. Speaker_2: Now *that’s* a plan I can get behind. Though, realistically, I’d probably just buy a really good gaming chair. Speaker_1: A gaming chair? Seriously? Speaker_2: Comfort is key, man.
