They hide behind a keyboard and just unleash. Speaker_2: Exactly! And it's always the most ridiculous things. I had someone complain the croissants weren’t flaky *enough*. Flaky enough! They’re, like, eighty layers of butter and pastry. What more do they want? Speaker_3: You just have to ignore them, right? I try to. But it still stings. Especially when you’ve poured your heart and soul into something. This one guy actually said my café "lacked ambition." Lacked ambition! I’m running a small business practically on my own, mate. Speaker_1: Proper cheek. Speaking of ambition, are you still thinking about that Margate place, then? The little art gallery/cafe hybrid? Speaker_3: Yeah, still noodling on it. Found a potential space, a tiny shop front just off the old town. It needs a *lot* of work, though. Seriously, the interior is… questionable. Like, floral wallpaper questionable. Speaker_2: Ooh, Margate is cool though, isn't it? It's had a real resurgence. You could do really well there. Design-wise, you've got a good eye. Speaker_3: Thanks. That’s the thing, I’ve got all these ideas, but then the practicalities hit. Like, permits, refitting, and the sheer volume of cleaning required. It's daunting. Speaker_1: It always is. But you’d be brilliant at it. You just need a good designer to tackle that floral wallpaper situation. It sounds tragic. Speaker_2: I could do a mood board! I've been playing with some colour palettes for some new cake designs and they might work for a café. Think muted tones, lots of natural textures… Speaker_3: That would be amazing, actually. Seriously. You’re a lifesaver. I keep getting bogged down in logistics and forgetting the fun part – making it *look* good. Speaker_1: Speaking of fun, I'm officially logging off for the night. This Twitter doomscrolling is making my brain hurt. I have a history essay to pretend to write tomorrow, and I need at least five hours of sleep to maintain the illusion of productivity. Speaker_2: Good plan. I’m going to attempt a face mask and then collapse. Honestly, all these sourdough complaints have aged me ten years. Speaker_3: Night, you two. And honestly, ignore the haters. Your sourdough is amazing, and my avocado on toast is a culinary masterpiece. Remember that. Speaker_1: Good night! And seriously, floral wallpaper… nightmares. Speaker_2: Good night! Speaker_3: Goodnight! Speaker_1: Sweet dreams. Speaker_2: Zzz. Speaker_3: Time for sleep. Goodbye. Speaker_1: Bye. Speaker_2: See ya.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Oisin, you’ve barely touched your peas. They’re lovely peas, honestly. Fresh from the garden. Speaker_2: They’re green and…round. I don’t *like* round. Speaker_3: Everything’s round, Lily. The table’s round-ish. Your plate’s round. Speaker_2: No, it’s not! It’s…mostly square. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) It’s a bit of both, sweetie. Just try one pea. For Grandma. Speaker_2: No! Peas are yucky. Can I have more raspberries instead? Speaker_1: We’ll have raspberries for pudding if you eat *some* of your dinner. A few peas. Just five. Speaker_3: Five peas is a pretty easy deal. I had to eat, like, ten broccoli florets to get dessert last night. Speaker_4: Oh, don’t remind me. He wouldn’t touch it. Said it looked like tiny trees. Speaker_1: He’s just being dramatic. Honestly, he’ll eat anything covered in ketchup. Speaker_3: It’s true. Ketchup solves everything. Want some ketchup, Lily? Speaker_2: No! Ketchup’s red. And sticky. Speaker_1: Right, okay. No ketchup. Maybe if you finish your chicken...though your brother ate most of his already. Leo, honestly, you were like a little vacuum cleaner. Speaker_3: It was good chicken! Dad made it. Speaker_4: He did indeed. Though he did spend half an hour trying to identify a bird’s egg he found in the garden before he started marinating it. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even *mention* that egg. I nearly stepped on it. Thought it was a discarded ping pong ball. Speaker_3: It was a robin’s egg, apparently. He was very careful moving it. Said it was a scientific investigation. Speaker_2: Did it hatch? Speaker_4: No, sadly not. Something happened. A badger, I think. Or maybe one of the cats. Speaker_1: Well, that’s nature, isn’t it? Speaking of nature, how was your bike ride this morning, darling? Speaker_4: It was lovely, actually. Went down by the river. Saw a heron fishing. Though I definitely need to get back into it – I was completely breathless going up that hill. Speaker_3: You should get an electric bike. Then you can fly up hills. Speaker_1: An electric bike! That defeats the object, doesn’t it? It's supposed to be exercise. Speaker_4: I know, I know. But it’s tempting. And then we could all go for rides together. Even Lily! Speaker_2: I want chocolate ice cream. Speaker_1: (Sighs) After your dinner, Lily. Now, back to the peas…What about a little walk after dinner? Maybe we can spot some birds? Speaker_3: Can we get ice cream afterwards? Specifically, chocolate ice cream? Speaker_1: We’ll see. If you’re both good. Speaking of good, remember Mrs. Higgins' gerbils? Speaker_4: Oh, the tiny ones? They were adorable. She brought them in for show and tell last week. Speaker_1: Exactly! She said they were eating all her prize-winning marrows. Apparently, gerbils *love* marrows. Go figure. Speaker_2: Marrows are orange! Speaker_1: They can be! And now, can we please focus on these perfectly good, green, round peas?

Speaker_1: Honestly, the supermarket was chaos this morning. Absolute chaos. Everyone seemed to be doing a massive shop. Speaker_2: Oh, don't even. I went yesterday and it was rammed. Needed just a loaf of bread and ended up buying half the biscuit aisle because I couldn't move for people! Speaker_3: (Chuckles) You two are terrible. I haven’t been to a proper supermarket in months. Far too much hustle and bustle for me. Just little shops, you see. Get what I need and be done with it. Speaker_1: That sounds idyllic, honestly. Though I do like the convenience of getting everything in one go. I need to get some more spinach, I’m trying that recipe from that healthy eating blog. Speaker_2: Oh, the one with all the kale and things? Looks a bit… rabbit food to me. Speaker_1: It’s not *all* kale! There’s quinoa and… well, a bit of kale. I need to be healthier. My cholesterol’s been creeping up. Speaker_3: Cholesterol! Fancy that. In my day, we just ate what we liked and got on with it. Though I did give up smoking when I was seventy-five. That was a shock to the system. Speaker_1: Seventy-five! Good for you, Mum. That’s fantastic. It’s never too late, is it? Speaker_2: No, it isn’t. My sister's trying to quit, she’s on those patches. Says they make her dream about cigarettes! Speaker_3: (Laughs) Oh, dear! They need to try hypnotherapy. Old Mr. Henderson down the road, he gave it up that way. Said he just suddenly didn’t want one anymore. Speaker_1: That’s amazing. Speaking of wanting things, my eyebrows are a disaster. They’ve gone completely wild. I need to book an appointment with Sarah. Speaker_2: Ooh, go for it! She does a brilliant job. Though I’ve been meaning to ask, have you had your hair cut yet? You said you were going to the new salon in town. Speaker_1: Not yet, I’m still working up the courage. I heard they're a bit scissor-happy. I’m terrified of ending up with a bob when I specifically asked for layers. Speaker_3: Oh, that's awful! You need a reliable hairdresser. I’ve been going to Doreen since… well, since before you were born, dear! She knows exactly what I like. Speaker_1: Doreen's brilliant. Though she’s getting on a bit, isn’t she? I worry she won’t be able to do it forever. Speaker_2: That's true. It’s good you’re loyal, but you might need to find a backup plan. Speaker_1: Maybe. Anyway, let’s talk about something more cheerful. Shall we try and book that meal out we talked about? At The Watermill? Speaker_2: Oh yes, that would be lovely! I haven’t been there in ages. Are you free next week? Speaker_1: I think so. Let me have a look at my diary. Mum, are you up for it? Speaker_3: Oh, I’d love to! A nice meal out is always a treat. And I can tell you all my gossip about the neighbours. You wouldn’t believe what Mrs. Higgins has been up to… Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, go on then. Tell us! This is getting better by the minute. Perhaps a glass of wine would help with the storytelling? Speaker_2: Yes, definitely a glass of wine. I think we’ve earned it after navigating those supermarket queues!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weaning is… a whole thing, isn’t it? I feel like I'm constantly covered in pureed sweet potato. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Mum, it's the classic first-time mum experience! Honestly, it gets easier. Though, you’ll find yourself assessing every public surface for ‘splatter potential’ for months. Speaker_1: Splatter potential! That’s exactly it! And the faces! The absolute disgust when she tries something new. You’d think I was poisoning her. Speaker_2: It’s hilarious, though, isn’t it? Remember when Leo did that with the broccoli? Completely launched it across the highchair. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh god, yes! Covered the cat in it! She wasn’t impressed. Anyway, enough about baby food warfare. What are you up to this week? Any plans with… well, anyone? Speaker_2: Not much planned, actually. Just work, mostly. Though, Sarah mentioned a pub quiz on Wednesday. Said she’d ask if Mark and Chloe were free. Would you fancy joining us, if they are? Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds nice. Quiet, though, isn’t it? Just the four of you? I was hoping we could maybe get a bigger group together? Perhaps next weekend? Speaker_2: Maybe. I'll see what people say about Wednesday. Everyone’s so busy. Speaking of busy, I’ve finally booked myself onto that baby sign language course! Speaker_1: Oh, brilliant! That’s a good idea. I was thinking about doing that. Does it actually work, though? Speaker_2: Apparently! I spoke to another teacher at school whose little one did it, and she said it really helped with frustration as they get older. It’s just a few basic signs to start with - ‘milk’, ‘more’, ‘tired’ - stuff like that. Speaker_1: That sounds really useful, actually. Less screaming, potentially? I'm in. Maybe we could do it together? They probably have another course starting soon. Speaker_2: I’ll check! It’s at the community centre, Tuesdays after work. It’s a bit of a trek from school, but worth it, I think. Oh! And Auntie Brenda is coming down on Friday. She’s promised to bring her famous lemon drizzle cake. Speaker_1: Brenda and her cake... a lethal combination! The whole house will smell of lemons for days. She’ll want to see the little one, of course. Are you ready for the interrogation about how I'm coping? Speaker_2: (Smiling) Prepare for the 'are you getting enough sleep?' and ‘are you sure you’re eating properly?’ routine. She means well, you know she does. Speaker_1: I know, I know. It’s just… exhausting, isn’t it? Being a mum, even just a few months in. I’m officially accepting all offers of help this week. Anything to get five minutes peace to drink a hot coffee. Speaker_2: Consider it done. I'll be around most evenings after the sign language class, so I can pop over and give you a hand. We’ll tackle the spaghetti bolognese explosion together. Speaker_1: You’re a lifesaver, honestly. Now, pass the biscuits. I feel a sugar slump coming on. And more importantly, are you sure Brenda doesn’t want to help with the sweet potato clean-up? She’s remarkably resilient. Speaker_2: (Laughing) I think she’d rather stick to the lemon drizzle. Speaker_1: Fair enough!

Speaker_1: It’s funny isn't it? How even a tiny incline feels like a mountain when you’re not used to it. London is…well, it’s just flat. Speaker_2: Utterly pancake-like. I genuinely forgot hills *existed* for a while there. It’s nice though, isn’t it? To have a bit of undulation. Makes you feel like you’re actually *going* somewhere, even if you’re just walking in a circle. Speaker_1: Exactly! And the views. You can actually *see* things. Not just brick walls and the tops of buses. Look, you can see St. Mary’s tower from here, can’t you? Speaker_2: Just about. Through those trees. It’s a lovely little village, Little Barningham. Properly…Norfolk. Speaker_1: Properly Norfolk? What does that even *mean*? Speaker_2: (chuckles) You know. Quiet. Stone cottages. A pub that serves adnams. A general sense of…not being in a hurry. Speaker_1: You’re being awfully romantic about it. It’s a village with a shop that closes at four and probably a lot of gossip. Speaker_2: All the best places have a lot of gossip. It’s the social glue. Think about it. It's how people connect, how they understand their community. Speaker_1: I suppose. It’s still a far cry from the constant hustle and bustle of university life, though. Being here… it’s a good antidote. Speaker_2: Definitely. It makes you realise how much headspace the city takes up. I feel like I can breathe properly out here. And think. Not just…react. Speaker_1: I know what you mean. It’s funny, isn’t it? To spend so long studying the human condition, and then realise you need to occasionally escape the humans to actually understand it. Speaker_2: Precisely. Sometimes you just need to look at fields. And sheep. And appreciate the subtle curve of a hill. Speaker_1: (laughs) You’re sounding increasingly like a postcard. Speaker_2: I’m embracing the Norfolk vibe! Honestly, I think we should come back more often. It’s good for us. Good for the soul. Even if it *is* a bit hilly. Speaker_1: I have to admit, I'm starting to agree. It’s just…a lot quieter than we're used to. Speaker_2: That's the point though, isn't it? Just quiet. And space. And not having to worry about dodging cyclists on the pavement. Speaker_1: Good point. Let's make a plan, then. A proper, regular escape to the countryside. It’s just… what will we do if it rains? Speaker_2: We’ll find a pub. Drink Adnams. And listen to the locals gossip. It’s a foolproof plan. Speaker_1: Sounds perfect, actually. Speaker_2: Right, let's carry on. I want to see if we can get to that trig point before it gets dark. Speaker_1: A trig point? You’ve been reading too many walking guides. Speaker_2: Hey, a man’s gotta have hobbies. And a trig point offers a panoramic view! It’s…properly Norfolk. Speaker_1: (smiling) Oh, here we go again. Speaker_2: Come on! Let's go conquer that hill. . . Speaker_1: Right lets go. .............

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the CGI was just… dodgy. Like, really dodgy. It pulled me right out of it. Speaker_2: Which film was that again? You were mid-rant when I got in. Speaker_1: *Rebellion Rising*. Saw it last night with Chloe. Honestly, hyped it up for weeks, and it was just… a mess. The plot was okay, but visually it was just appalling. Looked like a Playstation 2 game at times. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Harsh. I’ve heard mixed things. Chloe’s usually pretty good with her film recommendations though. Speaker_1: She was gutted, honestly. Said she’d been completely sucked in by the trailers. They clearly spent all the budget on the marketing and none on the actual effects. Speaker_2: Classic. It happens. So, how’s work? Still drowning in corpus data? Speaker_1: You have *no* idea. Old Professor Davies keeps finding ‘errors’ which just turn out to be him not understanding how the system works. He emailed me at eleven last night asking why a particular word count was different from his handwritten notes. Handwritten! In 2024! Speaker_2: Oh, Davies. He sounds… delightful. Speaker_1: "Delightful" is one word for it. More like a particularly grumpy badger. Speaking of work, how’s the new project going? The one with the wind turbines? Speaker_2: It's… challenging. Lots of stakeholder meetings. Everyone has an opinion on where these things should go, naturally. And a surprising amount of opposition from… cyclists. Speaker_1: Cyclists? Really? What’s their problem? Speaker_2: Apparently, the shadow flicker. When the blades turn, it casts a moving shadow that they find incredibly distracting. And also, they’re worried about birds. Which, fair enough, is a legitimate concern, but they're focusing on the shadow flicker thing. Speaker_1: That's… specific. I mean, I get being annoyed by things, but shadow flicker? Seriously? Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Spent an hour and a half yesterday explaining to a group of very passionate cyclists why the calculations showed the flicker wouldn’t actually impact any major cycle routes. They weren’t convinced. Speaker_1: Sounds exhausting. You'd think they’d have bigger things to worry about. Like cars. Or those electric scooters that just appear out of nowhere. Speaker_2: Exactly! Honestly, the scooters are more dangerous. Honestly, have you seen some of the places people are riding those things? On pavements, going the wrong way… it's chaos. Speaker_1: It is! My auntie nearly got knocked over by one last week. Nearly gave the lad a piece of her mind, she did. She's a feisty one, my auntie. Speaker_2: Sounds it. So, anything exciting happening this weekend? Thinking of catching that new indie film, *Static Bloom*, on Saturday. Speaker_1: Ooh, I’ve heard good things about that one. Might be up for it. Depends if Davies decides to email me again at eleven pm. He's got a real knack for ruining weekends, that man. Speaker_2: Well, hopefully not. I'll keep my phone on just in case you need a distraction from grumpy badger emails. Speaker_1: You're a lifesaver. Honestly. Speaker_2: Anytime. Speaker_1: Right. I just need to mentally prepare myself for another day of corpus chaos, and badger-related grievances. Speaker_2: You’ll survive. You always do. Speaker_1: I hope so.

Speaker_1: It’s just…look at that field of oilseed rape. It’s breathtaking, isn’t it? That bright yellow. Speaker_2: It is pretty spectacular. Though, knowing what I know about agricultural subsidies, it probably shouldn't be. All that cash crop nonsense. Speaker_1: Cash crops? You’re bringing economics into a lovely walk? Speaker_2: I can’t help it! It’s ingrained. Thinking about the market forces behind pretty flowers. It’s a curse, really. Though, this is arguably more functional than pretty, I suppose. Oilseed rape isn't grown for aesthetics. Speaker_1: No, no. It's for…biodiesel or something? I always forget. It feels a bit odd, though, doesn’t it? To have something so visually striking be driven entirely by economic factors. Like it's only beautiful because it’s profitable. Speaker_2: Exactly! It's a manufactured aesthetic. And the impact on bee populations isn't great, is it? It's a whole complicated system. Still, it *is* yellow. Speaker_1: Very yellow. Look, there are some orchids over there, by that hedge. White ones. Do you know what kind? Speaker_2: Hmm…hard to tell from here. Maybe common spotted orchids? Though the conditions don’t look quite right. Too dry, perhaps. You’re the botanist. Speaker_1: I'm a linguist, remember. I just… appreciate plants. I can tell them apart, mostly. It's a useful skill for fieldwork, actually. Trying to describe environments to students who’ve never been anywhere rural. The vocabulary gets quite specific. Speaker_2: Fair enough. I suppose describing the nuances of a landscape requires a pretty detailed lexicon. It’s not all ‘green and pleasant land,’ is it? Speaker_1: Definitely not. There's a whole spectrum of greens, and then you get into the textures, the smells… it's surprisingly complex. It’s like analysing a particularly difficult poem, really. Finding all the layers of meaning. Speaker_2: Speaking of layers of meaning, have you seen that research paper on the linguistic relativity of colour perception? The one I sent you? Speaker_1: Oh, the one about how different languages categorize colour differently? I skimmed it. It was…dense. Speaker_2: Dense, yes, but fascinating! The idea that the way we perceive the world is shaped by the language we speak. It’s pretty mind-blowing. Makes you think about how much we miss when we try to translate. Speaker_1: It does. Makes you think about how much we miss even *within* a language. So many subtleties get lost. Just like the nuances of this countryside, I suppose. Speaker_2: Exactly. It's all about perspective. Almost makes me want to give up economics and become a poet. Speaker_1: Don’t even think about it. Who would explain the agricultural subsidies to me then? And did you see the football last night? Absolutely ridiculous refereeing decision. Speaker_2: Oh, don't even *start* me on the football. It’s a complete disgrace. We need a proper VAR system… Speaker_1: (Laughing) See? That's what I was afraid of. Economics and now football. You're incorrigible. Speaker_2: It’s a passionate debate! And it demonstrates complex systems of… oh, never mind. Let’s just enjoy the yellow fields, shall we? Speaker_1: Yes, let’s. And the orchids, if we can identify them properly.

Speaker_1: Right, so are we still on for Saturday then? Your mam’s birthday? Speaker_2: Yeah, absolutely. I’ve booked a table at The Black Horse for seven. Thought that was sensible, somewhere a bit… less chaotic than the pub in town. Speaker_1: Good shout. She’ll appreciate that, she hates all the noise. Are you driving, or shall I? It’s not far for either of us, really. Speaker_2: I’ll drive. My car needs a run-out, truth be told. Been parked up most of the week. Plus, you’ve been doing all the driving lately, fair’s fair. Speaker_1: True, true. Though I do enjoy a good drive, actually. Especially when the football’s on the radio. Did you see the match last night? Speaker_2: Bits and pieces. Was stuck on a Zoom call until late. Heard Sunderland got a good result though? Speaker_1: They absolutely smashed it! Three-nil against Sheffield Wednesday. Honestly, the atmosphere at the Stadium of Light must’ve been mental. I wish I’d been there. Speaker_2: Sounds like it. You get properly invested in your football, don’t you? It’s a different level to what I experience following Watford. It’s just… polite applause most of the time. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Polite applause! That’s Watford summed up. Speaking of cars, yours is looking good, by the way. Still loving the new wheels? Speaker_2: Yeah, they’ve grown on me. Still a bit gutted I couldn’t get the one with the heated seats, but it’ll do. Parking’s a nightmare though, isn’t it? Even just getting to work. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I swear, trying to find a space near the office is a full-time job. People just park anywhere. It’s like the Wild West. Speaker_2: Seriously! I saw someone park right across someone’s dropped kerb the other day. Honestly. Anyway, we should probably talk about presents for my mam. Have you got anything sorted? Speaker_1: I’ve got her a little something. A new scarf. She always complains she’s cold. And I was thinking of taking her to see the Angel of the North when we’re up there. Have you taken her before? Speaker_2: No, actually. She's always said she wanted to go, but never got around to it. That’s a lovely idea. Might be a bit windy up there though, mind. Speaker_1: Oh yeah, good point. We’ll need to wrap up warm then. Also, been thinking about flats again. Saw a few online that look alright, near the tennis courts. Speaker_2: Oh really? Still looking? I thought you were happy where you are. Speaker_1: I am mostly, but the kitchen’s tiny, and I’d really like a bit more space. And being near the tennis courts would be brilliant. I'm trying not to get too carried away though. It's so stressful finding a place. Speaker_2: Yeah, it is. We should really start looking properly too, shouldn’t we? We’ve been saying we will for ages. But the market’s insane at the moment. Speaker_1: Absolutely insane. Everything’s so overpriced. Okay, new plan. Saturday, The Black Horse, scarf, Angel of the North, and a serious discussion about flats over dessert. Sound good? Speaker_2: Sounds perfect. Now, if only the traffic would cooperate… Speaker_1: (Sighing) Don’t even start.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this Fred Sirieix trial is absolutely gripping, isn’t it? I can't believe he’s doing so well. Never pegged him as a dancer. Speaker_2: Ooh, is it on tonight? I missed it last week, had a right bad headache. My Elsie – that’s my sister, you know – she’s proper hooked. Says he’s a dark horse. Speaker_1: It is! Saturday night, BBC One. You absolutely must catch it. It’s a good bit of escapism, isn’t it? Something a bit silly. Speaker_3: (Chuckling from her armchair) Escapism! You young ‘uns need a bit of that, always rushing about. Back in my day, escapism was a good book and a cup of tea. No television until the 60s, you know. Speaker_1: Times have changed, haven't they, Margaret? Though I do still love a good book. Speaking of things changing… have you noticed the geese are already gathering down by the river? Feels earlier this year. Speaker_2: Oh, they are, aren't they? I saw a huge flock yesterday, heading south. Proper noisy bunch, too. Bit intimidating when they come waddling across the road, they do. Speaker_3: They know when it’s time. Instinct, pure instinct. Used to watch ‘em with my Arthur - my husband – down at the ‘Nene Washes. Magnificent sight, hundreds of them. Always said they knew more than most folks. Speaker_1: It's amazing, isn't it? The distances they travel. I read somewhere that some of those geese migrate all the way to Russia for the winter. Speaker_2: Russia! Blimey. Elsie’s son, Darren, he went to Russia on holiday once. Said it was freezing. Wouldn’t fancy a winter there, not for all the tea in China. Speaker_3: Always loved watching the smaller birds, though. The robins, especially. Such cheerful little things, even in the bleakest weather. Remember feeding them scraps out of the kitchen window. Speaker_1: We get a lot of blue tits in the garden. They’re so quick! And the squirrels are getting bolder. I saw one trying to get into the bird feeder yesterday. Complete menace. Speaker_2: Oh, squirrels! They dig up my bulbs! I planted some lovely tulips last autumn, and they were all gone by spring. Little devils. Had to put netting over them this year. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Always a battle, nature is. Always a balance. Give and take. My Arthur used to say… (trails off, momentarily lost in thought) …Oh, never mind. Old memories. Speaker_1: Is everything alright, Margaret? You seemed to… drift off. Speaker_3: Oh, just remembering. Lovely man, Arthur. Used to know everything about the wildlife around here. Used to point out all the different birds to me, names I’ve long forgotten now. It’s good to see them still thriving, though. Restores your faith, it does. Speaker_2: Right, well, I’d best get back to it. Just the kitchen to finish now. Is there anything else you need doing, love? Another cuppa? Speaker_1: No, you’ve been a lifesaver, thank you. And I definitely won’t miss Fred Sirieix now! We’ll have to chat about it next week. Speaker_3: He sounds a nice young man, this Fred. Perhaps I’ll watch it with you next time, dear. If my eyesight holds out.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the interview was… a disaster. I mean, genuinely. Speaker_2: Oh no! Really? I thought you were a shoo-in for that role at the language school. You've got loads of experience with their curriculum, haven't you? Speaker_1: That's what *I* thought! But the panel… they were so fixated on my experience with, like, phonetics. Which is fine, I’m confident with phonetics, but it was a general French teaching post! They kept asking me about minimal pairs and vowel sounds – I felt like I was back in my Masters, being grilled! Speaker_2: Ugh, that sounds awful. So rigid. Some schools are like that though, aren't they? All theory, no practical application. Were they at least nice? Speaker_1: Niceness is subjective when you're being interrogated about the intricacies of the French ‘u’ sound for twenty minutes. They were… efficient. Coldly efficient. And one of them kept interrupting me. Honestly, I nearly told him to let me *finish a sentence*. Speaker_2: Oh, the *nerve*! I hate that. I had a similar thing happen once, years ago, at an interview for a head of department role. This guy just kept talking *over* me, explaining my own experience back to me, but incorrectly. I just wanted to scream. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s so undermining. Anyway, I think I fluffed the lesson observation part too. I completely blanked on a past tense exercise. Blanked! Me, a French teacher. It’s mortifying. Speaker_2: Oh, don’t beat yourself up. Everyone has off days. You're brilliant with your students, you always have been. It was just one interview. Speaker_1: Easy for you to say, you’re happily teaching Year 5 and completely content. I'm apparently incapable of securing a proper job. Speaker_2: Hey! It's not always easy with Year 5, believe me. Especially when half of them have decided that glitter is a food group. But seriously, you'll find something. Have you thought about supply work again, just to tide you over? Speaker_1: I'm so over supply work. The constant traveling, the last-minute phone calls… it’s exhausting. Plus, half the schools don't even provide a proper staff room. You're expected to eat your lunch in a classroom surrounded by ten-year-olds and half-finished art projects. Speaker_2: True, that does sound… chaotic. Speaking of chaos, have you tried weaning little Leo onto anything other than purees yet? It's a battlefield over here. Speaker_1: Oh, God, don't even get me started! Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of Facebook now. It’s just… endless political arguments and people sharing those infuriating chain letters. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. This area really needs an infrastructure upgrade. Although, I suspect they're too busy arguing about parking restrictions to worry about something as important as reliable internet access. Cheers to glacial progress and reasonably priced gin! Let’s just hope Mark doesn’t turn up in his Mustang. I'm not sure this car park is equipped to handle that level of American muscle. Speaker_2: It's a disaster waiting to happen. Let's hope he sticks to Facebook for his grandstanding. Speaker_1: Agreed. Much safer for everyone involved. Speaker_2: Another gin, then? Just in case. Speaker_1: Definitely. You never know what Facebook – or Mark – might throw at us next. Speaker_2: Precisely. A little liquid courage is always a good idea. Speaker_1: And a good pub garden. This is why we moved here, isn't it? Despite the internet. Speaker_2: Exactly. The good outweighs the frustratingly slow connection, just about. Speaker_1: Just about! Speaker_2: Cheers.

Speaker_1: Right, pass us the remote will you, Liv? Honestly, this thing is a mystery. Three hundred buttons and I still can’t just…turn the volume up. Speaker_2: (Without looking up from fiddling with her phone) Just the red one, then the plus. Unless you want to go onto the guide. Speaker_1: The guide? Why would I want the guide? Remember when we watched this on repeat when we were little? Speaker_1: Vaguely. I mostly remember being desperate for a sandwich. And feeling slightly disturbed by the giant spaghetti tornado. Speaker_2: It’s about unchecked ambition, Ben. And consumerism. Don’t dismiss it. Speaker_1: Oh, here we go. A deep dive into the metaphorical significance of airborne spaghetti. Like, what happens when it *never* stops raining food? Speaker_1: Probably a lot of obesity. And angry farmers. Speaking of consequences, I had a right nightmare at work today. Old Mrs. Higgins was complaining about the price of biscuits *again*. Honestly, you’d think the end of the world was nigh. Speaker_2: Seriously? Biscuits? Speaker_1: Seriously. And then Gary spilled a whole display of fizzy drinks. It was chaos. I’m starting to think retail isn’t for me. Speaker_2: Well, no one said it was glamorous. At least you're earning money. I'm just living off student loans and the occasional handout. Speaker_1: Don’t sell yourself short. You’re smashing it at uni. And you’re getting loads of interesting stuff done in your art projects. Speaking of art, did you finish that piece you were working on? The…feminist one? Speaker_2: (Slightly defensively) I’m still working on it. It’s complicated. I’m trying to get the message across without being…preachy. Speaker_1: Just trying to sound out the topics for our assignment. Speaker_2: It’s about the male gaze, basically. How women are often depicted in art through a male perspective. And how *that* affects perceptions. Speaker_1: Right. Sounds…heavy. Speaker_2: It is! But important. It’s weird though, isn’t it, how different conversations are now? Like, when we were kids, you wouldn't have been asking me about the male gaze. Speaker_1: No, you'd have been trying to convince me Power Rangers were better than Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. Speaker_2: Exactly! And we definitely wouldn't have been discussing the socio-political implications of a cartoon about food. Speaker_1: Times change, I guess. Though, some things never do. Like my inability to operate a television remote. Seriously, is there a tutorial for this thing somewhere? And I'm feeling peckish, actually. All this talk of meatballs. Speaker_2: (Sighs) Just hold on a sec… I'll find a tutorial online. And there are crisps in the cupboard. Definitely crisps.

Speaker_1: So, you reckon they'll actually pull it off then? With the new regulations? Speaker_2: Pull what off, lad? You’re flitting about like a bleedin’ bluebottle. The regulations for what? Speaker_1: The football club, you know. Everton. With the new points deduction, and the stadium funding, the whole carry-on. Will they stay up? I’ve been reading all sorts of pessimistic punditry. Speaker_2: Stay up? Aye, they'll stay up. They always do, don't they? Bit of a wobble every now and then, keeps things interesting. But they've got grit, Everton. Unlike some of these soft southern sides. Speaker_1: Grit? I'm not so sure. It feels…different this time. It's not just on-pitch performance, it's all the financial turmoil. Reminds me a bit of the late nineties, actually. When everything felt a bit unstable. Speaker_2: The nineties? You mean when Major was stumbling about, trying to keep the Tories together? That was a right mess. Thought Blair was a breath of fresh air at the time, didn’t we all? New Labour, promise of a new dawn… turned out to be a bit more complicated than that didn’t it. Speaker_1: Complicated is putting it mildly. He was… persuasive, let's say. And the Iraq war… that casts a long shadow. Though, honestly, looking back, I’m not sure anyone had a good answer for Saddam Hussein. Speaker_2: Aye, but did we need to go sticking our noses into everything? America calling the shots, like always. The government then, thought they were invincible, didn’t they. Thought they could sell us anything. Speaker_1: That’s the danger of power, isn't it? And the spin. The constant spin. Remember ‘stakeholder society’? That was a brilliant bit of marketing, really. Sounded all inclusive, but basically meant everyone had a vested interest in propping up the system. Speaker_2: Stakeholder… aye, sounds posh. More like ‘stakeholder in the problem’ to me. Used to pick up MPs in my cab back then. All flash suits and promises. Never saw any of it filter down to the fellas working on the docks, you know? Speaker_1: That’s the rub, isn't it? The disconnect. It’s still there, really. Look at the cost of living now. While they’re arguing about tax cuts for the wealthy, people are choosing between heating and eating. Speaker_2: Aye, you’re right there. And they wonder why people are getting fed up. They need to spend a day driving a cab, listening to what people are *actually* worried about. Not just reading reports written by some jumped-up advisor in London. Speaker_1: Speaking of London, have you seen the latest polls? Starmer’s looking good, apparently. Though I still worry he’s a bit… bland. Lacks that charisma that Blair had, even if Blair *was* a bit of a rogue. Speaker_2: Bland is better than a liar, in my book. Though honestly, they’re all the same, aren’t they? Promised the world, delivered a handful of dust. Still, can't hurt to give someone else a go. Back to football though, you reckon Sean Dyche can turn it around? Speaker_1: I genuinely don’t know. He’s a solid manager, no nonsense, but Everton needs more than just a solid manager at the moment. They need a miracle, almost. And possibly a bit of luck.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I spent like, three hours yesterday just trawling through BNC recordings trying to find examples of specific discourse markers. It's… draining. Speaker_2: Three hours? Oh, no. That sounds genuinely awful. What markers were you after, specifically? Still the ‘like’ and ‘you know’ obsession? Speaker_1: (laughs) It started with ‘like’, naturally. But then it spiralled into trying to quantify the use of ‘so’ at the beginning of clauses. It’s a rabbit hole, I tell you. A linguistic rabbit hole. Speaker_3: (slightly muffled, from offstage) Sounds riveting. Are you two still on about work on a Sunday? Speaker_1: Sorry, Mum! No, we're just… commiserating. I’m complaining, mostly. How was your walk? Speaker_3: Lovely, thank you. Saw a very handsome pug in Victoria Park. Honestly, I’m considering getting one. Though your father would have a fit. Speaker_2: Oh, good luck convincing him! He's firmly a 'big dog' kind of man. Speaking of fits, I’m starting to think I need to seriously revamp my LinkedIn profile. Everyone seems to be landing amazing jobs, and mine feels… pathetic. Speaker_1: Don’t! You’re brilliant at what you do. LinkedIn is just a highlight reel, remember? People only post the good stuff. And you’ve been nailing the editing, haven’t you? Speaker_2: I have, yeah. It’s just… seeing everyone jetting off to conferences in the Maldives, or posting about their promotions… makes me feel a bit stuck. I really want to live abroad for a bit, you know? Like, Spain maybe. Speaker_1: Oh, Spain would be amazing! You’d love it. The food, the people… you’d fit right in. Though, you’d have to learn to embrace the siesta. Speaker_2: I could manage a siesta. It's just…the flying. I absolutely *hate* flying. It genuinely terrifies me. Speaker_3: You and your father. He practically needs sedating before every flight. Though he’d never admit it. Speaker_2: It's irrational, I know. I just… imagine everything that could go wrong. It's awful. Do you ever feel like that, Chloe? Speaker_1: A little. But I'm mostly just scared of turbulence. It feels so… uncontrollable. I was reading an article about someone who’s started a whole social media account dedicated to debunking flying myths. Apparently, turbulence is rarely dangerous. Speaker_2: Oh, interesting! Maybe I need to follow that. I'm spiralling already just thinking about booking a flight to Barcelona. Do you think Wales is nice? I’ve not really spent much time there. Speaker_1: Wales is *gorgeous*. Proper mountains, coastlines… it's very different from East London. You should visit. My aunt lives near Abergavenny, actually. You could come and stay. Speaker_2: Oh, really? That's so kind of you. Abergavenny, you say? That’s… well, that’s where I’m from! It’s been ages since I went back. My Nan still lives there. Speaker_1: No way! Small world. You could have a proper Welsh homecoming. And then we could all come with you. Mum would love a weekend in the mountains. Speaker_3: I absolutely would! Though preferably not involving any pugs. They’re cute, but rather… excitable. Speaker_1: See! Perfect. Operation Welsh Adventure is a go. Now, back to those discourse markers…

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, maybe a bit more chilli in this? It feels a little…flat. Speaker_2: A little flat is putting it mildly, darling. It tastes like tomato soup someone forgot to season. Definitely chilli. And maybe a squeeze of lime? Speaker_1: Lime’s good. You always know what this needs. Seriously, you should be a chef. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Don’t be silly. I just appreciate flavour. Speaking of flavour, did you ever get that tattoo you were talking about? The little fox? Speaker_1: Oh, yeah! Got it done last week. On my inner forearm. It's…surprisingly painful. Speaker_2: Oh, you poor thing! But worth it, I presume? Let me see… Speaker_1: (rolls up sleeve) Here. Be gentle, it's still a bit tender. Speaker_2: Oh, it’s *beautiful*. Really delicate. Clever choice. You’ve gone for proper artist then? Not one of those backstreet places? Speaker_1: Nah, proper studio in Shoreditch. Recommended by Maisie, actually. She had one done there a while back. *A knock at the door.* Speaker_2: That’ll be Chloe. Right on time. She said she was escaping the chaos of Christmas planning. *(Speaker 2 opens the door, and Chloe enters)* Speaker_2: Chloe, darling! Come in, come in. We’re attempting dinner, but it’s currently lacking…oomph. Chloe: (laughing) Sounds about right. Smells delicious regardless. What’s the Christmas situation looking like? My mother is already asking about guest lists and whether Aunt Mildred is bringing her questionable fruitcake. Speaker_1: Oh God, the fruitcake. That thing is a weapon. Speaker_2: I’ve told my sister I’m handling the turkey this year. It's a risk, I haven't done a turkey in ages, but at least I can control the seasoning. Unlike this chilli, apparently. Speaker_1: Hey! I’m adding the chilli now! It'll be perfect. So, Chloe, how’s work? Still drowning in submissions? Chloe: You have *no* idea. The interns are…enthusiastic, let's say. One sent me a manuscript entirely in Comic Sans. *Comic Sans.* I nearly lost it. Speaker_2: Oh, the horror! You’re a saint, Chloe, you really are. Speaker_1: Seriously? Comic Sans? That's…criminal. Is it a particularly terrible manuscript, at least? Chloe: It was a vampire romance, written entirely from the vampire’s perspective, detailing his struggles with online dating. It was… something. The cover was even worse. It looked like it was designed in MS Paint. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Sounds like you need a very large glass of wine. Speaker_1: Speaking of, I'm going to raid the wine rack. Anyone want a glass? While I’m there, does anyone know what’s happening with the bathroom renovation? I keep forgetting to call the builder. Chloe: Ooh, yes please to the wine. And I think I saw a quote from him on your phone yesterday? Something about needing to order tiles? Speaker_2: I'll remind you later. Honestly, that bathroom is going to be the death of me. It’s been six months now! But first, let’s focus on surviving Christmas…and a slightly improved chilli. I have attempted to abide by all given constraints in this conversation, including dialectal influence where appropriate.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this butternut squash risotto is taking *ages*. I think I underestimated how long it would actually take to properly toast the rice. Speaker_2: (Stirring a salad) Oh, you’ll be fine. It smells lovely though. Much more ambitious than my usual ‘throw some leaves together’ effort. Though, on that note, I did find a really good little Italian deli near work. They do these amazing pre-made salads with proper mozzarella and roasted vegetables. It’s a lifesaver when I’m on deadline. Speaker_1: Ooh, tell me more! I’m always looking for quick lunch options. Especially now I’m trying to be…well, less reliant on Pret. It’s a black hole for my bank account. Speaker_2: It’s called ‘Bella Italia’ - slightly unimaginative name, I’ll grant you. But seriously, it’s proper good. They do pasta boxes too, if you’re really desperate. Speaking of desperate, how *was* that pilates class you tried? You looked…determined on Instagram? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Determined is one word for it. Tortured is another. I genuinely thought my core was stronger than that. Everyone else was gracefully flowing through the exercises and I was… flapping. Like a stranded fish. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh no! I’m imagining the scene. I’m thinking of joining a barre class. Apparently, it's good for posture, which after hours hunched over a laptop, is probably vital for my survival. Speaker_1: Barre sounds terrifyingly elegant. I’m more of a ‘sweaty and vaguely in control’ kind of exerciser. Did you manage to book that weekend away to Lisbon then? You were talking about it ages ago. Speaker_2: I did! Finally. Flights are booked, and I’ve got a little Airbnb in Alfama. It’s supposed to be really vibrant. I’m proper excited. I was thinking of dragging Sarah along, but she’s got that conference in Barcelona. Speaker_1: Lisbon is amazing. You have to try the pastel de nata. Seriously, prepare to become addicted. And wander up to the São Jorge Castle, the views are incredible. Oh! And I bought this really ridiculous floaty dress when I was there last time. It’s completely impractical for everyday life, but it makes me feel like I'm in a film. Speaker_2: A film? What film? Speaker_1: I don’t know! A… romantic comedy? Something with a soundtrack and a lot of sunshine. I have a problem with buying clothes based on the *feeling* they give me, not whether they’ll actually fit into my wardrobe. Speaker_2: (Smiling) I can relate to that. Half my closet is a testament to impulse purchases I regretted five minutes later. Do you think this risotto needs more stock? It seems a little…solid. Speaker_1: Yes, definitely more stock. And maybe a bit more parmesan. It’s a work in progress, but hopefully, it won’t be a disaster. So, Lisbon…definitely pack comfortable shoes, you’ll do a lot of walking! Speaker_2: Noted. Comfortable shoes and a large appetite for custard tarts. It’s a plan. Speaker_1: Perfect. Now, let's rescue this risotto. Speaker_2: Right then, stock at the ready! And have you heard back about that grading for the French exams? You seemed stressed about it last week. Speaker_1: Oh, that. Yes, it’s all done. Apparently, they were really pleased with the standard this year. Which is good, I suppose, but it meant a *lot* more marking. My eyes are still recovering.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the things they come up with. I had a student today genuinely ask me if Plato was a real person. A *real* person! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You’re kidding. After a whole semester of reading him? Speaker_1: I wish I was. Said he thought it was a pen name, like, a collective of philosophers. I just… stared. It’s exhausting, isn’t it? Trying to build up from absolute zero with some of them. Speaker_2: It is. Though I had one who thought Machiavelli invented the word ‘Machiavellian’. Said he’d looked it up, and the etymology led straight back to him. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s good. That's a lovely little circle of misinformation. We’re fighting a losing battle, aren't we? Against the internet. Speaker_2: Probably. But at least it gives us something to talk about. Speaking of exhausting things… have you seen Sarah lately? She sounded completely frazzled on the phone. Speaker_1: No, not since… oh gosh, was it Ben’s birthday? She was complaining about her mum then, wasn't she? Speaker_2: Yes, the mum saga continues. Apparently, her mum’s decided she needs to ‘find herself’ and has booked a silent retreat in the Himalayas. Speaker_1: (Laughing) No way! That’s… ambitious. And Sarah’s stuck picking up the pieces with her dad. Speaker_2: Exactly. She said she hasn't slept properly in weeks. It’s amazing how one person can generate so much chaos. Speaker_1: It really is. And then she feels guilty for feeling stressed about it! It's a vicious cycle. Poor thing. We should probably invite her over for dinner soon, force-feed her carbs and wine. Speaker_2: Good idea. How about next week? Tuesday? We could try that new Sichuan place down the road. Speaker_1: Perfect. And maybe we can get her to talk about something other than her mother. Although honestly, that could be a full-time job in itself. Speaker_2: True. Oh, speaking of things needing attention… I think I need to cut my toenails. They’re starting to tap against my shoes. Speaker_1: (Grimaces) Oh, please, don’t. Not now. I’ve just managed to compartmentalise all thoughts of podiatric maintenance. Speaker_2: Sorry, sorry. Just a random thought. Occupational hazard of wearing uncomfortable shoes all day, I suppose. Speaker_1: You and your shoes. You'd choose comfort over style every single time. Speaker_2: Hey, practicality is key! Especially when trekking across Beijing. Besides, a man must be able to walk without fearing impalement by his own toenails. Speaker_1: Fair enough. Honestly though, the things I’ve seen students wear to lectures…it’s terrifying. Speaker_2: Don't even get me started. Speaker_1: It makes me long for the days of sensible shoes and tweed jackets. Speaker_2: Those days are long gone, my friend. Long gone. Speaker_1: Sigh. Well, at least we have Sarah's mother to provide some entertainment. The Himalayas, honestly. Speaker_2: It's brilliant, isn't it? Speaker_1: Absolutely brilliant. Speaker_2: Nearly home now. Speaker_1: Nearly. And hopefully, a shoe-and-toenail-free evening. Speaker_2: One can only hope. Speaker_1: One can only hope.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the whole thing was just *exhausting*. Three hours of polite conversation about pottery. Pottery, David! Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring his coffee) Right, your mother-in-law's pottery appreciation evening. You warned me. Still, gotta keep the peace, eh? Speaker_1: Peace? It was a hostage situation. And she kept referring to her latest…creation…as ‘organic’. It looked like a lopsided ashtray. Seriously. Speaker_2: Organic lopsided ashtray. Sounds… rustic. Did your husband ride to the rescue at any point? Speaker_1: He was being strategically charming to Uncle Bernard about the cricket. A full-scale tactical retreat. Left me to fend for myself against the earthenware onslaught. Speaking of strategic retreats, have you seen the new Bond film? Speaker_2: Not yet! Been completely swamped at work. Apparently, someone in accounts thought it was a brilliant idea to switch software mid-financial quarter. Chaos. Absolute chaos. Is it any good? Speaker_1: It’s… fine. A bit predictable, honestly. The villain was trying to take over the world by controlling the global supply of sustainably sourced quinoa. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Quinoa? Seriously? Speaker_1: I’m not making it up! And the love interest spent most of the film explaining the ethical implications of drone warfare. It felt less like a Bond film and more like a particularly tense university debate. Speaker_2: Sounds… woke. They’re really trying to update the franchise, aren’t they? Speaker_1: They are. And I’m not sure it’s working. Anyway, enough about culturally significant cinema. How’s Sarah? Still obsessed with that true crime podcast? Speaker_2: Oh, relentlessly. She’s convinced the local baker is a secret art thief. Apparently, he has a ‘shifty’ look and buys a suspicious amount of canvas. Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) A baker? Using canvas? Speaker_2: Apparently, he’s using it to… line his bread tins? It's a whole thing. She's spent hours researching the art world and the price of flour. She even tried to get me to go undercover and buy a loaf of sourdough. Speaker_1: That’s… dedicated. You didn’t, I hope? Speaker_2: Absolutely not. I have a company to run. Although, thinking about it, his sourdough *is* suspiciously good. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Don’t encourage her, David! She'll be staking out the bakery with night vision goggles next. It's like that Flat Earth thing my brother got into a few years ago. Completely unshakeable belief in the ridiculous. Speaker_2: Oh god, the Flat Earth thing. That was a fun Christmas. Trying to explain the concept of gravity to someone who genuinely believes the world is a pancake. Speaker_1: Exactly! And then he started talking about reptilian overlords… honestly. It’s worrying how easily people latch onto these things. Speaker_2: It is. Maybe it's the internet. Echo chambers and algorithms… it’s a perfect storm for conspiracy theories. Listen, I should probably get back to the software apocalypse. Anything exciting happening with the teaching next week? Any budding linguists causing mayhem? Speaker_1: Actually, yes… I have a student who’s convinced Shakespeare didn’t write Shakespeare. He’s building a PowerPoint presentation to prove it. Speaker_2: (Groans) Oh, dear god. Here we go again. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. It’s going to be a long week.

Speaker_1: Dad, are we nearly there yet? Seriously, my legs are going numb. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Nearly, love, nearly. Still a good few hours to go yet, though. Cornwall's a long way from Manchester, you know. Look out the window, isn’t the scenery lovely? All these fields… Speaker_1: It's… green. And fields. I’ve seen fields before, Dad. Are we going past Jamaica Inn at any point? I read that book for English and it sounded really creepy. Speaker_2: We should do, yeah. It’s a bit further down, near Bodmin Moor. Spooky place, supposedly. Your Grandma always said there were smugglers running around there back in the day. She used to tell us stories. Speaker_1: Did she? Grandma’s stories are always… exaggerated. Remember when she said she once met the Queen? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, she did love a good story, your Grandma. Speaking of colours, have you noticed how grey everything is? The roads, the houses… It’s all just fifty shades of grey. Like that book you were reading. Speaker_1: It’s not *just* grey, Dad! Look, there’s a yellow gorse bush. And those wildflowers are purple. It’s not all depressing. It reminds me a bit of the Wizard of Oz going from black and white to colour. Speaker_2: Good point, love. A good point. It does brighten up a bit when you look for it. You know, it’s amazing how much things have changed since I was a lad. Remember when you were learning about the telegraph? And Morse code? Speaker_1: Yeah, in History. It's like, why did people even bother? Just send a text! It’s so much easier. Speaker_2: Easier now, yes. But back then, it was revolutionary! Instant communication, even if it was just dots and dashes. Before that, it was telegrams, delivered by hand. Imagine waiting days for a message. Speaker_1: Sounds… awful. Though, I guess they didn't have their phones constantly buzzing. Speaker_2: True enough. It's a trade-off. Did you finish that Sherlock Holmes story for school? Speaker_1: Almost. It's good, but a bit… long-winded. And the language is really old-fashioned. Like Lewis Carroll. Why did they write like that? Speaker_2: They did things differently then. More descriptive. Building the atmosphere. It’s a skill, really. Like those old fairy tales. They're dark, aren't they? Not like Disney. Speaker_1: Really dark. But interesting. Hey, Dad, can we stop for chocolate when we fill up with fuel? I’m starving. Speaker_2: We can certainly discuss it. Depends how much fuel it’s going to take, and how much chocolate you think you need. We need to keep an eye on that caravan too, make sure it’s still attached. Speaker_1: It is! I checked. Are we going to be able to see the sea from the caravan park? Speaker_2: Should be able to, yeah. It’s right on the coast. We can walk to the beach. Build sandcastles, paddle in the sea… Speaker_1: And… can I have a bodyboard? Please? Speaker_2: (Smiling) We’ll see. First, let’s get to Cornwall. And then we’ll talk about bodyboards. Look, those wind turbines! They're massive, aren’t they? Producing all that clean energy. Speaker_1: They’re kinda cool. But they also kinda look like giants. I wonder what it would be like to live near one. Speaker_2: Probably quite noisy, I imagine. Oh, look! Those red houses… they look like they’ve been painted with strawberry jam. Speaker_1: (Giggles) Dad! You’re so weird. But… they *do* look a bit like strawberry jam.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this cake is amazing, Gran. Did you make it yourself? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Aye, lass. Old family recipe. Victoria sponge, it is. Though, truth be told, I had a little help with the jam. Betty down the road makes a proper set, you see. Mine tended to be a bit… runny. Speaker_3: It’s fantastic. Seriously.
