But I need a hobby that doesn't involve staring at a screen all day. Speaker_1: I get that. I've been trying to get back into painting. But… motivation is a struggle, you know? Netflix is just too tempting. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. It's a vicious cycle. We should have a 'no screens' night, just like we used to in school. Board games, terrible snacks… the works. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! That sounds perfect. We'll have to organise that soon.

Speaker_1: Right, okay, so I’m going to use my researcher to… build a research station in Atlanta. Because honestly, the outbreaks are popping up everywhere and we need to get ahead of this! Speaker_2: Atlanta? Bold move. Lots of potential for spread from there, though. Are you sure? I was thinking maybe Bangkok, to try and contain the Asian outbreaks. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Containment is a strong word, Rhys. We’re basically just delaying the inevitable with this game. Though I agree, Bangkok feels strategically smarter. Atlanta feels... ambitious. Speaker_4: I'm with Rhys. Atlanta feels like a gamble. Think about the connections, the airports… it’s a hub! Speaker_5: (Sighs dramatically) Oh dear. Another potential super-spreader city. Honestly, I’m convinced this game is designed to make us all feel inadequate. It’s a metaphor for life, isn’t it? Constant crisis management. Speaker_6: Oh, don’t be so gloomy, Gareth. It’s just a game! Though, you’re right, it is stressful. Anyway, I'm going to use my operations expert to fly to Cairo. We’ve got three cubes there already, and if we don’t deal with it now… Speaker_1: Okay, okay, Atlanta it is. I’m going for it. And I'm using my event dispatcher card to remove a cube from São Paulo. That's getting out of hand. Speaker_2: Good call on São Paulo. Right, my turn. I’ll use my scientist to treat a disease in Essen. Then I’m going to fly from Bangkok to… hmm… Chicago. I need to get closer to the action in North America. Speaker_3: (Grinning) Chicago? Prepare for chaos, my friend. That’s a risky move, right in the heart of everything. I’m going to use my medic to treat three blues in Moscow. Trying to keep that one under control. Speaker_4: Three blues in Moscow?! That’s… concerning. I’m going to try and build a research station in London and focus on treating the yellow outbreak. Speaker_5: Oh, London’s looking grim. I’m going to help out there. I’ll use my quarantine specialist to… quarantine London. Sacrificing a city to save the world, eh? It’s a tough choice. Speaker_6: Very dramatic, Gareth! (Laughs) I’m going to move my senior support worker from Cairo to Algiers. We've got a lot of support there to start treating. Speaker_1: Oh no, wait! I just drew an epidemic card! (Groans) And it’s… Asia! Oh, brilliant. More cubes in Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City, and… *another* one in Jakarta. Speaker_2: (Slams his hand on the table lightly) Seriously?! Jakarta again?! That’s the third time this game! It's cursed, I tell you, cursed! Speaker_3: (Laughing) Relax Rhys, it’s just a game... although, honestly, it *feels* a bit too real sometimes, doesn’t it? Reminds me of that time I got stuck in a typhoon in Phuket. That was properly chaotic. Speaker_4: Oh, tell us about that! Speaker_5: (Shaking his head) Honestly, all this talk of epidemics just reminds me of volunteering with the Red Cross after the Boxing Day tsunami. A truly harrowing experience. Games shouldn't remind you of things like that... Speaker_6: Well, here’s hoping we can cure these diseases before they cure *us* of our sanity. My turn again…

Speaker_1: Right, so, the CBeebies panto is booked! We’ve got tickets for the Saturday matinee. Are you both excited? Speaker_2: (Squeals) Yes! Will Mr Tumble be there? Speaker_3: Will they do the twelve days of Christmas song? That’s my favourite! Speaker_1: I think so, darling! They usually include all the favourites. It’s going to be brilliant. Now, about your birthdays… Elsie, yours is first, isn't it? Just after the panto. Speaker_2: Mummy, can we have a unicorn party? A really sparkly one! Speaker_1: A sparkly unicorn party sounds lovely! We'll have to start planning. And Leo, yours isn't far behind. Any thoughts on what *you* want to do? Speaker_3: I want a dinosaur party! With a big, big dinosaur cake! And a bouncy castle! Speaker_1: A dinosaur party, excellent! A bouncy castle might be tricky in the garden, depending on the weather, but we’ll see what we can do. Honestly, it feels like you two are growing up so fast. It was only yesterday you were obsessed with *In the Night Garden…*. Do you remember Upsy Daisy? Speaker_2: I remember! She always says ‘Upsy Daisy!’ Speaker_1: Exactly! You two have memorized entire episodes. Remember when Leo used to try and copy Makka Pakka's sounds? Speaker_3: (Makes a ‘Po!’ sound) Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh, you haven’t forgotten! It’s amazing how things stick with you both. Speaking of sticking with you, World Book Day is coming up. Have you started thinking about what you want to dress up as? Speaker_2: I want to be Princess Poppy! She's so pretty. Speaker_3: I want to be a pirate! With a sword and an eyepatch! Speaker_1: Perfect choices! We’ll need to get started on costumes then. And then, right after that… Mother’s Day. You two have got to think of something lovely to make me. Speaker_2: We could make you a card! With lots of glitter! Speaker_3: I can draw you a picture of a dinosaur *and* a pirate! Speaker_1: That would be the best gift ever! Honestly, I feel like we’re constantly juggling birthdays, celebrations, school events… it’s a whirlwind! Speaker_2: Mummy, are you tired? Speaker_1: (Smiling) A little bit, darling. But it's a happy tired. Having you both makes everything worthwhile. Now, who wants a biscuit? And then we can talk about the guest list for your parties... Speaker_3: Me! I want a biscuit! And I want all my friends from school to come to my dinosaur party! Speaker_1: Alright, alright, biscuits for everyone! And we’ll work on that guest list. But remember, a big party means lots of help packing up afterwards! Speaker_2: Okay! But can we have a unicorn piñata? Please? Speaker_1: We’ll see, Elsie. We’ll see… Let’s finish these biscuits first. Oh, and by the way, your Grandma called. She wants to know if you're both excited about seeing her this summer. Speaker_3: Yes! Grandma makes the best cookies! Speaker_1: She does, doesn’t she? We're planning a trip to the seaside with her in August. That’ll be lovely. It’s going to be a busy year, isn't it? But a good one.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weather is doing my head in. One minute it’s sunshine, the next it’s biblical rain. Makes planning anything… impossible. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I was going to cycle to that interview down by the river, but then the heavens opened. Ended up sprinting for the bus, looking a right state. Speaker_3: Did it go alright, the interview? You were a bit cagey about it earlier. Speaker_2: It was… okay. It’s a tiny little local paper, covering mostly council meetings and village fetes. Not exactly Pulitzer Prize material, but it’s a job. And nearish. Speaker_1: Better than nothing. You’ve been looking for a while now, haven’t you? Is the commute a killer though? That’s what put me off a place near Richmond. Speaker_2: It’s manageable. About forty minutes each way. Though, realistically, closer to an hour with the traffic. The real downside is the pay. It’s… modest. Speaker_3: Well, you’ve got to start somewhere, Liv. And it sounds like it would give you some good experience. Remember when I first started teaching? The kids were terrifying! Speaker_1: Speaking of terrifying, did you see what Mark put on Facebook? Another picture of his ‘perfect’ sourdough. Honestly, the man thinks he's Paul Hollywood. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, god. He's so competitive about baking. Remember that disastrous bake-off at Sarah's birthday? Speaker_3: Vaguely. Wasn't there some kind of incident with a collapsed Victoria sponge and a very offended aunt? Speaker_1: That was the one! Aunt Mildred hasn’t let him live it down. I’m still trying to figure out if moving to Bristol was a good idea. The job is good, genuinely, but I miss having proper pubs nearby. All they seem to have down there is craft ale bars. Speaker_2: Bristol’s lovely, though. Isn’t it a bit… gentrified now though? Everything's getting so expensive. Speaker_1: It is. That’s the problem. Rent is insane. I’m starting to think about maybe looking a bit further out, towards somewhere like Clevedon? Speaker_3: Clevedon's nice. Bit sleepy, maybe. Have you thought about Taunton? It’s a bit further, but the train links are good. Speaker_2: Ooh, Taunton. That’s an idea. What about you, Amelia? Still enjoying the language teaching? Have you had any particularly… interesting students lately? Speaker_3: Oh, you know. The usual mix. Couple of really enthusiastic beginners, one student who seems to think he’s fluent already, and a teenager who only signed up because his mum made him. It's never dull. I’m actually running a little online course this weekend, too. Trying to make a bit of extra cash. Speaker_1: Clever. You should put it on one of those… what are they called? Those dating sites? The ones where people list their hobbies and interests? You might attract a language enthusiast! Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) Now, now, Mark. Don’t go encouraging her to hook up with potential students. Speaker_1: I’m just saying! It's a good marketing opportunity! Plus, who doesn't love a man who can speak fluent French? Speaker_3: (Laughing) You are terrible. I’ll stick to the official language learning websites, thanks. Though, speaking of dating apps, have either of you had any luck? I briefly downloaded one, but it was mostly just pictures of men holding fish.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this book…it’s just…fluffy. All this talk about finding yourself through sourdough baking. Really? Like a complex emotional journey requires a perfectly proofed loaf? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, come on, Sarah. It’s a bit of escapism. We all need it. Besides, I’ve been meaning to try sourdough. Apparently, it’s all about the starter. My Nan used to have a starter, she called it ‘Bertie’. Speaker_3: Bertie? That’s amazing! My grandma just made everything from scratch, but she didn’t give it names. It was all just…practical. Yorkshire puddings the size of dinner plates. That’s her legacy. Speaker_1: My mum was a bit the same. Practical. She wasn’t one for hobbies, more for… well, making sure we had clean socks and decent packed lunches. I did have a weird obsession with My Little Pony though. Spent hours braiding their manes. Speaker_2: Oh, I had those! Rainbow Dash was my favourite. Remember how they smelled? That slightly plasticky, sweet smell? You can still buy them, apparently. For collectors. Ludicrous prices. Speaker_3: Everything’s collectible now, isn’t it? I vaguely remember having some…Stretch Armstrong? Was that a thing? Or am I making that up? He was all gooey, I think. Speaker_1: Oh yes! Stretch Armstrong. And the worry when he inevitably split and the goo got *everywhere*. My brother had him. He was absolutely furious when Mum binned him. It was a tragic loss in his eight-year-old world. Speaker_2: Speaking of tragic losses…work is driving me insane. Old Mr. Henderson is querying *every* expense claim. Even the postage stamps. Honestly, it’s like he thinks I’m personally trying to fleece the company. Speaker_3: Oh dear. Sounds familiar. I’ve got a new boss, used to be in finance in London. She’s all about “synergies” and “optimising workflow”. Which basically translates to ‘expect to work longer hours for the same money’. Speaker_1: (Sighs) It’s always something, isn't it? I'm dealing with a huge account at the moment, a shipping company. They want me to work miracles to get their costs down. They don’t understand that sometimes, cheap isn’t always best. Speaker_2: They never do. It’s the same with everything. You try to explain it logically, and they look at you like you’re speaking a different language. Honestly, sometimes I think people from Peterborough speak a different language. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, don't start! I get that with Essex all the time. "Oh, you're from Essex? So you… tan a lot?" It's just a stereotype! We're not all about the fake tan and the big hair. Though, admittedly, my mum *did* have some impressive hair in the 80s. Speaker_1: My dad always used to say people from Boston were the most sensible in the country. Which, honestly, I think was just his way of saying we were a little bit boring. But we got things done. No fuss. Speaker_2: Sensible is good. We could use a bit more sensible in the world. Right, anyone fancy another biscuit? I made flapjacks. And yes, they are from a packet mix, don’t judge. Sometimes practicality wins. Speaker_3: Flapjacks sound perfect! And no judgement, honestly. Practicality *always* wins. Especially after discussing gooey toys and demanding bosses.

Speaker_1: So, how was it then? Honestly? Was it as awful as you both made it sound leading up to it? Speaker_2: Awful is a strong word, love. Let’s just say it wasn’t *exactly* the idyllic seaside getaway we'd envisioned. Speaker_3: Idyllic? Ha! More like a seagull convention with chips. Honestly, they were brazen. Positively brazen. One tried to nick my sandwich right out of my hand! Speaker_4: (Chuckles) She wasn’t kidding. Brenda was wrestling a gull for a cheese and pickle. It was a sight to behold. Speaker_1: No way! You fought a seagull? Mum! Speaker_3: I didn’t *fight* it, I… defended my lunch. It was a perfectly good sandwich. And it had Branston pickle, you know how I like it. Speaker_2: The B&B wasn’t much better, mind. Right on the main road. Constant traffic. And the landlady… well, she was enthusiastic. About everything. Especially her collection of porcelain thimbles. Speaker_4: Oh, Doreen. She gave me a full tour. Each thimble had a story. A *very* long story. I think I aged five years just listening to her describe the history of one little German thimble. Speaker_1: A German thimble? That’s… ironic, considering. Speaker_3: Don’t start, dear. Yes, I know. Ironic. But at least she wasn’t talking about fishing all the time like Old Man Hemmings down at the harbour. Honestly, you couldn’t get a word in edgeways about cod. Speaker_2: Speaking of fishing, Dad did try to go out on a boat trip. Speaker_4: That was a disaster. Absolute disaster. The sea was choppy, I’ve got a dodgy back as you know, and the captain smelled strongly of kippers. I was seasick for three hours. Three hours! Speaker_1: Oh no, Dad! You and seasickness are not a good mix. Speaker_3: He turned green. A very fetching shade of green, I must say. They didn’t even catch anything! Just one tiny little whiting. Speaker_4: And a plastic bag. They hauled up a plastic bag. Symbolism, I tell you. Pure symbolism. Speaker_2: We did see a lovely beach though, one day, a bit further down the coast. We took Winston – he loved it. Chased the waves for hours. Speaker_1: Oh good! At least someone enjoyed themselves. Did you get any pictures? Speaker_3: Hundreds. Mostly of Winston looking utterly ridiculous. And Doreen’s thimbles. And a particularly aggressive seagull. Speaker_4: I’ve got one of me looking distinctly unwell on the boat. It’s a masterpiece of misery. Speaker_1: I want to see them all. This sounds like the most disastrous, and therefore hilarious, holiday ever. Speaker_2: It wasn't *all* bad. We did have some nice meals. There was a little seafood shack… Speaker_3: The chips were good. Despite the seagulls. Speaker_4: (Sighs) It was an adventure. A slightly chaotic, plastic-bag-and-thimble-filled adventure. Speaker_1: So will you go back? Speaker_2: Absolutely not. Speaker_3: Not if you paid me. Speaker_4: Unless Doreen promises to lock up the thimbles, and the sea agrees to be calmer. Speaker_1: (Laughing) I think we can safely say that’s unlikely.

Speaker_1: Right, who finished the milk? Seriously? I was going to make a proper coffee, not this… watery stuff. Speaker_2: Oh, was that you wanting milk? Sorry! I had a latte this morning. Didn’t even think. I'll grab some on the way back from yoga later, yeah? Speaker_3: Yoga already? You’re a morning person, aren’t you, Chloe? I'm operating on about four hours sleep. Deadline looming, you know how it is. I practically *lived* on coffee last week. Speaker_2: It's the only way to survive a Saturday deadline! But yeah, downward dog and a green smoothie are my attempt at being a functioning human being. How’s the article coming along? The one about the… dodgy property developer? Speaker_3: It’s… well, it's complicated. He’s got *layers*. And a very expensive lawyer. I’m trying to get a solid source who isn’t terrified to speak on record. It’s infuriating. Speaker_1: Sounds stressful. You need a proper breakfast, at least. I was thinking bacon sandwiches. Unless anyone's vegan-ing it up today? Speaker_2: Bacon sounds amazing, actually! I'm not vegan, just… trying to be mindful. But bacon is definitely mindful-worthy. Speaker_3: Oh, I'm in. Definitely bacon. Though maybe a slightly smaller portion. Trying to counteract the coffee and general life chaos. Speaking of which, did either of you see that ridiculous article about Harry Styles buying a goat farm? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) No way! A goat farm? What’s he going to do with a goat farm? Start a boy band for goats? Speaker_2: Apparently, it’s for sustainable wool production. Seriously! He’s trying to be all ethical and… fashionable? It’s a whole thing. Speaker_1: Ethical wool? That’s a new one. Honestly, celebrities. Anyway, less goats, more bacon. I'll get started. Anyone want brown or white bread? Speaker_3: Brown, please. Oh, and Liam keeps texting me about his phone. Apparently, it’s decided it doesn’t *want* to connect to the internet anymore. He’s convinced it’s a conspiracy. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Liam and his conspiracy theories! Honestly, he thinks everything is a plot. Probably thinks 5G is controlling his toast. Speaker_1: It’s probably just needs a restart. I could take a look later if he's still struggling. I'm pretty good with that sort of thing. Being an engineer and all. Though mostly I just fix robots that weld cars these days. Not exactly cutting-edge stuff. Speaker_2: Don’t undersell yourself! It’s still clever stuff. I just teach people how to say “hello” in French. It’s hardly saving the world. Though, arguably, good communication *is* important… Speaker_3: You’re enabling international understanding, Chloe! That *is* saving the world, one ‘bonjour’ at a time. Right, bacon sounds even better now. And maybe I’ll ask Liam to switch off his phone before I lose my mind. Speaker_1: Good idea. I’m going to put the bacon on now. Anyone want black pudding? Speaker_2: Ooh yeah, go on then! Treat yo’self on a Saturday! Speaker_3: Maybe just a small slice… I'm trying to pace myself before the article deadline descends again. Speaker_1: Pacing is good. Okay, bacon is sizzling! This is the life.

Speaker_1: Honestly though, I still don't trust Satnavs implicitly. Remember when yours sent us down that unmade farm track last summer? Speaker_2: Oh, don’t even! I was convinced it was taking us to a shortcut. Nearly lost the suspension on the car, I swear. Google Maps is generally better, though, isn’t it? At least it shows you what the road *looks* like beforehand. Speaker_3: Google Maps is alright. Still thinks Old Man Hemmings’ field is a public park. Keeps telling me to turn left into it. Speaker_4: (chuckles) Aye, they’re not always right are they? Used to navigate by the stars, we did. Less reliant on batteries and dodgy signal that way. Although, Saudi Arabia was a different story. No stars, just sand. And a lot of very stern men pointing things. Speaker_1: Saudi Arabia? You were stationed there, Reg? I didn’t know that. Speaker_4: A tour or two. Hot work. But good lads. Got a bit of a soft spot for the place, despite everything. Different world. Anyway, enough about sand. How's the decorating going at yours, Liam? Still haven’t managed to convince Sarah that magnolia isn’t a colour? Speaker_2: It’s an ongoing battle. We’ve got the living room done, thankfully. She finally agreed to a muted grey. But she wants bright orange in the spare bedroom. Bright *orange*, Reg. I’m fighting it, I really am. Speaker_3: Orange? That’s… bold. My Nan had orange wallpaper in the seventies. It was horrific. Speaker_1: Oh god, the seventies. I’m trying to avoid all design choices that scream ‘seventies’ at my place. It’s hard enough just finding affordable furniture, let alone stylish furniture. This admin job doesn’t exactly pay a fortune. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Project coordination is alright, pays the bills, but it’s not exactly setting the world alight. You thinking of moving on anytime soon, Chloe? Speaker_1: I might look around. It’s just… stable, you know? And the commute’s decent. Plus, it gives me time to do my masters. But yeah, maybe something a bit more… fulfilling. Speaker_3: I’m happy enough with the labouring. Keeps me fit, I reckon. And the money's alright. Though my back’s starting to complain a bit now. Speaker_4: You gotta look after your back, lad. Years I spent lifting things, marching. Wrecked my knees. Now it’s just a constant ache. Speaking of aches, how’s your mum doing, Liam? Haven't seen her since Christmas. Speaker_2: She’s alright, thanks Reg. A bit lonely since Dad passed, but she’s got her book club and her gardening. Keeps her busy. She keeps asking when you’re going to visit, you know. She misses your stories. Speaker_4: Oh, right. I must get around to that. Life just gets in the way, doesn’t it? Tell her I send my love, will you? And I’ll give her a ring next week. What about you, Chloe? Still in touch with any of your university mates? Speaker_1: A few. Lena's living in Berlin now, working as a translator. We video call occasionally. It’s hard to keep up with everyone, though. Life just… happens. We should all make more effort, really. Speaker_3: Anyone fancy another pint? I’m parched. Speaker_4: Go on then, lad. One more for the road. And let’s raise a glass to a good man, leaving for a new adventure. And to staying in touch, eh? We can't let another Christmas roll around without seeing each other.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I feel like I’ve been fighting off a cold for a week. Just this persistent tickle in the throat. Probably all the recycled air on the flights. Speaker_2: Oh, you poor thing. You need to be diligent with the hand sanitiser, you know. Everything goes around on planes. I swear I bring back a new germ with every trip. Are you taking vitamin C? I’ve started chucking a sachet in my water every morning. Speaker_3: Are you seriously still doing that, Helen? Vitamin C is basically useless unless you’re already deficient. It’s a marketing ploy. Honestly. Speaker_2: Oh, don’t be like that, Sarah! It can’t *hurt*, can it? And it feels like I’m doing *something*. Speaker_1: I’m trying to get loads of sleep, which is hard when you’re constantly shifting time zones. This garden is beautiful, though. Such a calming influence. Do you know what that one is? *points to a sprawling shrub* It looks almost prehistoric. Speaker_3: That’s a Rhododendron maximum. Quite invasive, actually. They’re constantly battling to keep them contained here. Apparently, they’re a nightmare in the Pacific Northwest – smothering everything in their path. Speaker_1: Invasive, huh? So beautiful, but a bit of a rogue. Sounds a bit like my uncle, actually. Speaker_2: *laughs* You’re terrible, David! But true. He’s a charmer, but he’ll walk all over you if you let him. Speaking of walking all over things, have you noticed how meticulously maintained everything is here? The paths, the borders… It's incredible. Speaker_3: It's down to a team of incredibly dedicated horticulturalists. And a huge budget, I suspect. The Swedish are very good at investing in green spaces. You see it all over Stockholm. It’s a real point of pride. Speaker_1: Makes you think about the council back home, doesn’t it? Half the flowerbeds are just weeds and the grass is knee-high. Speaker_2: Don’t even get me started. They keep threatening to cut the library budget. As if books aren’t important enough already! I’m going to write a strongly worded letter. Speaker_3: You and a million other people, Helen. It rarely makes a difference. I tell you what *does* make a difference – volunteering. Maybe we should suggest a garden clean-up day with the school? Get the kids involved, teach them a bit about botany. Speaker_1: That's a brilliant idea, Sarah. They could learn something, and it gets them off their screens for a few hours. Speaker_2: I’m in! Although I suspect a lot of them would prefer to be playing Fortnite… Still, worth a try. Oh, and David, seriously, go find some hand sanitiser. You’re glowing with impending doom. Speaker_1: Dramatic as ever, Helen. I think I just need a coffee. And maybe a slightly less intense shrub to contemplate. Speaker_3: There’s a lovely little café just beyond the rose garden. We could grab a fika and strategize about the school garden. Speaker_1: Sounds perfect. Lead the way. And I’ll invest in some potent hand sanitiser on the way. You two are relentless. Speaker_2: Only because we care! Now, don’t touch anything on the way. Speaker_3: Especially not your face, David. Especially not your face. Speaker_1: *groans playfully* You’re killing me. Literally.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Dad, you've lost *all* your London in the last few years. You sound practically Kentish now. Speaker_2: Kentish? What are you on about, love? I've always spoken like this! It's just… people don't talk properly anymore. All mumbly, you know? My ears ache trying to understand some of these youngsters. Speaker_3: Oh, don't start on the youngsters, Arthur. It's the sound systems on their phones. They're all shouting into little boxes. My ears are permanently ringing after a shift. Speaker_4: (Muttering) It's not their fault the signal's rubbish around here. You try getting a decent connection in Chatham. Speaker_1: It’s true though, Dad. You used to have that proper East End drawl. Remember when you'd tell us stories about growing up in London? You sounded like Michael Caine. Speaker_2: Michael Caine? I don't sound like Michael Caine! I sounded like my father, that’s who I sounded like. And he sounded like *his* father. It's… diluted, I suppose. Everything gets diluted. Like that washing-up liquid, always ending up too watery. Speaker_3: Speaking of watery, did young Daniel finally manage to sort out the custody arrangement with Sarah? I saw her in town, looking absolutely shattered. Speaker_4: (Scoffs) Sort it out? She's demanding half his benefits, that's what she's doing. And trying to paint him out to be some sort of terrible father because he…well, you know. Speaker_1: Because he struggles with a drink? Look, it's not helping anyone, Daniel. You need to get help. Honestly, watching you two is exhausting. Speaker_4: Easy for you to say, you're not the one stuck in the middle. She’s threatening to take little Maisie away for good. And she’s using his, you know…problems against him. Speaker_2: It’s a sad state of affairs, that. A child needs their father, even if the father's a bit…flawed. Back in my day, you stayed together. You worked at it. Speaker_3: Oh, Arthur, don't romanticize the past. You and Mum weren’t exactly a picture of marital bliss. Remember those shouting matches? And him locked in the shed with a bottle of whiskey? Speaker_2: (Grumbling) That was different. That was stress. The war… losing his job… Speaker_1: Okay, can we *please* not revisit the war again? I'm trying to write my dissertation and this is distracting me. Honestly, the stories… it's like living in a soap opera. Speaker_4: You should write about this! A family saga. You could make millions. Speaker_3: More likely end up needing therapy. And speaking of needing support…Arthur, are you still sleeping on that ancient mattress? It looks like it’s been through a war *itself*. Honestly, you'll do your back in. Speaker_2: It's perfectly comfortable! It's broken in. Like a good pair of shoes. Speaker_1: It's lumpy and smells faintly of mothballs. Honestly, I've slept on camping mats more comfortable. You deserve better, Dad. We could get you a new one. Speaker_4: Yeah, a memory foam one. They're supposed to be amazing. Though, knowing my luck, I’d probably fall *off* it. Speaker_3: Speaking of falling… did anyone see young Jamie on his bike yesterday? Nearly took out Mrs. Higgins' prize-winning roses. Speaker_1: Oh god, I did! He was zooming down the hill like a maniac, shouting about Minecraft. He needs to learn some road safety. This whole area is a nightmare for cyclists. And drivers. Honestly, it's a miracle anyone gets anywhere without a dent. Speaker_2: Everything was closer in my day. You could walk everywhere.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the Baked Alaska was a disaster. Utterly. Speaker_2: Why? What happened? Did it melt? Speaker_1: It didn't *melt* exactly. It… slumped. It slumped dramatically. I think the meringue wasn’t stiff enough, and the freezer isn’t quite cold enough. It looked like a sad, sugary island. Speaker_2: Haha! A sad sugary island. Did anyone eat it? Speaker_1: Your brother demolished most of it. He said it tasted fine, just looked ‘a bit wonky.’ He’s remarkably unfazed by culinary catastrophes. Speaker_2: Yeah, he’s like that. He’d eat anything. Sometimes, people’s own experiences colour their views, and they forget what it’s like to be young. It's not always intentional, but it doesn’t make it okay. It made me think about that thing you were telling me last week, about when you were starting out at work and people were… well, not very nice. Speaker_1: Oh, right. Yes. That was a long time ago, thankfully. There was a lot of… implicit bias back then, let's put it that way. And frankly, some explicit discrimination too. It was a very different climate. Speaker_2: What kind of discrimination? Speaker_1: Oh, all sorts. Being a woman in a male-dominated field, for starters. Having ideas dismissed because… well, because I was young and female. It took a long time for things to change. You have to be resilient and believe in yourself. Speaker_2: That sounds horrible. Speaker_1: It was. But it made me very determined to create a more inclusive environment for others. Which is partly why I’m so involved in recruiting now. Ensuring everyone has a fair chance. It's also why I get so very cross at any hint of unfairness. Speaker_2: Did they ever get into trouble? The people who discriminated against you? Speaker_1: Some did. Eventually. But it often takes a lot of courage to speak up. And honestly, sometimes it's a very slippery slope trying to define what counts as discrimination,

Speaker_1: This bacon’s lovely, mind you. Proper back bacon. You don’t get this stuff in Leeds anymore, not consistently anyway. Everything's streaky, all fancy. Speaker_2: (Mouth full) Mmmph. Speaker_1: Right, okay, my go. Ugh, seriously? Another vowel. This is hopeless. I’m never going to get rid of these ‘A’s. Speaker_2: Just play ‘AEIOU’, make a word. Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Very funny. A sign I need to disconnect. Although… disconnecting means missing important Candy Crush updates. It’s a dilemma. Speaker_4: Speaking of disconnecting, are you still hating your coursework? Depending on whether I can finish writing about the symbolism of pavlova in Victorian poetry. It’s…complex. Speaker_1: Right, I’m playing ‘ARE’. Eight points. Just to prove I can still function. And someone remind me to throw my phone in the sea later.

Speaker_1: Right then, finished that crossword, didn’t I? Took me a good hour. Dreadful clues, honestly. Speaker_2: Oh, good for you, Arthur. I haven’t had the patience for crosswords lately. Speaker_1: This is lovely, honestly. You both always outdo yourselves with these meals. What *is* this amazing sauce with the chicken? It’s got a bit of a…zing. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Well, good luck with the sourdough. And send pictures of the basil’s demise. It’s good to have realistic expectations, you know? Do you want me to continue the conversation? Or perhaps explore a different scenario? Speaker_1: Okay now I'm going to give a little pep talk to the basil. Speaker_2: Oh no. Speaker_1: The old man does not get the attention he deserves. It's going to start getting some love or I have nobody to blame but myself. Speaker_2: You're a little maniac you know that. Speaker_1: I'll own it. Now would you like a biscuit with this tea? Speaker_1: Right, so, Auntie Maureen’s definitely coming for Lily’s christening, then? She confirmed this morning? Speaker_1: Right then, who’s for another cuppa? Mine’s gone a bit cold, hasn’t it? Speaker_2: Oh, go on then, Arthur. I wouldn’t mind one. Though I really shouldn’t, should I? Doctor said… you know. Speaker_3: Said you shouldn’t enjoy life, did he? Nonsense. A good cuppa solves most things. I’ll have one too, thank you. Earl Grey if you’ve got it, Margaret? Speaker_4: Of course, Bernard. Just brewing a fresh pot now. Though honestly, Arthur, it’s the third you’ve had since lunch! Speaker_1: Well, what else is a retired man supposed to do? Sit and count the dust bunnies? Besides, it keeps the circulation going. You know what the doctor says about that. Speaker_2: He said you were to moderate your caffeine intake, Arthur, not have a free-for-all. Speaker_1: Moderate! That’s a strong word, isn’t it? I’m not a racing driver, am I? Just a simple man enjoying a simple brew. Speaker_3: He’s got a point, you know. A bit of tea and a biscuit – what harm can it do? Though I do remember your late wife, Elsie, keeping a close eye on your tea consumption. Speaker_1: Elsie was a force of nature, that one. She could silence a room with a single glare. And she had a particular fondness for strong tea herself, ironically enough. She'd say "Arthur, you'll be bouncing off the walls!" Speaker_4: (Bringing over the tea) Here we are. Earl Grey for Bernard, and… Arthur, I’ve made yours a bit weaker this time, just for peace of mind. Speaker_1: Weaker? Oh, now you’re just being cruel, Margaret. It'll taste like coloured water. Speaker_2: Oh, don't be silly, Arthur. She's just looking out for you. You know she worries. Speaker_3: It’s a thoughtful gesture. And a good brew needs to be appreciated. Though I confess, I’m rather partial to a digestive with mine. Anyone? Speaker_4: I’ve got some ginger biscuits, Bernard. They’re a little bit healthier, perhaps? Speaker_1: Ginger? Oh no, I can’t abide ginger. Gives me heartburn something terrible. A plain biscuit will do nicely. Speaker_2: Honestly, you lot. Arguing about biscuits now. It's a wonder we ever got through a childminding course together, Margaret. Remember little Timmy and the jam? Speaker_4: Oh, don't remind me! That was a disaster. Jam everywhere. It took me hours to clean up. And Timmy just sat there, giggling. Speaker_3: Children. They’re little agents of chaos, aren’t they? But they keep you on your toes. And honestly, a quiet life isn’t all it’s cracked up to be. Though a good cup of tea certainly helps. Now, pass the sugar, would you Margaret? Speaker_1: Just a half a spoon mind. Not wanting to go overboard. Speaker_4: Here you go Arthur. Always a sensible one you are. Speaker_3: Sensible? Arthur? Now *that's* a first. Speaker_1: Cheeky! I’ll have you know I’m a pillar of the community. Speaker_2: (chuckling) That’s a good one Arthur. A pillar! Speaker_4: Alright you two. Let’s enjoy our tea in peace.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this roast is amazing, Mum. You’ve outdone yourself. Speaker_2: Oh, go on! It’s just a bit of effort, isn’t it? Glad you all like it. Rhys, you having enough Yorkshire pudding? Speaker_3: (Mouth full) Loads, thank you. Best Yorkshire puddings ever. Seriously. Nothing beats a good Norfolk roast. Speaker_4: Absolutely. Reminds me of Sunday dinners at my Nan’s. Though hers were… considerably less refined. More gravy, less finesse. Speaker_1: Less finesse is putting it mildly, darling. Remember the time she put a whole clove of garlic in the custard? Speaker_4: (Laughing) How could I forget? I nearly choked! She insisted it was “for the flavour”. Speaker_2: She was a character, your Nan. Speaking of characters, did you lot see that protest in London on the news? The one outside the art gallery? Speaker_1: Oh, vaguely. Something about… funding cuts? Speaker_3: Yeah, apparently they're trying to shut down a really important community art space. Always happens, doesn't it? First the libraries, now the art centres. Speaker_4: It’s depressing. London’s losing its soul a bit, I think. Everything’s becoming too polished, too expensive. I was down there last week for a conference and the hotel was… astronomical. Honestly, five hundred quid a night for a room the size of a shoebox. Speaker_2: Five hundred! You're joking! I wouldn’t pay that for a week in the Bahamas. Speaking of which, are we still on for Cornwall this year? Speaker_1: I think so. We need to look at somewhere that’s dog-friendly, though. And not too far from a decent pub. That’s crucial. Speaker_3: You and your pubs! Though, I can’t blame you. Finding a good pub in Norfolk is easy, but elsewhere can be a nightmare. Speaker_4: It’s a skill, honestly. A highly refined skill. Did anyone hear back about those CRB checks for volunteering at the school, by the way? I’m supposed to be helping with the art club next week. Speaker_1: I got mine through yesterday. Everything seemed okay. They were surprisingly quick. Speaker_2: I’m still waiting. Honestly, the bureaucracy is ridiculous sometimes. It's not as if I've been up to no good. Speaker_3: You? Never! (laughs) You’re the most organised person I know. Speaker_2: That’s kind of you to say. Though, I did once accidentally hotwire a go-kart when I was eight… long story. Speaker_4: (Raises an eyebrow) *Hotwire* a go-kart? Now *that’s* a story. We need to hear this. Speaker_1: Oh, Mum, please! You always have the best stories. Before you start, though, anyone fancy another glass of wine? I think I can just about manage it. Speaker_3: Definitely. This Malbec is lovely. And I'm all ears for the go-kart saga. Seriously. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh alright. It involved a field, a slightly dodgy shed, and a very confused farmer… and before you ask, no, I don't know how I even *thought* about doing it. It was a strange childhood. And it definitely didn’t involve… well, it's a long story involving my cousin and a very difficult conversation about circumcisions, which is another story altogether. There is a pause as everyone laughs, anticipating a further detailed story.

Speaker_1: Right so spill. How was Italy? Honestly, give me all the details. Did you eat ALL the pasta? Speaker_2: Oh my god, it was incredible. Honestly, the best. And yes, I ate approximately my body weight in pasta. Carbonara, cacio e pepe, you name it, I devoured it. Seriously, I'm going to need to live on salad for a month. Speaker_1: Worth it though, right? Did you do much sightseeing or was it mostly just… food-focused? Speaker_2: A bit of both actually. Rome was amazing, obviously – Colosseum, Vatican City, all that jazz. But honestly, some of the best bits were just wandering around little towns, finding hidden restaurants, and people-watching. Oh, and the gelato. Don't even get me started on the gelato. Speaker_1: Sounds idyllic. Did you meet anyone interesting? Apart from all the handsome Italian chefs, obviously. Speaker_2: Haha! Well, there was this guy at a wine tasting… very charming, spoke terrible English, but we managed to communicate through gestures and a lot of laughter. It didn’t go anywhere, but it was fun. How was work while I was gone? Did everything implode without me? Speaker_1: It was… chaotic. Old man Hemmings decided to completely overhaul the project schedule on the Tuesday, then complained when no one could implement it immediately. Classic Hemmings. And Sarah keeps asking about Daniel. Speaker_2: Ugh, *still* going on about Daniel? Seriously? It’s been, what, two years? Speaker_1: I know! It's exhausting. She keeps hinting that maybe they were meant to be and I'm like, ‘Sarah, he cheated on you with his personal trainer. Move on!’ Speaker_2: Honestly, some people just love wallowing. Speaking of exes, have you heard anything from Leo? He messaged me a couple of weeks ago asking about you. Speaker_1: Oh god, no. Please tell me he didn’t try to get your number for ulterior motives. Speaker_2: No, no, it was just a genuine ‘how are you?’ message. I didn’t reply, obviously. I forwarded it to you, remember? Speaker_1: Oh yeah! Right! I completely forgot. I probably ignored it. Good. He’s a menace. Anyway, let’s not talk about awful people. What are you doing tonight? Fancy ordering a takeaway and having a proper catch-up? I’ve got that new true crime documentary everyone’s been talking about. Speaker_2: Ooh, yes! Perfect. I’m starving after all that healthy airport food. What kind of takeaway are we thinking? Indian? Thai? Speaker_1: Hmm, leaning towards Indian. I’m craving a proper curry. And we need to plan something for the weekend. I was thinking maybe that new escape room? Or we could finally go for a hike in the Peak District? Speaker_2: Escape room sounds fun. I'm always up for a challenge. Plus, it'll get me out of the house. Honestly, it's so weird being back. Feels like I've been gone for ages. Oh! And Mum wants to know if we’re free for Sunday lunch. The usual interrogation about my nonexistent love life to follow, I presume. Speaker_1: Oh definitely. Prepare for the third degree. And yeah, let's do Sunday lunch. It’s a tradition, after all. Right, curry it is then? I’ll get on ordering… and mentally prepare for Sarah’s Daniel-related ramblings tomorrow. Speaker_2: Sounds good. I'll grab some drinks. And brace yourself for Mum, she was *very* specific about wanting to hear about whether you’ve met “a nice young man” recently.

Speaker_1: Did you speak to Sarah today? How’s she doing? Speaker_2: Yeah, I gave her a call this morning. She sounded… tired. Really tired. Said the chemo’s hit her hard this week. Mostly just nausea, apparently, but it's knocking her for six. Speaker_1: Oh, poor thing. It’s awful isn’t it? Seeing her go through all of this. I keep wanting to *do* something, but she’s so resolute about just getting on with it, you know? Doesn’t want a fuss. Speaker_2: Exactly. And she’s really good at putting on a brave face. She was mostly asking about the kids, actually. Wanted to know how Leo’s doing in football practice. She didn’t want to talk about herself for long. Speaker_1: She’s incredible. It just feels so… unfair. I keep thinking about that holiday we all took to Cornwall last year. She was so vibrant, full of energy. It feels like a lifetime ago. Speaker_2: It does. It really does. Anyway, shifting gears slightly, I was having another look at Rightmove this evening. Anything new pop up in the village? Speaker_1: Just the old Miller place. Still ridiculously overpriced, even after that price drop. And the description is full of estate agent waffle. “Charming character property…” it's basically a crumbling cottage with a damp patch. Speaker_2: Right? It's taking the mickey. I’m starting to think we’re just going to be stuck here for the foreseeable. There's literally nothing coming up that ticks all the boxes. Four bedrooms, garden big enough for the dog, and not needing a complete gut renovation. It’s a tall order. Speaker_1: And affordable! Let’s not forget affordable. We need to think about the planning permission too, don't we? If we did manage to find something that needed work, getting permission for an extension could be a nightmare. Old Mrs. Henderson next door would object to anything. Speaker_2: You’re right. She'd probably argue it blocked her sunlight. Honestly, I sometimes think she just enjoys complaining. I saw her glaring at Mr. Davies for mowing his lawn before 9 am last week. Speaker_1: Oh, *please*. It's a lawn. It's not a sacred ritual. But you know what she's like. I think we need to lower our expectations. Maybe look at places a little further out, even if it’s a longer commute? Speaker_2: I’m reluctant to do that. I like being close to everything, the school, the shops… And I’m already spending enough time on the train as it is. But you’re right, we can’t afford to be too picky. We just need to keep looking, I suppose. It’s exhausting though, isn’t it? The whole house hunting process. Speaker_1: It is. And with everything going on with Sarah, it feels a little… frivolous to even be focusing on it. Speaker_2: I know. But we need to think about our future too. And we’ve been talking about moving for ages. Maybe just a bit less looking this evening, and more… telly? Speaker_1: Sounds good to me. And I’ll text Sarah later, just to see if she needs anything. Even if it’s just a chat. Speaker_2: Good plan. Speaker_1: Right then. What’s on? Speaker_2: I was thinking of starting that new David Attenborough series. Speaker_1: Perfect. Speaker_2: Although I suppose after talking about Sarah, maybe something a little less… existential?

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to dread coming in on a Monday. Not because of the work, but because of *them*. Speaker_2: Oh, don't even get me started. Who’s set you off this time? Is it the overflowing bins again? Because I swear, some of them think the communal kitchen is their personal dumping ground. Speaker_1: Worse, actually. It’s the music. Always the music. Boom, boom, boom, rattling the windows. And it’s always the same three songs on repeat. Like, do they not *own* headphones? Speaker_2: Ugh, the bass. It travels, doesn't it? I can feel it in my flat sometimes, and I’m two floors up. It's inconsiderate, plain and simple. I had a complaint last week about a student playing acoustic guitar at 11 pm. Acoustic guitar! Can you believe it? Speaker_1: Seriously? An acoustic guitar is hardly a rave. They're focusing on the wrong things. It’s the thumping bass I can’t stand. Makes my teeth ache. And it’s always when I'm trying to read. Speaker_2: Oh, reading. Don’t even. I tried to mark essays in the common room yesterday. Impossible. Between the music and the constant chatter, it was like trying to concentrate in a nightclub. Speaker_1: Right? And the leaving dirty dishes everywhere. I genuinely don’t understand how some people can live like that. It’s not hard to rinse a plate! Speaker_2: It’s a complete lack of respect, that’s what it is. For the building, for other residents, for *us* who have to clean up after them. I spent half an hour this morning clearing a mountain of pizza boxes. Speaker_1: Pizza boxes, yeah. That's a classic. It’s always pizza. Or instant noodles. Honestly, it’s like they’ve never seen a proper kitchen. Speaker_2: And the smell. The lingering smell of stale food… it’s disgusting. I've started carrying air freshener with me just to survive. Speaker_1: Good shout. I’ve considered industrial-strength bleach, but I suspect that would get me in trouble. It’s just… exhausting, isn’t it? Dealing with all this nonsense day in, day out. Speaker_2: It is. And the worst part is, you try to politely ask them to be considerate, and they just look at you like you’re the unreasonable one. “It’s a student hall,” they say. “It’s meant to be lively.” Speaker_1: Lively is one thing, a complete free-for-all is another. Honestly, sometimes I dream of a quiet life, far away from student accommodation and booming bass. Maybe a lighthouse keeper… Speaker_2: A lighthouse keeper? Now *that* sounds peaceful. Although, knowing my luck, even lighthouses have noisy neighbours these days. Speaker_1: You're probably right. Never mind. Another Monday, another wave of chaos. At least we can moan about it to each other. Speaker_2: Exactly. Misery loves company, as they say. Now, where did I put that air freshener…? Speaker_1: Is it going to be awful tonight? Speaker_2: I've got a feeling… I really have a feeling. And have you seen how many Deliveroo bikes are parked outside? Brace yourself. Speaker_1: Oh god. Here we go again. Speaker_2: Yep. Here we go. Speaker_1: Want a coffee? Maybe caffeine will dull the pain. Speaker_2: Yes, please. Make it a strong one. I think I’m going to need it.

Speaker_1: Honestly, seeing those people in Bruges pretending they’d *discovered* Belgium was hilarious. Like, you're on a package tour, Sheila, it's not an archaeological dig! Speaker_2: Package tours aren’t so bad, love. Keeps things… organised. Though I did overhear a bloke complaining the beer wasn’t ‘British enough’. British enough! In Belgium! Speaker_3: Oh, don’t get me started. My sister Doreen went on one to Germany last year. Came back moaning the sausages weren't Cumberland. Honestly. You can’t take some people anywhere. Speaker_1: Exactly! And they all flock to the Christmas markets. It's just a load of overpriced trinkets and gluhwein, isn't it? Though, I did get a lovely hand-painted bauble in Antwerp… Speaker_2: Antwerp’s nice. Bit busy, though. Reminds me of Brighton on a Bank Holiday. Traffic’s murder. Though, Brighton's traffic is always murder, isn't it? Even *walking* along the seafront is a contact sport these days. Speaker_3: Tell me about it. I had to fight my way through a gaggle of stag-dos just to get to the pier yesterday. Honestly. And then a swarm of pigeons descended on my ice cream. Speaker_1: Oh, no! That’s dreadful! I'm trying to learn Dutch, actually. Figured if I’m going to be traipsing around the Low Countries, I should at least be able to order a waffle without sounding like a complete idiot. Speaker_2: Dutch, eh? Good luck with that. Sounds like someone gargling pebbles. I tried a bit of Spanish once, when we were thinking of retiring to… somewhere warm. Didn’t get very far. Speaker_3: Speaking of retiring, how’s your neighbour, Mr. Henderson, coping? He seemed dreadfully lost when he finished work. Speaker_2: He's alright, I think. Mostly potters about in the garden now. Says he’s taken up birdwatching. Apparently, there’s a rare spotted flycatcher visiting his apple tree. Can't say I've ever noticed a flycatcher. Speaker_1: That sounds…peaceful. It’s just, I’m already dreading the thought of finishing my degree and then… what? The ‘real world’ seems terrifying. Speaker_3: You'll be fine, love. You're a bright girl. Remember my Terry? Always said university was the best thing he ever did. Though his boys were his pride and joy. Raising boys is… a different kettle of fish. Speaker_2: It is that. All mud and noise. Mine were always covered in something or other. Though they turned out alright. One’s a solicitor, the other’s… well, he’s a musician. Pays the bills, eventually. Speaker_1: Sounds like a good mix. Mum keeps reminding me I need to start thinking about Christmas shopping. It's only October! Speaker_3: Oh, don’t leave it till December, darling. Herne Bay is a nightmare then. Full of day-trippers and people arguing over parking spaces. Speaker_2: You know, I saw a little puppy in the park the other day. Tiny thing, a Jack Russell. Reminded me of Buster, bless him. Twenty years gone now. Speaker_1: Oh, Dad. It still gets to me, you know? Just… vanished. So quickly. Speaker_3: It does, love. It really does. Still miss my mum, even after all these years. Remember her awful rhyming slang? She used to call money ‘Barnet Fair’. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, she was a character, your mum. Always had a phrase. Hers was ‘apples and pears’ for stairs, wasn’t it? Speaker_1: Yes! And everything was ‘trouble and strife’, which, looking back, was probably quite accurate. Still, good times. Do you think we should head for a walk along the seafront after this?

Speaker_1: Seriously though, this Ireland thing is huge, isn't it? All that stuff about legalising same-sex marriage… it's mad to think it wasn't already. Speaker_2: It *is* massive. And genuinely moving. My auntie Maureen was over there for a bit, visiting her friend, and she said the atmosphere was electric. Everyone just…happy. Speaker_1: It’s just… basic equality, isn’t it? Like, why even *have* a vote on that? Should just be a given. Makes you think about all the other stuff that's still messed up. Speaker_2: Exactly! And it's not like Ireland’s some super-progressive place, historically. That makes it even more impressive. It shows things *can* change, you know? Even quickly. Speaker_1: Yeah. Mr. Henderson was talking about it in history today, saying it showed a real shift in societal values. He went on a bit, as he does. Speaker_2: Oh, Mr. Henderson. Always one for a lecture. Did he mention anything about how much the Catholic church opposed it? Speaker_1: Yeah, he did. Apparently, they were throwing everything at it, trying to scare people. Didn’t work, though. Speaker_2: No! Good. Honestly, some of the things my mum says… you wouldn’t believe it. She was going on about ‘the sanctity of marriage’ and I was like, “Mum, you've been married three times!” Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, that's brilliant! My mum wouldn’t say anything like that, she’s too… embarrassing in other ways. Like, she tries to be cool and ‘down with the kids’ but it just never works. Speaker_2: Oh, we all have those mums. Mine tried to use a TikTok dance at my cousin’s wedding. It did not go well. Speaker_1: No way! Oh god. That's amazing. Speaker_2: Traumatic, actually. Anyway, back to Ireland. It’s just… uplifting. It gives you a bit of hope, doesn't it? Speaker_1: It does. It’s a lot better than listening to the news about everything else going on. Speaking of which, have you seen what old man Peterson is saying now? He’s claiming that… Speaker_2: Oh, don't even get me started on Peterson. That man lives in a bubble of his own making. Honestly, it's like he’s deliberately trying to provoke people. Speaker_1: Exactly! It's just… tiring. Speaker_2: It is. Right, enough politics. It’s nearly your birthday, isn't it? Are you thinking about a party? Speaker_1: I don’t know. Maybe just a few mates. Don't want anything too big. Plus, I'm worried Mum will try and organise another TikTok dance. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Fair enough. We'll protect you. We’ll form a human shield. Rest assured, no unwanted choreography will be inflicted upon you. Although, maybe we should film it if it happens… for posterity. Speaker_1: Seriously, don't. Please. Speaker_2: Okay, okay. Deal. But you have to promise me one thing. Speaker_1: What? Speaker_2: You have to have a proper cake. Last year’s “cake” was basically a biscuit with a candle stuck in it. It was a tragedy. Speaker_1: Hey! It was efficient. And tasty! Speaker_2: It was a biscuit, Liam! A biscuit! We need a real cake. With frosting. And sprinkles. Speaker_1: Alright, alright. A real cake. You’re boss. But you're helping me bake it, just so you know. My baking skills are limited to making toast.

Speaker_1: Right well, that was a good bit of sausage, that was. Not quite Doreen’s, mind you. She could make a sausage sing, Doreen could. Speaker_2: She could indeed. Remember that time she entered that sausage competition at the village fete? Proper Norfolk sausage, it was. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Oh, I remember. Old Mr. Henderson nearly had a fit when he found out she’d used his secret spice blend. Thought she’d stolen it! Speaker_1: Aye, a right kerfuffle that was. But Doreen, she just batted her eyelashes and said it was a tribute. Worked a treat, it did. Won her a blue ribbon, it did. Speaker_2: She always was a charmer. Though, speaking of…Have you seen young Timmy’s hamster? I can’t find Mr. Nibbles anywhere. Speaker_1: (Frowning) Now that *is* odd. He usually squeaks like a rusty gate whenever you’re about. Speaker_3: Good heavens, don't tell me… did anyone leave the microwave door open again? Speaker_2: Oh, don’t even *say* that, David! Little Alfie did it last year with his goldfish! We didn’t speak to him for a week. Speaker_1: (Eyes widening) A goldfish? In the microwave? Good Lord. They don’t learn, do they? Remember when I was an apprentice, old Mr. Finch…he had a lad, just starting out, put a lathe tool in the grinder? Speaker_2: Oh dear. Not a good idea. Speaker_1: No, not a good idea at all! Thing exploded, sent sparks flying everywhere. Nearly took his eyebrows off. Mr. Finch went absolutely purple. Said something about ruining a perfectly good tool and a perfectly good Friday afternoon. Speaker_3: Lathe tools are serious business. Precision engineering, and all that. You wouldn't put one in a microwave, would you? Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Wouldn’t dream of it! Though, I reckon a bit of steel would probably do more damage to a microwave than a hamster. Speaker_2: (Standing up) Right, I’m going to have a look. This is giving me palpitations. Honestly, these children… it’s a wonder anything survives. I’m checking the microwave *first*. Speaker_3: Just be prepared for the worst, Margaret. It’s probably just hiding, though. Hamsters are notoriously sneaky. Speaker_1: Sneaky little blighters, they are. Give me a good piece of sausage any day. Less stress involved. More flavour, too. Speaker_2: (Calling from the kitchen) Oh… my… goodness. You are *never* going to believe this. Speaker_3: (Exchanging a worried glance with Speaker_1) What is it? What’s happened? Speaker_1: (Sighing) Oh dear. Here we go. Speaker_3: Well, don’t leave us in suspense, Margaret! Speaker_2: (Returning, looking utterly bewildered) It's not *in* the microwave... it's *on* top of it… wearing Alfie’s little cowboy hat. Speaker_1: (Bursting into laughter) On top of the microwave?! Wearing a cowboy hat?! That little rascal! Speaker_3: (Smiling) Well, that’s a relief, at least. And certainly a story for the grandchildren. Speaker_1: A story indeed! Mr. Nibbles, the cowboy hamster! Now *there’s* a tale.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of things… I saw a headline today about a cat who’d apparently ordered things online using its owner’s Amazon account. Just… pawing at the screen! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You’re kidding! A cat? Ordering what, cat food? More scratching posts? Speaker_3: It's a sign of the times, isn't it? Everything online, everything automated. Reminds me of those stories about mirror writing. Did you know Leonardo Da Vinci was a prolific mirror writer? Though I suspect this cat wasn't making a grand artistic statement. Speaker_1: No, I think it was… Christmas decorations, apparently. The owner woke up to a dozen inflatable Santas arriving. It’s just utterly bizarre. Speaking of bizarre, did you see the latest figures on house prices? They’re absolutely ludicrous. Speaker_2: Don’t even *start* me on house prices. We’re effectively priced out of moving anywhere remotely decent. It's discouraging. I was looking at a tiny terraced place near the park, and it’s gone up £30,000 in six months. Speaker_1: It's madness. You'd think they’d want people to *be able* to buy houses. It all feels so… unfair. And the banks aren’t helping, are they? Still offering ridiculously small interest rates on savings, while simultaneously making a fortune off mortgages. Speaker_3: Banks have always been… opportunists. I remember back in the 80s, the building societies… even then, they weren’t known for their generosity. Though, things were simpler then. Less reliance on technology, less debt, less… everything. Speaker_2: Simpler, maybe. Not necessarily better. Remember when you had to actually *go* to the bank to pay bills? Queuing for ages? Speaker_1: (Sighs) I do. And now we’re all worrying about online security, passwords, phishing scams… it's exhausting. I’m trying to do that cryptic crossword, but even *that* feels tech-influenced. Clues about algorithms and social media influencers! Speaker_3: Cryptic crosswords are a dying art. They require a certain… lateral thinking. Something I fear is diminishing in the younger generation. Although, perhaps I’m just being a grumpy old woman. Speaker_2: You’re not grumpy! Just… discerning. Have you been following the American political scene at all? It’s like watching a train wreck in slow motion. Speaker_1: Don't even mention it. I try to avoid it. It’s all so… draining. It feels like the world is perpetually on the brink of some sort of disaster. Speaker_3: Exactly. It's best not to dwell. Have either of you noticed they’re charging for plastic bags again? Five pence? As if that’s going to solve anything. It’s just another way to squeeze money out of people. Speaker_2: It’s performative environmentalism. Makes them *look* like they’re doing something, without actually addressing the core problem. And frankly, I always forget my reusable bags anyway. Speaker_1: Me too! It’s a constant struggle. Speaking of struggles, how are things going with…? Oh, never mind. Probably not the best time to bring up marital issues before dinner. Speaker_3: Nonsense, dear. We are family. What's on your mind? It’s always better to talk. Speaker_1: Oh, well… it's just… David and I have been bickering a bit lately. Over finances, mostly. He thinks I spend too much on… well, everything. Speaker_2: That sounds familiar. It’s always about the money, isn't it? Speaker_3:Indeed. A common source of discord in any marriage. Perhaps you need to sit down and have a proper chat, lay everything out on the table. Gentle persuasion, darling. It often works wonders.

Speaker_1: Right, books away. Tablets away. It’s nearly bedtime, and we’ve talked about this. No screen time thirty minutes before bed. Speaker_2: But Mummy! I was *just* about to finish building the Ninja temple in Lego Ninjago Tower! It’s almost done! Speaker_3: Yeah, and I was about to fight the End Dragon in Minecraft! I needed one more diamond! *One* more! Speaker_1: I know, I know. It’s frustrating, isn't it? But your eyes need to rest. All that glowing… it makes it harder to fall asleep. Speaker_2: But Kai has a new spinjitzu master technique! I haven’t even tried it yet! Speaker_3: And the End Dragon has a new armour! It's super strong! I think I need another one after the thought of that stock take. Speaker_3: Me too. Oh, and Mum, did you ever manage to find out what happened with Auntie Brenda’s cat? You were saying something about it being missing when you were on the phone last week? Speaker_1: Oh, poor little Winston! Yes, she found him. Always getting into mischief. Speaker_3: He is! Last time I saw him, he was trying to steal a biscuit off my plate. It was hilarious. Speaker_1: He’s a little rogue, that one. Alright, refill time. Then maybe we can start brainstorming Gran’s birthday, and then maybe a little trip into town? Sound good? Speaker_2: Perfect. Speaker_3: Sounds lovely, Mum. Thanks for having us. Certainly, let me know if you would like me to continue the conversation further or tweak it in any way! Speaker_1: Oh, yes by the way, I got a call from Uncle Geoff whilst I was sorting through photos. Boxing Day lunch sounds good. Hopefully, it doesn't clash with any work commitments for me. Speaker_3: Yeah, that'd be brilliant. It'll be chaos, as always, but a good kind of chaos. I'm sure everyone will want to make up for lost time. Speaker_1: That's what I said to him. Although, knowing the family, there's bound to be some sort of drama, isn't there? Someone will inevitably fall out over something silly. Speaker

Speaker_1: This sandwich is… underwhelming. Seriously, five quid for this? It’s mostly bread. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I got the chicken and bacon and it tastes like sadness. Should’ve gone to Greggs. Speaker_3: Honestly, Greggs is a lifesaver. Or we could’ve just gone to that little cafe near the station. Remember, the one where Old Man Hemmings always is? He went on about tactical disadvantage the other day and didn’t even mention logistics. It’s like he thinks war is all glory and no, you know, actual stuff. Speaker_3: Speaking of which, did you see that documentary on Channel 4 last night about the Ukrainian conflict? It was… intense. Speaker_1: Yeah, I caught bits of it. Proper bleak. Makes you think, doesn’t it? All that stuff happening, and we’re here worrying about sandwich fillings. Speaker_2: It does. Although, honestly, I need a distraction. Anyone fancy a game of Magic: The Gathering after this? I finally built my new deck. Speaker_3: Ooh, yes! I’m in. I’ve been practicing with my enchantress build. Prepare to be defeated, boys. Speaker_1: Oh, it is *on*. I’ve got a new rare card I’ve been saving. It’s going to wreck everyone. By the way, did they announce the new Head Boy and Girl yet? Speaker_2: Not yet. Apparently, Mrs. Harris is making a whole song and dance about it during assembly on Friday. I heard Lizzie Thompson is a frontrunner. Speaker_3: Ugh, Lizzie? Really? She’s so…perfect. Like, suspiciously perfect. I bet she’s got a whole team of people stage-managing her life. Speaker_1: Maybe. I'm hoping for Raj. He's actually a decent guy, and not afraid to speak his mind. Although he did get in trouble for pointing out that the school’s Diversity and Inclusion policy felt…a bit tokenistic. Speaker_2: Yeah, that was a bit awkward. Then Mr. Peterson went all red in the face. It’s just, sometimes it feels like they're ticking boxes, you know? Like they *have* to have a certain number of kids from different backgrounds, even if it doesn’t feel genuine. Speaker_3: It’s like when they made that whole fuss about Black History Month, but then nothing changed the rest of the year. It’s performative activism. Speaker_1: Exactly! Anyway, enough about school politics. Anyone watching the new season of 'Stranger Things'? Speaker_2: Dude, yes! It’s so good. Vecna is terrifying. Speaker_3: Totally! And the 80s soundtrack is amazing, as always. Right, game time? I'm shuffling my deck. Let's see who's the Magic master.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mr. Davies is the *worst* physics teacher ever. He just stands there and drones on and on. You can tell he doesn't even *like* teaching. Speaker_2: Seriously! I thought it was just me. He explains everything so… complicatedly. Like, he’s trying to be clever but it just makes it harder to understand. Remember when he was trying to explain momentum? It took him like, fifteen minutes to get to the actual formula. Speaker_1: Oh my god, YES! And then when someone finally asked him to simplify it, he just sighed and repeated it louder. As if volume equals comprehension? Speaker_2: Exactly! And he keeps using phrases like ‘as we’ve previously established’ when half the class has literally just switched off. It’s so condescending. Speaker_1: Ugh, and Mrs. Peterson, our form tutor, is just… absent. She never seems to notice anything. Like, Ben was crying in the corner yesterday and she just walked past! Speaker_2: What?! No way! I didn’t even see that. Honestly, she just spends the whole time on her phone. I swear she's playing Candy Crush or something. Speaker_1: I think she is! Seriously. She barely makes eye contact. Speaking of eye contact, did you see Chloe trying to flirt with Mr. Harrison in the library today? Speaker_2: *No way!* Chloe? Mr. Harrison? That's… ambitious. He's like, ancient. Speaker_1: I know, right? It was so awkward. He just sort of stared straight ahead and pretended she wasn’t there. It was glorious. Speaker_2: Haha! Oh, did you finish that English reading assignment? The one on *To Kill a Mockingbird*? I’m so behind. Speaker_1: Nearly. I’m on chapter… ten, I think? It's actually really good, though. A bit slow at the beginning, but it's picking up. Speaker_2: Really? I’m struggling. It just feels… heavy. And Miss Evans keeps asking us really deep questions about symbolism and I just want to scream ‘I don’t know!’ Speaker_1: I know what you mean. She’s intense. Oh! Have you seen the trailer for that new film, *17 Again*? Speaker_2: Ooh, no! Is it good? Speaker_1: It looks hilarious! Like, Matthew Perry goes back to being seventeen? Imagine! It’s totally my fantasy to relive high school, but like, knowing everything I know now. Speaker_2: That would be amazing. You could avoid all the embarrassing moments. Oh, speaking of embarrassing moments, did you hear what happened with Liam and the custard in the canteen? Speaker_1: *Oh my gosh!* Tell me everything! Speaker_2: Apparently, he was trying to throw it at George, but he missed and it landed right on Mrs. Bell’s head! She was NOT impressed. Speaker_1: NO! Liam is so reckless! Honestly, that boy. What a disaster. I bet he's in detention for a week. Speaker_2: Pretty sure. It was epic, though. Everyone was trying not to laugh. It was so hard! Speaker_1: Seriously. School is… a lot. Speaker_2: You have no idea. Sometimes I just want to disappear. Speaker_1: Me too. Maybe *17 Again* will make everything better. Speaker_2: Hopefully! Or at least distract us for a couple of hours. Speaker_1: Definitely.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the thought of Monday… it’s actively making my stomach churn. Need a plan, *something* to look forward to after this weekend’s done. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Though, work wasn’t *terrible* today. Managed to perfect that sourdough recipe, finally. Old Man Hemmings practically wept with joy when he tasted it. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Hemmings cries over everything! Remember when Brenda accidentally put salt instead of sugar in his coffee? Thought the world was ending. Speaker_4: Right? Drama king. Speaker_3: (Grimaces) I know, I know. It’s a last resort. Honestly, the man’s tastebuds are…questionable. Besides, down under, we say “sharp as a tack,” not “sharp as a hawk.” Different hemisphere, different metaphors. Speaker_2: That’s a good one! You’re really starting to sound like a proper Aussie, Liam. Speaker_3: What are we all up to this weekend then? Anyone got plans beyond wallowing in post-work freedom? Speaker_1: I was thinking of hitting up that new exhibition at the Tate Modern. Anyone fancy it? Speaker_2: Ooh, that sounds good! I’m in. I need a bit of culture after a week of flour and sourdough. Speaker_4: Count me in too. And then maybe we could grab dinner somewhere afterwards? I’m craving a decent curry. Speaker_3: Perfect! I’ll check the rota and see if I can escape Hemmings’ clutches. Speaker_1: Right, so the playlist for the party… I was thinking a bit of everything? Some 80s, some current stuff, a little bit of… what do you guys like at the moment? Speaker_1: Right, well, that was a good bit of pizza, wasn’t it? Not too much garlic, thankfully. Reminds me of when your mother… bless her… tried to make a pizza from scratch. Though, I do wish she wouldn’t post everything online. It’s just… everything is out there now isn’t it? Like when I tried to take a photo of your hair yesterday, Arthur, and you threatened to wrestle me… Speaker_1: (Grumbling) I did *not* threaten to wrestle you! Speaker_1: Right, your move, love. Don’t think too long, you’ll wrinkle your forehead. Speaker_2: (Examining the board) It’s just… so many possibilities. It’s quite overwhelming, isn’t it? Looked a right mess. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even *start* on variations. Stick to the proper rules, that’s what I say. Speaking of rules, are you remembering about the cannon? Thinking three steps ahead. Like a good politician. Though looking at Westminster these days, maybe that’s not a good example. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You’re not wrong there. Did you see that piece about Scotland wanting another independence referendum? Honestly, it’s just back and forth, isn’t it? Never ending. Speaker_2: It’s… complicated. A lot of it stems from Brexit, I think. And a feeling of being ignored. I was reading a linguistics paper about how language shifts are tied to political movements. Fascinating, actually. Speaker_3: Fascinating, eh? I’m more interested in whether or not it’ll affect the price of petrol. Honestly, everything’s gone up. It's daylight robbery. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I was at Brenda’s yesterday, and she was moaning about the dentist. Apparently, they’re wanting another fifty quid just for a check-up. Fifty quid! Speaker_2: That’s ridiculous. Dental care should be free at the point of use. Speaker_3: Should be, shouldn’t it? Reminds me of when I was a lad. Old Mr. Harrison, the dentist, used to give us a lollipop after every appointment. Now *that* was good service. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, those were the days. Right, stop reminiscing and move a piece. You're letting me get ahead. You know, I had a recording of Winston Churchill I found on an old reel-to-reel. Trying to get it digitised. It’s a nightmare with all this new technology. Speaker_2: I could probably help with that. I've got some software that can do audio restoration. It's surprisingly effective. Speaker_3: That’s good of you, lad. Always helpful. I’m trying to get the greenhouse sorted. The tomatoes are going mad, but the beans are refusing to sprout. It’s a right mystery. Speaker_1: You need to talk to them nicely. Plants respond to encouragement, you know. Speaker_3: (Scoffs) Don’t be daft, woman. They’re plants. Though, I did read something about… never mind. Your move, young man. And think about that cannon. It's a sneaky little piece. Speaking of sneaky pieces, have you heard from your friend, the one who was studying in South Korea? Speaker_2: Oh, Liam? Yeah, he messaged me last week. Said things are getting pretty intense with North Korea testing more missiles. He's thinking about coming home early. It's a shame, he was really enjoying the language learning, but… safety first, I guess. Speaker_1: Goodness me! That doesn't sound very pleasant. Right then, let's think about lunch. I was thinking of a simple salad, or maybe beans on toast?

Speaker_2: Honestly, some of the things they come up with… this one student, bless her, tried to tell me that “irregardless” is a real word. I had to gently explain… again. It’s exhausting sometimes. Speaker_1: Oh, you get that all the time, don't you? It’s the confidence, isn't it? They’re so sure they’re right, even when demonstrably… not. Reminds me of some politicians, actually. Makes you grateful to be here, I suppose. Not dealing with all that. Speaker_1: Exactly. Though, being here does make me think about pensions, and how utterly terrifying that whole system is. I mean, will there *be* anything left? I haven't paid in properly for years, you know, with not really… working. Speaker_2: Ugh, don't even go there. I'm still battling with student loan repayments. It feels like it will follow me to my grave. And the interest rates are ridiculous! They say they're helping young people, but it feels like they’re just trapping us in debt. Speaker_1: It’s a joke, isn't it? And then everyone acts surprised that people are choosing to move abroad. I was reading an article about how many qualified teachers are leaving the UK because of all the…stuff. It's a brain drain. Speaker_2: It is. I’ve been thinking about it myself, to be honest. Not permanently, but maybe another year or two somewhere different. South Korea, maybe? Or Vietnam. The opportunities are decent, and the money is good. Speaker_1: Ooh, Vietnam sounds exciting! You'd be brilliant at that. Though, you’d miss proper tea. And a decent MOT. Remember when the car failed last year? That was a nightmare. Speaker_2: Don’t remind me! The exhaust was completely shot. Still, could be worse. At least I'm not stuck doing paperwork all day. How are you passing the time, apart from correcting grammatical errors and contemplating the end of civilisation? Speaker_1: Largely Netflix, to be honest. I finished that new series, “The Serpent.” Gripping, but slightly disturbing. And I've been attempting to learn Polish. Duolingo is…challenging. Speaker_2: Oh, good luck with that! Polish is supposed to be fiendishly difficult. I’ve picked up a few phrases just from being here, but anything beyond “Dzień dobry” is a struggle. Rest assured, I’m ready to unleash the northern glare if he comes anywhere near. He looks like he’s trying to work out the bill, though. Probably just confused. Speaker_1: Possibly. Speaker_1: Right, so you’re still pretty set on Human Sciences then? At Oxford? Speaker_2: Yeah, pretty much. It just… feels right, you know? It's broad enough, isn't it? Oxford's not *that* far, though, is it? We could still meet up, weekends and stuff. Plus, we've got to learn to be independent eventually, right? New experiences, new people… Speaking of new experiences, you finally tried a proper Old Fashioned last night, didn’t you? Not just a sip of my dad’s? Speaker_1: Yeah, well… one. And regretted it immediately. That stuff is strong. It tastes nice going down, but then… woah. Speaker_2: Told ya! It’s an acquired taste, definitely. You're better off sticking to cider, mate. Less chance of ending up questioning your life choices. Speaker_1: Cider's good. Speaking of things I regret, I tried to make pasta carbonara on Tuesday. It was a disaster. Speaker_2: No way! You and cooking. Name a more iconic duo. What went wrong? Speaker_1: Everything. The sauce was watery, the bacon was burnt, I think I put too much pepper in… It looked nothing like the pictures online. Honestly, I think I need lessons. Speaker_2: (chuckling) You definitely do. Speaker_1: So, did you watch that debate last night, Grandma? The one with… all of ‘em? Speaker_2: Oh, aye lad, I did. Though honestly, it all just sounds like a load of shouting to me these days. Speaker_2: (laughing) Well, of course it is! It was written a long time ago. You'll get used to it. It’s a beautiful language. More beautiful than what they use on those debates, that’s for sure.

Speaker_1: Now, Liam, put down the fork when you’re talking, will you? It's not a very good look, son. Like you’re stabbing the air with it. Speaker_2: Sorry, Dad. I have that appointment with the… well, never mind what the appointment is for. It's just easier if she's with someone she loves. Speaker_1: And who's better with a wriggling toddler than her Granny? Now finish your dinner, and remember your manners.

Speaker_1: So, did you catch any of that Scottish referendum coverage last night? Absolute chaos, wasn't it? Seems like it’s going to be a long few days, honestly. Speaker_2: A bit, yeah. Flicked it on and off. Honestly, I’ve lost track of what they’re arguing about anymore. Just seems to go round and round. More interested in what’s happening with the price of petrol, to be frank. Dreadful, isn’t it? Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Filled up this morning and nearly choked. Speaking of stressful things, how did that job interview go on Tuesday? Did you get any feedback yet?
