More worried about the bills, naturally. But she knows I’m putting the feelers out. It’s just… different, isn’t it? After running my own business for thirty years, the thought of answering to someone else again… feels a bit strange. Speaker_1: I can imagine. It's a big shift. Remember old Mr. Henderson, from the school? Tried to retire, then lasted a week before going back part-time. Said he was bored silly. Speaker_2: Ha! That sounds like him alright. Still, I've got a few leads. And frankly, a bit of a break might do me good. Been burning the candle at both ends for years. Speaker_1: You need to look after yourself. Speaking of family, how’s Sarah doing? How’s university treating her? Speaker_2: She’s good. Stressed, obviously. Final year. Endless essays. Keeps moaning about having to do group work. Says she ends up doing all the work herself! Sounds familiar, eh? Speaker_1: Oh, absolutely. The joys of group projects. My Emily's just landed a graduate scheme with a marketing company in London. So, she's buzzing. Still trying to work out how she’s going to afford to live there, though. It's ridiculous, the cost of everything. Speaker_2: London. Forget it. Robbery. I wouldn’t live there if you paid me. Still, good for Emily. That’s fantastic news. Speaker_1: It is. It’s just… things are a bit precarious at the moment, aren’t they? With everything going on. You know, trying to juggle work, family, worrying about the future... It’s exhausting. Speaker_2: You’re telling me. It is. Still, we’ve weathered worse, eh? A cup of tea always helps, though. Fancy another one? I’ll stick the kettle on. Speaker_1: That sounds perfect. Thank you, mate. Always good to have a moan and a cuppa, isn't it? Cheers to weathering storms. Speaker_2: Absolutely. Cheers to that. Right, tea time. And then I might just check that email again… you never know. Speaker_1: Don't hold your breath, but hope springs eternal! Speaker_2: Right you are.

Speaker_2: Right, well that was a bit of a kerfuffle getting out of Sainsbury’s, wasn’t it? Honestly, you wouldn’t believe the parking. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Speaker_1: Classic Dad. Always finding a way to compare everything to your mum. Speaker_3: They really were good, though. Speaking of baking, I was looking at this recipe for sourdough online…seems ridiculously complicated. Speaker_2: Sourdough! Oh, don’t even go there. I tried that once. It ended up like a brick. A very sour brick. I think it’s one of those things you need a specialist course for. Like that pottery class I did. Speaker_1: How did that go? Speaker_2: Well, let’s just say my ‘vase’ looked more like a lopsided ashtray. Everyone else made these beautiful things, and mine…well, it’s in the shed. It might be supporting a tomato plant now. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) You’re modest, love. You've always been creative. Remember that knitted penguin you made Aaron when he was little? Speaker_1: Oh god, please don’t remind me. That thing was terrifying. It had one eye and a wonky beak! Speaker_3: Sounds…unique. So, how much further, Dad? My phone’s lost signal. I need to tell my students I’m on my way back. Speaker_4: About ten minutes. Signal’s patchy around here. Makes you wonder how people managed before mobile phones, doesn’t it? We used to just…wing it. Turn up when we turned up. No one knew where anyone was. Speaker_2: It was simpler, in some ways. Less pressure. Although, getting lost was a regular occurrence. Remember that time we ended up in that tiny village in Norfolk, completely by accident? Speaker_1: And you insisted on buying that ridiculously oversized teapot from the antique shop? Speaker_2: It was a bargain! And it looks lovely in the dining room. Well, it *would* if we ever used the dining room. Speaker_4: It's a good job we don't have a dog anymore. Remember Buster? He used to try and drink out of that teapot. Speaker_3: (Looking out the window) Ooh, look at those fields. It’s so green. Completely different to London. Makes you appreciate the countryside, doesn't it? Speaker_4: It does. Right, nearly there. Just bracing for the lane. It’s a bit bumpy. Hold on tight. Speaker_1: Oh brilliant. Here we go. Speaker_2: Honestly, you’d think they’d fix it by now. They’ve been promising to resurface it for years. It's like the pension promises, all talk and no action. Speaker_4: Don't get me started on pensions. It’s a complete mess. Speaker_3:

Speaker_1: Honestly, this traffic is mental, isn’t it? Didn’t realise leaving at six would still be this bad. Speaker_2: Aye, it’s a right bother. Used to be able to get across Manchester in fifteen minutes, back in my day. Fifteen minutes! Now look at it. All these cars… and for what? Speaker_3: It's mostly the M62, isn't it? Seems to be perpetually jammed. They really need to do something about that stretch. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I swear, I aged about ten years just merging onto it. Did you see that tractor? Honestly, right in the outside lane. Speaker_2: A tractor? On the motorway? What’s the world coming to! Back in my day, tractors stayed in the fields where they belonged. Speaker_3: Probably heading to market. There’s a lot of farmland around here still, even with all the development. Speaker_1: Still, a bit of consideration wouldn't go amiss, eh? Held everyone up something awful. And then, right behind it, a trailer full of sheep! Honestly, a woolly roadblock. Speaker_2: Sheep, you say? Now that's interesting. My Auntie Bessie used to raise sheep. Lovely creatures, but a right mess, they are. Always getting into the vegetable patch. Speaker_3: I spent a summer on a farm once, helping out a friend. The smell… wasn't exactly pleasant. And the early mornings. 4 am starts, just to milk the cows. Speaker_1: Oof, no thank you! I need my sleep. I can barely function before nine, never mind four in the morning. Though, I did see some really cute piglets. Tiny little things, all pink. Speaker_2: Piglets are clever, you know. Surprisingly intelligent animals. Cleaner than people give them credit for, too. My Auntie Bessie had pigs as well. Always loved a good belly rub, she said. Speaker_3: That’s a new one! I always thought pigs were just…muddy. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Apparently not. Everything I thought I knew about farm animals is being challenged right now. Maybe we should have just stayed home and watched a documentary. Speaker_2: Nonsense! You wouldn’t get this kind of insight watching a documentary. You need to *experience* it. Besides, I enjoy a good bit of traffic. Gives me time to think. Speaker_3: Think about what? The good old days when you could cross Manchester in fifteen minutes? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Amongst other things. It reminds me… there was this time, back in ‘58, when I got stuck behind a herd of cows… Speaker_1: Oh lord. Here we go…Another story. Speaker_3: (Smiling) I am all ears. Speaker_1: Honestly though, the amount of livestock on the roads today is unbelievable. You'd think they'd have designated 'animal routes' or something. Speaker_2: Designated animal routes? Now *that’s* an idea. They ought to put that to the council! Speaker_3: They’d probably just build a new housing estate on it. Speaker_1: Probably. Although, a housing estate full of sheep would be… interesting. Speaker_3: (Laughing) That *would* be something. Speaker_2: Well, it’d certainly be quieter! No noisy neighbours, just baa-ing. Speaker_1: Right, I'm officially losing it. Just need to get to Newcastle, grab some food, and forget this whole ordeal.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this shepherd’s pie is lovely, Margaret. Much better than anything I could manage now I'm retired. My hands aren’t what they used to be for all that mashing. Speaker_2: It *is* good, isn't it? You always did make a good one though, Eileen. Remember that one Christmas, you practically lived in the kitchen, perfecting the potato topping? Speaking of forces of nature, have you been keeping up with your walking, Eileen? I know you were aiming for a couple of miles each day. Speaker_1: I have, mostly. Volunteering, he said. Some scheme in South America. I’m trying not to overreact. Speaker_3: South America! Goodness. That's a long way to go. A bit ambitious, perhaps? Speaker_1: Exactly what I said! I told him there’s plenty to do closer to home. Volunteering at the animal shelter, maybe. Or helping at the village hall. Though, truth be told, I secretly hope he’ll realize how expensive university is and decide to get a job for a year. Speaker_2: Well, it *is* expensive. I’m still paying off my student loan, and I finished years ago! You know, my sister was saying they’re thinking of starting a scholarship fund at her old school. To help kids from less well-off families get a decent education. Speaker_3: That’s a lovely idea. It’s important to give back, isn’t it? I always meant to do more with the oil money, but… well, life got in the way. Speaker_1: Don’t beat yourself up about that, Arthur. You always had a good heart. Though, speaking of being helpful, did Mrs. Higgins ever manage to get the hang of that new telly? I offered to show her last week, but she said she’d ask her grandson. Honestly, the youngsters think they know everything. Speaker_2: It’s always the way! My Nan wouldn’t let anyone touch her remote control. Said she was the only one who knew which button did what. Even if it meant watching the shopping channels all day. Speaker_3: They’re set in their ways, aren’t they? Which reminds me, is the choir still meeting on Tuesdays? I might pop along and see if I can remember the words to a few of the hymns. It’s been a while. Although, I'm not sure my voice has improved with age, more likely the opposite. Speaker_1: Oh yes! And Mrs. Peterson rejoined, which is wonderful. She was away for ages with her hip. And they’re learning a new piece – a lovely arrangement of ‘Danny Boy’. You *must* come, Arthur. It’ll do you good. And it gets you out of the house. Unlike some people who spend all day tinkering with… whatever it is you tinker with.

Speaker_1: Right, so, Parent's Evening. Overall, pretty good, wasn’t it? Both of you seemed really happy with your teachers. Speaker_2: (Mumbling with a mouthful of peas) Yeah. Speaker_2: Yes! ‘Wingardium Leviosa!’ But I keep saying it wrong. Speaker_3: I'm going as… (pauses thoughtfully) …a knight! With a shiny sword! I need to make a helmet. Speaker_1: Fantastic! We can get some cardboard and decorate it tomorrow. Speaking of tomorrow, I’ve booked tickets for the circus! Remember we talked about it? Speaker_2: Ooh yes! With the acrobats? And the lions? Speaker_1: Probably. Do you like clowns? Speaker_3: They’re a bit scary. Speaker_1: Okay, we can sit further away from the ring then. Right, after school tomorrow… I need to pop into the shops, then we’re heading straight to the circus. And then bath time. Speaker_2: Can we get ice cream at the circus? Speaker_1: We'll see, let's get through dinner first. Actually, that reminds me. This chicken… it smells a bit funny, doesn’t it? Speaker_3: (Sniffs dramatically) No! It smells like chicken! Speaker_1: No, it’s… I was reading this article online… apparently, forensic anthropologists can sometimes tell if something is human flesh just by the smell. It’s really weird. They said it smells… sweet? And smoky? Speaker_2: (Eyes widening) Ewwww! Speaker_3: (Stopping mid-chew) What?! Human flesh?! Speaker_1: (Quickly) Oh, don’t worry! This definitely isn't human flesh! Speaker_1: So, did young Leo manage to finish that curtain job then? His mother was saying he was working down in O’Connell’s, wasn't he? Speaker_2: Oh, aye, he did. A wee gathering is far more manageable. And less stressful for everyone. I’ve seen it all, you know, teaching wee ones for forty years. Speaker_3: Party! Balloons! Cake! Speaker_2: He's already obsessed with the cake. He keeps asking if it’s going to have dinosaurs on it. Speaker_1: Dinosaurs it is, then. I’ll order it tomorrow. We'll need to send out invites too, that’s a job for me I suppose. Speaker_2: I could do that, if you’re busy with work. Though honestly, getting a response from people these days…it’s like pulling teeth. Speaker_1: True enough. Speaking of busy, I’ve got a treasurer meeting for the garage owners on Tuesday. It’s a thankless task, honestly. Everyone wants something for nothing. Speaker_4: Ah, the garages. Always a source of drama, aren’t they? I remember old Mr. Henderson, down the road… he was forever complaining about someone parking over his space. Speaker_1: It's hardly parking disputes, Mother. It’s invoices and accounts and trying to figure out the latest tax regulations on rented houses. The government keeps changing things, it’s a nightmare. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Honestly, the tax on rental properties is ridiculous. It’s like they want to discourage people from letting them out. Speaker_4: They do love to make things tricky, don't they? Anyway, back to happier things. Oisin was saying “wanty” again today. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, no! Still with the “wanty”? Speaker_1: “Wanty”? What’s that now? Speaker_2: He says "wanty" instead of "want to". It’s adorable, but a bit… grammatically incorrect. Speaker_4: It's a phase. They all go through phases. Little Fergus used to call everyone “daddy.” Even the postman! Speaker_1: (Smiling) That's brilliant. I received three calls from charities today, wanting donations. Absolutely relentless. Speaker_2: They are persistent, aren't they? I just tell them I'm too busy looking after a toddler, and they usually hang up fairly quickly. Though one tried to convince me I needed to donate to help children in Africa…while I was trying to stop Oisin from drawing on the walls. The irony!

Speaker_1: Right, I’m telling you, it’s impossible. Absolutely impossible. I’ve been thinking about it for ages. Speaker_2: What’s impossible? You've been muttering about ‘it’ for five minutes now. Is it a particularly difficult Sudoku? Speaker_1: No, it’s the word game, the one Liam set us. A word with, like, four different vowels in a row. I just…it’s not happening. Speaker_3: Oh, that one! Aye, it's a brutal challenge. I’ve been having a go on and off all evening. I’ve got three vowels, but getting a fourth feels like finding hen’s teeth. Speaker_1: See! It *is* hard, right? I thought I was going mental. I've tried everything – queuing, audio, plateau… nothing's working. Speaker_2: Queuing? Is that even a word? Speaker_1: Well, it is now! I’m inventing words if I have to. I just need any four vowels in a row! Think about it, you’ve got a, e, i, o, u… it's like trying to fit a square peg in a round hole. Speaker_3: You’re overthinking it. Think about digraphs, or vowel teams. Sometimes they sneak in where you least expect them. Speaker_1: Vowel teams? Like… 'eau'? Is that enough? Speaker_2: No, that’s only three vowels. Though it’s a good thought. What about words with diphthongs? 'Au' or 'oi' are technically vowel sounds… Speaker_1: Oh, clever. But that still doesn't give me four in a row, does it? It’s just teasing me. Honestly, Liam just likes making us suffer. Speaker_3: He does enjoy a good mental workout, doesn't he? I was trying to think of words with ‘iou’ in them – that's a tricky combo. Speaker_1: Oh god, ‘iou’? That sounds like something a pigeon would say. Speaker_2: (Laughing) A pigeon saying ‘iou’? That’s brilliant. Okay, okay, let’s brainstorm. If we forget about it needing to be a *real* word for a second, could we construct something ridiculous? Like… "beauious"? Speaker_1: Beauious? What even *is* that supposed to mean? Speaker_3: It doesn’t have to *mean* anything! Liam didn’t say it had to be legitimate English. Speaker_2: Exactly. It just needs four vowels in a row. Speaker_1: Hmm... you know what? That’s… actually a really good point. Okay, "beauious"— it’s horrific, but it might just work. I’m going to text Liam. Wish me luck. Speaker_3: Good luck, you’ll need it. He’ll probably say it doesn't count though. He's a stickler for the rules. Speaker_1: Rest assured, I’m ready to argue the case for the beauty of “beauious”. I'll report back. Anyone fancy another biscuit while I wait for his judgement? Speaker_2: Yes please. Although, I'm starting to think this word game is less about linguistic skill and more about sheer stubbornness…and perhaps a willingness to invent words. Speaker_3: Absolutely. It’s a battle of attrition. And Liam knows it. He’s probably sat there, sipping tea, watching us suffer. Speaker_1: (After a moment, looking at her phone) He says… he says “acceptable, but only because I’m feeling benevolent. Prepare for the next round.” Oh brilliant. Just brilliant.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I napped for like, four hours solid today. Four. I feel like I've wasted the entire day. Speaker_2: No way! Four hours? You must have been *exhausted*. What even made you nap for that long? Speaker_1: I don't even know! I sat down on the sofa to just check my emails, and next thing I know, it’s nearly seven. My neck is properly stiff. Speaker_2: Classic. Happened to me last week. Remember that essay we had to read for Dr. Hayes’ class? Knocked me right out. It was brutal. Speaker_1: Oh god, that one. So dry. Speaking of brutal, have you seen what Chloe’s posted on Instagram? Another picture from her holiday in Tenerife. She’s living her best life, while we’re stuck here. Speaker_2: (Scoffs) Ugh, don’t even. I saw. Another infinity pool photo. Honestly, it’s exhausting looking at her 'perfect' life. It's just... curated, isn't it? Speaker_1: Totally. Remember when we were digging through old photos last week? The ones from primary school? Chloe had a full-on tantrum because her hair wasn't "just right" for the picture. Some things never change. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh my god, yes! And she was wearing that awful sparkly pink jacket. The one her nan made her. Speaker_1: The one she swore she'd never be seen in again! Look at her now, posing like she's a model. Speaker_2: It’s hilarious. Still, she's got good taste in music, I'll give her that. Have you heard that new Arctic Monkeys track? Speaker_1: Oh yeah, it's good. A bit different, though, isn't it? More… orchestral. I was listening to it on repeat earlier. Then I promptly fell asleep. Full circle, I guess. Speaker_2: Different, yeah, but still undeniably them. It's growing on me. Hey, have you spoken to Liam recently? Haven’t seen him in ages. Speaker_1: Not really. He messaged me a couple of weeks ago asking about the assignment, but that was it. Said he was swamped with work at the pub. He's always working. Speaker_2: Yeah, he needs to chill out. He's gonna burn himself out. Remember when we tried to convince him to come to that awful karaoke night with us? He refused, said he had a shift. Speaker_1: (Bursting out laughing) Oh god, that was a disaster. Ben attempting Bohemian Rhapsody… that'll haunt me forever. Speaker_2: Seriously! It was the most painful thing I’ve ever witnessed. You know what, I am starving. Fancy getting another portion of chips? Speaker_1: Absolutely. And maybe we should dig up some more embarrassing photos later. For research purposes, of course. Speaker_2: Naturally. For scientific advancement. Restoring balance to the universe, one terrible primary school photo at a time. Speaker_1: Exactly. Speaker_2: Chips it is then. Speaker_1: Chips it is. . . . (A brief pause as they both look around the pub) . . . Speaker_2: My mum's here again. Speaker_1: (Groans playfully) Oh, not again. She's a social butterfly, isn't she? Speaker_2: A force of nature. Here she comes… brace yourself. ........

Speaker_1: So, did you manage to get a look at the application properly before the council planning committee meeting? It felt a bit rushed, didn’t it? Speaker_2: I did, skimmed it mostly on the train. Honestly, it’s a mess. The drawings are…optimistic, to say the least. They’ve conveniently ‘forgotten’ to include the existing trees, haven’t they? Speaker_1: Exactly! And the shadow analysis is completely bogus. Old Man Hemmings was right to be furious. The whole thing will overshadow his garden. They’ve tried to downplay it, saying it’s ‘minimal impact’. Speaker_2: Minimal! It’ll be like living in permanent twilight. And the access road… it’s already a bottleneck in the mornings. Adding another twenty houses’ worth of traffic will make it absolutely gridlocked. Did you see Councillor Davies trying to justify it? Speaker_1: Oh, God, yes. All that talk about ‘sustainable development’ and ‘meeting housing needs’. It’s just a greenfield site, Peter! It’s a lovely field, and they’re just going to slap a housing estate on it. Speaker_2: He was clearly siding with the developer, wasn't he? I think there’s more to it than meets the eye. A little bird told me Malcolm at the pub knows Davies’ brother-in-law works for the firm doing the build. Speaker_1: No way! Honestly, it's disgusting. You'd think they’d have some kind of ethical obligation. And the structure of the meeting itself was…odd. They rushed through the objections so quickly. Speaker_2: They did. And then gave the developer's representative ages to make his presentation, full of carefully curated photographs that made it look like paradise. Speaker_1: It was infuriating. I wanted to stand up and just read out the objections properly, but I knew it wouldn't make a difference. They’d already made their minds up. Speaker_2: I think they were hoping everyone would just roll over. Which is why Hemmings going in guns blazing was actually quite effective, even if he did come across a bit…forceful. Speaker_1: He *was* forceful, but he had a point. It’s his quality of life they’re messing with. Do you think there’s anything we can do now? Appeal, perhaps? Speaker_2: Possibly. We'd need to get a solicitor involved. It’s going to be expensive, and there’s no guarantee of success, but…I think it’s worth exploring. Especially if we can gather more evidence about those dodgy drawings. Speaker_1: Right. I'll have a look online to see about solicitors specialising in planning appeals. And maybe check the council’s website for the full application details. It's just so frustrating. It feels like no one actually cares about preserving anything nice anymore. Speaker_2: It’s just profit, isn’t it? Pure and simple. They don't care about communities, they care about filling their pockets. Let’s get that solicitor sorted, and then we can see what our options are. A good fight might do us good, anyway. Speaker_1: It certainly will. A good, righteous fight. Speaker_2: Exactly. Now, fancy a cup of tea to fuel the battle? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Strong one, please. And maybe a biscuit. We'll need the energy. Speaker_2: Coming right up. Speaker_1: Good. Speaker_2: How is the selling going? Speaker_1: It’s such a headache. Speaker_2: I know. Speaker_1: It’s just so slow.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I am *starving*. I’ve been surviving on biscuits all day. Did you manage to grab anything decent for dinner after your shift? Speaker_2: Ugh, tell me about it. Shifts were…a lot today. I just grabbed a meal deal from Tesco. It's pathetic, I know. Tuna and sweetcorn, the height of culinary excellence. There’s still some chicken in the fridge, though, if you fancy it. I can knock up a quick stir-fry? Speaker_1: Oh, you are a lifesaver. Yes please! Chicken stir-fry sounds amazing. I’ll get the rice on. You know, I was thinking about Chloe from school the other day. Speaker_2: Chloe? Chloe…Miller? The one who was obsessed with horses? Speaker_1: That’s the one! I found her on Instagram. She’s…a lifestyle influencer now, apparently. All avocado toast and yoga poses. It’s wild. Speaker_2: No way! Seriously? That’s… peak Chloe, actually. Always had a flair for the dramatic. Remember when she tried to organise a protest about the school uniform? Speaker_1: Oh god, yes! So passionate about freedom of expression through clothing. Such a rebel. Speaking of dramatic, have you *seen* Mrs. Henderson’s garden lately? It’s like a jungle. Speaker_2: Oh, don't even get me started on Mrs. Henderson. It's overgrown, the gnomes are multiplying, and I’m pretty sure she’s been yelling at the postman again. I swear, she's plotting something. Speaker_1: I heard a rumour she's started a birdwatching club as a front for surveillance. I’m not even joking. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You are awful! Seriously though, she’s a bit…intense. Change of subject, desperately. Did you catch that new film, “Midnight Bloom”? Everyone’s raving about it. Speaker_1: No, not yet. Is it worth braving the crowds for? I saw the trailer and it looked a bit…slow. Speaker_2: It *is* slow, but beautifully slow. It's one of those films that stays with you. It’s all about grief and…well, blooming again, I guess. Bit heavy, but good. Though, honestly, after today, I just want something brainless. Like a rom-com where everything goes perfectly. Speaker_1: Oh, you need “Set it Up” on Netflix then. It’s pure fluff, but exactly what's needed after a hard day. Speaking of needing things… are you still seeing that guy, Ben? Speaker_2: (Sighs) Ben… It's complicated. We're “taking a break.” He just… doesn’t understand what I do, you know? He keeps suggesting I “just relax” when I’m stressed from work. As if I *choose* to hear sad stories all day. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s terrible. You deserve someone who gets it. Someone who won’t tell you to just "relax" when you're dealing with genuine trauma. Honestly, some men. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Anyway, enough about my disastrous love life. I was thinking, we haven’t been on a proper day out in ages. How about that botanical garden we talked about? Next weekend? Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! That sounds perfect. We can wander around, pretend we have green fingers, and then get a ridiculously overpriced coffee. I’m in! Perhaps we could hit up that new vintage shop afterwards? I need retail therapy. Speaker_2: Deal. Botanical gardens and vintage finds. Definitely needed. Right, let’s get this stir-fry going. And then… maybe a rom-com, and a very large glass of wine.

Speaker_1: Right, honestly, the state of this place, eh? I swear, dust breeds in here. It's like a self-replicating organism. Speaker_2: (Without looking up from her phone) You say that every time, Liam. And you’re just as bad as me, you know. You leave your shoes everywhere. Speaker_1: That's different! Shoes have a designated… area. Near the door. A strategic placement, really. Though, even then, sometimes they migrate. Speaking of migrating, did you see that advert for the new travel company? The one with the llamas? Speaker_2: Llamas? No. Was it on telly or online? I’ve been scrolling through TikTok all evening. It’s a black hole, honestly. Speaker_1: On telly, during *Corrie*. It was ridiculous. A bloke trying to ride a llama through the Andes. Selling holidays, supposedly. Honestly, the things they come up with. Makes you wonder how advertising execs sleep at night. Speaker_2: Probably on a bed of money, thinking about the next llama-based campaign. It’s all manipulation, isn't it? Like that diet ad earlier with the ridiculously toned woman. Speaker_1: Oh, aye. She looked like she hadn't eaten a proper meal in her life. Reminds me of Auntie Brenda. Still going on about cabbage soup diets, even after all these years. She started smoking again, you know. Speaker_2: No way! After everything she said about it giving her a cough that sounded like a dying walrus? Speaker_1: The very same. Apparently, old habits die hard. She says it calms her nerves. I reckon it just makes her cough more. It's grim, that. Speaker_2: It is. What are you thinking of doing at the car boot sale on Sunday? Any treasures you’re hoping to unearth? Speaker_1: I’m on the lookout for vinyl. Found a couple of decent Beatles records last month. You were brilliant at haggling for those, by the way. You've got a real talent. Speaker_2: Years of practice, bartering with market stallholders with my nan. She could get a fiver off a bag of potatoes. It’s a skill, I tell you. Speaking of skills, I was reading about NLP - Neuro-Linguistic Programming - at work today. Fascinating stuff. Apparently, it can help people with all sorts of things, even dyslexia. Speaker_1: NLP? Sounds a bit… woo-woo, to be honest. Speaker_2: Maybe. But it’s based on understanding how the brain processes information. We had a training session focusing on how it relates to helping patients with trauma. It’s quite clever, actually. Do you remember Mark Jenkins from uni? Speaker_1: Yeah, vaguely. The bloke who wanted to be a journalist? Always scribbling in a notepad. Speaker_2: That’s the one. He messaged me earlier. He's doing really well, apparently. Freelancing, covering local crime. Said it’s hectic but rewarding. Speaker_1: Local crime, eh? Bet Birkenhead’s providing plenty of material. What about you? Anything exciting happening at work? Speaker_2: Same old, same old. Assessments, reports… though, I've got a family therapy session booked for tomorrow. That'll be interesting. What are your plans for the week, apart from wrestling with dust bunnies? Did you order that new phone case online, by the way? Speaker_1: Nah, haven’t got round to it yet. Too busy thinking about llamas and Auntie Brenda’s lungs. And yes, more dusting. Definitely more dusting. This place is a lost cause.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weather is doing my head in. One minute it’s sunshine, the next it’s biblical rain. Makes planning anything impossible. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I was hoping to get the car washed this weekend, but it's looking…optimistic. Speaking of cars, anyone seen those new electric Minis? They look surprisingly good. Speaker_3: Yeah, I’ve seen them. Properly smart. Though the price tag is a bit…ouch. Still, better than shelling out for constant petrol, I suppose. Speaker_4: It’s a huge investment either way. I’m still saving for a deposit on a house, and it feels like a never-ending task. Especially with interest rates doing…whatever they’re doing. Speaker_5: Don’t even *start* me on house prices. I’ve been looking up north, thinking maybe Leeds is more affordable, but it’s still mental. I saw a two-bed terrace going for nearly three hundred thousand! Speaker_1: Three hundred thousand?! You’re joking! Even in Hitchin, that’s…significant. Speaker_3: It's the same down here. My mate just bought a place in Bournville, tiny garden, needs a full refurb, and he remortgaged himself to the hilt. Speaker_2: Speaking of stressful things, has anyone tried that new meditation app, Headspace? I downloaded it, figured I need *something* to calm the nerves with the workload I’ve got at the moment. Speaker_4: I’ve heard good things. I tried Calm a while back, but I found the voice a bit…patronising, if you know what I mean? Like it was talking to me like I was five. Speaker_5: Oh god, yes! That’s exactly it. I need someone to tell me to breathe, not explain *why* I need to breathe. I've started writing again, actually. Short stories. Keeps me sane. Speaker_1: That’s brilliant, Sarah! You always had a knack for that. Remember that piece you wrote for the university magazine? The one about the…what was it? The haunted library? Speaker_5: (Laughing) Oh, God. Yes! That was awful. Terribly melodramatic. But it did win a prize, which was nice. Speaker_3: I’ve been listening to loads of music lately. Discovered this amazing new band, The Mysterines. They’re a bit grungy, bit psychedelic. Perfect for gloomy Birmingham evenings. Anyone heard of them? Speaker_2: Nope. Add them to the list. My Spotify is already overflowing with recommendations I’ll never get around to listening to. Speaker_4: I’ve been catching up on films. Watched “Everything Everywhere All at Once” last night. Utterly bonkers, but incredible. Michelle Yeoh is phenomenal. Speaker_1: Oh, I’ve heard good things! Is it…difficult to follow? I sometimes struggle with very layered films. Speaker_4: It is a bit, yeah. You kind of just have to go with it. Though honestly, the chaos is part of the charm. We should go to that new Thai place next week, the one near the canal? I heard the Pad Thai is amazing. Speaker_5: Ooh, yes! I'm in. I'm starving just thinking about it. And I need a proper meal that isn’t toast. I’ve been living on toast since Tuesday. Speaker_3: I'm good for Thai. Although, I did attempt to make a curry last night and it was…an experience. Let’s just say it didn’t exactly transport me to India. Speaker_2: (chuckling) I think we’ve all been there. My attempt at sourdough bread last month was a disaster. It ended up looking like a weapon.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the houses around here were fields! Proper fields. We moved in ‘68, you know, and it was all farmland. Lovely farmland, mind, but nothing like it is now. Remember old Man Hemmings’ place? Where the estate is now? Just cows. Speaker_2: Oh yes, Hemmings. Used to deliver milk, didn't he? Lovely man. It was a proper village then, wasn't it? Everyone knew everyone. Quite a shock coming from Ramsgate, I can tell you. Very different pace. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) You think *that* was a shock? Try coming here from Birmingham in ‘65! I’d secured the dental practice, thankfully, which obviously eased things, but finding somewhere decent to live… that was a trial. Everything was either brand new, horribly expensive, or falling down. Speaker_3: Falling down was the norm in Manchester. Though even there, it was getting a bit spruced up by then, early sixties. But you, Brian, a dentist… you’d have been in demand. Must’ve had your pick. Speaker_4: Oh, I did alright. Eventually found a little semi near the high street. Needed *everything* doing to it, though. Damp, dodgy wiring, the whole shebang. But it was affordable, and it was mine. I spent the next five years renovating it. Nearly bankrupted me, if I’m honest. Speaker_2: We rented for ages, Margaret and I. Couldn’t afford to buy, not on a teacher’s salary back then. Found a little cottage just off the Common. Damp, naturally. Every winter, the wallpaper would peel off. But it was cosy. Speaker_1: We bought almost straight away, didn’t we, John? Lucky really. My father helped with the deposit, thank goodness. It was a new build, one of the first on the estate. Bit boxy, but solid. Where did you two meet, actually? Margaret and you? Speaker_2: Now that’s a story. A training weekend, down in Bournemouth. Awful weather, freezing cold, and surrounded by trainee teachers. But Margaret… well, she stood out. Even then, she had that… sparkle. Speaker_1: Oh, I remember Bournemouth training weekends! Horrible organised fun. John and I met at college. St. Martin’s, in London. He was a bit of a charmer, even then. Speaker_3: St. Martin’s! Good college. I was up at Manchester, of course. English Literature. Then did my postgrad at Leeds. Though I did spend a rather… eventful time in Athens. Speaker_4: Athens? Oh, do tell! Speaker_3: So, I’d secured a place on a post-grad course at the University of Athens. Brilliant opportunity. I flew out in ‘67. Landed, checked into my student digs, and the next day… the military coup. The Colonels. First day of the dictatorship. Absolute chaos. Speaker_1: Oh my goodness! Speaker_3: Complete lockdown. Curfew, soldiers everywhere. Now, because I'd arrived the day before, I hadn’t registered with the university yet. They thought I was a spy! They grilled me for hours. Couldn't understand a word I was saying, and I certainly couldn't understand them. Speaker_2: You must have been terrified! Speaker_3: Terrified doesn’t quite cover it. And the time difference! I’d arranged for my wife, Mary, to ring me the next day, back home. So she rings, expects me to be happily settling in, and instead, I’m being interrogated by a bunch of armed soldiers. She was beside herself! It took weeks to sort it all out, get the university to vouch for me, and eventually, continue the course. But it was an adventure, I suppose. A rather stressful adventure. Speaker_4: Good Lord! And you say you’re a man of letters! You've got a bit of a story to tell, haven’t you? That’s far more exciting

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the dust! You’d think being antiques, they’d be… cared for. But people just didn’t bother. Polish was a rare sight, let me tell you. Mostly just layers and layers of grime. I specialized in small furniture, you see. Boxes, chests, the occasional little table. Not the big, imposing pieces. Too much hassle. Speaker_2: Oh, fascinating. That sounds… physically demanding though, doesn’t it? Lifting and shifting things all the time? My work was decidedly less so. Speech therapy. Mostly sitting and listening, and trying to coax sounds out of people. Though, some of the children… they could be quite energetic! Speaker_1: Oh, it was! Years of it. Back problems, naturally. But worth it, in a way. I always loved the stories things held, you know? Imagining the lives they'd witnessed. Who’d sat at that table, what secrets were kept inside that box. It’s silly, I suppose, but… Speaker_2: Not at all. I think that’s lovely. It’s about connection, isn't it? To the past. My work was about connection too, in a different way. Helping people *make* connections, through language. I spent thirty years working with children who had difficulties communicating. Autistic children, children with Down’s Syndrome, all sorts. Speaker_1: Thirty years! Goodness. That must have been… rewarding. And exhausting. I imagine there were some heart-wrenching stories too. Speaker_2: Oh, absolutely. It wasn’t always easy. But the little victories… when a child finally said their first word, or strung a sentence together… those were magical. What about your childhood, Marion? Did you grow up around antiques, or was that something you came to later? Speaker_1: Oh, no, not at all. Very ordinary childhood, really. Somerset farm. Mud, animals, a lot of fresh air and even more chores. My father was a dairy farmer, a proper old-fashioned one. Roses down the rows, everything perfect. My mother painted, watercolours mostly. Landscapes. She encouraged me, always had paper and brushes about. That’s where it started, I suppose. The art, not the antiques. The antiques came much later, a way to fund the art, really. Speaker_2: A Somerset farm… that sounds idyllic. Though I imagine it was hard work. I grew up in Sydney, Australia. Quite different! Sunshine and beaches, and a much more… laid-back lifestyle. My father was a solicitor, quite a respectable profession. My mother was a teacher. They were very keen on me having a ‘sensible’ career. Hence the speech therapy. Speaker_1: Sensible, yes. A very good word for it. My parents were more… pragmatic. They wanted me to be happy, but also self-sufficient. An artist needed a hobby to pay the bills, they said. A very sensible view, in retrospect. Did you ever regret not following a more… artistic path? Speaker_2: Sometimes, perhaps. I always enjoyed painting, but it never felt… strong enough. A passion, I suppose. I found real satisfaction in helping others. And truthfully, I’m not sure I’m terribly good at it! You, on the other hand, clearly have a gift. Do you still paint now that you’re retired? Speaker_1: Oh, yes. When my hands allow! Arthritis, you know. It’s a nuisance. But I still dabble. Mostly still life – flowers, fruit, the occasional pot or two… a little nod back to the past, perhaps. Speaker_2: That sounds delightful. I might have to commission something one day.

Speaker_1: Right, so onions are caramelising nicely. You sure we’ve got enough balsamic? Last time, it was a bit…understated. Speaker_2: I bought two bottles! Relax. It’s in the cupboard next to the paprika. Honestly, you'd think I deliberately sabotaged dinner last time. Speaker_1: No, no, it wasn't sabotage, just…a lack of tangy sweetness. Though, remember Old Man Hemmings at the tattoo parlour? He always said balsamic needs to *bite*. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh god, Hemmings. He probably thinks balsamic is a prerequisite for getting a decent dragon. Speaking of, are you still thinking about getting more ink? Speaker_1: Maybe. I've been sketching up ideas. Something floral, I think. A bit of a contrast to the…geometric chaos on my arm. It’s just, money is tight, being a ‘highly educated’ unemployed graduate and all that. Speaker_2: You'll get there. And honestly, a floral design would suit you. It’s a palate cleanser after all that blackwork. This smells *amazing* by the way. What are we having with this? Speaker_1: I was thinking roasted potatoes and some green beans. Simple, but effective. Speaking of effective, how’s the bakery going? Still selling out of those salted caramel brownies? Speaker_2: Sell out every. Single. Day. Honestly, I need to hire someone, but finding reliable staff is a nightmare. Plus, I'm thinking about doing Christmas cookie boxes, you know, fancy decorated ones. Thinking of a pre-order system. *Doorbell rings* Speaker_1: That’ll be Chloe. Right on time, as always. Prepare for Christmas overload. She starts planning in July. *Chloe enters* Speaker_3: Hello, my loves! Something smells divine. What culinary masterpiece are you two concocting? Speaker_2: Caramelised onions and impending potato perfection. Chloe, you are officially banned from mentioning Christmas until at least November. Speaker_3: (Gasps dramatically) Banned? But it's practically here! I’ve already been sketching out decoration schemes. I'm thinking rustic chic this year, lots of pine cones and fairy lights…and I’ve started compiling a spreadsheet of candy cane suppliers. Speaker_1: Spreadsheets? For candy canes? Speaker_1: Yes, as usual. Though old Reverend Thompson was rambling on something fierce last week. Couldn’t follow a word he was saying. I think he's getting a bit… lost in his thoughts, poor man. Speaker_4: We should probably pop round and see him. He’s a good man, even if his sermons are a bit meandering. We could take him some biscuits. Speaker_2: That’s a lovely idea. And Arthur, perhaps you could help him sort out his heating? I hear his boiler’s been acting up. Speaker_1: Oh, I could take a look. Though, honestly, these modern boilers… they’re beyond me. Everything’s digital these days. Give me a good old-fashioned gas fire any day.

Speaker_1: Right, so I genuinely think my mum thinks I’m still sixteen. Honestly. She was going on about needing to check what time I was getting the train back up north, and then proceeded to ask if *Dad* was picking me up from Doncaster station. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring a pan) Oh, bless her. Is she alright though? Is she…forgetful, generally? Speaker_1: No, not particularly! It’s just…me, I think. She treats me like I haven’t got a brain cell between them. Like I’ll just wander off a platform and get lost. Last time I visited, she packed me a bag with like, three jumpers and a hot water bottle, even though it was July! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh my god. That’s… peak Mum behaviour. My nan is the same. She still tries to slip me £20 when I see her, convinced I’m a struggling student. I’ve got a *Masters*! Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s just… patronising! Still, she means well, I suppose. Speaking of parental units, did your dad ever tell you that story about when he tried to build a shed? Speaker_2: Oh god, the shed saga. Don't even get me started. That story’s practically family folklore. It took him six months, involved a near-hospitalisation with a rogue hammer, and the final product leans at a frankly alarming angle. Speaker_1: (Grinning) I remember him telling me that! He made it sound like it was a feat of engineering. "It required precision, you see, and a level of commitment..." Meanwhile, it looks like it's about to fall apart in a stiff breeze. Speaker_2: The sheer *pride* he took in that wobbly monstrosity. It’s endearing, isn’t it? Right, dinner’s almost ready. Did you want to put the film on now, or after? I was thinking we could watch that new Wes Anderson one. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! Definitely after. I need sustenance first. And maybe another glass of wine. This conference I’m organising is *killing* me. The AV guy keeps cancelling on me, apparently his van broke down. Again. Speaker_2: Honestly, the drama with event planning. It’s a whole other level. I’ve got a similar thing happening with a supplier for the new theatre project. They’re threatening to pull out at the last minute because…apparently, they have a dispute with the catering company? It’s ridiculous. Speaker_1: It always is ridiculous. It’s like, everyone’s got to have a problem, right? Oh, this smells amazing, by the way. You’re a culinary genius. Speaker_2: (Blushing slightly) Don’t be silly. It’s just pasta. Although, I did spend a good twenty minutes trying to find decent basil in this neighbourhood… Honestly, Cambridge is surprisingly lacking in good Italian delis. Speaker_1: You’d think, wouldn't you? A university town, you’d expect a bit of sophistication. Maybe we should make it our mission to find one. Research for…cultural enrichment. Speaker_2: (Laughing) That's a very good idea. Cultural enrichment, indeed. Right, get your plate. And then we can judge Wes Anderson’s colour palette while shovelling pasta into our faces. Speaker_1: Perfect! Speaker_2: Perfect. Speaker_1: Good plan. Speaker_2: Ooh, don't burn your tongue! Speaker_1: Okay, okay, I'm being careful.

Speaker_1: Aye, well, it's a right pickle, isn't it? This Scottish referendum. Speaker_2: Yeah, Dad keeps going on about it. Says it’ll be a disaster if they go. Speaker_1: Your Dad's got a point, lad. Though I can understand why they want to, mind. They've always been a bit…different, haven't they? Thinking they're superior and all that. Speaker_2: He says it’ll mess up the whole UK, like. Everything's all connected. Speaker_1: It will. Absolutely will. Think about the borders, for a start. All that paperwork, the lorries queuing up. It’ll be a right mess at the border crossings. More hassle than crossing the Channel. Speaker_2: What about the money, then? He said something about the oil. Speaker_1: Oh, the oil. That’s where it gets tricky. They reckon they'll be rolling in it, don't they? But it’s not that simple. The price of oil goes up and down like a yo-yo. And then there's the decommissioning costs…getting rid of all the old rigs. That’s a fortune. Speaker_2: So it’s not as easy as just taking the oil and being rich? Speaker_1: Not at all, love. It's never that easy, is it? Remember when Maggie Thatcher shut down the mines? Said it'd be better for the economy. Look what happened to those communities. It tore them apart. This could be a bit like that, only on a grander scale. Speaker_2: I think Mr. Henderson, our history teacher, said it's about identity, too. That a lot of Scots feel like England tells them what to do. Speaker_1: Aye, there's a bit of that in it, I suppose. A lot of history there, you see. Old grievances and all. My grandma used to go on about the Jacobites, always siding with the Scots. Though she couldn’t tell you a thing about politics, just that they were ‘our people.’ Speaker_2: Did she have a Scottish accent? Speaker_1: Not really. She grew up down south. But she always felt a connection. It’s a complicated thing, identity. More than just a flag and a bit of tartan. Speaker_2: So, what do you think will happen? Speaker_1: Honestly? I don't know. I think it’ll be close. Very close. People are passionate about it, on both sides. It'll be a nervous night when the results come in, that's for sure. I just hope they think it through properly. It's not a decision to be taken lightly. It's something they’ll be living with for generations. It’s not like changing your mind over what tea to have. Speaker_2: Dad said he’s going to watch it on telly with his mates, get some beers in. Speaker_1: Your Dad loves a good political drama, doesn't he? He’d probably enjoy a proper war, the way he gets worked up! But seriously, it’s a big thing. A really big thing. Let’s hope they make the right decision, for everyone's sake. Speaker_2: Yeah. I just want to know what’s going to happen, so we can get back to…you know…normal. Speaker_1: You and me both, lad. You and me both. Now, are you finished with your dinner? You've barely touched your peas. Speaker_2: (Grumbling) Nearly…just…gotta get through them.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this Jeremy Kyle is a car crash, isn’t it? But you can’t look away. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! It's awful, but I’m proper hooked. Listen to that fella, though. You can barely understand a word he’s saying. It’s like… is he even *speaking* English? Speaker_3: It’s the elision, innit? Dropping all the ‘t’s and ‘h’s. Makes it a right mess. Speaker_4: Elision? What’s that then? Speaker_1: Basically, like, when people run words together and leave bits out. Like, instead of “want to” they say “wanna”. It’s common, but some people take it to the extreme. Speaker_2: Yeah, it's proper common where I'm from. "Gonna," "shoulda," the lot. But that guy… he's on another level. Speaker_5: It’s a Scouse thing, isn’t it? The accent generally kinda… swallows things. My auntie Sheila sounds like that when she’s had a few sherries. Speaker_3: So does my nan, but she’s always sounded like that, sherry or no sherry. It’s just how she’s always talked. It’s quite endearing, actually. Speaker_1: Endearing? He sounds like he’s mumbling into a sock! Honestly, this is why people poke fun at accents. It's not about being superior, it's just... some are harder to decipher. Speaker_4: You think our accents are easy to understand, then? Because I get stick for sounding ‘broad’ when I go down South. People ask me to repeat myself all the time. Speaker_5: Aye, me too. They think we’re all extras from *Emmerdale*. It's a bit insulting, really. Speaker_2: It's funny, isn't it? Everyone thinks *their* accent is normal, and everyone else’s is weird. Like when I first came to Chester, everyone thought I was speaking gibberish. They were all like, "What did you *say*?" Speaker_3: Oh, it’s the same for me coming down here from Derby. Everyone's like "What are you saying?" and I'm thinking, "I'm speaking English, love!" Just a slightly different flavour. Speaker_1: Still, you’ve gotta admit, Jeremy Kyle brings out the best – or worst – in everyone’s accents. It's like the stress makes it even more pronounced. Speaker_4: It does, doesn’t it? Listen to that woman now, she sounds like she's about to explode. Speaker_5: Ooh, here we go… someone’s about to yell something dramatic. Pass the crisps. This is getting good. Speaker_2: Oh, God, she's accusing him of sleeping with her sister... right this is going to be a good one. Speaker_3: Honestly, you couldn't write this stuff. Speaker_1: I'm honestly starting to think these people are professional actors or something. It's too ridiculous to be real. Speaker_4: No way, they are real. This is the wild west of daytime television. Speaker_5: Do you think they get paid to be on it? Speaker_2: Probably not much, but it's free publicity for their drama, innit? Gets their name out there. Speaker_3: Well, for all the wrong reasons! Speaker_1: I'm honestly stunned. Speaker_4: It's only going to get worse.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the refereeing in this game is absolutely shocking. Shocking! Speaker_2: (Eyes glued to the screen) Aye, it’s a bit ropey, isn’t it? Gave that away far too easily. Should’ve held their ground. Speaker_1: Held their ground? They were practically *inviting* a foul! Honestly, I swear some of these refs have never actually *played* football. Speaker_2: You’re telling me. It’s all about speed and physicality now, isn't it? No one actually *thinks* about the strategy anymore. Reminds me of when my grandad used to complain about the game changing in the 70s. Said it weren’t proper football without a good old-fashioned tackle. Speaker_1: Ha! My Nana’s the same, but she’s more concerned with if the players have “decent haircuts”. She judges the entire team on that. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) That’s brilliant. You know, it’s funny, you spend all this time doing academically rigorous research, and then you just end up shouting at a telly about twenty-two lads kicking a ball around. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. It’s therapeutic, though, isn’t it? A good release. Speaking of therapeutic... how’s the knitting going? Still on that scarf for your mum? Speaker_2: Slowly. Very slowly. I’m attempting a cable knit, which, apparently, requires a level of dexterity I simply do not possess. It looks less like a scarf and more like a… a tangled fishing net. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, no! Send me a picture, I want to see the carnage. I’ve started a little hat for the… well, for when we potentially have a little one. Speaker_2: Oh, seriously? Already thinking about hats? That’s moving fast! Speaker_1: Well, I was browsing baby names again last night, and it’s just… happening. I'm deep in the rabbit hole. I found one that means 'star' in Gaelic. Speaker_2: That’s nice. We haven't even gotten to names yet. We're still firmly in the 'is this even possible?' stage. Though, I did see someone suggest 'Ragnar' the other day. Speaker_1: (Bursting out laughing) Ragnar?! Seriously? Where did they even *find* that? Speaker_2: Apparently it’s making a comeback. Viking chic, apparently. It's good to have a list ready incase the Olympics are on again. They always get name trends soaring. Speaker_1: Oh, good point. Remember when everyone suddenly decided to name their kids after cyclists after London 2012? It was madness. Speaker_2: Totally. It's funny how easily influenced people are. Although, Ragnar… I think that might be pushing it a bit. Speaker_1: Definitely pushing it. Stick with something a bit more… conventional. Unless you want a toddler running around yelling 'I am Ragnarok!' Speaker_2: (Smiling) You're probably right. Maybe I'll leave the naming to you. You're clearly already prepared. Speaker_1: (Eyes back on the screen) Oh, for goodness sake! Another dodgy decision! This is unbelievable! Speaker_2: (Sighing) Well, at least it's giving us something to shout about. And providing ample material for your Nana’s haircut critiques. Speaker_1: True, true. It is a good game even though they are cheating. Speaker_2: It is. It’s a good game.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the Bee Movie is… a cinematic masterpiece. Don’t you think? The legal arguments were surprisingly sound. Speaker_2: (Giggles) Bees talking! It's so funny when they all fly around! Speaker_3: And the bee gets lost in human world! Is it real bees talking, Mummy? Speaker_1: Well, not *real* real, darling. It’s a cartoon. But it’s a very clever cartoon. It makes you think. Speaker_2: I want to be a bee! I’d collect all the pollen! Speaker_3: I want to be King Arthur! With a really big sword! Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You both want to be… powerful figures, it seems. Speaking of powerful figures… all this talk about the Royal Family. It’s just… odd, isn't it? Paying to go and look at where they live. Speaker_2: But they have nice gardens! Speaker_1: They *do* have nice gardens. And apparently, they’re very fussy about what fruit they eat. I read an article about how they only have specific varieties of peaches and plums. Royal fruit, apparently. Speaker_3: So they don't eat apples? Granny makes the best apple crumble! Speaker_1: They probably eat apples, sweetheart. Just… very *particular* apples. It just feels a bit… wrong, doesn’t it? That we’re effectively paying to peek into someone else's life. I’m leaning more and more towards being a Republican, honestly. Speaker_2: What’s a Republican? Speaker_1: It means you don't think we should have a King or Queen. You think everyone should be equal. It's a bit complicated for now. Speaker_3: I want to be King! Then I could have ALL the apples! And a big sword! Speaker_1: (Laughing) You would be a very generous King, I suspect. But you know, it does make you think. Would you actually *want* to be royal? All that scrutiny… or a politician, for that matter? No privacy. Speaker_2: I don't want people looking at me all the time. Speaker_1: Exactly! It sounds exhausting. Now, have you both taken your vitamins this morning? Don't forget, we’re going to the Olympic Stadium on Saturday! Speaker_3: For the diving! Can I wear my goggles? Speaker_1: Absolutely! But remember, we need to be super quiet. It’s a competition, and we don't want to disturb the divers. Total silence. Speaker_2: Like a bee! Quiet flying! Speaker_1: Precisely! Very good comparison. Remind me again, did I book that restaurant for after? We *always* struggle taking you two to restaurants. It's either too loud or too boring or… Speaker_3: I just want chips! Speaker_1: (Sighs playfully) We’ll figure it out. Oh, I really must call Granny later. She was saying the roof is leaking again in the old house. I keep meaning to go over and help, but…life just gets in the way. It’s such a shame to see it falling apart. It was a lovely house, wasn't it? Speaker_2: Granny makes yummy biscuits! Speaker_3: And reads me stories! And lets me build forts! Speaker_1: She does, doesn’t she? A very special Granny. Okay, vitamins, then maybe we can finish planning our bee-like, quiet trip to the diving! Speaker_1: Honestly, the Bee Movie is… a cinematic masterpiece. Don’t you think? The legal arguments were surprisingly sound. Speaker_2: (Giggles) Bees talking! It's so funny when they all fly around! Speaker_3: And the bee gets lost in human world! Speaker_1: Honestly, that tip was chaos. Absolute chaos. People hauling furniture, old carpets… you’d think it was a free-for-all. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I saw a woman trying to load a complete bathroom suite into a Mini. A *Mini*, Elsie! Speaker_3: (Eyes glued to his phone) Sounds… intense. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Typical Saturday afternoon. Did you manage to get rid of everything, Mum? Speaker_1: Nearly. Just the attic left now. Honestly, the amount of junk accumulated over the years… it’s frightening. Your father, bless him, never threw *anything* away. Said it might be useful. Speaker_2: That’s men for you. Mine’s the same. I found a box of screws he’d been saving “just in case” from 1987. 1987! Speaker_3: (Looking up briefly) Seriously? What were they even *for*? Speaker_2: He couldn’t remember. That was the point! Speaker_4: Speaking of useful things, did you see that antique dresser went for a fortune at Thompson’s auction last week? The one Old Man Hemmings had? Speaker_1: Oh, I did! I was quite surprised. I always thought it was a bit drab. Though, it was probably good quality. Everything was better made back then, wasn’t it? Not like the flatpack stuff they sell now. Speaker_2: Absolutely. We’re redecorating the spare room, trying to go for a sort of… shabby chic look. It’s proving tricky. There's so much *stuff* out there labelled ‘shabby chic’ that’s just… cheap. Speaker_3: Shabby chic is just a polite way of saying ‘old and falling apart’, isn’t it? Speaker_4: Pretty much. Though a genuinely good antique can look amazing. You wouldn't believe the price of original William Morris wallpaper these days. Speaker_1: William Morris… lovely man, wasn’t he? Always thought he was a bit of a socialist though. Remember the debates at university? Speaker_2: Oh, don’t get you started on politics! I've got enough to deal with trying to explain the curriculum changes to my Year 9s. Honestly, it’s like they're deliberately making it more complicated. Speaker_3: Miss, can I get another scone? These are good. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Of course, love. Just don't fill up entirely on scones before dinner. Speaker_4: Have you heard about Brenda's hen do? Apparently, she’s insisting on a medieval-themed weekend in Thirsk. Speaker_1: Thirsk? Oh dear. That sounds… ambitious. What are they planning? Jousting? Speaker_2: Something like that, apparently. They’re hiring costumes and trying to find a falconry centre. It's going to be a disaster, I tell you. A complete disaster. Speaker_3: Falconry? Cool. Speaker_4: It’s Brenda, after all. She always goes all out. Remember her stag do for Dave? He ended up dressed as a giant banana. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, I’d forgotten about that! He was furious. Poor Dave. Though he did look rather ridiculous. My knees have been giving me gyp again, by the way. I really must make an appointment with Dr. Peterson. It’s just… the waiting lists are so long. Speaker_2: They are, aren’t they? It’s a disgrace, frankly. Still, better to get it checked out. You don't want to leave it. Speaker_3: Can I have jam *and* cream with my next scone? Speaker_4: Of course you can. You've earned it. You suffered through listening to us old folks ramble on for long enough.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, for your birthday, we could actually go to the museum. Not just wander around town, proper museum. The Walker Art Gallery, maybe? Speaker_2: Ooh, that’s nice. I haven't been in ages. But parking's a nightmare around there, isn’t it? Remember last time we tried, we ended up miles away and practically had to take a bus back? Speaker_1: Yeah, I do. Nightmare. We could get the train, easy peasy. Though, then we’re limited to what we can bring back if we do any shopping. Speaking of which, have you started thinking about Christmas presents at all? I’m completely behind. Speaker_2: A little bit. I've got a few ideas, mostly online shopping. It's less stressful than fighting through Liverpool One. How's work been? Still battling the year sevens? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Honestly, some of the things they come out with, you wouldn’t believe. Tried to explain irregular verbs to one lad, and he genuinely thought 'ate' was another animal. Like a type of bird. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh, you’re kidding! They're brilliant, aren't they? But exhausting. My day was… interesting. Had a really difficult session with one of my patients. He's going through a really rough patch, and it’s hard not to get completely emotionally involved. Speaker_1: That sounds tough. You’re too good at your job, you care too much. Need a massive chocolate biscuit to cheer yourself up. Speaker_2: Definitely. You know, Sarah and Ben are finally setting a date for the wedding. Apparently, it’s next summer. They’re looking at that venue near Formby, the one with the gardens. Speaker_1: Oh, lovely! That’ll be a good one. Hopefully, the weather will be decent. Have they asked us to be ushers or anything yet? Speaker_2: Not yet. I think they're still figuring everything out. Listen, about moving… I was looking at places in Allerton again. Found a couple with gardens. Imagine, a garden for a dog! Speaker_1: Hold your horses! We haven't even *talked* about a dog! It's a big responsibility. And gardens are expensive to maintain. Speaker_2: I know, I know. Just daydreaming. But imagine, a little scruffy thing running around! Anyway, have you heard back about that interview for your Masters? Speaker_1: Not yet. I'm trying not to think about it. The waiting is the worst part. I’ve been checking my emails every five minutes. I really want to do it, though. It feels like the next step. Speaker_2: You’ll be brilliant. You always are. Don’t worry so much. And if it doesn’t work out, it’s not the end of the world. We'll figure it out. We're good at figuring things out. Speaking of figuring things out, how are we doing financially? Christmas is going to be expensive. Speaker_1: Yeah, we need to sit down and really look at that. I’ve been trying to save, but… well, you know. Takeaways and football tickets have a way of eating into the budget. What about your sister? Is she still talking about moving back up north? Speaker_2: She is, actually. She says she misses being close to family. And she's a bit fed up with London prices. She was asking me about schools around here for her little one. It would be nice to have her closer, honestly. Speaker_1: Yeah, it would. Right. Biscuit time? And then maybe we can actually start making a list of Christmas presents. Before it’s too late.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…an experience. I think that’s supposed to be pasta. It tastes vaguely of sadness. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I swear they just boil everything in the same water. Yesterday’s curry flavour seemed to have permeated the mashed potato. It was… unsettling. Speaker_1: Oh god, no! You're right, it *did* taste faintly of spice. I just assumed I was imagining things. Speaking of unsettling, have you seen the new series of ‘Bridgerton’? Speaker_2: Oh my god, yes! It's so ridiculous. I’m fully on board though. The costumes are insane, and honestly, I’m living for the drama. Lord Debling is… something. Speaker_1: He's *awful*! But you can’t look away, can you? Like a train wreck. Though Daphne and Simon in the first series were on another level. I keep rewatching clips on YouTube when I should be, you know, *studying*. Speaker_2: Don’t we all? I’ve been down a whole Disney rabbit hole this week. Watched ‘Hercules’ for the first time in ages. Philoctetes is a mood. Speaker_1: Oh my god, YES! Phil is the best. He’s so cynical and sarcastic. It’s perfect. I need a Disney rewatch. It’s been way too long. What are you doing this weekend? Anything exciting planned? Speaker_2: Not much, actually. My brother's having a football viewing party, but I’m not massively into football. I might just chill, try and finish that assignment for Modern History, and maybe go to that new café, ‘Bloom,’ on Albion Street. Have you heard of it? Speaker_1: Ooh, no! What’s it like? Is the coffee good? That’s the important thing. I’m desperate for a decent flat white. This uni coffee is basically coloured water. Speaker_2: Apparently, it's amazing. My friend, Priya, went yesterday and said their pistachio croissant is life-changing. Also, they have all these cute fairy lights and plants everywhere. Super Instagrammable. Speaker_1: Pistachio croissant… okay, you're selling this. We should go! Saturday? Speaker_2: Yeah, Saturday sounds good. We could grab some lunch there, maybe do a bit of window shopping afterwards. I need to browse some new clothes. The temptations of Shein are too strong. Speaker_1: Honestly, same. It’s a dangerous website. Speaking of dangerous, have you seen what Liam did on his Instagram story? He got a tattoo! Speaker_2: No way! What did he get? Another questionable nautical thing? He's obsessed with anchors, it’s baffling. Speaker_1: Worse! A tiny pizza slice on his ankle. An actual pizza slice. I screenshot it. It’s… a choice. Speaker_2: (laughs) Oh, Liam. That is spectacularly awful. I love it. He’s fully leaning into the chaotic energy. Speaker_1: Right? He's a menace. I haven't slept properly all week honestly. Between the coursework and the relentless hum of the student halls, I feel ancient. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I’m running on caffeine and sheer willpower. I think I saw a cartoon playing on someone's laptop last night and just stared at it for a solid ten minutes. It was strangely soothing. Speaker_1: That sounds… necessary, actually. Maybe we need a cartoon-and-pizza night. A distraction from the impending doom of deadlines. Speaker_2: Absolutely. I'm in. Maybe after Bloom on Saturday? We can order a ridiculous amount of pizza and watch ‘Rick and Morty’. Speaker_1: Perfect. It's a plan. Honestly, you’re a lifesaver. Now, I’m going to attempt to salvage what’s left of this… pasta. Wish me luck.

Speaker_1: Right, so I finally got Charizard. Took ages to evolve him, honestly. It was brutal. Speaker_2: Oh, good for you! Is that the really… fiery dragon one? Oisin loves dragons. He keeps pointing at pictures in books, shouting “Drah-gon!” It’s adorable, but mostly just noise. Speaker_3: Drah-gon! Nana! Speaker_1: Yeah, that's the one. It took like, a million Charizard candies. Honestly, Pokémon Go is taking over my life. Speaker_2: It’s good you’re getting out and about though, isn’t it? Instead of just glued to a screen all the time. Speaking of screens, have you Skyped your Dad this week? He was asking about you. Speaker_1: Not yet, I was going to tomorrow. He wants to hear about the school trip. Speaker_2: Good. He misses you. Listen, I was thinking… we could maybe go for Ramen on Saturday? There’s that new place opened down by the river. Speaker_1: Ooh yeah, I’ve heard it's good. Is Oisin coming? Speaker_2: Probably. He's been obsessed with noodles lately. Although getting him to *stay* in his seat while eating is another matter entirely. He just wants to chuck them about. Speaker_3: Noodles! Up! Speaker_2: See? Exactly. Speaking of chucking things, have you seen where you’ve left your skinny jeans? I need to get them in the wash. They’re practically growing legs and walking around on their own. Speaker_1: They're probably under my bed. Sorry. I was practicing guitar in them. Speaker_2: Guitar in skinny jeans? That sounds… restrictive. Speaker_1: It’s fine! It doesn’t hinder my shredding. Much. Hey, do you think we could get ice cream after Ramen? Speaker_2: We’ll see. Depends on how well Oisin behaves. Although, honestly, a bribe might be necessary. He’s been saying “more” all day. Just… “More! More! More!” It’s driving me slightly insane. Speaker_3: More! Juice! Speaker_2: See! More juice now, apparently. Honestly, I swear he understands more than he lets on. He just likes the reaction. Speaker_1: He's a clever one, that Oisin. Hey, did you manage to find those fluffy slippers I left here last time? The dinosaur ones? Speaker_2: Actually, no. I think he’s hidden them somewhere. He loves carrying them around. It’s a whole thing. We’ll find them eventually. Probably under the sofa, with the remote control and a half-eaten biscuit. Speaker_1: Classic Oisin. Right, gotta go finish evolving my Squirtle. It’s a matter of national importance. Speaker_2: Alright, alright. Just remember to Skype your dad! And maybe put the skinny jeans *in* the wash, not *under* the bed. Speaker_3: Drah-gon! Biscuit! More! Speaker_2: Oh, good grief. Here we go again. Speaker_1: (Muttering as he heads off) Squirtle… must… evolve… Speaker_2: Honestly, boys. They're all the same, aren't they? Speaker_3: Nana! Up! Biscuit! More! Then Peter Pan, and maybe a little bit of research about Great Ormond Street. It's a good night for stories and helping people.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this M5 is just relentless isn’t it? Seems to be permanently gridlocked these days. Used to be able to do this run in… well, not quickly, but without wanting to age visibly. Proud of her, I am. Right, well, we’re getting closer. So, Christmas… have we confirmed what we’re all doing? You two coming to us, I hope? Speaker_2: We are, Dad. Unless something completely catastrophic happens at school. Though, I suspect even a school pandemic wouldn’t stop me from having your Christmas dinner. Speaker_3: We’re looking forward to it. And we should start thinking about a house-warming for you both, once you’ve fully settled in. A proper one, not just a quick cup of tea while unpacking boxes. Speaker_1: Oh, yes! A proper party. We’ll need to get the garden sorted first. Still a bit of a mess after all that building work. Speaker_2: Don't worry about that, Dad. We’re happy to help clear it up. It's looking good though, honestly. The new extension is fantastic. Speaker_3: It really is. It’ll be lovely to have the space. And for Sarah when she comes home… she'll have her own room at last. Speaker_1: Precisely. Everything for my granddaughter. Now, look at that traffic… still crawling along. I swear, they’re building a new roundabout every five miles and it doesn’t make a bit of difference. Does this fit what you were looking for? Let me know if you'd like me to continue the conversation or modify it in any way. Does this fit what you were looking for? Let me know if you'd like me to continue the conversation or modify it in any way. Speaker_2: Okay, well. Does this fit what you were looking for? Let me know if you'd like me to continue the conversation or modify it in any way.

Speaker_1: Oh, bless me, this queue is dreadful, isn’t it? Though, I suppose, it's expected on a day like this. Lovely weather for it, all the same. Though a bit too bright for my eyes, really. Speaker_2: You’re telling me. I’ve been stood here ten minutes already, just to get a ticket to…well, never mind where to. It’s the principle of the thing, isn’t it? They should have more staff on. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Though, I was saying to my neighbour just last week, it’s all about efficiency these days. No one wants to pay for proper service anymore. It’s all self-service and machines. Gives me a headache trying to work them. Speaker_2: They expect everyone to be tech-savvy now, don't they? I struggle with the telly remote half the time. My wife, God rest her soul, she was the one who sorted all that out. Always had a knack for gadgets. Speaker_1: Oh, I am sorry to hear about your wife. It’s never easy, losing a partner. I lost my husband some years ago. Though, he wasn’t much for gadgets either, thankfully. More interested in his garden. He used to say a garden kept a man honest. Speaker_2: That’s a nice thought. Mine was a teacher, you know. Nursery education. Said it was the most important stage. Shaping little minds, she called it. Used to volunteer at the hospice too, after she retired. Incredible woman. Speaker_1: That’s wonderful. It’s good to give back, isn’t it? I used to run an art gallery, years ago, before I retired completely. Did a bit of painting myself, though mostly landscapes. Lovely, peaceful thing to do. Though, it never paid the bills, not really. Speaker_2: Art’s a difficult game, I imagine. Everything’s about money these days, isn't it? Speaking of which, I was reading in the paper about this ME event next year, the one they're holding…somewhere around here, I think. Speaker_1: Oh, you mean the big one? Yes, they're planning it for the field down by the river. I’ve heard a bit about it. Speaker_2: Apparently, they’re trying to get more women involved. Which is good, I suppose. Though sometimes I think all this talk of ‘female equality’ becomes a bit… much. It’s like they have to label everything, make a fuss. Women are perfectly capable without being constantly reminded. Speaker_1: Now, I'm not so sure about that. It's a bit like when I used to deal in antiques, you see. The men would always try to undervalue things, assuming I didn’t know my stuff. They couldn't believe a woman could have such knowledge. It’s a subtle thing, but it’s there. And the terminology! ‘Handmade’ versus ‘craftsmanship’...it always felt like they were diminishing the skill simply because *I* was the one doing the work. Speaker_2: Hmm. A good point, actually. I hadn’t really thought of it like that. My wife used to say the same thing about the school board. Always a struggle to get her voice heard. Speaker_1: Exactly! And with this event, they need to ensure the women are involved at every level, not just asked to make the tea and cakes. Proper representation. Speaker_2: I suppose you’re right. It’s just… I’m an old-fashioned man, I suppose. I still open doors for ladies. Speaker_1: (chuckles) Well, that's certainly a gentlemanly habit. Though, don't be surprised if I open the door for *you* next time, just to keep you on your toes! Oh, look, the queue's moving. Finally.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was looking at flights again, and it’s still looking…optimistic, to get something remotely reasonable. Speaker_2: Optimistic as in expensive, or optimistic as in doesn’t actually exist? Speaker_1: Both, honestly. Expensive *and* they involve about three layovers in places I’ve never even heard of. Oh, that’s a bit grim, isn’t it? Is it worth trying to shift the dates even by a day or two? Sometimes just a slight change can knock a load off. Speaker_1: I’ve played around with it a bit. It’s just that Mark already has that work thing on the Friday, so we’re trying to fit it around that. And I really wanted five full days, not four, squeezed in with travel. Speaker_2: Hmm. Okay. Well, have you thought about…and this might be a bit radical…trains? Speaker_1: Trains? Mum, that’s…that’s a long way to go by train! Speaker_2: I know, I know. But just think about it. No airport faff, you can actually *see* the country, you can take your time… it’s a different kind of holiday. And you could break it up, stop off in Paris for a night, maybe even Bordeaux. Speaker_1: Bordeaux does sound nice…but honestly, the thought of being on a train for two days solid… I’d get so restless. I need a bit of space, you know? Plus, it’d probably work out more expensive, wouldn’t it? Speaker_2: Possibly. But I’ve been reading about these Interrail passes. They do deals sometimes. It's worth a look. It might be a bit of an adventure. Speaker_1: (sighs) Maybe. I'll look into it. It just feels like such a fuss getting there. I was picturing just flopping on a beach, not meticulously planning train schedules. Speaker_2: Well, you won't flop on a beach if you don't *get* to the beach, will you? Have you booked accommodation yet? At least get the apartment sorted, that might focus your mind. Speaker_1: I’ve shortlisted a few, yeah. This one, near the Alfama district…it's got a little balcony overlooking the rooftops. It looks gorgeous, and it’s not massively expensive. Speaker_2: Alfama? Oh, that’s the old part, isn’t it? Really atmospheric. You’ll love it there. Just be careful with your belongings, that area can be a bit…picked-pocket-y. Speaker_1: Oh good tip, thank you. I'll remember that. I was also thinking about doing a day trip to Sintra. Have you been? Speaker_2: Oh, Sintra is *magical*. That Pena Palace… it’s like something out of a fairytale. Absolutely breathtaking. You *have* to go. But book your tickets in advance. The queues are horrendous.

Speaker_1: Right, so I checked the bank again, and they’ve actually taken *both* Spotify subscriptions this month. Both mine and Mum’s. Speaker_2: Seriously? That’s… inefficient, to say the least. Did you call them about it last time, when it happened with yours? Speaker_1: Yeah, and they said it was a glitch, refunded it, and told me it’d be sorted. Apparently not. I’m on hold now, it’s been twenty minutes. The hold music is genuinely criminal. It's like a midi file of a pan flute. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, that *is* rough. Banks and their terrible hold music.
