Root looked alright for a bit, but then just…gone. They needed him. I was watching it with Ben, he was proper fuming. He’s convinced it’s all down to the pitches being too bowler-friendly. Speaker_2: It's a bit of both, I think. The bowlers *were* on fire, but the batting just wasn't up to scratch. No application, you know? Seems like nobody wants to just stick around and build an innings these days. Speaker_1: Exactly! It's all slog, slog, slog, and then out. No patience. Remember when Cooky used to just…wear the bowlers down? Solid as a rock. Speaker_2: Ah, Alastair Cook. A proper craftsman. Different times. Speaking of different times, how was your Auntie Carol’s birthday weekend? Did everyone make it down to Devon? Speaker_1: Yeah, everyone except Uncle Dave. He said his back was playing up again. Mum was proper disappointed. She’d made his favourite lemon drizzle cake. Speaker_2: Oh, that’s a shame. He always does appreciate her baking, though, doesn’t he? I remember him smuggling bits of it out to the garden last time. Speaker_1: (Laughing) He’s a terrible sneak! But yeah, she was a bit miffed. It was a good weekend overall though. Lots of catching up, a few embarrassing stories about Mum’s youth… the usual. Speaker_2: Sounds perfect. Family chaos is the best kind, isn't it? Still on hold, I presume? Honestly, just email them. It'll be quicker. Speaker_1: I'm tempted. But I'm stubborn. And I want to *speak* to someone and make them acknowledge their terrible system. Plus, I'm avoiding starting that essay on post-structuralism. Procrastination at its finest. It’s supposed to be on Foucault. Speaker_2: Foucault? Good luck with that. Sounds…dense. I'm glad I'm just dealing with spreadsheets and budgets. Much less existential angst. How’s the new team at work settling in? Still causing you headaches? Speaker_1: Honestly, they’re better than I expected. A couple of them are really quick learners. Although, one keeps trying to convince me that TikTok is the future of marketing. Speaker_2: (Groans) Oh, no. Don't tell me about TikTok. My nephew is obsessed. It's just endless dancing and lip-syncing. Where’s the substance? Speaker_1: Exactly! I tried to explain that our target demographic is slightly above the age of fifteen, but he just didn’t get it. I think I’m losing a battle here.

Speaker_2: Honestly, this Skype thing is a marvel, isn't it? Seeing your faces like this, feels almost like you’re both here. Though, a proper cuppa and biscuit with you two is always better. Speaker_1: Aye, it's alright for a quick catch up. Though I still can't get on with these newfangled contraptions. Always fiddling about with the volume. You can hear everything but what you *want* to hear, eh? Speaker_3: Dad, you say that every time. It's probably just your hearing, honestly. Are you managing alright with your leg today? Speaker_1: Oh, it's a rum do, this leg. A rum do. On a bad day, it feels like someone's taken a hammer to it. Though, I managed a little potter in the garden earlier. Just deadheading the roses, mind. Can’t be doing any heavy lifting. Speaker_2: Good for you, dear. Roses are looking lovely, according to the photos you sent. You always did have a way with the garden. Remember that time you tried to grow pumpkins for Halloween? They were enormous! Speaker_1: Ha! Enormous is right. Nearly took out Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning dahlias! She wasn’t best pleased, I can tell you. She gave me a right telling off. Speaking of holidays, I was looking at those globes you sent, David. Lovely things. Reminded me of our trip to Yorkshire, years ago. Speaker_3: Yorkshire? That was ages ago! I was still at school, wasn’t I? Mum and Dad took me and…was it Auntie Brenda who came too? Speaker_2: It was. A terrible trip! Rain the whole time. We tried to make the best of it, visited those little villages. And you, David, insisted on staying in a youth hostel. Speaker_3: It was cheap! And a good experience. Though admittedly, the shared showers weren’t ideal. I had a school project due, remember? Geography, all about the Peak District. That trip really helped. Speaker_1: Aye, a proper soaking it was. Remember climbing that hill? Could barely see a thing through the mist. And then you got us lost following a sheep track! Speaker_2: Oh, don't start that again, Arthur. It wasn’t a sheep track, it was a public footpath! And we weren't *lost*, just…temporarily misplaced. We found our way back eventually. Speaking of being lost – have you been watching that new drama on the television? About the underground system during the war? Speaker_3: Oh, yeah! It's brilliant, isn’t it? So well done. Makes you think about all the stories hidden beneath our feet. Speaker_1: Television. All that noise and flashing. Give me a good book any day. Though I did watch a bit of that gardening programme this morning. They were building a raised bed. Might have to try one of those next year. If this leg allows. Speaker_2: You could ask young Emily for help, dear. She’s quite handy. Now, you two, are you eating properly? I worry about you both. David, you’re always working, and Arthur, you barely touch a thing. Speaker_3: Mum, I'm fine. Just busy with marking. End of term rush. And Dad…you know how he is. He'll eat when he's hungry. Speaker_1: I'll have another biscuit, thank you very much. And a little more tea. Best tea in the world, this. Though not quite as good as a proper cuppa *with* you both. Still, this’ll do for now.

Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve been looking at flights again, and honestly, it’s just…criminal. Everything’s gone up, hasn't it? Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I was checking prices for my mum to come up for Christmas, and it's ridiculous. Even EasyJet are trying it on now. They used to be the budget champions. Speaker_1: Exactly! Speaker_2: Oh, no! Barcelona’s brilliant. You absolutely have to go. Have you tried, like, looking at different airports? Sometimes flying into Girona or Reus can be cheaper. Speaker_1: Yeah, I’ve had a look. Adds another couple of hours on the journey though, which kind of negates the saving, doesn’t it? I spent ages yesterday comparing different sites – Skyscanner, Kayak, directly with the airlines… I’m starting to dream in flight numbers. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, I know the feeling. When I was booking flights for Italy last year, I was convinced I’d found a glitch. Spent an hour triple-checking, then it turned out I'd just misread the airport code. Speaker_1: Oh, classic! I did that with a hotel once. Booked a ‘luxury suite’ thinking it was in the city centre. Turns out it was 20 miles out in the middle of nowhere. Lesson learned: always check the location properly. Speaker_2: Definitely. So, what are you having for your tea? I'm starving. This day has just flown by. Three meetings back-to-back, then a crisis with the new supplier… honestly, it’s been a mess. Speaker_1: I made a chilli. It's not fancy, but it's easy. And warming. Do you want some? It’ll take your mind off crisis suppliers. Speaker_2: Oh, yes, please! That sounds perfect. You're a lifesaver. I think I need a bowl of something spicy and a long sit-down. Plus, you promised we could watch that new true crime documentary. Speaker_1: Deal. Chilli, documentary, and hopefully, a flight to Barcelona that doesn't require remortgaging the house. Speaker_2: Fingers crossed! Oh, and I brought biscuits. Chocolate digestives. Because every crisis deserves a biscuit. Speaker_1: You are officially the best friend ever. Chocolate digestives *and* escaping a crisis. Perfect. Now, let's get this chilli dished up, and then we can solve all the world’s problems – starting with the extortionate price of flights. Speaker_2: Agreed. World domination, one biscuit and one documentary at a time. Speaker_1: Exactly. Speaker_2: So tell me everything about Barcelona. Do you have a rough plan or are you just going to wing it? Speaker_1: I've got a few things… Park Güell is definitely on the list… and La Sagrada Familia. But mostly, I want to just wander around and get lost. Chloe’s the planner, I’m the… improvisor. Speaker_2: Sounds good. You’ll have to get some tapas, obviously! I had the best patatas bravas in Barcelona, ever.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the price of a loaf of bread now… it’s scandalous. Used to be you could get a decent sliced white for… well, less than a pound, certainly. Now? Nearly two fifty. Speaker_2: It is awful, isn't it? Everything is going up. I was looking at the cost of cat food the other day… ridiculous. Jasper's getting picky, too. Only wants the salmon flavour, the expensive stuff! Speaker_3: Don’t even *start* me on pet food. Honestly, they’ve got you by the short and curlies. You love ‘em, you pay through the nose. It's the same with everything. I was at the supermarket yesterday, and a tin of tomatoes… used to be sixty pence, now it’s nearly a pound twenty. Speaker_1: It's daylight robbery, that's what it is. And the banks… don't even get me started on the banks. Charging for everything now. I tried to withdraw some cash yesterday, and they wanted a fee! A *fee*! For using *my* money. Speaker_2: I switched mobile phone providers last month, hoping to save a bit. Worst decision ever. The signal is terrible, and the customer service is… nonexistent. I spent an hour on hold yesterday trying to sort out a billing issue. An hour! Speaker_3: Oh, customer service. Don’t even ask. I had a problem with a dodgy neighbour last week, had to call the police. Took them nearly three hours to turn up. Three hours! And then the officer just said there wasn't much they could do without further evidence. Honestly, the justice system is falling apart. Speaker_1: It's the same everywhere, isn't it? No one seems to care about doing a proper job anymore. Everyone’s just trying to get by. Speaking of getting by, have you seen what’s happened to interest rates? Absolutely crippling. I’ve got a bit of savings, you know, for a rainy day… but earning next to nothing on it. Speaker_2: It’s so frustrating. You try to be responsible, save for the future, and then the banks just… swallow all the benefits. I’ve been thinking about investing, but it all seems so risky. Speaker_3: Risky is right. Remember Uncle George and that ‘guaranteed’ investment scheme? Lost the lot, he did! Still talking about it, years later. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Aye, George was always a bit too trusting. Honestly, it's a minefield. What about you, have you managed to put anything aside, dear? Your job must be fairly secure. Speaker_2: It is, thankfully. But even so, with the cost of everything going up, it's hard to know what the future holds. I am putting a little bit away each month, but it doesn’t feel like enough. Maybe I should look at a LISA? Speaker_3: LISA? What's that, some new type of banking scam? Speaker_2: (Laughing) No, it's a Lifetime ISA. The government adds a bonus to your savings. Good for a first house or retirement, apparently. Speaker_1: Sounds complicated. I’ll stick to my building society, thank you very much. Though, admittedly, it’s not doing me much good. Listen, are you two free next weekend? My sister’s having a birthday… a small gathering at her place. Thought it’d be nice if you both came. Speaker_3: Oh, lovely! Yes, I’d love to. It’s been ages since I’ve seen Mabel. Speaker_2: I’d like that very much. We can bring cakes. Though, knowing supermarket prices, they’ll probably cost a fortune by then!

Speaker_1: Right, so we’re doing favourites, yeah? Favourites of everything. I’ll start with holidays. Mine’s gotta be… South Africa. Obvious, innit? Seeing as I practically grew up there. But honestly, the beaches are just… another level. Speaker_2: Ooh, good shout! South Africa does sound amazing. Mine’s probably Italy, actually. Florence, specifically. All the art and the pasta… I could live there. Speaker_3: Italy’s gorgeous! Though I'm a bit biased towards Ireland, obviously. The Cliffs of Moher are just breathtaking. And the pubs, like, you can’t beat a proper Irish pub. Speaker_4: Oh, definitely! I went to Ireland a few years ago, lovely. For me, though, it’s gotta be Greece. The islands are incredible. So much history and the food is just… *chef’s kiss*. Speaker_5: I’m a bit boring, I think. Mine’s Spain. Benidorm. Don’t judge me! It’s just proper chill, sunshine, sangria… exactly what I need after a stressful semester. Speaker_1: Benidorm’s a classic! No judgement here. Right, what about animals? Favourite animal then? Speaker_2: Oh, that’s easy. Dogs. 100%. Especially Golden Retrievers. So fluffy and sweet. Speaker_3: I’m a cat person, through and through. Always have been. They’re so independent and sassy. Plus, mine absolutely loves a cuddle when *she* decides it's cuddle time, which is the power move. Speaker_4: I have a soft spot for elephants. They’re just… majestic. And so intelligent. I watched a documentary about them once and I was sobbing. Speaker_5: I love meerkats! They’re just so funny, always standing on their little hind legs, looking around. They proper brighten my day. Speaker_1: Meerkats are brilliant! Okay, last one. Food. Favourite food, go! Speaker_2: Oh god, that’s the hardest one. Okay… Pizza. Definitely pizza. Any kind, honestly. But especially a good Margherita. Simple perfection. Speaker_3: I’m going to go with a full Irish breakfast. Sausage, bacon, black and white pudding, fried egg, the works. It’s a proper cure for everything. Speaker_4: Welsh Rarebit! It's a classic, it's cheesy, it's perfect with a side of chutney. You can't beat it. Actually, anything with cheese, really. Speaker_5: I'm gonna say… a proper Sunday dinner. Yorkshire puddings, roast potatoes, gravy… the whole shebang. My nan makes the best. Speaker_1: Ooh, a good Sunday dinner is hard to beat. Mine's… Bobotie. It’s a South African dish, minced meat baked with an egg-based topping. It’s amazing. You'd have to try it. Honestly, I’m getting hungry just talking about all this food! Maybe we should order something. Speaker_2: I'm in! Pizza maybe? To stick with my favourite. Speaker_3: I’m not complaining if we order pizza. Speaker_4: Definitely ordering something. This conversation has made me ravenous. Speaker_5: Pizza sounds amazing. Let's do it! Speaker_1: Alright then, pizza it is! Who's on ordering duties? Speaker_2: I'll do it. I know a good place that delivers round here. Speaker_3: Perfect! And I'll put the kettle on for tea. Or maybe something stronger. Speaker_4: Sounds like a plan! Speaker_5: Excellent. This flatmate favourite game has been a success, I think.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to freak out a bit about what comes *after* uni. Like, properly freak out. Speaker_2: Oh god, same. Feels like everyone else has a ten-year plan mapped out, and I’m just…here. Still figuring out what I want for breakfast. Speaker_1: Exactly! And it's not even like, a career thing necessarily. Seriously, commitment like that takes dedication. And you're brilliant at art, remember? You should focus on that. Speaker_1: Easier said than done. This essay on the Pre-Raphaelites is killing me. “Discuss the influence of Medievalism on Rossetti’s artistic vision.” It’s just…words. Meaningless, pretentious words. Speaker_2: Oh, I feel you. Mine's on Post-Structuralism. I’ve read the same paragraph five times and I *still* don't understand it. It's like they're deliberately trying to sound complicated. Speaker_1: Exactly! It's all just intellectual showing-off. I wish I could just paint all day instead of writing about it. Imagine, just losing myself in colour and texture, not worrying about semiotics or whatever. Speaker_2: You totally should. Maybe during the break? Actually, proper break. No uni work allowed. Just paint, play Stardew, maybe even attempt a flower arrangement. You know, prepare for old age. Speaker_1: (Laughs) You’re awful. But yeah, maybe. I keep thinking about entering some of my stuff into that student exhibition, but I'm too scared it’ll be rubbish. Speaker_2: No way! Your work is amazing. Remember that portrait you did of old Mr. Henderson from down the hall? It was incredible. You need to believe in yourself more. Speaker_1: Thanks, you’re sweet. You always know what to say. Have you made any progress with your dissertation topic then? Still thinking about video game addiction? Speaker_2: Yeah, I think so. I found a really interesting study about dopamine levels and reward mechanisms in MMOs. It's a bit dense, but I think I can make something of it. Speaker_1: Morning, Chloe! Chaos as usual, I see. You’re practically sprinting towards Falmer House. Speaker_2: (Slightly breathless) Morning, Ben! You have *no* idea. I refuse to spend £50 on a pumpkin spice latte. Speaker_1: Good for you. I saw Liam from the TEFL course last week. He's already booked his flights to Thailand. Speaker_2: Right, so you need one part rice to two parts water. It’s really simple, honestly. People make such a fuss about rice. Speaker_1: Two parts water? Are you sure? Though, honestly, a little bit of what you fancy doesn’t hurt. We're having a treat tonight. Remember that restaurant we went to in Bristol, the one with all the amazing food? Speaker_1: Yeah! The one with the really weird art on the walls? Speaker_2: That’s the one! We should go back someday. They did amazing curries, but they were so expensive. These vouchers I've got might cover a main course each, though. We could try and go next month. Speaker_1: Cool. What about that weird thing you were reading about… the person with the face… you know, the one who couldn’t make facial expressions? Speaker_2: Oh, right! That was… fascinating and quite sad, actually. It’s a really rare condition. Something to do with the nerves in their face. Imagine not being able to smile properly. Speaker_1: That’s… grim. It makes you appreciate your face, I guess. Speaker_2: Definitely. Speaking of grim, have you ever been stung by a jellyfish? Speaker_1: No! But I saw a picture of one on the beach once. It looked really painful. Speaker_2: It is! My cousin got stung when she was little. She was screaming for ages. Right, rice is bubbling nicely. How about you give it a stir? Careful, it's hot. Speaker_2: You’ve only been looking properly for a couple of weeks, Liam. Don’t beat yourself up. Have you tried widening your search? Maybe looking further afield? Speaker_1: Right, so then Brenda, bless her, she’s gone and booked a pottery class for us all. A *pottery* class, Liam. Can you imagine? Speaker_2: Pottery? Cor, sounds…messy. And a bit slow, innit? The keynote speaker keeps changing his mind about the AV setup. Speaker_2: Oh, the joys. Folks are always right at the last minute. Makes your head spin, doesn’t it? It comes naturally. Besides, someone’s gotta keep the armchair warm. Though I miss being busy, I won't lie. Used to enjoy a bit of physical graft, actually. Building stuff, fixing things. Like Brenda, even if she is trying to turn me into a ceramic artist. Speaker_2: Aye, that it does. Pass the gravy, would you? This roast’s lovely, you’re a good cook. Speaker_1: Thank you! Glad you think so. It's a far cry from a collapsed ashtray, anyway. Speaker_2: Definitely a far cry. And way more filling. Speaker_1: So, pottery on Saturday then? Prepare to be amazed by my utter lack of talent. Speaker_2: I'll bring a towel. Just in case. And maybe a camera. For posterity. Speaker_1: (Groans) You’re awful. Speaker_2: I try my best.

Reminds me a bit of Federer, honestly. Speaker_2: Dad, you always say that about anyone good at tennis. Speaker_3: Well, Federer *was* the best. Still is, in my eyes. Speaker_4: I don’t know... it looked a bit close. Like, holding hands close. Speaker_3: Right, well, that’s a conversation you need to have with her, son. It reminds me a bit of what happened with Auntie Maureen, you know, slowly… disappearing. It's just awful watching someone you love…fade. Speaker_3: (Quietly) It is the worst thing. My mum… forgetting my name. That was hard. Still hard, even now. Speaker_2: (Changing the subject slightly) Did you see that new building they're putting up on the Silk Road? It looks… huge. Speaker_1: Hideous. Honestly, it's completely out of character with the town. It’s like someone just plonked a spaceship down. And the traffic…it’s already chaos. Speaker_3: They never think things through, do they? Just build, build, build. Don’t care about the consequences. Remember that Beaver Scout Christmas party last year? Little Timmy swore after losing at pass the parcel. His mum was mortified. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, I remember that! Poor Timmy. Did you ever see Darren from primary school? The one with the ridiculously curly hair? Speaker_1: Darren?! Blimey, it must be twenty years! No, haven't a clue what happened to him. Last I heard he was obsessed with Network Scouts. Speaker_2: That’s what I heard too! Apparently, he's still involved. Runs a whole troop now. Speaker_1: Good for him! I mean, good for him finding something he's passionate about. I never understood all that scouting stuff. Always seemed a bit…muddy. Speaker_3: Your Uncle George was a scoutmaster, you know. Anyway, enough about work doom and gloom. What are your plans for the weekend? Anything fun? Speaker_2: Your Grandad's birthday, remember? We’re going over to his on Saturday for lunch. Though, honestly, I think he'll just want to talk about his garden. Speaker_1: Definitely. He could talk about gardening for hours. You know, I really should try and go to the gym more. I've been terrible with my eating lately. Speaker_2: Oh, don't beat yourself up about it. Everyone indulges now and then. Though, speaking of ice cream, I saw some lovely salted caramel in Waitrose yesterday. We could pick some up on the way home? Speaker_1: Ooh, yes, please! You know my weaknesses. We should also think about getting some bits for the house. We still haven't chosen tiles for the downstairs toilet extension... it's been ages. Speaker_2: I know, honestly! It’s dragging on. Let’s have a proper look online this weekend. We need to make a decision soon before the builder starts getting impatient. And maybe a little retail therapy afterwards? I saw a lovely cardigan in John Lewis... Speaker_1: You and shopping, Mum! Always a good distraction. Alright, salted caramel ice cream, tiles, potential cardigan… sounds like a plan. And hopefully, no redundancy announcements! Speaker_2: Let’s keep our fingers crossed. Now, watch out for that lorry!

Speaker_2: Right, nearly finished. Nearly dinner ready. Peas and fish fingers, is that alright? Speaker_1: Yeah, sounds good. Can I watch Mick after? Speaker_2: After you’ve eaten *all* your peas. No arguments. Honestly, you’re worse than Finn sometimes. Finn, darling, stop trying to climb the curtains! *to Speaker_3* No, down! Speaker_3: (Gurgles and points at the curtains) Uh-oh! Speaker_1: He's a proper little monkey, isn’t he? Speaker_2: You have no idea. Honestly, it’s a full-time job. Now, what are you planning to do tomorrow? It's raining again, isn't it? No good for a park visit. Speaker_1: Liam said we might go to his house and build a massive Lego castle. He’s got all the Star Wars sets. Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds good. Who’s Liam again? Remind me. Speaker_1: From school! We were talking about it on the bus. It’ll take ages, apparently. He's got, like, three different Millennium Falcons. Speaker_2: Goodness. Well, as long as you’re having fun. What if it rains all summer? Have you thought about what you’d like to do then? Speaker_1: I dunno. Learn more guitar? Mr. Henderson said I'm getting good, but I keep forgetting the chords for ‘Smoke on the Water’. Speaker_2: Well, practice makes perfect. Maybe we can find some easy tutorials online? Or, we could try and go to the swimming pool more often. Speaker_1: The Quays? It's always busy. And sometimes those older kids splash everyone. Speaker_2: We could go early, before it gets too crowded. Or maybe try the one in Midleton? It’s quieter there, I think. We could even pack a picnic. Speaker_1: That’d be good. Finn could come too, if he's being good. Speaker_2: He’s two. “Good” is a relative term. *to Speaker_3* No, Finn, don't put that in your mouth! It's a sock! Speaker_1: What was that you were saying earlier? About…Japan-ease? Speaker_2: Oh! Japanese! I was trying to learn a few phrases for a holiday, ages ago. It’s so complicated. All those different writing systems. I got to ‘hello’ and ‘thank you’ and then gave up. Speaker_1: I saw a video on YouTube about it. They said it's not that hard if you break it down. Speaker_2: Easy for you to say, you’re a quick learner. Right, dinner’s getting cold. Peas first! And no complaining. Are you doing any chores this summer? Mr. O’Malley next door was saying his son helps him with the garden. Speaker_1: Ugh, chores? Dad said I might have to mow the lawn...but it's so boring. Speaker_2: Well, helping out around the house is important. It’s good to learn responsibility. We’ll have to see. Now eat up, and then you can watch your…Mick. As long as you’ve finished your peas! Speaker_3: (Points at Speaker_1’s plate) More! More! Speaker_2: Oh, for goodness sake, Finn! He doesn't need more peas! Speaker_1: (Grinning) He wants to share. He thinks they’re funny.

Speaker_1: Right, that was a bit… much, wasn’t it? All that slow-motion running. Like a music video from 1998. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Tell me about it. Could’ve fast-forwarded half of it, honestly. Proper cheese. Though, I’ll give ‘em this, the villain's got style. Proper menacing. Reminds me a bit of that bloke from *Peaky Blinders*…Arthur Shelby, yeah? Speaker_1: A bit, yeah. Though Arthur’s got a bit more… well, desperation in his eyes, hasn't he? This guy just looks… bored of being evil. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Bored of being evil! That's brilliant. You're spot on. Speaking of unsettling, remember old Mr. Henderson, the dentist back in Leicester? Speaker_1: Oh *god*, Henderson. Don’t even *mention* him. That man was a menace. Always smelled of mint and regret. Speaker_2: Regret! Exactly! And the way he'd just…stare. While drilling. Like he was contemplating the existential dread of teeth. Speaker_1: And he’d always talk about his holidays. Every single appointment revolved around hearing about his caravan trips to Skegness. “Oh, and the wind was *terrible* this year, you know, awful for the awning.” As if I cared about his awning while he was assaulting my molars! Speaker_2: (Wipes away a tear of laughter) Awning! Oh, that's perfect. It's amazing the things you remember. I’ve got a dentist here, thankfully, who mostly just asks about work. Which leads to me inevitably having to explain what I actually *do* to people. Speaker_1: The curse of the English Language Teacher. “So, you… teach people *how* to speak?” Like it's some kind of complex alchemy. What are you working on at the moment, anyway? Any brilliant new lessons brewing? Speaker_2: Actually, yeah. Trying to get them to grapple with regional accents. It’s a nightmare. I played a recording of you talking the other day, just a little snippet, and they were *convinced* you were speaking a foreign language. Speaker_1: (Feigning outrage) What?! Me? My accent is perfectly reasonable! It's classic Midlands speech! Speaker_2: Reasonable to *you*, maybe. To a group of eighteen-year-olds from all over Europe, it was utter gibberish. Apparently, the “oo” sounds were particularly perplexing. Speaker_1: (Grinning) Oh, they haven't heard me really lay it on thick, then. I can do a Leicester accent that’ll melt your ears. Speaker_2: Please, no. My students are easily traumatised enough. So, how's the writing going? Still battling with the novel? Speaker_1: Slowly but surely. I’m stuck on chapter twelve. It feels like… like I’ve written myself into a corner and the only way out involves a time-travelling badger. Speaker_2: (Bursting out laughing) A time-travelling badger?! That sounds…fantastic, actually. Honestly, lean into it. Make it happen. Although, maybe dial back the slow-motion running when you’re describing its exploits. Speaker_1: I think that’s fair. You fancy a cuppa? Or maybe we should order some food? All this talk of dentists and badgers has made me peckish. Speaker_2: Ooh, food sounds good. What about that pizza place down the road? They do a decent Margherita, yeah? And maybe a cheeky side of garlic bread. Speaker_1: Sorted. Oh, and I saw a bunch of those Citibikes around today. Tempted, but terrified. I’d probably end up cycling into the Mersey. Speaker_2: Best avoided. Stick to pizza. And maybe time-travelling badgers.

Speaker_1: So, how was the school run this morning? Any little horrors? Speaker_2: Honestly, Mum, chaotic. Little Leo decided today was the day to protest wearing shoes. Full-on meltdown in the car park. I swear, I got judging looks from everyone. Speaker_1: Oh, Leo. Always a character. Remember when he refused to wear trousers to the supermarket? Speaker_2: (Laughing) How could I forget? He insisted he was a mermaid. It’s exhausting, but… mostly wonderful. How was your morning? Did you manage to get to the garden centre? Speaker_1: I did, eventually. It was rammed, though. Everyone preparing for Easter, I suppose. I got those little daffodil bulbs you like, and a couple of those iced Easter cakes – the ones with the chicks on. I’ll bring them over later. Speaker_2: Oh, you shouldn't have! But thank you. The kids will *love* those cakes. They’re already talking about the Easter egg hunt. Are you free to help me hide them? Speaker_1: Of course, love. Any time. It's good to have something to do, now I’m… well, you know. No work to fill my days anymore. Still feels a bit odd. Speaker_2: How *are* you feeling about everything, actually? It’s been a few weeks since you finished. Speaker_1: It’s a bit of a rollercoaster, to be honest. Some days I feel incredibly liberated - like a weight’s been lifted. Others… I miss the structure, the people. And the pay, let’s not lie. It's a big adjustment. Speaker_2: I can imagine. But you've always got us, Mum. And you’ve got loads of things you’ve always wanted to do. That painting course, for example? Speaker_1: Yes, I’m looking into that. It starts next month, I think. And I’ve been trying to get back into reading. Though, honestly, I just end up scrolling through Facebook. Old habits die hard. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Anyway, exciting news… I finally got confirmation about the new job! The Head of Year position at Elmwood. Speaker_1: Oh, Sarah! That's fantastic! I knew you’d get it. You're brilliant with those children. When do you start? Speaker_2: September. Which is good. It gives me time to properly finish the year with my current class. It’s a lot more responsibility, though. More meetings, more paperwork… but it's what I want. Speaker_1: It sounds perfect for you. And it's a real achievement. We're all so proud. Speaking of big events… Have you and Ben finalised details for Amelia’s christening? Speaker_2: Nearly. We’ve got the church booked, and Ben’s mum’s doing the catering. It’s just finding godparents. We’ve asked Auntie Carol, obviously, but we're still deciding on the other one. Speaker_1: Carol will be thrilled. She adores Amelia. Perhaps Mark? He’s always good with children. Speaker_2: That’s who we were thinking. We’ll chat to him properly this weekend. It’s all getting a bit hectic, but in a nice way. Do you think you can come on Saturday to help with some of the decorations? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Consider it done. I'm already picturing little Amelia in her christening gown. It goes so fast, doesn’t it? It feels like yesterday you were a little girl yourself. Speaker_2: (Smiling) You’re going to make me cry. It does, though. It really does.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this marking is never-ending. I feel like all I do is read essays about… well, usually just badly paraphrased Wikipedia articles. How are things with Year 11? Any closer to sanity? Speaker_2: Don’t even *start* me. They're driving me round the bend. The drama, the entitlement, the sheer refusal to engage with anything that vaguely resembles effort. It’s exhausting. I had one girl actually *ask* me if she could have extra credit for having a bad day. Speaker_1: You’re joking! Speaker_2: I wish I was. Honestly. It’s like they think school is some sort of personal entertainment service. How’s Leo taking to Year 4? Settled now? Speaker_1: He’s loving it, actually. He’s started doing this little science club after school, which is brilliant. He came home yesterday trying to explain the water cycle using just ping pong balls and a watering can. It was… chaotic, but adorable. Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds like him! He's always been a little inventor. My niece, Chloe, is obsessed with animals at the moment. She wants to be a vet, a marine biologist *and* a dog groomer, all at the same time. It changes weekly! Speaker_1: That’s lovely. It’s good they’ve got passions, isn’t it? Though slightly terrifying when they start talking about wanting to rescue every stray animal in the country. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Her mum's trying to gently steer her towards something more…realistic. Speaking of animals, how’s Winston? Still shedding like a snowstorm? Speaker_1: Oh, Winston. Always shedding. I swear he multiplies fur overnight. I’ve invested in one of those robotic vacuum cleaners, and it’s constantly battling a losing war against the fluff. But he’s worth it. He's started stealing socks again though. Speaker_2: (laughs) Oh, Winston! He’s a menace. My sister had a Labrador who used to do the same thing. Found one in the washing machine once. Mid-cycle. Speaker_1: Oh, the horror! I’d probably cry. Although, I did try this new face mask last night… it was a clay one, supposed to be detoxifying. It made me look like a Martian. Speaker_2: Oh, I know the type! I’ve been trying to find a decent retinol serum; everything seems to either do nothing or completely strip my skin. It's a minefield out there. Have you seen anything good? Speaker_1: Not recently, I'm afraid. I've been sticking to the basics lately. Too much stress to experiment with complicated skincare routines. It's just work, home, cat-related chaos, and attempting to maintain some semblance of adult functionality. How's your mum doing, by the way? I haven’t spoken to her in ages. Speaker_2: She’s alright. Still complaining about the neighbours, naturally. Apparently, they’ve started a garden gnome collection. She’s convinced it's a deliberate act of provocation. She's considering retaliating with a flock of plastic flamingos. Speaker_1: (laughing) Oh, your mum! She's legendary. You really need to get her on Instagram. She'd be a sensation. Speaker_2: I’ve tried, honestly. She thinks it’s all a waste of time. Says she prefers a good crossword puzzle and a cup of tea. Which, frankly, is perfectly reasonable. Anyway, enough distractions! Back to Year 11… I think I’m going to need another glass of wine just to face the mountain of marking.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this charoset is incredible, Eliana. Seriously. What *is* your secret? It’s not too sweet, it's got a good bite… Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, stop it! It's just my grandmother’s recipe. The key is really good quality dates, and a tiny bit of orange zest. Don't tell anyone, it’s a closely guarded family secret. Speaker_3: It's delightful, dear. Far better than the one my mother used to make. Too much apple, not enough… well, everything else. Though she tried her best, bless her. She always felt slightly guilty she couldn't keep a properly kosher kitchen. Speaker_4: It’s a nice break from all the matzah ball soup, though, isn’t it? No offence to anyone’s matzah ball soup, of course. Mum’s is legendary. Speaker_1: Absolutely no offence. Matzah ball soup is foundational. But, yeah, a bit of textural variety is appreciated. So, anyone making any exciting plans for after Pesach? I’m thinking of finally taking that trip to Italy. Speaker_2: Oh, Italy! That sounds amazing. I’ve always wanted to go to Naples – proper pizza, you know? And all the pastries! Though truthfully, I’m happy just being here, perfecting my sourdough. Speaker_3: Italy is lovely, darling. Florence is a must. But you *must* be careful with the restaurants. Some of them are… rather overhyped. And absolutely avoid anything that sounds remotely like ‘ortolan’. Utterly barbaric. Speaker_4: Ortolan? What even is that? Sounds… medieval. Speaker_1: Apparently, it’s a small bird, they fatten it up in the dark, then you eat it whole, head and all, with a napkin over your head to catch the bones and juices. Don’t ask. Saw it on a documentary. Truly horrifying. Speaker_2: Oh my god! No thank you. I'll stick to biscotti. Speaking of which, has anyone seen my recipe for the almond biscotti? I was hoping to try it out this week. Speaker_3: I think I might have it, darling. It's somewhere amongst my chaotic collection of recipes. Your Great Aunt Ruth sent it over, didn’t she? She always had the best ones. Reminds me, she insisted on calling you “Leah” for years, even after you corrected her! Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh, Aunt Ruth. She was convinced I was supposed to be named Leah. She had a whole elaborate story about Hebrew names and destiny. Speaker_1: My mum is always trying to get me to learn more Hebrew. She keeps saying it'll ‘connect me to my roots’. I can barely manage ‘Shalom’. Speaker_4: I took a bit of Hebrew at uni, just as an elective. It’s… a completely different structure to English. Everything feels backwards. Speaker_3: It is, isn’t it? But it’s a beautiful language. And you’d be surprised how many words we use in English that come from Hebrew. Speaker_2: True! Plus, knowing a bit helps with deciphering some of the older family recipes. Like, some of the ingredients are listed in Yiddish, and you need to know the Hebrew root to figure out what they actually are. Speaker_1: Right, okay, this is officially too much brain work for a post-Passover dinner. Speaking of eating… anyone want more charoset? Seriously, Eliana, this is a masterpiece. Or maybe we should talk about New York? I was thinking of visiting my cousin…

Speaker_1: Right, so, who actually finished “The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo”? Because honestly, I started it and just… couldn’t get into it. It felt a bit… much. Speaker_2: Oh, I adored it! Absolutely adored it. Cried buckets, naturally. Though, I do think it’s massively overrated, if I’m being honest. Everyone was raving about it, and it was good, but not *that* good. Speaker_3: I’m with Sarah, actually. I sped through it. Had to know what happened. I did the audiobook though, which might have helped. The narrator really brought Evelyn to life. Though, I’m slightly side-tracked. Has anyone been watching “The Diplomat” on Netflix? Speaker_1: Oh! Yes! I binged that in two days. Brilliant, wasn’t it? The twists and turns… and Rufus Sewell is just… *chef’s kiss*. Speaker_2: Rufus Sewell does have a certain… something. But I found it a bit implausible, didn’t you? All that international intrigue happening so quickly. Felt a bit like a James Bond film dressed up as a political drama. Speaker_3: I thought it worked *because* it was a bit heightened. It’s entertainment, after all. You’re not expecting realism. Speaking of entertainment, I’ve been trying to get back into knitting. Remember when we all tried that during lockdown? Speaker_1: Oh god, yes. My attempt at a scarf looked like something a cat dragged in. I stuck to eBooks, far less stressful. Honestly, I’ll never understand the appeal of physically making things. I like instant gratification. Speaker_2: I rather enjoy it! It’s meditative. I’m crocheting a blanket for my nephew’s new baby. It’s going to be… a process. And I’m definitely more of a physical book person. I love the smell, the feel of the paper... you just don't get that with a Kindle. Speaker_3: I'm on team both, really. eBooks for when I’m travelling or need something light, and physical books for when I want to really *savour* a story. Though I did get my mum a Kindle for her birthday. She’s a committed physical book fan, but her eyesight is getting worse. Speaker_1: Good thinking. My dad is refusing to get a Kindle, says it ruins the experience. He's still ploughing through Tolstoy, bless him. Speaking of family, did anyone manage to get through to Auntie Mavis to wish her happy birthday? She's been a bit off the radar lately. Speaker_2: I tried yesterday, went straight to voicemail. She’s probably busy with her gardening. She lives for her roses, you know. I did send a card though. Speaker_3: I’ll give her a ring tomorrow. She always enjoys a good chat. Oh, and I saw that new film, “Everything Everywhere All at Once”? Anyone seen it? Speaker_1: Oh my god, yes! Utterly bonkers. But brilliant. Michelle Yeoh was phenomenal. I had no idea what was going on half the time, but I was completely hooked. Speaker_2: I’ve been meaning to watch that. It’s been on my list for ages. I’m a bit wary of films that are overly hyped, though. Usually end up being disappointed. Speaker_3: It lives up to the hype, honestly. It’s… a lot. But in a good way. Right, shall we decide on next month’s book? I’ve got a few suggestions… I was thinking maybe something a bit lighter after “Evelyn Hugo”, perhaps a good thriller? Speaker_1: Sounds good. I’m open to suggestions. As long as it doesn't involve too many husbands, I think I’m good. Speaker_2: Ooh, I've got one! "The Guest List" by Lucy Fokley, its a great mystery with big twists and turns. I finished it just last week!

Speaker_1: Right, so this… this is the bit I’m most worried about, innit? Transferring everything over. You’d think, wouldn’t ya, after all these years, it’d be seamless. But it never is. Speaker_2: Seamless is a strong word for technology, especially when we’re dealing with Android to Android. It *should* be relatively straightforward though, yeah? I mean, Google’s supposedly got everything backed up in the cloud. Speaker_1: Supposedly. That's the key word, isn’t it? “Supposedly.” Remember last time? With the Samsung? It was a nightmare. Lost half me photos, contacts were a mess. Took weeks to sort it out. Speaker_2: Oh god, don’t remind me. You were apoplectic. This is a Pixel though, supposedly Google's own hardware. It *should* play nicer. Have you got the cable? I can try and plug mine in and show you how the quick transfer thing works? Speaker_1: Aye, here. USB-C to USB-C. Brand new, still in the bag. Go on then, you’re the tech wizard. I still think it’s a conspiracy, you know? They *want* you to struggle. Keeps people buying new ones. Like Nokia back in the day. Solid as a rock, nearly indestructible. They just… vanished. Speaker_2: Vanished is a bit harsh. Apple happened. And Android. Nokia were slow to adapt. Remember everyone had a 3310? You could literally throw that thing down the stairs and it wouldn’t break. Speaker_1: You could. And they still worked! My first proper mobile phone. Texting was a revelation. Now look at ‘em, all glass and fragile. Honestly, I’m scared to even *hold* this thing properly. Speaker_2: Right, okay. So, let’s power yours on. Okay, it’s asking if you want to copy data from your old phone. Yes, obviously. Now, it should detect mine. It says… “Nearby Devices.” Give it a sec… Speaker_1: What about the SIM card? That's a faff, isn’t it? They never made those a standard size. Always a different one. Speaker_2: It’s nano-SIM, thankfully. I’ve got that little tool thingy with my phone. One sec… okay, got it. Just need to pop that in. So, it’s connecting now. It’s saying it’ll copy apps, data, photos… it looks like it’s actually recognising everything. This is good. Speaker_1: Fingers crossed. How long does it reckon it’ll take? I don't wanna be sat here all night. We've got a sauna booking, remember? Speaker_2: It’s estimating about… twenty minutes. It says it depends on how much data there is, obviously. Maybe plug it in to charge as well? Just in case. Speaker_1: Good shout. Right, done that. So, twenty minutes then? We could have another Lapin Kulta while we wait? Speaker_2: Tempting, but maybe just the one. Don’t want to be attempting a Finnish sauna while mildly legless. It might not end well. Speaker_1: Fair enough. Alright, let's see if this damned thing actually works first before we celebrate. And if it doesn’t, I’m blaming Google. And Apple. And the ghost of Nokia. Speaker_2: Haha, deal. Let's just hope it works, yeah? It really is a beautiful phone though, isn’t it? And the camera… I’ve heard amazing things about the camera.

Speaker_2: Right, so Leo’s party. Are you still set on having it at the soft play centre? Speaker_1: Yeah, definitely! All my mates said it’s the best one. They’ve got like, a massive slide and everything. Speaker_3: (Babbling excitedly, pointing at a picture book) Doggy! Doggy! Speaker_2: Yes, darling, that’s a doggy. A very fluffy doggy. Now, Leo, we need to finish talking about your party. Have you made a list of who you want to invite yet? Speaker_1: Almost. I’ve got most of them, but I need to check with Mum about Ben. She said something about his mum being a bit… difficult? Speaker_2: She’s just a bit overprotective, love. It’s fine. Just make sure you say everyone's invited. We don’t want anyone feeling left out. Oh, and did you decide on the theme? You were talking about Red Pandas yesterday? Speaker_1: Yeah! Red Pandas! They’re awesome. They’re like, tiny bears but super fluffy and they eat bamboo. I saw a documentary about them. Speaker_3: (Clapping) Panda! Panda! Speaker_2: He loves pandas too. They’re very cute. Now, we need to think about the cake. Do you want a Red Panda cake? We could get one with little bamboo shoots on it. Speaker_1: Ooh, yeah! That’d be amazing! Can it be chocolate? Speaker_2: Of course. Chocolate Red Panda cake it is. Right, let’s see... soft play centre booked, theme decided, cake sorted… what about presents? You’re getting something for Finn, aren’t you? His birthday’s next week. Speaker_1: Yeah, I was thinking a new Malamute puppy toy. He loves dogs, but he's always wanted a Malamute. He saw one at the park last week and wouldn’t stop talking about it. Speaker_2: That’s a good idea. He'll love that. Do you want me to take you shopping for it this weekend? We can also get a card. Speaker_1: Yeah, that’d be good. Oh, and can we watch that Japanese film you downloaded? The one about the girl and the cat? Speaker_2: *Whispering to herself* …Studio Ghibli one? Yes, of course. We can watch it on Saturday. After we go to gymnastics with Rory. Speaker_3: (Reaching for the iPad) ‘Pad! ‘Pad! Speaker_1: Can I use the iPad after? I need to finish my research for school. We’re learning about different ecosystems, and I want to find out more about Red Panda habitats. It’s much easier to type on a laptop though, isn’t it? Speaker_2: It is, but the iPad’s portable. Perhaps we could get you a little keyboard for it? That way, you can use it like a laptop. Speaker_1: Ooh, that’s a good idea! Would that cost a lot? Speaker_2: We’ll see. We’ll have a look online. Now, what about after the party? Do you have anything planned for the holidays? Your Dad said he might take you to Bristol to see your cousins? Speaker_1: Yeah! I’m really looking forward to that. We could go to the aquarium and play some board games. I’ve been learning how to play Settlers of Catan, it’s really hard. Speaker_3: (Pointing at Speaker_1) Play! Play! Speaker_2: Well, it sounds like you’ve got a busy few weeks ahead of you. It’s good to be organised. Now, finish your juice. We need to get Rory ready for his nap.

Speaker_1: Honestly though, Christmas at Nana’s was *always* mental. Not in a bad way, just… chaotic. Speaker_2: Chaotic is a polite word for it. It was a full-on assault on the senses. All the aunties crammed into that tiny kitchen, smelling of sherry and burnt Brussels sprouts. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Oh, don't I know it. I’ve lost count of the Christmases where someone inevitably ended up arguing over the last Quality Street. It was a tradition in itself, really. Speaker_4: You lot had Quality Streets? We never had those. It was always Roses down in Bognor. Though, the arguments were exactly the same. The coffee creams were the most fought over, naturally. Speaker_1: Roses are worse! They’ve got those weird coconut ones that nobody likes, but someone *always* gets stuck with three. Speaker_2: It’s funny, isn’t it? How deeply ingrained these little traditions are. I remember my Lola – my grandmother from the Philippines – would always make this dish called *lechon*. Roast pig, whole, on a spit. It was incredible, but… incredibly messy. Speaker_3: Oh, that sounds lovely! Bit different from our turkey and stuffing. We always had a proper British Christmas dinner. Though, I did once try to introduce a mango chutney. Didn’t go down well. “Too exotic,” they said. Speaker_4: Exotic? Honestly. People are so stuck in their ways. I remember when we first went to Italy, decades ago, and tried to order a proper English breakfast. The look on the waiter’s face! He thought we were mad. Speaker_1: Speaking of different cultures, I was reading an article about how Christmas is celebrated in Japan. They eat KFC! Apparently, it’s a huge marketing success story from years ago, and now it’s just…normal. Speaker_2: KFC? Seriously? That’s bizarre. Though, I suppose it's no weirder than stuffing a whole pig with spices and roasting it. It just…doesn’t scream ‘Christmas’ to me. Speaker_3: It's the thought that counts, dear. Though, I must say, I’ve noticed things have changed a lot over the years. It feels…more commercial now. Less about family and faith, and more about getting the perfect present. Speaker_4: Absolutely. When I was a boy, Christmas felt… simpler. We didn't have all this fuss. And people weren’t so quick to judge, either. I remember a chap moved to Bognor, an Indian fella. Got some terrible stick for it, initially. Made me so angry. Speaker_1: It’s awful, isn’t it? Still happens now, unfortunately. I had a lecture a few weeks ago where one of the students made a really inappropriate comment about someone’s background. It was…bad. Speaker_2: Ugh, that’s just disgusting. You’d think, in this day and age… I mean, I grew up with so much diversity in London. It was just *normal* to be around people from all different backgrounds. Speaker_3: I think it’s important to remember everyone’s story. Everyone’s journey. You never know what someone else might be going through. And a bit of kindness can go a long way. Speaker_4: Hear, hear to that. And a bit of good food and a glass of something nice, too. Anyone fancy another sherry? I think I spotted a bottle lurking in the cupboard earlier. Speaker_1: Ooh, don’t mind if I do! Christmas isn’t Christmas without a bit of sherry, is it? Even if it *does* lead to arguments over Quality Streets. Speaker_2: I’ll join you. Though, I'm sticking to a small one. Gotta be responsible, even at Christmas. What about you two? One for the road? Or another blast from the past?
