Speaker_1: Sounds… adventurous. You weren’t allowed much freedom, were you? Speaker_2: Freedom? In my day, freedom was a cup of tea and a good book. We didn’t *need* all this… fuss. Speaker_3: Still, it sounds nice. We're always rushing around. I saw that new Bond film last night, though. Brilliant. Bit long, but brilliant. Speaker_1: Oh yeah? I’ve been meaning to go. Is it as good as everyone says? Speaker_3: Definitely. Proper action, good story. Though, honestly, Daniel Craig’s getting a bit old for all the running and jumping. Speaker_2: Bond… They keep changing him, don’t they? Never as good as Sean Connery. Now *he* was a Bond. Speaker_1: You always say that, Grandma. Speaker_2: It’s true! And he had manners. These new ones just swagger about. No respect. Speaking of respect, has your cousin David fixed that car of his yet? The red one? Speaker_3: Oh, that’s a disaster. Apparently, it was a faulty sensor. Cost him a fortune. Said he’s thinking of getting a bike. Speaker_1: A bike? David? He wouldn’t last five minutes. He’s about as coordinated as a newborn giraffe. Speaker_3: (Laughing) I know! But he’s saying it’s better for the environment. And cheaper. Speaker_1: More likely he’s skint. Work’s been slow lately. I’ve been putting in ridiculous hours on this project. Trying to get this new software implemented. Total chaos. Speaker_2: Software? What's all that about? Give me a good cookbook any day. I made a lovely Victoria sponge yesterday. Would you like a piece? Speaker_3: Oh, yes please! Your Victoria sponge is the best, Mum. Speaker_1: I’d love some, actually. Stress baking is a life skill, you know. Honestly, the things I deal with at work... it's like herding cats. One minute everything is going smoothly, the next… bang, complete meltdown. Speaker_3: You need a holiday. Somewhere warm. Maybe Spain? Speaker_1: Maybe. Just need to get this project over the line first. Then, escape. Then… maybe Spain. Or just a long lie-in. That sounds good too. Speaker_2: A lie-in… Now *that* is a good idea. Though nothing beats a proper cup of tea and a biscuit for starting the day right. And a bit of gossip, of course. Have you heard from your Auntie Brenda? Speaker_3: Not recently. She’s been very quiet. I wonder if she's managed to get that hip replacement sorted. Speaker_1: I’ll give her a call tomorrow. It's easy to lose touch, isn’t it? Especially when everyone is so busy.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Leo, you've barely touched your pancake! It’s Pancake Day! You made a wish *with* it – that’s the rule! Speaker_2: (Muffled, mouth full) It's yummy, Mummy, but I'm full now. Speaker_3: Mine’s gone! Can I have some sprinkles now? Please? Speaker_1: Yes, you can have sprinkles, darling. A little bit. And Leo, just *one* more bite. It’s a waste if you don’t finish it. Honestly, sometimes I think children in my class eat more than you do! And they don’t even *have* pancake on Pancake Day. Speaker_2: Why not? Speaker_1: Well, some families don’t have much money, sweetheart, and they can’t always afford special treats. It's just...sad. Makes you appreciate what we have, doesn’t it? Speaker_3: Sad. Speaker_1: It is. Right, sprinkles are happening. Anyway, how was school today? Did you both have a good day? Speaker_3: I did a really good painting of a dinosaur! Miss Jones said it was the best one. Speaker_1: Oh, fantastic! I bet it was! And you, Elsie? Anything exciting? Speaker_2: We had assembly. And Mrs. Peterson told us a story about Green Knowe. It was spooky. Speaker_1: Oh, Green Knowe! That's a lovely story, isn't it? All those children visiting the past… it makes you think about how much things change, and how quickly everything goes by. Makes *me* feel old! Speaker_3: Mummy, when we grow up, will we be old? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Eventually, yes, you will. But not for a very long time! You’ll have lots of adventures first. We're thinking of going to the Science Museum this weekend, aren't we? Speaker_2: Yay! Can we see the dinosaurs? Speaker_1: Absolutely. And maybe we can go to that festival at the Festival Hall next week. They’re doing something with puppets. Speaker_3: Puppets! Speaker_1: Yes! Now, before we get too carried away planning fun things, have you both brushed your teeth properly? And washed your hands? I saw chocolate on your face, Leo! Speaker_2: I washed my hands! Speaker_3: (Grumbling) I brushed mine. Speaker_1: Good. Because we are going to Paris soon, remember? And we don’t want any germs ruining our trip. I’m thinking next half term. Speaker_2: Paris! Will we see the Eiffel Tower? Speaker_1: Of course! And we can eat croissants and go on a boat on the river. It will be lovely. Although, knowing you two, you’ll probably just want to go to the beach, won’t you? Speaker_3: The beach is best! We can build sandcastles! Speaker_1: Exactly. Although, last time we went to the beach, someone – and I won't mention any names – didn’t want to share their bucket and spade. Speaker_2: That wasn't me! Speaker_3: Was too! You said it was *your* favourite bucket! Speaker_1: (Sighing fondly) Oh, honestly. It’s always something, isn’t it? Right. Finish your pancakes, then it's teeth brushing and bedtime stories. And Leo, even one more bite! Think of the children who don't *have* pancakes…

Speaker_1: This is actually really good. I was worried ordering from here, their online reviews are…mixed. Speaker_2: Mixed is putting it mildly. I saw someone claim their chow mein tasted exclusively of despair. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Despair? That’s… a strong culinary critique. Honestly, I’m just glad it arrived in under an hour. Remember that time we ordered Indian and it took two and a half? Speaker_4: Oh god, the Great Curry Wait of ‘21. I was starting to suspect the delivery driver had decided to *become* a curry chef. Speaker_1: Seriously! I was pacing. Anyway, this egg fried rice is surprisingly decent. Speaker_2: Yeah, I’ll give them that. Although, it does taste a bit… suspiciously yellow. Speaker_3: Don't look a gift horse, or suspiciously yellow rice, in the mouth. So, anyone catch the news today? More depressing stuff as usual. Speaker_4: Briefly. Something about another politician being investigated. Honestly, it's just a relentless cycle at this point. It feels like you can’t trust anyone. Speaker_1: Exactly. Remember old Mr. Henderson? He used to say politicians were all the same, just different shades of grey. Speaker_2: He was a character, old Mr. Henderson. Always muttering about Bob the Builder and claiming he knew the secret to a perfect lawn. Speaker_3: (Smiling) And perpetually offering everyone digestive biscuits. I miss his biscuits. Speaker_4: Speaking of missing people, have you heard anything from Liam? I haven’t seen him post on social media in ages. Speaker_1: No, not since he went to that cricket match last weekend. I messaged him, no reply. Hopefully, he’s just enjoying a digital detox. Speaker_2: A digital detox? Liam? The guy who live-streamed himself making toast? I find that hard to believe. Speaker_3: Maybe he finally realised he needed a break. Or maybe he’s gone off-grid to become a professional lawn enthusiast, inspired by Mr. Henderson. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Now *that* would be a twist. We should probably check in with him properly though. It's just, he’s been a bit down lately, about… you know. Speaker_1: Right. About Sarah. It’s awful what happened. That funeral was… something. Just so many people. Speaker_2: It was. And so sad. She was way too young. I keep thinking about how much she loved terrible rom-coms. Speaker_3: She truly did. We had a marathon the week before… watched five in a row. Pure cinematic trash. Speaker_4: She had such a good spirit. Do you guys fancy going to the cinema next week? There’s that new sci-fi film everyone’s talking about. A distraction might be good. Speaker_1: I’m in. Though, knowing our luck, it’ll be full of people live-streaming the entire thing. Speaker_2: Deal. Count me in too. What about you, Three? Speaker_3: Absolutely. Cinema sounds perfect. Although… if anyone starts comparing the special effects to Bob the Builder, I'm walking out. Speaker_4: Agreed. Despair-flavoured chow mein and Bob the Builder commentary are both deal breakers. Speaker_1: Alright then, cinema next week it is. Now, pass the prawn crackers, I'm feeling a sugar rush coming on. Speaker_2: Coming right up! Though, fair warning, they’re slightly stale. Just adds to the authentic Chinese takeaway experience, really.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Old Man Hemmings next door… you wouldn’t believe what he tried to tell me this morning. He’s convinced Mrs. Peterson is secretly a spy. Speaker_2: (Chuckles softly) A spy? That woman? Goodness me. She can barely remember where she put her spectacles, let alone orchestrate international intrigue. Speaker_3: It's probably just loneliness getting to him. He did lose his wife last year, didn’t he? Though, to be fair, she *was* rather secretive about her garden club meetings. Speaker_1: That’s what I said! But no, apparently, she’s using the prize-winning marrows as a cover. A cover, I ask you! He was utterly serious. He said he’s been watching her… “for weeks,” he said. Speaker_2: Reminds me of your Uncle Arthur. Used to be convinced the milkman was reporting back to the Soviets. Claimed the bottles were coded messages. Always drank his milk straight from the bottle, wouldn’t trust a glass. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, Arthur! We all used to tiptoe around him, afraid to say the wrong thing. So, what did you say to Mr. Hemmings? Speaker_1: I just gently suggested he might be letting his imagination run away with him. He grumbled something about “young people these days” and went back inside. Honestly, he’s a sweet man, but… a bit. Speaker_2: They’re all a bit, at that age. Memory starts to play tricks, and a bit of drama fills the void. It’s sad, really. Although, thinking about it, I rather liked Arthur's milk-from-the-bottle habit. Seemed rather… efficient. Speaker_3: Efficient and slightly alarming. Speaking of efficiency, did you see that article about driverless cars? Apparently, they’re doing trials on the A38 now. Speaker_1: I did! Terrifying, isn’t it? I can barely trust *people* to drive properly, let alone a computer. What if it malfunctions and just… goes rogue? Speaker_2: Progress, my dear. Progress. They said the same about aeroplanes, you know. Remember when people thought flying was the height of recklessness? Now look at us, jetting off to Spain for a week with barely a thought. Though I must say, the queues at security are getting worse every year. Speaker_1: That’s an understatement. Honestly, it's a nightmare. I was thinking about those scan-as-you-go things in supermarkets. Do you use those? I'm always too worried I'll accidentally scan something twice. Speaker_3: I do! It makes such a difference, especially when you’ve got a full trolley. It’s just… weird, isn’t it, doing your own checkout? It feels like the end of an era. Speaker_1: It is. Remember when Mrs. Davies used to work on till three at Somerfield? She always gave the kids a little sweet. Speaker_2: And you could put things on ‘layaway’! Remember that? Pay for it in installments. Can’t do that anymore. Everything’s instant these days. No patience. Oh, and the price of rice krispy cakes! Absolutely scandalous. They're practically gold dust now. Speaker_3: You are obsessed with those things! It’s a wonder you haven’t started growing your own rice. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Don’t give her ideas! Though, she *is* rather keen on the garden… Speaking of which, I was looking at house insurance quotes yesterday. The new build estate near the village is pushing premiums up for everyone. Apparently, they're all claiming for subsidence. Speaker_2: New builds… always something with those. Never properly settled. Reminds me of the house we lived in back in Wolverhampton. Lovely house, but the foundations… Oh, the foundations. And the garden! I used to spend hours tending to my roses. A good sturdy English rose, that’

Speaker_1: Right, so, Chinese New Year! Did you two have fun at school making lanterns? Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Yeah! Mine was red and sparkly! And I drew a dragon on it! Speaker_3: Mine was… blue. And my dragon had, like, *lots* of teeth. Scary teeth. Speaker_1: Ooh, scary! Dragons are very important in Chinese New Year, aren’t they? They bring good luck. Did you learn about that? Speaker_2: Miss Davies told us! Dragons fly in the sky and… and breathe fire! Speaker_3: And they're really long! Longer than our garden! Speaker_1: That’s right! They are very long. Speaking of the sky… what did you learn about in science today? Was it planets again? Speaker_2: Yeah! Saturn has rings! And Jupiter has a big red spot! Speaker_3: Miss Thompson said the red spot is a storm! A *really* big storm! It’s been happening for ages. Speaker_1: Wow, that’s incredible. It’s amazing how long those storms can last. Right, I think I smell something burning… oh dear. The spring rolls! Speaker_2: Spring rolls! Are we having Chinese food for Chinese New Year? Speaker_3: I love spring rolls! Especially with the sweet chilli sauce! Speaker_1: You are both obsessed with that sauce! Yes, we're having spring rolls, noodles, and a little bit of everything. It's not *proper* Chinese food, I know, but it's a start! Speaker_2: Can I help set the table? I can put the chopsticks out! Speaker_3: I wanna get the plates! The red ones! Because red is a lucky colour! Speaker_1: Excellent! Teamwork makes the dream work. Now, after dinner, how’s the practicing going? Are you still enjoying piano, Leo? Speaker_3: It’s okay. Mr. Peterson makes me do scales. Scales are boring. Speaker_1: I know they can be, but they're important! It's like learning your ABCs before you can write a story. And Maya, are you excited for your drum lesson tomorrow? Speaker_2: Yes! I'm learning a new beat! It’s really loud! Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, wonderful. I’m sure the neighbours will love that! And what about aerial hoop on Saturday? Are you still brave enough? Speaker_2: (Hesitantly) It’s scary, but fun. I can almost do a roll now! Speaker_1: That’s amazing! You're getting so strong. Oh, and I nearly forgot! You two were telling me about a film you want to watch, wasn’t it? Something with Barbie? Speaker_3: *Barbie and the Great Adventure*! It’s got horses and a secret kingdom! Speaker_2: And Barbie has to save everyone! It's so good! Speaker_1: Right, *Barbie and the Great Adventure* it is, after Chinese food and maybe, just maybe, if you eat all your noodles… a small piece of chocolate fortune cookie. Speaker_2 & Speaker_3: (In unison) Yay! Speaker_1: Alright, let's rescue those spring rolls before they become charcoal rolls! Speaker_2: (Running towards the kitchen) I’m helping! Speaker_3: (Following close behind) Me too! I'm the plate getter-upper! Speaker_1: (Chuckling) Very good! Speaker_1: (Under her breath) Right, controlled chaos. My life in a nutshell.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this is… bliss. Proper bliss. Needed this. Rome is doing bits, innit? Speaker_2: It really is. Sun’s actually out, which is a miracle considering the forecast. And this little bar is perfect – not rammed, good vibes… and the Aperol Spritz is *chefs kiss*. Speaker_3: It's lovely, yeah. Way better than that AirBnB though. Seriously, the photos were…optimistic. I thought we were getting a balcony overlooking the Colosseum, and it was overlooking a bin alley. Speaker_4: (With a noticeable Australian accent) Fair dinkum? A bin alley? That’s rough, Rach. I thought you were the AirBnB queen. You always find the hidden gems. Speaker_3: I *usually* do! I think I got caught out by the hype. Everyone raves about Rome AirBnBs, I just… trusted too much. Lesson learned. Speaker_1: Right, so, dinner. We sticking with the plan to wander around Trastevere? I heard there's some proper authentic stuff over there. Speaker_2: Yeah, I'm up for that. I did a little research – there’s a place called Roma Sparita, apparently their Cacio e Pepe is legendary. We *have* to try it. Speaker_3: Oh, I've heard of that place! It’s supposed to be tiny and booked solid, but we can give it a shot, right? Maybe if we go early? Speaker_4: Early’s good. I’m still adjusting to the Italian timeframe, everything happens… later. Like everything. It’s a vibe, but my internal clock is confused. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I tried to order a coffee at like, ten past seven this morning, and the barista looked at me like I’d asked him to solve world peace. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, bless him. They take their coffee seriously here. You’ve gotta commit to the whole ritual. No grabbing a takeaway latte on the go. Speaker_3: Speaking of serious… my mum keeps texting me asking if I'm speaking Italian yet. She's convinced I should be fluent after two days. Speaker_1: Oh, mums. Ours is the same. She called yesterday to ask if I'd learned to haggle in Italian. Apparently, that's the key to a successful holiday. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Haggle? I tried to buy a postcard this morning and completely butchered the pronunciation of ‘prego’. The shopkeeper just looked… amused. They probably charged me extra. Speaker_2: You'll get there. It's a tricky language. I did a bit at uni, but mostly I just remember how to order wine. Which, let's be honest, is the most important skill. Speaker_1: Exactly! Although, I’m starting to pick up a few phrases. Like "un altro Spritz, per favore!" That’s essential. Speaker_3: You’re fluent already, then. What about after Rome? Anyone got plans beyond this weekend? I was thinking maybe Florence next week? I know Liam’s always wanted to go. Speaker_1: Florence sounds good, yeah. I’m fairly flexible. I need to check with work, but I should be alright. Speaker_2: I'm in! I need more pasta in my life. And maybe a leather jacket. Florence is famous for leather, right? Speaker_4: Reckon I'm up for Florence too. Heard the art scene is unreal. Plus, if we’re going to keep eating this much, I need to walk it off. My jeans are starting to feel a bit… snug.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the planning for Chloe’s hen do is *stressful*. I feel like I'm her mum, not a friend! Speaker_2: Oh, tell me about it! Whose bright idea was it to make personalised bunting? It's going to take forever. Speaker_3: It's Sarah, isn't it? She always goes overboard. Remember her 30th? The glitter… *everywhere*. Speaker_4: (Laughing) Oh god, the glitter. We were finding it for weeks! But Chloe will love the bunting, she’s really into that crafty stuff. I’m more worried about the escape room. Apparently, it's really hard. Speaker_1: Hard is good! We need something challenging. Although, knowing the group, someone will probably start panicking and yelling within five minutes. Speaker_2: Probably Jess. She gets super competitive. Remember that game of charades at New Year’s? She nearly threw the TV remote. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Classic Jess. I volunteered to do the cake, by the way. I’m thinking maybe a lemon drizzle? Or something with raspberries? Speaker_4: Lemon drizzle is always a winner! Oh, and you *have* to make those little sugar flowers you did for my birthday. They were gorgeous. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! Those were amazing. I'm rubbish at baking, so I’m happy to leave the cake to you. I've been put on decorations duty. Which, as we established, involves a lot of bunting. Speaker_2: I’m handling the playlist. I'm trying to get a good mix of cheesy pop and stuff everyone knows. Any requests? Speaker_3: 90s classics are essential! And definitely some Spice Girls. Speaker_4: Oh, and anything by Destiny’s Child! Perfect for belting out on the dance floor. Speaker_1: Right, noted. Okay, so we've got bunting, cake, playlist, escape room... have we sorted out a photographer? Speaker_2: I asked Liam's cousin, he does wedding photography, and he said he'd do a few hours for a good price. He’s coming. Speaker_3: Perfect! That's one less thing to worry about. I'm a bit worried about Auntie Maureen though. She promised to come but she's always a bit...much. Speaker_4: Oh dear. True. We might need to strategically position ourselves away from her. Speaker_1: We could distract her with the cake? She loves a good slice of lemon drizzle. Speaker_2: Good thinking! Right, I'm going to quickly check on the venue. I need to confirm the booking and make sure they've got enough space for our chaos. Speaker_3: I’m off to the supermarket to gather supplies for the cake. Raspberry jam, lemons… it’s a mission! Speaker_4: I’m going to try and get some inspiration for little games we can play at the pub before the escape room. Just to get everyone hyped up. Speaker_1: Sounds good! This is going to be…an experience, isn’t it? But a fun one. For Chloe, at least.

Speaker_1: Right, so you reckon this much chilli is good for a curry for four? Seems… ambitious. Speaker_2: Trust me. It's not that bad. Unless you're, like, *really* sensitive. Remember that time you had that vindaloo in uni and spent the next hour regretting every life choice? Speaker_1: (grimaces) Don't remind me. That wasn’t a vindaloo, it was a weapon. I swear the chef was actively trying to harm me. Honestly, I felt sick for a full day. This feels different though, you’re actually, you know, cooking properly. Not just throwing a load of things in and hoping for the best. Speaker_2: Hey! My student cooking was perfectly adequate. Relatively speaking. Anyway, this chilli is mild in comparison. Speaking of sick, how are you feeling? You sounded a bit rough on the phone yesterday. Speaker_1: Just a bit of a bug, I think. Woke up feeling dreadful, achy and all that. Definitely couldn’t face work. Slept most of the day. Still a bit knackered, to be honest. Probably needed the sleep anyway. Been running myself ragged with that commission. Speaker_2: Yeah, you were complaining about the deadlines. Seriously though, look after yourself. Don’t push it. Remember what happened last time you tried to work through a cold? Ended up in bed for a week. Speaker_1: Point taken. This is why I have a brother who's a sensible English teacher. You'd be terrible at art though. Too…precise. Speaker_2: And you’d be terrible at explaining grammar to a class of teenagers. Trust me, it's a skillset. Anyway, hotel situation sorted for Barcelona? You said you were looking at places. Speaker_1: Yeah, booked it actually. Found a little place near the Gothic Quarter. Looks alright, bit basic, but it’s close to everything. And surprisingly cheap. Always worry though, you know? Hotels. Bed bugs, dodgy plumbing, weird smells… Speaker_2: (laughs) You’re such a worrier. It’ll be fine. Barcelona’s amazing. You'll have a blast. Just… maybe pack some disinfectant wipes. For your peace of mind. Speaker_1: Good shout. Right, shall we get this onion diced? I’m suddenly feeling a bit peckish, despite feeling awful yesterday. This curry better be worth it. Speaker_2: It will be. And before you ask, yes, I’ve already chopped the garlic. I’m not a complete monster. Though, I am considering adding a *tiny* bit more chilli… Speaker_1: (eyes widen) Don’t you dare. I’m already bracing myself for a mild burn. Don't test me. Do you even *like* curry that hot? Speaker_2: I enjoy a challenge. Plus, you said you’re feeling better. A little spice will clear your sinuses. Think of it as medicinal. Speaker_1: (sighs) You're incorrigible. Just…promise me a yoghurt on standby. And maybe a fire extinguisher. Speaker_2: Deal. Now, pass me the tomatoes. And stop looking like I’m about to poison you. It’s just a curry. Speaker_1: Famous last words. Speaker_2: Very funny. Speaker_1: I'm serious! Speaker_2: Okay, okay, no extra chilli. Happy? Speaker_1: Happier. Much happier. Speaker_2: Good, because I’m starving. Let’s get this cooked. Speaker_1: Right. Let's do it. And you're washing up.

Speaker_1: Right, shopping list. We need milk, definitely. And…oh, biscuits. Chocolate digestives, your favourite. And bread – a proper loaf, not that sliced stuff. Speaker_2: Ooh, lovely. And some apples, I fancy a baked apple later. Do you remember Mrs. Higgins from primary school? She used to make the most amazing apple crumble. Speaker_1: Mrs. Higgins… vaguely. She was the art teacher, wasn’t she? Always covered in paint. She made us do the most awful papier-mâché. I remember being utterly disgusted with the mess. Speaker_2: Oh, she loved her papier-mâché! And the glitter. Everywhere, glitter. Honestly, it took weeks to get it out of the classroom. Speaking of the classroom, do you remember those calendars they used to sell, with little fob bits on? Each month had a different one. I always collected them. Speaker_1: Oh, the plastic fobs! Yes! I had a whole string of them. Usually animals, weren’t they? Or little cartoon characters. I wonder what happened to those. Probably thrown away. Speaker_2: Me too. It's funny the things you remember, isn’t it? Remember young Timmy Bates playing hockey? He was dreadful! All legs and no coordination. He always needed help with his boots. Speaker_1: Oh, dreadful! He'd fall over his own feet. And that new ‘sports day’ initiative wasn't very effective. I remember Miss Davies trying to explain the importance of teamwork. It all fell apart when little Jenny Smith started crying because she didn’t win the egg and spoon race. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, she was a drama queen, that one! It's amazing how much primary school stays with you. It forms you, doesn’t it? I sometimes wonder what direction my students went in. Did they fulfill their potential? Speaker_1: It’s interesting thinking about what I’d study now, if I was going to University. I think I’d love to do something with sound recording. All those old radio programs… capturing and preserving that. Speaker_2: That's fascinating. Though you always had a knack for history. Social history, specifically. Really digging into how people *lived*. Speaker_1: That’s true. But I find the technology side appealing too. Imagine, going back and restoring recordings from the 1920s... It's practically archaeology, isn't it? Speaker_2: It is. Speaking of technology, you’re getting rid of that old computer, aren't you? The one you bought back in… what was it, ‘98? Speaker_1: Yes! It’s ancient. It barely runs anymore. I was thinking of donating it to that computing museum, the one near Bradford. They seem very keen on old equipment. Speaker_2: Oh, that’s a brilliant idea! They’d be thrilled. I’ve been meaning to volunteer there myself, actually. I'm sure they could use some help cataloging things. It would be good to put something back. Speaker_1: You should! You’d be brilliant at it. You remember all the changes, from those massive rooms filled with machines to everything fitting in your hand. It's a remarkable evolution to have witnessed. Speaker_2: It is. It really is… Right, back to the shopping list. Do we need any washing up liquid? And I must remember to pick up a card for Elsie’s birthday. She'll be eighty-two next week! Goodness, where does the time go? And should I put “82” or “Eighty-Two” on the card?

Speaker_1: So, Old Man Hemmings next door, apparently he’s been complaining about the lights on the barn. Says they’re too bright. Speaker_2: Oh, really? He’s always moaning, isn’t he? Mum said he complained about her hanging washing out on a Sunday! Speaker_3: Honestly, some people. It’s a barn, for goodness sake! What’s he expect, darkness? Though, I suppose it *is* quite a bright light. Did you get a chance to talk to him, David? Speaker_1: I did. Popped over with a mince pie, tried to be neighbourly. He grumbled on for about ten minutes about light pollution and the disruption to the badgers. Badgers! As if a barn light is going to bother a badger. Speaker_2: (laughing) Oh, Hemmings. He sounds… delightful. It's good you took a mince pie, though. Defuses things, usually. Speaker_3: Absolutely. Works wonders. Although, knowing him, he probably checked for walnuts before accepting it. He’s allergic, you know. Speaker_1: I did! Made sure they were walnut-free. Learned that lesson last Christmas. He practically had an anaphylactic shock over a trifle. Speaker_2: Oh dear! That sounds dramatic. How’s the decorating going, by the way? Have you managed to tackle the living room yet? Speaker_1: Slowly. Very slowly. I tried to put up that shelf yesterday, you know, the big one for all my books? And it kept falling down. Nearly took out the cat. Speaker_3: Oh, David! You and DIY are not a good combination. Remember the time you tried to fix the garden gate, and it ended up hanging sideways? Speaker_1: (grumbling) Don’t remind me. That was a disaster. Ended up calling Phil in the end. He’s the only one who can actually wield a screwdriver properly around here. Speaker_2: Phil’s a lifesaver, isn’t he? Speaking of which, did you manage to find that local walking group I told you about? The one that does the coastal path? Speaker_1: I did! I emailed them. Apparently they meet every Saturday morning. Thinking of joining next week, try and get some fresh air. And get away from that blasted shelf. Speaker_3: That sounds lovely. It’s such a beautiful coastline round here, you'll love it. Though, wrap up warm, it can get quite blustery. Speaker_2: And don’t forget your walking boots! It can get muddy. I've been meaning to ask – have you tried the pub yet? The Badger’s Holt? Speaker_1: Not yet, no. Been a bit busy unpacking and fighting with furniture. But I’ve heard good things. Apparently, they do a fantastic Sunday roast. Speaker_3: They do! Best in the village, easily. And they've got a lovely garden, perfect for sitting out in the summer. You must take me. Speaker_1: Definitely. First opportunity. And you two *must* come over for dinner once I’ve managed to get the kitchen looking presentable. It's currently a disaster zone of boxes. Speaker_2: We'd love that! Like taking away their toys? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) A bit like that, yes. A very grown-up version of taking away toys. Right, who wants more peas? Speaking of grown-up things, are you two excited about birthdays coming up? Speaker_2: I’m hoping for the new Lego Star Wars set. The Millennium Falcon one. It’s massive. Speaker_3: I want a new skateboard. Mine’s completely wrecked. Speaker_1: We'll see what we can do. We need to start thinking about what you both want to *do* for your birthdays as well. Party? Quiet meal? Speaker_2: Definitely a party. With friends. And cake. Speaker_3: Yeah, a party! And pizza. Maybe laser quest? Speaker_1: Laser quest sounds… energetic. We'll see. We’ll look at dates and stuff. Just finish your supper first, alright? And no requesting butterfly forks, please. Speaker_2: (Grinning) No promises. Speaker_3: (Mouth full of peas) I don’t even *like* asparagus. Speaker_1: That’s probably a good thing. Speaker_2: Honestly, a butterfly fork. What *is* the world coming to? Speaker_1: Don’t even ask. Speaker_3: Can we watch a film after? Speaker_1: Of course. After homework. And clearing your plates. Speaker_2: Deal. Speaker_3: Deal. Speaker_1: Good. Now eat your greens. Speaker_2: Mum! Speaker_1: What? They're good for you! Speaker_3: Yeah, Mum, they're just… green. Speaker_1: (Smiling) That’s the point.

Speaker_1: Right, so Adventure Island is officially booked for the last week in July. Four days, Monday to Thursday. Think that’s manageable, yeah? Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Adventure Island! Are we going on the Scorpion Express first? It's *so* fast! Speaker_3: Can I go on it, too? Even though I'm a bit scared? Speaker_1: You absolutely can, darling. We’ll all go on it together. Maybe we’ll start with something a bit gentler first, eh? There’s that lovely little train ride. Remember that one? Speaker_2: But the Scorpion Express has loops! And drops! Speaker_1: Yes, it does. And we’ll get to it, promise. So, Adventure Island sorted. Now, Cornwall… I was looking at cottages yesterday. There's one near Padstow, looks really nice, sea views… but it’s pricey. Speaker_3: Cornwall again? We *always* go to Cornwall. Can’t we go somewhere different? Like… Scotland? Speaker_1: Scotland is lovely, but it's a very long drive. And with marking exams looming, I don’t think I can manage a massive road trip. Cornwall is… reliable. We know what to expect. Plus, you both love building sandcastles on the beach. Speaker_2: And getting ice cream! Speaker_1: And getting ice cream. Exactly. Though, speaking of things we know, I’m still trying to work out what’s triggering my tummy issues. I swear it was that sourdough bread last night. I feel dreadful. Speaker_3: Mummy, are you sick? Speaker_1: No, sweetie, just a bit… uncomfortable. It’s probably just a food intolerance. I’m going to cut out gluten again and see if that helps. It’s just annoying, I really like sourdough. Speaker_2: Maybe it was the chocolate cake at Nana’s house? You had loads! Speaker_1: (Laughing) You are not wrong. Possibly. Right, back to Cornwall. This cottage has a games room, which is promising. And it’s close to the Eden Project. Have you two been before? Speaker_3: I liked the big bubbles! Speaker_2: And the rainforest bit! It was all hot and steamy! Speaker_1: Exactly! Okay, I think we’re leaning towards Cornwall. It’s just… I saw this amazing exhibition at the V&A in London – “Alice: Curiouser and Curiouser”. It looked incredible. But again, London feels like too much effort right now. Speaker_3: Alice in Wonderland! I like the Cheshire Cat! Speaker_1: Me too! Maybe another time. Right, Cornwall it is. I’ll book it this weekend. In the meantime, has anyone started thinking about what they want to pack for Adventure Island? Suncream is essential, obviously. Speaker_2: I want to pack my mermaid tail! Speaker_1: (Smiling) A mermaid tail… right. We’ll have to see about fitting that in the suitcase. And you, darling? Speaker_3: My dinosaur! And my bucket and spade. Speaker_1: Perfect. A bucket and spade are *always* a good idea. Now, let’s finish these packed lunches and get you two ready for school… then, I’m facing a mountain of exam papers. Wish me luck! Speaker_2: Good luck, Mummy! Speaker_3: I hope you find lots of good answers! Speaker_1: That’s the spirit! Now, sandwiches or wraps today?

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mr. Davies is *obsessed* with the semicolon. Like, every feedback point is just “Semicolon usage needs improvement.” It’s a coursework essay, not a grammar test! Speaker_2: Tell me about it. He marked down Liam for using “like” in a sentence. “Like,” as a filler word. It’s a natural thing to say, innit? He’s such a stickler. Speaker_1: It's worse than Mrs. Patel. She actually smiled when she told me my analysis was "adequate." Adequate! That’s basically a polite way of saying it’s rubbish. Speaker_2: Haha, brutal. Did you finish the physics practical report though? I’m still stuck on calculating the uncertainty. Speaker_1: Nearly. Just gotta tidy up the conclusions. It’s boring as heck, though. Speaking of boring, did you see Sarah in art today? She was attempting pottery and it looked… disastrous. Speaker_2: No way! Really? She’s usually so good at everything. Speaker_1: Yeah, she just kept collapsing the clay. Mr. Henderson was trying not to laugh. It was pretty funny, actually. Speaker_2: Right, speaking of funny, did you hear about what happened with Ben and the prefects? Speaker_1: No! Spill the tea. Speaker_2: Apparently, he was trying to film a TikTok in the library. Like, full-on dance routine. The head prefect, Emily, went ballistic. Speaker_1: No! Ben? Seriously? That’s so… Ben. Did he get in trouble? Speaker_2: Got a detention, obviously. Plus, he’s banned from using his phone on school grounds for a week. Which, let’s be real, is like torture for him. Speaker_1: He’ll survive. Anyway, are you still going to Jamie’s party on Saturday? Speaker_2: Yeah! Should be good. Apparently, he’s hired a DJ. Just gotta convince my mum I’m not going to cause any trouble. Speaker_1: Good luck with that. My parents are cool as long as I'm back by midnight. Oh, and they made me promise not to cycle home after. Said it’s too dangerous. Speaker_2: Annoying, right? It’s only a ten-minute bike ride. Saves loads of time. I hate waiting for the bus. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Hey, have you seen the new Marvel movie? I was thinking of going next week. Speaker_2: Ooh, yeah! I’ve heard it’s really good. But… I’m allergic to something in the cinema popcorn. Makes my face swell up. It's a nightmare. Speaker_1: Oh, blimey. That’s… not ideal. Maybe we could just grab something afterwards then? Speaker_2: Yeah, that’d be good. Unless you wanna risk me looking like a pufferfish. Speaker_1: Definitely not. Hey, remember that time old man Hemmings caught us trying to sneak into the sports hall? Speaker_2: Oh my god, yeah! He gave us the longest lecture ever about respecting school property. He was proper fuming. Speaker_1: He was! I thought he was going to call our parents. I was so scared. Speaker_2: Honestly, he’s terrifying. Alright, almost home. See ya tomorrow. Hopefully, Mr. Davies won’t ruin my life with semicolons. Speaker_1: See ya! And don’t let Ben inspire you to TikTok in the library. Hopefully, this conversation meets your requirements. Let me know if you’d like any adjustments.

Speaker_1: This road is absolutely mental, isn’t it? Honestly, the traffic is building up for no reason. Speaker_2: It always does at this time, doesn’t it? People just seem to decide to merge into one lane for fun. It's baffling. Speaker_1: Aye, it’s daft. Remember when we were trying to get to Durham last summer? Took us ages just to get past Washington. Speaker_2: Oh god, don’t remind me. That was a nightmare. At least we had a good view of the cricket ground, though. Did you see England were playing India last week? Speaker_1: I caught a bit of it on the radio. Sounds like they did alright? I’m not the biggest cricket fan, mind. Speaker_2: They won! Ben Stokes was on fire, apparently. It was a really good match. You should come with me next time, it’s a good atmosphere. Speaker_1: Maybe. I’m more of a football person, you know? Though I appreciate a nice sunny day for watching *something* sporty. Speaking of sunny days… are you still planning on cycling to Brighton next month? Speaker_2: Yeah, definitely. I’ve booked the route and everything. Hoping the weather holds up. It's a fair distance, but it’ll be worth it. Have you ever done a long distance cycle ride before? Speaker_1: No, never. I can barely manage a trip to the shops and back on my bike without getting completely out of breath! You’re proper keen, you are. Speaker_2: Well, I've been training a bit. Trying to build up my stamina, mostly. It's less about speed and more about endurance, you know? It's all about pacing. Speaker_1: That sounds… sensible. I’d probably just sprint for the first five miles and then collapse in a heap. Speaker_2: Don’t do that! Seriously, you'll ruin your entire trip. You need to start slow and steady. Plenty of water, lots of snacks… and a comfortable saddle. That's crucial. Speaker_1: A comfortable saddle? That sounds like a very important piece of cycling advice. I’ll remember that if I ever decide to take it up. Speaker_2: It is! Trust me. I learned that the hard way. You wouldn't believe the state of my… well, never mind. Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh, I can imagine! You and your fancy bikes. Honestly, you're a machine. Speaker_2: Just trying to stay active. It beats sitting in front of a computer all day, anyway. This traffic isn't helping my stress levels though...think we're going to be here a while. Is there anything else you'd like me to add to the conversation or adjust? Speaker_1: How's that project going, the one with the new bridge design? Speaker_2: Slow. So slow. Bureaucracy is a nightmare, honestly. Every decision has to go through seventeen different committees. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds stressful. Speaker_2: It is. But I'm hoping we'll get the green light next month. Then the real work begins. Speaker_1: Well, good luck with that. You'll smash it. Speaker_2: Thanks. I hope so. You're doing alright with work are you? Still enjoying the corpus stuff? Speaker_1: Yeah, not bad. It's a bit repetitive at times, but it's a good environment, and the people are nice. Speaker_2: That's good to hear. Always helps when you enjoy who you work with, doesn't it?

Speaker_1: Right, okay, so Golden Dragon or Lucky House? Honestly, I’m struggling. Last time from Golden Dragon the sweet and sour sauce was… questionable. Speaker_2: Questionable? It tasted like straight vinegar. I swear they just emptied a bottle in. Lucky House is usually a safer bet, though their portions are a bit smaller, aren't they? Speaker_3: Definitely smaller. I remember ordering a portion of chicken chow mein from there once and I genuinely thought they’d forgotten the chicken. It was like, 90% noodles. Speaker_1: See, that’s my fear! I want *food*, not a noodle mountain. But the vinegar… oh, the vinegar. Did you see my face when I tried it? Speaker_2: It was a picture! You genuinely recoiled. Honestly, I think you made a noise usually reserved for accidentally touching something really hot. Speaker_1: It was a reflex! It was *that* bad. Right, okay, new plan. What about New City? They’re a bit further, but apparently their sesame prawns are amazing. Speaker_3: Ooh, I’ve heard good things about New City. Apparently, they actually use sesame seeds, which is a revolutionary concept for some of these places. I’ve had prawns that tasted suspiciously of… nothing. Speaker_2: Sesame seeds *and* prawns? Bold. I'm worried about the delivery charge being astronomical though, especially if it’s coming from further out. Remember the last time we ordered from that Thai place? It was nearly ten quid just for delivery! Speaker_1: Okay, valid point. Let’s quickly check their delivery charges. One sec… Oh, it’s… six fifty. Not terrible. But still. Speaker_3: Six fifty. Hmm. Maybe Lucky House is the least offensive option. We could order extra portions to compensate for the noodle deficiency. Speaker_2: That’s…actually a sound strategy. We could get two portions of chow mein, just in case. And maybe some spring rolls. Always a safe bet, spring rolls. Speaker_1: Okay, okay. Lucky House it is. But if I get another vinegar-based sauce, I’m writing a strongly worded letter. And possibly leaving a scathing online review. Speaker_3: You do you. I'm happy with spring rolls. And maybe some dumplings? Do they do good dumplings? Speaker_2: I think so. They had a picture of them on their online menu, and they looked…promising. Right, shall I order? I’m feeling proactive. Speaker_1: Yes, please! You’re a lifesaver. And maybe, just *maybe*, order a small portion of sweet and sour chicken. But if it's vinegary, you have my permission to throw it at the wall. Speaker_3: Ooh, good rule. Definite wall-throwing permission. And can you get some prawn crackers? It’s not a proper Chinese takeaway without prawn crackers. Speaker_2: Prawn crackers are already on the list. Don't worry, I *know* the essentials. Right...ordering now. Don't answer the door to anyone suspicious, just in case it’s a vinegar-smuggling operative. Speaker_1: Good call. Speaker_3: Honestly, that vinegar was a crime against cuisine. Speaker_1: It really was. Speaker_2: Okay, order placed! Estimated delivery time is 45 minutes. Prepare for stomach-filling deliciousness... hopefully. Speaker_3: I'm already excited. Speaker_1: Me too! Now, what are we watching while we wait?

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of it, eh? Been trying to get me mum an appointment with the GP for weeks now. You’d think being retired she’d get priority, wouldn't ya? Speaker_2: Tell me about it. It's a nightmare. I'm a nurse practitioner, I *work* in the system, and even *I* struggle to navigate it sometimes. It’s just… constantly fire-fighting. Never enough resources, never enough time. Speaker_1: Aye, well you’re on the front line, love. I can only imagine. It’s a miracle any of it still functions, really. I was reading an article the other day about the Finnish healthcare system… apparently it's completely different. Preventative, properly funded, the whole shebang. Speaker_2: Oh, I’ve heard good things. Everything's centralised isn't it? No postcode lottery like we have here. They invest properly in primary care. It's a totally different philosophy. But, you know, good luck trying to implement that here. Too many layers of bureaucracy, too many vested interests. Speaker_1: Exactly. It's always the same story, innit? Anyway, speaking of frustrating situations… have you heard anything more about old Mrs. Delaney next door? Speaker_2: Oh, her? Not really. Just seen her pottering about in the garden, same as always. Why? Speaker_1: Well, I saw her son, Kevin, the other day, loading a van full of her stuff. Said she was "downsizing." Downsizing at eighty-five? Seems a bit dodgy, if you ask me. Speaker_2: Oh, that doesn't sound right. She always seemed alright to me. Little bit of a gossip, maybe, but harmless enough. Is he taking her with him? Speaker_1: That's what I'm worried about. He’s never been one for looking after anyone but himself, that Kevin. Always asking her for money, always "borrowing" things. I’ve seen him, sneakily, taking her post. Speaker_2: Oh, that’s awful! He’s always struck me as a bit of a scoundrel. Has anyone else noticed anything? Speaker_1: Old Mr. Henderson across the road said he saw a removal firm he didn't recognise. Apparently, they weren’t local. He said they looked a bit shifty. Henderson’s nosey, but he’s usually spot on. Speaker_2: That *is* concerning. Maybe someone should just pop round and have a chat with her, see if everything's alright? I can slip round after work if you like. Speaker_1: That would be brilliant, honestly. Just a friendly face, ask her if she's happy. I'd do it myself, but I’m stuck with marking essays until the cows come home. University life, eh? All intellectual stimulation, no actual time. Speaker_2: You lecturers have it tough, honestly. Grading endless piles of work. I get enough drama at the hospital, I don’t need it at home! Speaker_1: Tell me about it. And then they wonder why we all drink. Listen, if you do go round, just… be discreet, alright? Don't want to cause a scene, but it's better to be safe than sorry. Poor woman. This area used to be lovely, but it's going downhill. These new houses they’re building… all crammed in, no gardens. It's a disgrace, really. Speaker_2: Aye, it’s changing. Still, good people live here. Hopefully Mrs. Delaney is okay. I’ll have a word, don’t worry. I'll let you know what I find out.

Speaker_1: …and then young Kevin, bless ‘im, he’s arguing with the postman about a parcel. Said it weren’t his, despite bein’ addressed to ‘K. O’Connell, Number 7’. Said the postman was tryin’ to scam ‘im! Speaker_2: (Chuckles, a dry rasping sound) Kevin, eh? Always a drama with that lad. Reminds me o’ me brother, Billy. Now *he* could argue the hind legs off a donkey. Once argued with a copper over a parking ticket, said the lines weren’t clear enough. Ended up gettin’ a bigger fine for bein’ obstructive. Speaker_1: Ah, the police. There’s been a lot of ‘em around lately, hasn’t there? Seems a bit heavier handed than usual. Heard they raided that flat on Upper Stanhope Street again. Speaker_2: Aye, heard that. Drugs, they say. Though I reckon half the trouble is caused by these…these newcomers, comin’ over here takin’ our jobs. Not all o’ them, mind, but there’s a good few. Speaker_1: That's…a complicated issue, isn’t it? A lot of these jobs aren’t ones people *want* to do, to be honest. And a lot of them work incredibly hard. I teach a few students who came over with their families. Bright kids, desperate to learn. Speaker_2: Hard work don't fill an empty belly, lad. And desperate… desperate people do desperate things. Back in my day, you knew everyone on the street. Now? Faces you've never seen before. It’s not the same, not the same at all. Used to be able to leave your door unlocked. Not anymore, not anymore. Speaker_1: Things certainly change. Though I remember me Nan always sayin’ you could never truly trust anyone, even your own neighbours. She'd seen a bit in her time, lost her husband in the war. Speaker_2: She was right, y’know. She was a smart woman, your Nan. Mine… well, she worried about everything. Especially me. Said I was too soft. Used to say, “Arthur, you’d let a burglar help himself to the silver and then offer him a cup of tea!” Speaker_1: (Laughs) Sounds like her. My Dad was the worrier. Constantly fretting about the welfare state, said it was breeding dependency. He used to say if everyone had to work for a livin’, there’d be less trouble. Speaker_2: He weren’t wrong, y'know. Though it’s alright sayin' that when you *have* a livin’. What about the ones who can't work? The sick, the disabled… the old like me? Relyin’ on a pittance from the government just to keep the lights on. It's a disgrace, truly. Speaker_1: It *is* tough. I’ve seen it, workin’ with students from disadvantaged backgrounds. The system’s… flawed, let’s say that. Still, you’ve got your family, haven’t you? Your daughter visits regular, doesn’t she? Speaker_2: She does. Bless her. Comes every Sunday with a bit o' shopping and a gossip. Says I need to get out more, but frankly, I haven’t got the energy. Nor the money, for that matter. Everything’s gone up, hasn't it? Even a loaf of bread costs a fortune these days. Speaker_1: Everything is. It's alarming, really. Still, family’s what matters, isn’t it? And a good cup of tea. Fancy one? I’ve just put the kettle on. Speaker_2: (A small smile) Now *that*’s an offer I can’t refuse, lad. A good cup of tea and a bit o’ company. That’s all an old man needs, really.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…an experience, isn’t it? I think I’ve identified at least four different shades of beige on my plate. Speaker_2: (Laughing) It’s Cambridge University Press, not a Michelin-starred restaurant, Liv. You get what you get. Though, I’ll admit, the ‘mystery meat’ is always a gamble. Speaker_3: It’s functional. Fuel. That's all it needs to be. I’ve got a stack of transcripts to annotate this afternoon, I need the energy. Speaker_4: You guys are too polite. It’s… institutionally bland. Though, I’m used to American university dining halls. They often operate on a similar principle of mass-produced lukewarmness. Speaker_5: I’m just grateful I managed to snag a seat. It was like the Hunger Games in here. Did anyone see old Mr. Henderson elbowing that poor PhD student out of the way for a Yorkshire pudding? Speaker_1: No way! Henderson? He’s usually such a gentle soul. Though, he *does* have a legendary appetite. Speaker_2: I heard he single-handedly cleared out the biscuit tin at the last departmental meeting. Apparently, he said they were “a vital component of cognitive function.” Speaker_3: (Chuckles) That’s amazing. He’s a character, isn't he? Reminds me of my grandad, always sneaking extra portions. Speaker_4: It’s funny how consistent those little personality quirks are across generations. My grandfather was the same way with pudding. Couldn’t resist a good custard. Speaking of which, is anyone braving the dessert selection? Speaker_5: I might. I’ve heard whispers of a chocolate brownie. Though, it’s probably 90% icing and 10% actual brownie. Speaker_1: You’re brave, Ella. I’m sticking with the vaguely fruit-like substance they’re calling ‘compote’. It’s…texturally interesting. Speaker_2: So, anyone actually made any progress on the phonological analysis today? I’m hitting a wall with the Northern English vowel shifts. It’s… complex. Speaker_3: I’m slowly getting there. It’s the subtle variations that are killing me. You think you've got it pinned down, then you find a recording with a completely different pronunciation. Speaker_4: It's fascinating though, isn’t it? The way language evolves and changes with geography. Keeps things interesting. That’s why I love working on these dialect projects. Speaker_5: It’s mad how different things are even just between Leeds and Sunderland, Liv. You’d think being relatively close, it'd be more similar. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I was trying to explain to my aunt what you meant by ‘quid’ last week and she just looked at me like I’d grown a second head. She’s from down south, everything’s ‘pounds’ there. It’s exhausting sometimes. Speaker_2: It *is* a constant negotiation of meaning. I had a colleague from Devon convinced I was speaking a different language entirely when I said "bairn." Speaker_3: Oh, that’s a good one! I bet. Speaker_4: This is what makes linguistics so wonderful. It's not just about rules and grammar; it's about people and their stories and how they connect through language. Even if it means deciphering beige-plated canteen food fuelled conversations. Speaker_5: Hear, hear! To linguistics, and surviving lunchtime at Cambridge. Speaker_1: Cheers to that! I think I need a second cup of tea to help me process this meal.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the buffering was atrocious. I mean, I’m paying for fibre, supposedly ‘superfast’ fibre, and I was watching a nature documentary, right? David Attenborough, majestic stuff. But every time a particularly stunning shot of a snow leopard emerged, it would freeze. Freeze! Ruined the whole dramatic effect. Speaker_2: Oh, the indignity! You’re missing the apex predator in its natural habitat because of… BT? Is that who you’re with? Speaker_1: Yeah, BT. They claim it’s the line, the ancient wiring in this Victorian house. I’m starting to suspect it’s just a conspiracy to keep me from discovering the secrets of the snow leopard. Speaker_2: (Laughs) A snow leopard conspiracy. I like it. Makes more sense than their customer service, anyway. I’ve been thinking about trying to pick up some Mandarin. Speaker_1: Mandarin? Seriously? That’s a bold move. Speaker_2: Well, I’ve been working with a couple of Chinese colleagues on this latest project, and it’s become acutely apparent how hopeless I am. I mean, I can manage ‘Ni hao’ and ‘Xie xie’, but beyond that… nothing. It’s frustrating. You feel like you're constantly relying on translation, missing nuanced understanding. Speaker_1: I can imagine. I attempted Spanish once. Got as far as ordering beer and asking where the toilet was. Highly practical, admittedly, but not exactly fluent conversation. What are you thinking of doing? Online course? Speaker_2: Probably. Duolingo’s tempting, but I worry it’s a bit… superficial. I was looking at some evening classes at the local college. It’s just fitting it into the schedule is the killer. You’re still teaching that adult education class, aren’t you? Speaker_1: Sadly, yes. Though ‘teaching’ might be a generous term. It's mostly trying to coax reluctant learners through basic essay structure. It’s surprisingly draining. You get one or two who are genuinely enthusiastic, then a sea of blank stares and sighs. Speaker_2: Sounds familiar. The joy of public service, eh? I’ve always admired people who are good at teaching. It requires a patience I definitely don’t possess. Speaker_1: It’s more about lowering your expectations, honestly. And having a good sense of humour. One lady last week honestly thought footnotes were some sort of secret code. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, bless her. That's brilliant. You'd think in this age of instant information, footnotes wouldn't be so mysterious. It’s funny, isn’t it? How differently people approach things depending on their cultural background, their education… Speaker_1: Absolutely. You realise how much is just *assumed* knowledge. I was reading an article about the different ways various cultures perceive time, and it was fascinating. Some see it as linear, others as cyclical… totally impacts everything from business dealings to personal relationships. Speaker_2: Right, I’ve heard that. Makes you think, doesn’t it? Maybe Mandarin isn’t just about learning a language, but about trying to understand a whole different way of looking at the world. Speaker_1: Precisely. It's not just verbs and nouns, is it? Say, are you free next week? We should finally get around to that pub quiz. Apparently, The Red Lion is doing a theme on obscure geographical facts. You’d crush it. Speaker_2: Obscure geographical facts? Is that even a thing? Okay, you’ve talked me into it. Next week sounds good. Let me just check my calendar… avoiding snow leopard conspiracies and footnote decoding, obviously.

Speaker_1: Right, now then, love, you’ve made a proper mess of this cushion arrangement, haven’t you? Looks like a flock of pigeons landed on it. Speaker_2: (Groans) Grandma! I didn’t *make* a mess. I was just…rearranging. It needed a bit of life. Speaker_3: Life? It needed a good plumpin’ and settlin’, not scatterin’ about like confetti. Your grandad always said a tidy room is a tidy mind. Though, mind you, his mind was often a bit of a muddle anyway. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Aye, that’s true. Used to look for his glasses when they were on his head. Happened more times than I care to remember. Speaker_1: Don’t encourage him, Arthur! Now, are you two hungry? I’ve made a victoria sponge. Proper one, with raspberry jam and a dusting of icing sugar. Speaker_2: Ooh, yes please! That sounds amazing. Speaker_3: Lovely. Though, I’m not sure I should. Doctor said I need to watch my sugar. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t be daft, Margaret. One slice won't hurt. Besides, a little bit of what you fancy does you good. I’ll cut you a small one. Speaker_4: I'll have a slice then, whilst you're at it. Can’t let all that good cake go to waste. Speaker_1: That’s what I thought. Now, that dripping from the guttering… I really need to get someone to look at that. It's been like that for weeks. Speaker_2: I told you, Gran, I could have a look. I’m pretty good with DIY stuff. I fixed Mr Henderson’s shed last summer, remember? Speaker_1: You *helped* Mr Henderson. His son did most of the work. And you nearly took your finger off with the hammer. Speaker_2: (Muttering) It was a slight mishap. Speaker_3: Always best to get a professional in for something like that. Don't want you falling off a ladder, lad. We'd have another one to worry about then. Speaker_4: Speaking of worrying, have you seen that new program on the telly? About the escaped emu? Speaker_1: Oh, Arthur, honestly! Emus! It's ridiculous. Speaker_2: It’s hilarious! Apparently it ran through a primary school playground. Speaker_3: Well, I never. Imagine the chaos. Speaker_1: I'm more concerned about the heating. It’s been acting up again. Keeps going on and off. I've tried everything. Do you think I should call Billy next door? He's quite handy. Speaker_4: Billy? He charged Mrs. Patterson a fortune for changing a light bulb. Speaker_1: Oh, don't remind me. He's a bit of a rogue, that one. Maybe I should just suffer in silence. Speaker_2: I could have a look at the thermostat, Gran. It might just be a loose wire or something. Speaker_1: (Sighs) Oh alright, go on then. But be careful! And don't go fiddling with anything you don't understand. I don't want the house plunging into darkness. Speaker_3: He's a good lad, your grandson. Always willing to help. Unlike some I could mention... Speaker_4: (Winks at Speaker_2) Aye, he’s a chip off the old block, that one.

Speaker_1: Oh, look at that little courtyard. Isn’t it lovely? All those potted plants… makes such a difference, doesn’t it? Speaker_2: It does. It's amazing what a bit of green can do. I was thinking about old Mrs. Higgins’ garden back in Norwich, remember? She had prize-winning roses. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, *Mrs. Higgins*! Yes! She was utterly terrifying if you dared to step on her lawn. She’d be out there with her watering can like a weapon. Speaker_2: Exactly! But the roses were spectacular. Do you think we’ll ever… I don’t know… have a proper garden again? Just space to potter about? Speaker_1: Eventually, I hope so. It feels a bit… surreal, doesn’t it? Being here, so far from everything that feels normal. Though, increasingly, ‘normal’ feels a long way away. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I was scrolling through photos on my phone earlier. Liam and Chloe’s wedding… feels like a lifetime ago. Everyone looking so happy and… *there*. Speaker_1: Oh, God, that was a good wedding. So much gin. Did you see Sarah’s photos too? She posted loads of them from her trekking trip in Nepal. Incredible. Makes you want to just… go. Speaker_2: Completely. Though Nepal feels a little ambitious at the moment. Maybe something closer to home, when we get back. A week in the Lake District? Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! That sounds perfect. We should start planning something. A proper break. I keep meaning to look at the flight prices, but I always get distracted with marking. Speaker_2: It's the same story. Honestly, marking essays about the symbolism of rain in Victorian poetry is not nearly as appealing as a walk in the fells. Speaker_1: (Smiling) You’re telling me. I had one student write an entire essay arguing that rain represents the repressed desires of the upper class. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, *seriously*? That’s… dedicated. Or completely bonkers. Speaker_1: A little of both, I think. Speaking of slightly bonkers…did you hear back from Mark about his trip out here? He was talking about trying to visit over the summer. Speaker_2: He emailed! He’s decided to postpone. Something about work commitments. He said he’s gutted, though, and promised to try next year. Speaker_1: Ah, that’s a shame. It would've been lovely to show him around. He’d love the food, I think. Or, at least, complain about it in a very amusing way. Speaker_2: Absolutely. He's the master of polite complaints. Well, let's enjoy this walk. The air’s actually quite nice today, even with the… particulate matter. Speaker_1: Yes, let's. It's good to just… be. Away from emails, away from essays, away from everything for a little while. Speaker_2: Definitely. Sometimes you just need a bit of… perspective, you know? And a good cup of tea later. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Perspective and tea. The cornerstones of a sensible life. Speaker_2: Couldn’t have said it better myself. Look, there's old Mr. Chen… always tending to his bonsai trees. Speaker_1: He takes them very seriously. They're like his children, aren't they? Speaker_2: They are. Come on, let’s keep walking. I want to see if the dumpling shop is open.

Speaker_1: Honestly, my feet are *killing* me. I swear those shoes were designed by someone who's never actually walked anywhere. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I think I’ve permanently ruined my blisters. Did you see Liam trying to dance? Honestly, it was… a choice. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, God, Liam. He thinks he’s John Travolta, doesn’t he? It’s tragic. He was practically knocking people over. Speaker_2: He was! And then he kept trying to offer everyone shots. Shots of what, I don’t even want to know. He was a menace. Speaker_1: At least it was a good laugh though, right? I haven’t laughed that much in ages. Even Chloe managed a smile, and you *know* how grumpy she gets when she’s not getting enough attention. Speaker_2: True. She was glued to Ben all night. Honestly, I don't get it. He's nice, yeah, but he talks about football *constantly*. It’s exhausting. Speaker_1: I know! My dad talks about football less, and he literally watches it every single day. Speaking of dads, mine’s been going on about getting a dog again. Speaker_2: Oh no, not again! He was obsessed last time. Remember when he was researching Great Danes? In our tiny flat! Speaker_1: (Groaning) Don't remind me. He forgot we live in a shoebox. He’s now talking about a Labrador puppy. Says it’ll “get us all out more.” Speaker_2: Right, because hours of puppy training and cleaning up accidents is exactly what we need to make our lives more exciting. Tell him to get a goldfish. Speaker_1: Honestly, I will. He’s already sent me links to breeders. It’s terrifying. Did you manage to eat anything last night, by the way? I was too busy dodging Liam's shots to even look at the food. Speaker_2: I had a chip. One. It was swimming in grease, but it was a chip and I was starving. I spent all day at placement, honestly I’m wrecked. Speaker_1: Placement sounds brutal. I'm just doing essays, which is… another kind of brutal. I'm trying to get motivated to start mine on Victorian literature. It's so dull. Speaker_2: Oh god, Victorian lit. That sounds awful. I’d rather have Liam offering me dodgy shots. What’s the essay on? Speaker_1: Dickens. Specifically, the portrayal of poverty. Riveting stuff. I think I’m going to need a lot of coffee. Speaker_2: You and me both. I saw Jess posting photos on Insta this morning, looking *amazing*. She went to some fancy party. It's so unfair. Speaker_1: Don’t even go there! She’s just good at posing. Remember she tripped over her own feet at that dinner last week? She was so embarrassed. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh yeah! She pretended it was a sophisticated move. “Oh, I just *glided*…” Speaker_1: (Joining in the laughter) Glided! Into a table. Oh, Jess. Anyway, we should probably actually go to a lecture at some point today. Speaker_2: Ugh, don’t remind me. I’m seriously considering faking a fever. Speaker_1: Maybe. I think I'm up for a nap, truth be told. And potentially, a very stern word with my dad about the Labrador puppy situation. Speaker_2: Sounds like a plan. And seriously, goldfish. Definitely a goldfish.

Speaker_1: Right, so have we actually finalised when your mum’s coming? I keep forgetting to ask. It feels like it’s been 'next week' for a month now. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) It has, hasn’t it? She’s confirmed for the 18th. She’s booked the train, everything. Luckily she managed to get a reasonably priced ticket, though she was grumbling about the cost. She's aiming to arrive around lunchtime. Speaker_3: The 18th… that’s good. Gives us time to… well, to generally tidy up. This place isn't exactly presentation-ready, is it? Speaker_1: Oh, don't be daft, John. It's perfectly homely. She’s not expecting the Ritz. Though, maybe a quick once-over with the hoover wouldn't go amiss. And I’ll get the guest room aired. Speaker_2: I can help with that. I’ve finished most of the transcription work for today, so I have a bit of free time. Speaking of which, did you see the latest FIFA update? They’ve completely reworked the player movements. Speaker_3: Oh, no, I haven’t touched it since… well, since last month, probably. I’m getting too old for these things. My reflexes aren’t what they used to be. I was getting utterly thrashed by that young lad, Ben, online. Speaker_1: (Smiling) You’re just being modest, John. You’re still very competitive. Remember that time you beat your brother at tennis when you were… oh goodness, must have been forty years ago? He never let you forget it. Speaker_3: (Sighs) That was a different time. And it was partially due to him having a dodgy knee. He’d just come back from a football injury. Though, he’d never admit that. Stubborn man, your father. Speaker_2: Speaking of stubborn, I was reading an article about the situation with that football manager, Gareth Southgate. Everyone’s blaming him for the team’s performance, but I think the board are just as culpable. They haven't invested properly in youth development. Speaker_1: It's always easier to blame the visible figure, isn't it? No one wants to admit their own part in a failure. It reminds me of school – a student failing a maths test and instantly blaming the teacher, rather than acknowledging their own lack of preparation. Speaker_3: Exactly. No accountability. It’s a modern malaise. It's all about passing the buck. Honestly, you see it in politics, you see it in business… Speaker_2: It’s frustrating. It's like, where does the responsibility *actually* lie? Do you think your mum will want to play a game of cards when she comes? She always enjoys a good game of rummy. Speaker_1: Oh, she will love that. She’s been asking about it. And she wants to hear all about this new life up here. She’s still a bit sceptical about us moving so far north, you know? Thinks we're mad, swapping Dublin for Cumbria. Speaker_3: (Grinning) Well, we *are* a bit mad, aren’t we? But it’s a good kind of mad. It's peaceful here. And… well, we’re happy. That's what matters. Are you sure you've got enough peas, Mary? These are lovely. Speaker_1: Plenty more, dear. Help yourself. And don't let John hog all the chips. He's been eyeing them up for the last five minutes.

Speaker_1: Right, well, that was lovely wasn’t it? Biscuits were a bit stale, but…you can’t win ‘em all. Speaker_2: They weren't *that* stale, honestly. It’s just you're a biscuit snob, Liam. And honestly, Dad, complaining about free biscuits is a bit much. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) No, no, she’s right. A bit crumbly, maybe. Still good with the tea though. Lovely tea, actually. Better than what I make, I’ll admit. Speaker_4: You always say that, Reg. You make a perfectly good cup of tea. It’s just…we use posh tea here, isn’t that right? Speaker_1: It’s just a slightly fancier blend, yeah. Worth the extra quid, I reckon. Anyway, are you sure you’ve got everything? Bags packed? Speaker_2: Yep. Phone charger, toiletries, emergency chocolate...the essentials. Speaker_3: I’ve got my glasses. Found them under the cushion, of all places. Honestly, I swear they have a life of their own. Speaker_4: Tell me about it. I’m *always* losing mine. It’s the age, I think. Everything starts to go. Speaker_1: It’s not age, it’s just being…distracted. Like when I tried to fix that wonky shelf last week and ended up nearly taking the whole wall down. DIY is officially beyond me. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You and DIY are a tragic combination. Remember the time you tried to assemble that flat-pack bookcase? Speaker_1: Don't remind me. It took three of us and a lot of colourful language. Anyway, did you two manage to figure out that phone, Dad? The Blackberry? Speaker_3: Ah, that thing. Still a mystery. It’s…complicated. Young Liam here was trying to show me, but it’s all touchscreens and swipes. I miss a good button. Solid, you know? Speaker_4: It’s different, definitely. I’m pretty good with technology, but even I find some of it a bit baffling. Speaking of baffling, did you hear about the bin strikes? Absolute chaos. Speaker_2: Oh god, no. Still going on? That’s disgusting. Brighton will be a tip in a week. Speaker_1: Apparently the water company’s involved somehow. Something about…waste processing and needing more water? Typical. They’re always finding a reason to increase the bills. Speaker_4: It’s mad isn’t it? You can’t even trust them to just take your rubbish away. And the water, honestly, I’ve been reading about different filters you can get, to improve the taste. Apparently, tap water isn’t as clean as they say. Speaker_3: I just drink it straight from the tap. Always have. Never done me any harm. Bit of chlorine, maybe, but…character building! Speaker_2: Dad! You’re incorrigible. Speaker_1: Right, well, you’re both off then? The train’s not going to wait. It's getting a bit gloomy out there. Looks like we're in for another downpour. Speaker_4: Yeah, best get going. It was lovely to see you both. And thanks for the tea and the… slightly stale biscuits. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Anytime. Always a pleasure. Good to get out of London for a bit, even if it’s just for a few days. Speaker_2: We’ll ring when we get back. And Liam, don’t attempt any more DIY projects. Promise me. Speaker_1: No promises. But I'll try. Right, then. Give us a wave, and be careful on the journey. Goodbye!

Speaker_1: Right, have you checked the football? Any sign of a miraculous recovery from United? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You know it's pointless even looking, honestly. It was another…well, let’s just say it wasn’t a good weekend for them. I saw a few headlines. Didn’t bother digging deeper, saved myself the pain. Speaker_1: Sensible. It’s just…it's getting to the point where I dread even glancing at the scores. It’s affecting my mood, which, given the general grey-ness of everything, is not ideal. This gloom is really getting to me, actually. Proper SAD vibes going on. Speaker_2: I can imagine. Poland in November isn’t exactly known for its sunshine, is it? Is it worse than Cambridge this time of year, do you think? Speaker_1: Oh, massively. Cambridge gets damp, but it doesn’t have *this*…oppressive feeling. Everything feels heavy. Though, this coffee is good. Really good. This place is a find. Have you tried the latte macchiato? Speaker_2: Not yet, but I will. I'm on my second flat white, and it’s perfect. Bit stronger than what I’m used to back home. Speaking of home… I had a message from Sarah this morning. She’s booked a weekend away, hiking in the Lake District. Speaker_1: Oh, lovely! Good for her. Are you feeling…homesick? Speaker_2: A little, if I’m honest. It's not so much missing *things*, it's missing having everything familiar. You know? Like knowing where to get your favourite biscuits, or just being able to pop to the pub without needing to translate the beer menu. And my students… I’m starting to feel so responsible for them all. Their exams are looming, and I’m terrified I haven’t prepared them well enough. Speaker_1: Ah, that's awful. The weight of expectation, right? You’re a good teacher, though, you’ll have done your best. It's easy to get caught up in worrying. Speaker_2: I know, I know. It’s just…Agnes, one of my students… she’s so bright, but she struggles with speaking. I've been trying to build her confidence, but I feel like I'm failing. I spend hours thinking about different approaches. Speaker_1: That sounds exhausting. You’re such a conscientious person. Remember that time you volunteered on the organic farm in France for a summer? You threw yourself into everything. Absolutely covered in mud, but happy as could be. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh god, don't remind me! The blisters… and trying to herd those goats. It was… an experience. Though, I did learn to make a mean goat cheese. Speaker_1: See? You’re adaptable! You’ll handle this. Are you going to get fitted for new boots this week? The ones you were looking at online? Speaker_2: Yes, I’m going to try and squeeze it in. I really need waterproof ones. It's perpetually drizzling here. I saw someone trying to navigate the market with a tiny, ridiculous umbrella earlier. It was practically inside out. Speaker_1: Bless them. Honestly, the people here are so resilient. And… I was reading an article about the Polish media, just trying to get a sense of what’s going on. It’s…different. A lot more focused on local issues, which is refreshing, actually. Speaker_2: It is, isn’t it? Less obsession with celebrity gossip. Although, I did see a magazine with a very enthusiastic article about a dog who can apparently paint. Speaker_1: (Smiling) A *painting* dog? Now *that’s* news. See? There’s always something to brighten the day. Perhaps another latte macchiato is in order?

Speaker_2: Right, this sauce needs a proper good stir, doesn’t it? I swear, pasta sauce always separates when you’re not looking. Speaker_1: It does, it's the law. Honestly, you'd think it *wants* to look sad and watery. So, how was work today, Liam? More heavy lifting? Speaker_2: You know it. Pallets of… something. Honestly, I rarely look. It’s just shift it from A to B. The lads are alright though, keeps you sane. You? Still wrangling conference centres? Speaker_1: Still wrangling. Honestly, it was a nightmare. Apparently, someone booked the main hall for a poodle grooming competition *and* a taxidermy convention on the same day. Speaker_3: (Laughing) No way! Seriously? That's…quite a clash of interests. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I had to explain to Mrs. Higgins – the poodle lady – why she couldn’t have glitter cannons during the taxidermy demonstration. Apparently, the stuffing is flammable. Speaker_2: Woah. Okay, *that's* a story. See, my day lacked any kind of drama like that. Just sweat and splinters. Speaker_3: Sounds… fulfilling. I swear, corporate life is just a constant fire drill these days. Had a full meltdown from Brenda in marketing because the font on the new brochure was “too assertive.” Speaker_1: Oh, Brenda. She's a special breed, isn't she? Still, at least you get paid a decent wage for handling assertive fonts. Speaking of which, have you guys seen that new shop that opened on Mill Road? The vintage one? Speaker_2: Nah, not yet. Is it any good? I’m always needing new work clothes, something that doesn’t look like I’ve been wrestling with timber all day. Speaker_1: It’s brilliant! I found this amazing leather jacket, secondhand of course, for like thirty quid. It's proper 80s, all oversized and a bit rebellious. Speaker_3: Ooh, send me a pic! I’m always on the hunt for a statement piece. I’ve been trying to avoid fast fashion lately, it feels…wrong. Speaker_1: Will do! It's definitely a good find. It’s a shame you're always working, Liam, we could have gone browsing this afternoon. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Shifts are crazy at the moment with Christmas coming up. Everyone’s panicking about deliveries. Speaking of Christmas, are we still doing Secret Santa this year? Speaker_3: I think so. I was thinking we could set a limit of twenty quid. Keeps it reasonable. Speaker_1: Sounds good to me. Have either of you had any luck on the dating front? Still swiping endlessly? Speaker_2: Swiping is a waste of time. All the good ones are either already taken or want you to be a professional footballer. Speaker_3: (Smiling) You’re exaggerating. Slightly. I’ve been on a couple of dates. One guy spent the entire time talking about his cryptocurrency investments. Speaker_1: Oh dear. Red flag alert! Speaker_3: Massive red flag. Although, the other one was a surprisingly good conversationalist…and a chef. He made me pasta from scratch. Speaker_1: Ooh, a chef! Now *that’s* promising. What’s he like? Speaker_3: Nice, a bit quiet maybe, but really thoughtful. We’re going out again next week. Perhaps I will have found someone after all.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this square is…odd. It’s all these straight lines, isn’t it? Very formal. Reminds me of a chessboard. Not a patch on a proper park with meandering paths and… well, character. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s a bit stark. Though I suppose it’s useful for, you know, meeting people. Look at that kid though, actually caught a pigeon! Bit rough, isn’t it? The poor thing. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Kids will be kids. Makes you wonder what they’re teaching them these days. Speaking of which, I’m still reeling from Mrs. Chen’s stories about teaching English in China. The sheer scale of it… thirty students in a class? And the emphasis on rote learning. Speaker_2: It’s a world away from our TEFL courses, eh? I remember old Professor Davies banging on about communicative methodology. She said the Chinese system is changing, slowly. More demand for conversational English, especially with the rise in tourism. Speaker_1: Tourism… that’s an interesting one. Apparently, Paris is completely overrun. Chinese tourists, specifically. All wanting the Eiffel Tower selfies. I read something about it – queues stretching for miles. Speaker_2: Yeah, it's a bit mad. I was talking to Li Wei last week and he was saying the Chinese middle class are desperate to travel, see the world. They’ve been cooped up for so long. He was telling me about his family’s trip to Tibet. Said it was… transformative. Speaker_1: Tibet… wow. Must be incredible. Completely different landscape, isn't it? He also mentioned seeing pandas, of course. Apparently, they're obsessed with pandas. They used to keep bears as pets, apparently. Real, proper bears. Speaker_2: Really? That sounds… perilous.
