Bit different from a golden retriever. You realize how much about China I’m learning through anecdote, don’t you? It's all second hand from students and Li Wei. Speaker_1: It’s the best way, sometimes. Textbooks can only tell you so much. Speaking of textbooks… how’s the PhD going? Still battling with Professor Albright? She's notoriously… demanding. Speaker_2: Oh, Albright. Don’t even get me started. She wants me to completely re-frame my argument. Says I’m being too… optimistic about the role of social media. She's practically breathing down my neck. It’s exhausting. Fancy another coffee? There's that place on Tottenham Court Road. Speaker_1: Absolutely. I need the caffeine. Plus, I saw they do that coconut cake… the one you like. And we need to avoid those chuggers, though. They're relentless. Always wanting donations for… well, everything. Speaker_2: They are the worst. Just standing there, trapping you. You’d think they’d have figured out that nobody wants to be accosted in the middle of Gordon Square. Did you read that article about the death penalty in China? Pretty grim stuff. Speaker_1: Sadly, yes. And the drug laws… incredibly strict. Li Wei’s cousin got into trouble for possessing a tiny amount of… well, never mind. It’s a complicated country, isn't it? Complicated and fascinating. Speaker_2: It really is. I still can’t get over how… ubiquitous WeChat is. Everything happens on that app. Birthdays, payments, messaging… it’s a whole ecosystem. I tried explaining Facebook to Li Wei and he just looked at me like I was explaining hieroglyphs. Speaker_1: I suppose it’s like trying to explain West Ham United to someone. Completely incomprehensible if you’re not already invested. Speaking of investments, are you still thinking about driving down to Devon for Christmas? Speaker_2: Possibly. But the thought of navigating those country lanes… the tractors, the tourists… it fills me with dread. Trying to get to the Isle of Wight by car feels easier, honestly. Speaker_1: (Laughs) You and rural driving.

Speaker_1: Right, so are we still on for Friday then? Speaker_2: Yeah, Friday's good. Unless… oh wait, actually, Sarah’s mum is coming to stay. Friday night. Blast. Speaker_1: Oh no, really? Thought she was away on that cruise? Speaker_2: She was, but it got cancelled. Bad weather, apparently, in the Mediterranean. So, she’s descended on us. Friday’s a non-starter, then. Sorry. Speaker_1: No worries, happens. What about Saturday? Are you free Saturday afternoon? We could finally hit that new climbing place. Speaker_2: Saturday… hmm. Let me just check. *taps on phone* Okay, yeah, Saturday's looking clear. No pre-booked doom and gloom. Climbing sounds brilliant, actually. Been needing to get back into it. Speaker_1: Wicked! It's supposed to be really good there. Proper high walls and everything. I've been watching videos online, looks intense. Speaker_2: Excellent. Should be a good workout. What time were you thinking? Speaker_1: How about… 2pm? Gives us time to grab a coffee beforehand, maybe a quick bite to eat? Speaker_2: 2pm sounds perfect. There’s a little café just round the corner from the climbing centre, does cracking sandwiches. Speaker_1: Proper sandwiches, or the sad, pre-made kind? Speaker_2: Proper, I promise. Fresh bread, actual fillings…the works. They even do a decent veggie option, which I know you'll appreciate. Speaker_1: You know me too well. Okay, brilliant. Let's do 2pm Saturday then. Speaker_2: Sorted. And have you managed to get hold of Liam about that gig next week? Speaker_1: Aye, yeah, I spoke to him yesterday. He’s in, definitely. Says he’s already started thinking about the setlist. Apparently, he's unearthed some old gems from university. Speaker_2: Oh lord. That sounds… potentially concerning. Liam's university tunes are a bit… experimental. Speaker_1: That's what I said! I told him we're aiming for "fun" not "avant-garde jazz fusion". He assured me he's toning it down. We'll see. Speaker_2: Right. Well, as long as there's something vaguely recognisable. I'm bringing my sister, and she has zero tolerance for anything that sounds like a dying cat. Speaker_1: Noted. I'll subtly steer him towards the more mainstream choices. Maybe slip a bit of The Killers into the mix. Speaker_2: Excellent plan. Operation: Keep Sister Happy is a go. Speaker_1: Aye. Operation: Keep Sister Happy. It’s a crucial mission. Speaker_2: Absolutely. So, Saturday, climbing, and a delicate negotiation with Liam. Sounds like a plan. Speaker_1: Sounds perfect. Now, if you don't mind, could you turn the music down a *little*? My ears are still ringing from that bass solo. Is there anything else I can help you with? Or perhaps you'd like me to continue this scene? Speaker_1: Oh, nearly forgot. My Mum asked if you were still coming for Sunday lunch. Speaker_2: Oh yes! Definitely. I wouldn’t miss it. Is she making her Yorkshire puddings? Speaker_1: Of course she is. It wouldn't be Sunday lunch without them. She’s already been muttering about getting the perfect rise. Speaker_2: Bless her. She takes those Yorkshire puddings *very* seriously. Speaker_1: You have no idea. They're practically sacred. She once refused to let my uncle sit at the table because he suggested adding herbs to the batter. Speaker_2: *laughs* No way! That's brilliant. Your mum is a legend. Speaker_1: She certainly thinks so. Just don't even *mention* herbs. Consider yourself warned.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I feel like I’ve been run over by a bus. This cold is absolutely brutal. Speaker_2: You look it, lass. Proper peaky. You shoulda stayed in bed, should’ve you? Speaker_1: I *tried* to, but I had that conference call first thing. Absolutely essential, apparently. Felt like my head was going to explode during it. I kept having to mute myself to cough. So professional, right? Speaker_3: Oh, the joys of working from home when you’re ill. At least you weren’t spreading germs around the office. Still, sounds awful. Are you taking anything? Speaker_1: Just paracetamol, loads of hot lemon and ginger, and trying to sleep. Feel like a zombie, though. Everything smells weird. Speaker_2: Lemon and ginger’s good stuff. Me nan swore by that. Though she always added a good slug of brandy, said it ‘opened up the airways’. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Your nan sounds…sensible. Speaker_1: She was! Right, practical woman. Speaking of practical, I need to sort out my dating life, or lack thereof. It's a disaster. Speaker_2: Oh, go on then. Spill the beans. What’s happened now? Speaker_1: Well, remember Mark? The vegan architect? Speaker_3: Vaguely. Wasn’t he a bit… intense? Speaker_1: Intense is an understatement. He messaged me yesterday, after barely speaking for a week, to tell me I wasn’t “aligned with his energy” and therefore we shouldn’t see each other anymore. Speaker_2: *Aligned with his energy*? What in the world does that even mean? Sounds like something off a mindfulness retreat brochure. Speaker_1: Exactly! I said as much, actually, but he just sent back a load of emojis - a sprout, a crystal, and a little meditating person. I blocked him. Speaker_3: Good. You did the right thing. That’s just… weird. Honestly, dating apps are a minefield. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I'm considering deleting them all and taking up knitting. Least then my biggest problem will be tangled yarn, not questionable life choices. Speaker_2: Knitting's alright. Me mum makes amazing jumpers. You could learn, might meet someone at a knitting circle! Speaker_3: (Smiling) You never know! Although, maybe stick to recovering from this cold first. We’re going out on Saturday, remember? You need to be semi-functional for that. Speaker_1: Oh god, Saturday. I'd forgotten. Right, operation ‘get better’ is now in full swing. I'm accepting all medicinal offers – chicken soup, a hot water bottle, terrible reality TV… It’s all on the table. Speaker_2: I can certainly offer terrible reality TV. I’m currently obsessed with that show where people renovate caravans. It's baffling. Speaker_3: And I can bring the chicken soup. My mum's recipe, it’s practically a cure-all. Although, warning, it contains a suspicious amount of garlic. Speaker_1: Perfect. Honestly, you two are the best. I’m so glad I have friends who can tolerate my melodramatic illnesses and questionable dating decisions. Speaker_2: That's what friends are for, eh? Now eat your pasta, you look like you need it. Speaker_3: Exactly. And maybe lay off the lemon and ginger for a bit, you’re starting to smell like a cleaning product! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, shut up! But yes, more pasta please.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the day just… wouldn’t *end*. Mr. Henderson kept asking me to re-format the same spreadsheet, like, five times. Five! And each time he’d just squint at it and say “Hmm, doesn’t quite *pop*.” Pop?! It's a budget spreadsheet, not a fireworks display. Speaker_2: Oh my god, Henderson. He sounds… intense. You’d think after all this time he’d have learned to specify what ‘pop’ means. Speaker_1: Exactly! I tried to ask, but he just waved his hand dismissively and said “You know, *pop*.” It felt like being back in art class with a painfully vague brief. Speaker_2: Ugh. Well, at least you're home now. Wine time? I need to decompress after a twelve-hour shift dealing with… well, everything. Speaker_1: Definitely wine time. Though, you won’t believe who I saw today at lunch. Speaker_2: Oh? Spill. Speaker_1: Liam. From university. Remember him? The one who was obsessed with interpretive dance? Speaker_2: Liam! Oh god, yes. The tights. I’ve blocked a lot of that out. What was he doing there? Speaker_1: Apparently, he’s working for that marketing firm near the office now. He looked… good. Scarily good. Like, actual adult human being good, not ‘needs-to-be-chaperoned-through-Freshers’ good. Speaker_2: No way! Good for him, I guess. Still doing the dance thing on the side? Speaker_1: I didn’t ask! He saw me and just sort of… froze. Then mumbled something about “catching up sometime” and practically sprinted back to his office. It was awkward. Speaker_2: That’s hilarious. Okay, that's a good story. Mine's less funny, more… sad. Chloe from work just told me she's splitting up with Ben. Speaker_1: Oh no! Seriously? I didn't even know they were having problems. They always seemed so solid. Speaker_2: Apparently, it’s been brewing for a while. Something about him wanting kids now and her… definitely not. It’s a big thing. She was absolutely gutted. She was crying in the stationary cupboard. Speaker_1: Oh, the stationary cupboard. The professional weeping place. That’s awful. Poor Chloe. It’s just… everyone’s going through something, isn’t it? Speaker_2: It really is. It's exhausting. Makes you appreciate the small things, like not having to explain to a man what ‘pop’ means in a spreadsheet. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Absolutely. And a good glass of wine. Pouring now! So, interpretive dance Liam, crying Chloe… anything else exciting happen in your day? Speaker_2: Just the usual. A patient trying to convince me they could fly, a locked medication cabinet, and a near-miss with a rogue sandwich. Just a typical Tuesday. Speaker_1: A rogue sandwich? Don't leave me in suspense! Speaker_2: Okay, so Carl, lovely guy but a bit… distracted, was bringing his lunch in and tripped. It went flying, narrowly missing Mrs. Davies who’s eighty and has the sharpest elbows I’ve ever seen. It narrowly missed *her* and landed squarely on the head of the agency worker who was observing. It was chaos. Speaker_1: (Bursts out laughing) Oh my god! That is amazing. You really do have the most interesting job. Speaker_2: It’s never boring, that’s for sure. Now, tell me more about Liam’s glow-up. Was it a beard? Because a beard can explain a lot.

Speaker_1: Right, so the thing about Baba Yaga is, she’s not *always* evil. It depends how you treat her, doesn’t it? It’s a bit like… well, like Mrs. Higgins next door. She seems grumpy, but she always brings us apples from her tree. Speaker_2: (Small voice) Is Baba Yaga grumpy? Speaker_1: Sometimes. She’s… complicated. She lives in a house that walks on chicken legs! Can you imagine? Speaker_3: Woah! Does it *really* have chicken legs? Big ones? Speaker_1: Huge ones! And it spins around, so you have to shout the right words to make it stop and let you in. It’s a very old story, a Russian folk tale. They used to tell these stories to teach children lessons, you see. About being polite, and not being greedy. Speaker_2: So, if you’re nice to Baba Yaga, she helps you? Speaker_1: Sometimes. Or she tests you. Like, she might ask you to do a really difficult job, just to see if you’re kind and brave. And if you are, she’ll reward you. Speaker_3: What kind of jobs? Like tidying her house? Speaker_1: Maybe! Or sorting seeds, or helping her clean the oven. She has a very big oven, you know. And some stories say she eats people! Speaker_2: (Gasps) Eeeeew! Speaker_1: But those are usually the stories told to naughty children! She’s much more likely to give you advice, or a magic object. It’s all about respect, really. Respecting your elders and respecting the forest. Speaker_3: So, she’s like a… a witch? Speaker_1: Well, she *is* a witch, but not like the witches in fairy tales who just want to turn everyone into frogs. She’s powerful, and she represents the wild, untamed parts of nature. And sometimes, that can be scary. Speaker_2: What about dragons? Are dragons always evil? Speaker_1: That’s a good question! Dragons are… tricky. In some stories, they’re horrible monsters who hoard gold and breathe fire. But in others, they’re wise and noble creatures who help heroes. It really depends on the story. Remember St George and the Dragon? Speaker_3: Yeah! He killed the dragon! Speaker_1: He did, but that dragon was terrorizing a village. Sometimes, you *have* to fight evil, even if it's scary. But it's also important to remember not all scary things *are* evil. Speaker_2: So, Baba Yaga might not be evil? Speaker_1: Exactly. And that’s what makes these stories so interesting, isn’t it? Nothing is ever quite as simple as it seems. Now, who wants hot chocolate with marshmallows? We can read more stories while we drink them. What shall we read next? Maybe something about King Arthur? Speaker_3: Yeah! King Arthur and the sword in the stone! Speaker_2: With Lancelot! Speaker_1: Okay, okay. Arthur it is. Let’s go get the hot chocolate sorted first. Speaker_3: Can I have extra marshmallows? Speaker_1: We’ll see… if you promise to be brave like King Arthur. Speaker_2: I promise! Speaker_1: Right, then. Let's go. Speaker_3: I want a bigger cup! Speaker_1: (Sighing playfully) One cup at a time, my little dragon slayer. One cup at a time.

Speaker_1: So, how was the filming trip today, Lily? Did you enjoy it? Speaker_3: It was really good! We filmed at the castle! It was HUGE! And there were knights! Speaker_2: Knights? Proper knights in armour? Speaker_3: No, silly! People *dressed* as knights. But they had swords and everything! And I got to be an extra! I had to pretend to be a village girl bringing bread. Speaker_4: Did you drop the bread? Speaker_3: (Giggles) No! I held it *really* tight. It was pretend bread anyway. It was plastic! Speaker_1: Sounds brilliant. Was it cold though? I was worried about you all being out in that wind all day. Speaker_2: They said it was quite bracing. Honestly, I’m still trying to convince myself it’s properly warming up at night. I had the heating on a little bit last night. Speaker_1: Me too. Just a little bit. I’m a wimp, I know. Speaker_3: My legs hurt. Speaker_2: Oh, darling. Still hurting from yesterday? From falling off your scooter? Speaker_3: Yeah. It feels… stingy. Speaker_1: Let me have a look. (pause) Oh, it’s already looking much better. Just a bit of a scrape. We put the cream on, didn’t we? Speaker_2: We did. She was very brave. Right, I’m thinking I need to get myself to the gym tonight. I feel like I haven't done anything proper all week. Speaker_1: Good idea. I might join you. I'm feeling restless. Speaker_4: Are you going to run on the… the thing? Speaker_1: The treadmill? Maybe. I usually walk. It feels less… punishing. You know, less like I'm actively trying to hurt myself. Speaker_2: I just switch it to ‘hills’ and pretend I’m climbing a mountain. It distracts me from the pain. Speaker_1: That’s… dedication. I usually just people-watch. See who's struggling the most and feel slightly better about my own suffering. Speaker_3: Can we get doughnuts after? Speaker_4: Yeah! With sprinkles! Speaker_2: (Laughing) We’ll see. Maybe if you both behave yourselves. And maybe if *I* manage to run up a virtual mountain without collapsing. Speaker_1: Fair enough. Although, if you do collapse, I’m definitely getting a doughnut. For medicinal purposes, of course. Speaker_3: I want a pink one! Speaker_4: Mine needs chocolate! And sprinkles! Lots of sprinkles! Speaker_2: Alright, alright! We’ll discuss the sprinkles later. Now, who wants a snack *before* dinner? Don't tell your father. Speaker_1: (Winking at the children) Our lips are sealed. Although, he always finds out, doesn’t he? Speaker_3: He has magic ears! Speaker_4: Yeah! Magic ears! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Something like that. Let’s sneak some fruit then, shall we? Before the magic ears detect biscuit intentions. Speaker_1: Good thinking. Before the donut negotiations begin. Speaker_2: Exactly. Speaker_3: Fruit is boring. Speaker_4: Yeah! Doh-nuts! Speaker_1: (Sighs, smiling) The negotiations have begun. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Here we go. Speaker_1: This is going to be a long evening.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this paella is… perfectly adequate. Not exactly transporting me back to Spain, is it? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Adequate sums it up, Arthur. It's fuel, isn't it? Fuel for moaning about the state of the world. Speaking of which, saw old Maggie down at the boot sale on Sunday. Speaker_1: Maggie? Still at it, is she? Always had an eye for a bargain, that woman. Find anything good? Speaker_2: She snagged a rather alarming ceramic gnome for a quid. Said it reminded her of Brenda’s garden. Brenda being her sister, who’s got… well, let’s just say a *robust* garden aesthetic. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh, lovely. Sounds about right. She’s a character, Maggie. How’s business, by the way? Still keeping busy with the shop? Speaker_2: Keeping afloat. Just. It's tougher now, isn't it? Everyone's online. Trying to compete with Amazon is like bringing a water pistol to a tank battle. Thinking about maybe… scaling back a bit. More time for myself, perhaps. Speaker_1: You deserve it, Geoff. Run that place for years. Though what you’d *do* with yourself is another matter. You’d be under my feet at school within a week, volunteering to tell stories. Speaker_2: Don't you start! I can already picture it. “Mr. Thompson, the shop’s quiet, I thought I'd regale Year 7 with tales of retail life…” Speaker_1: Exactly! Seriously though, you need to look after yourself. I had old Mrs. Higgins in last week, practically collapsed in my office. Blood pressure through the roof. Stress, she said. The modern world is exhausting. Speaker_2: That’s what I’m saying. You know, I’ve been thinking about this Green Party stuff. They’re gaining traction, aren't they? Speaker_1: They are. Getting a lot of support locally, surprisingly. Though some of their proposals… a bit radical for my taste. Still, anything to get people talking about the environment. Speaker_2: I’m tempted to give them a vote. Though I worry it’s all a bit idealistic. My son, Ben, he's fully on board. He’s lecturing me about carbon footprints now. The irony! He spends his life flying around the world as a photographer. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Ah, the contradictions of youth. It’s all part of the learning process. Speaking of families, how’s Sarah? Still happily married to the barrister? Speaker_2: Oh, they’re fine. No dramatic news there, thankfully. She sends her love, by the way. Says she saw you at the theatre last month. Speaker_1: Did she? Lovely. We were seeing “A Streetcar Named Desire.” Quite powerful, actually. Reminded me a bit of Carol… Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) Oh? In what way? Speaker_1: Restless spirit, you know? Always seeking something more. Though I wasn’t suggesting she was particularly… Blanche Dubois-esque. Just a fleeting thought. It’s been a while since I’ve talked about Carol, hasn't it? Speaker_2: It has. It's alright to talk about her, Arthur. It doesn’t have to be a taboo subject. Speaker_1: I know, I know. Sometimes it just… feels raw, even after all these years. Anyway, enough morbid reflection. More paella? Perhaps if we add enough salt, it will resemble something edible.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m convinced my fiddle leaf fig is actively plotting my demise. It’s just *judging* me with its leaves. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, they’re dramatic, aren't they? Mine just drops leaves whenever I look at it wrong. It’s passive aggressive horticulture. Speaker_1: Exactly! Like, I water you, I mist you, I even talk to you… what more do you want? It's worse than trying to explain Brexit to my grandad. Speaker_2: Speaking of which, did you see Trump’s latest… pronouncements? Honestly, the man is a walking, talking headline generator. It’s exhausting. Speaker_1: Don't even get me started. It's just…constant. And people actually *believe* it. It’s terrifying. I had a whole debate with someone on Twitter last night – needless to say, it ended with me muting them. Speaker_2: Sensible. Twitter is a wasteland. I try to avoid it after 6pm. Too much… energy. How’s the research going, by the way? Still battling the data demons? Speaker_1: Oh, always. I’ve hit a bit of a snag with the qualitative analysis. It’s all just… opinions. So many opinions. And trying to find themes is like finding a needle in a haystack made of other needles. Speaker_2: Sounds delightful. My PhD is feeling increasingly like a very expensive exercise in self-doubt. I’m starting to question if anyone will *actually* care about the migratory patterns of garden snails. Speaker_1: Oh, come on! Garden snails are fascinating! Think of the tiny adventures! Seriously though, it *will* be valuable. You’re doing important work. And at least you're not dealing with… people’s opinions on everything. Speaker_2: True. Though sometimes I think snails are more opinionated than people. Have you seen what they do to your hostas? Speaker_1: (Grimaces) Don’t remind me. My mum’s garden is a battlefield. Oh! And my new blazer arrived. I got the one we were looking at online - the teal corduroy. Speaker_2: Ooh, nice! Teal suits you. It’ll look great with that patterned shirt you have. You always have excellent style. I’m still stuck in a rut of jeans and vaguely academic-looking jumpers. Speaker_1: You pull off the academic look! It’s very… distinguished. Although, we should probably both be thinking about saving a bit more money, to be honest. These Cambridge pubs are draining my account. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I swear, a pint costs more here than a pasty back home in Brum. And a good Cornish pasty is a basic human right, you know? It’s in the Geneva Convention, probably. Speaker_1: (Laughing) You’re right! It should be. And it should be subsidised for PhD students. We deserve pasties! Right, another drink then? To snails, opinions, and affordable pasties? Speaker_2: Absolutely. Cheers to that. Though maybe just half pints this time… for the sake of my dwindling funds. Speaker_1: Aye, alright. Half pints it is. It's a sensible decision, like. Speaker_2: It is. A very sensible decision… though still slightly disappointing about the lack of a pasty. Speaker_1: We'll get pasties on our next trip home. I'm promising you that. Speaker_2: Alright, you've got a deal. Speaker_1: Good. Now, tell me more about these snails…

Speaker_1: Honestly, the student feedback this year was… bracing. Apparently, I “lack energy.” Can you *believe* it? Speaker_2: (Chuckles, swirling his wine) Lack energy? You’re practically a dynamo in seminars! They just want someone to spoon-feed them everything, don’t they? Speaker_1: It's more than that. One said my lectures were “visually dull.” Visually dull! I showed them Rothko! Rothko! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, that’s brilliant. What did they want, flashing lights and interpretive dance? Speaker_1: Honestly, I wouldn’t be surprised. I was trying to explain post-structuralism and I swear one of them was scrolling TikTok. Speaker_2: The eternal struggle. Mine were complaining about workload. Apparently, reading a 20-page article is “too much.” Speaker_1: Ugh, the entitlement. Speaking of which, have you seen that documentary about killer whales in captivity? It’s absolutely harrowing. Speaker_2: No, not yet. Is it the Blackfish one? I heard it was pretty bleak. Speaker_1: It is. It completely changed my perspective. I mean, these incredibly intelligent, social creatures, stuck in tiny tanks... it's awful. Makes you think about everything, really. All sorts of captivity. Speaker_2: It does. It’s like that debate about TV violence. Everyone worries about kids being desensitized, but then you see something like that and you think maybe it's not the *violence* that's the problem, it's the lack of empathy it fosters. Speaker_1: Precisely! Although, I did see a rather alarming thing on the news today about a rise in squatting in abandoned properties. Apparently, they're getting quite organised. Speaker_2: Really? That's a bit unsettling. Though, I suppose it’s a symptom of the housing crisis, isn’t it? No easy answers. Speaker_1: None at all. It just reminds me of being a kid, and all those stories about squatters in London. Mum was terrified we’d end up living in one. Speaker_2: (Smiling) She worried about everything. Remember when you were obsessed with getting a Blue Peter badge? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh God, *obsessed*. I sent in, I swear, at least fifty letters. Designs for puppets, poems... everything. All for that orange badge. Speaker_2: And you never got one. The injustice! Speaker_1: Never! I was heartbroken. Actually, I think it fuelled my academic ambition. Proof I needed external validation from a young age. (She takes a sip of her wine.) Speaker_2: (Raises his glass) Well, you've got a doctorate *now*, darling. I think you've done alright for yourself. And you don’t need a Blue Peter badge to prove it. Speaker_1: Cheers to that. Though, secretly, I still want one. Just for the nostalgia. Speaker_2: I'll keep an eye out for competitions... although, I suspect the criteria have changed a bit since the 80s. Speaker_1: Probably. They’d want a viral TikTok video now, I bet. It's a different world. Speaker_2: A very different world. But we're still here, complaining about students and killer whales… and occasionally reminiscing about unachieved childhood dreams. Speaker_1: Exactly. And that’s quite a good thing, isn't it? Speaker_2: It is. It very much is. Speaker_1: More wine?

Speaker_2: …and then young Timothy, bless him, decided to paint the dog. With glitter glue. Honestly, the state of poor Winston! Took me an hour to get it all out of his fur. Speaker_1: Glitter glue, eh? They'll think of anything, these youngsters. Reminds me of when my sister, Mabel, tried to give our old terrier, Buster, a haircut. Ended up looking like he'd been attacked by a particularly vicious sheep. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Sounds chaotic. It’s amazing how much energy small children have. Though I’m starting to think my Year 9s have a similar level, just…directed differently. More towards eye-rolling and passive aggression. Speaker_2: Oh, teenagers. Don't get me started. At least the little ones are honest about wanting to make a mess. Speaking of messes…did your cousin Arthur ever manage to sort out that hostel he was running? I heard it was a bit of a…situation. Speaker_1: Arthur? Bless his heart, he tried. He always had big ideas, that one. But managing a hostel full of…well, *people*… wasn’t quite the same as tinkering with engines in his shed. Said he found it all a bit overwhelming. Too much paperwork, too many complaints. Said one chap tried to pay his rent with a jar of pickled onions. Speaker_3: Pickled onions? Seriously? Speaker_1: Swears on it. Honestly, the stories he used to tell. Remember old Mrs. Higgins? She kept insisting the hostel was haunted by the ghost of a former cook. Speaker_2: Oh yes! She was convinced. Always talking about cold spots and the smell of roasting beef. Though, knowing Arthur, the ‘smell of roasting beef’ was probably just his questionable cooking. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Speaking of smells…my grandfather used to work in an abattoir. He always said he lost his sense of smell years before he retired. I used to go with him occasionally, as a kid. It was…an experience. Certainly put me off sausages for a while. Speaker_1: Abattoirs. My mother’s father had a butcher's shop, you know. A proper family business. They worked so hard, my grandparents. Up at dawn every day, sorting through the meat, serving customers. No fancy refrigeration back then, just ice and a lot of elbow grease. And they ran it alongside a little greengrocery too. Hardworking folk. Speaker_2: It’s true, isn’t it? That generation really knew the value of hard work. My parents had a little sweet shop. Always bustling, always full of sweets. They didn't have much, but they always provided. Look at these old photos, though. (She rummages in a bag, pulling out a faded photo album). Here’s your mother behind the counter, Arthur! Doesn't she look lovely? Speaker_1: (Takes the album, peering at the photo) Oh, aye. Lovely she was. And quick with a sixpence change, she was too. Always smiling. She always wanted me to learn engineering you know. Thought it was a good trade. Told me I had a knack for taking things apart. Never had the patience to put them back together though. Speaker_3: It’s funny how our parents envision our lives, isn’t it? My dad was convinced I'd be a lawyer. Said I was always arguing. Thankfully, I found a way to channel that into teaching. Less paperwork than being a lawyer, hopefully. Though sometimes… Speaker_2: Ah, the paperwork. The bane of all existence. Poor Harold’s in hospital again, you know. His prostate’s been playing up. He was saying the NHS forms are more complicated than astrophysics these days. Speaker_1: Poor Harold. Tell him I’m sending my best. I always admired his knowledge, that man. Knew everything about cars, he did. Could tell you the engine size and the horsepower just by looking at it. A real petrolhead.

Speaker_1: So, recruitment, huh? That’s… quite a leap to lecturing, isn’t it? I mean, no disrespect intended, it's just a very different world. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Yeah, tell me about it. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I’m speaking a different language. Not just academically, though that’s a big part of it, but… the motivations, the timescales. Everything is so much slower paced here. Speaker_1: Slower paced is good, isn't it? After the fire drills of teaching teenagers, a bit of contemplative academic work feels rather lovely. But really, recruitment? What drew you to that in the first place? Speaker_2: Money, to be honest. Straight out of undergrad, needed to pay off a student loan the size of a small house. It was… easy enough to get into. A lot of phone calls, a lot of rejection handling, a lot of pretending to care about people’s career aspirations when really you just wanted to hit your targets. Speaker_1: (grimaces) Sounds… draining. Speaker_2: It was. It really was. You become very good at reading people, though. Spotting the BS a mile off. Which, oddly, is a skill that’s surprisingly useful in academia. Students can be very skilled at… let’s say *optimising* their work. Speaker_1: (laughs) Optimising. That’s a polite way of putting it. Speaking of students, how are you finding the academic literacy levels on your course? It’s something we’ve been discussing in the department. I’m worried they’re just not prepared for the demands of university-level writing. Speaker_2: Honestly? It's… patchy. I’ve got a handful who are genuinely brilliant, can construct a coherent argument with sources, the whole shebang. But then you get others who struggle to even form a proper paragraph. It’s less about the actual content and more about the structure, the referencing, the ability to synthesize information. Speaker_1: Exactly! It feels like they’ve been taught *what* to think, but not *how* to think. And the referencing! It’s a disaster. I had one essay last week with a bibliography that included… a meme. Speaker_2: (bursts out laughing) No way! Seriously? Speaker_1: I wish I was joking. It was a picture of a slightly disgruntled cat with the caption “Academic Integrity.” Speaker_2: (still laughing) Oh, that’s incredible. You have to show that to the department. That’s… peak student. Maybe it’s a commentary on the futility of academic pursuit? Speaker_1: (smiles) Maybe. Or maybe they just don’t understand what a source is. We've been trying to implement more scaffolding, more workshops on essay writing, but it's an uphill battle. Especially with the sheer volume of students. Speaker_2: I’m finding the same. I've built in a mandatory workshop on critical analysis, hoping that’ll help, but it’s hard to get them engaged. They seem to see it as extra work, rather than something that will actually *help* them. It's a frustrating cycle. Speaker_1: It really is. Sometimes I wonder if we're expecting too much. Or if the school system is just failing them. Speaker_2: Probably a bit of both, to be honest. But hey, at least it’s never dull, right? And at least it's a far cry from having to convince someone that their skills are 'transferable' for a job they're completely unqualified for.

Speaker_1: Right, so you’re saying you’ve never actually *been* to Blackpool? Seriously? Speaker_2: Never. It just… never happened. Family holidays were always the Lake District. Nice enough, but no donkeys and sticks of rock, you know? Speaker_3: Oh, the Lake District is lovely. Bit… subdued, though. Blackpool's a full-on assault on the senses. That’s the whole point! Speaker_4: (Smiling hesitantly) Hi. Sorry to eavesdrop, but… Blackpool sounds… chaotic. I’ve only been in the UK a few years. I’m Priya, by the way. Speaker_1: Oh, hello! No worries at all, we’re just being ridiculously northern. I’m Chloe. This is Liam, and that’s Sarah. Speaker_2: Nice to meet you, Priya. Yeah, Blackpool *is* chaotic. Gloriously so. Speaker_3: I’m Sarah. Where are you from originally, Priya? Speaker_4: India. Mumbai. It’s… a bit different to Salford, to say the least. Though, Salford’s growing on me. The people are very friendly. Speaker_1: Aw, that's good to hear! Mumbai must be amazing. Do you miss the food the most? Because I’d be gutted if I couldn’t get a good curry anymore. Speaker_4: The street food, definitely. And my grandmother's cooking. Nothing compares. Although, I did discover a fantastic Indian restaurant just around the corner from campus… Speaker_2: Oh, which one? I’m always on the lookout for somewhere decent. Speaker_4: It’s called ‘Spice Haven’. It’s small but the food is authentic. Speaker_3: Ooh, noted! I’m a fiend for a vindaloo. Liam, you’re not brave enough for a vindaloo, are you? Speaker_2: (Feigning offense) I am so brave! I once had a… a medium strength korma. It was fiery. Speaker_1: (Laughing) A medium strength korma? That barely registers on the Scoville scale! You’re such a softie. Speaker_3: So, Priya, what are you studying here at Salford? Speaker_4: I’m doing a Masters in Environmental Science. It’s a big change from what I did for my undergrad - film studies. Speaker_1: Wow, that’s a leap! What made you switch? Speaker_4: I loved film, but I realized I wanted to do something more… practical. Something that could actually make a difference. Speaker_2: Good for you. It's good to know what you want to do, isn’t it? I’m still working that out. I’m just plugging away at a retail job while I figure things out. Speaker_3: Don’t beat yourself up about it, Liam. It takes time. I’m doing a PhD, and honestly, some days I wonder if I made the right choice. Endless research can be… draining. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I’m doing a postgrad in creative writing. So basically, I get paid to stare at a blank page and pretend to be profound. Speaker_4: Sounds… challenging. Speaker_2: Sounds brilliant, actually. I’ve always wanted to write a novel. Maybe after I figure out what I want to *be* when I grow up. Speaker_1: You should, Liam! We could all form a writers’ group! Priya could give us feedback on authenticity if we ever write about India… Speaker_3: And I could provide relentless, brutal honesty. It’s a gift. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) I think I’d enjoy that very much. Perhaps, after this, we could all grab a coffee? I need to warn you, though. My attempts at British humour are still… developing. Speaker_2: Oh, you’ve come to the right place for a masterclass in self-deprecating awkwardness

Speaker_1: Right, so then Uncle Barry starts going on about his time in the Falklands, again. Honestly, you’d think he single-handedly won the war, the way he carries on. Speaker_2: Oh god, not Barry with the war stories. Does he still claim he was a sniper? Speaker_1: Claims he *trained* as a sniper. Which is, like, drastically different. And then started questioning why everyone's so obsessed with, like, Marvel films instead of documentaries about actual bravery. Speaker_2: Ugh. Family dinners, eh? It’s always something. I had to actively disengage to avoid getting drawn into a debate about Brexit with my dad. He’s convinced everything is going to fall apart. Speaker_1: Sounds delightful. At least yours doesn’t dredge up the Falklands every five minutes. Though, speaking of things falling apart, have you seen the new issue of ‘Wired’? They’ve got this long piece about the potential for cyber warfare. Proper scary stuff. Speaker_2: Oh, I skimmed that online! It’s a bit… intense. My brother's really into all that, building his own computers and stuff. He's convinced we’re all heading towards a digital apocalypse. He keeps trying to get me to learn coding. Speaker_1: Oh, bless him. Coding sounds like my personal hell. I can barely work the office printer, let alone write algorithms. Though, I did try that online course on graphic design, remember? Lasted about a week. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh yeah! And then you realised Photoshop was way more complicated than Instagram filters? Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s just… too many options. I like things simple. Speaking of simple, I’ve been rewatching ‘Paddington 2’. Honestly, such a feel-good film. It genuinely makes me happy. Speaker_2: You and ‘Paddington’. It's inspiring. Speaker_2: Ooh, that sounds amazing. I’m terrible with spices. I always end up just using curry powder. Speaker_4: That’s alright, dear. Curry powder is good. Simple and effective. Though, honestly, I’m more worried about all those little…things. The accessories. All your bits and bobs on the kitchen shelves. It's a bit…much. Speaker_1: (Laughing) It's a work in progress! We're still settling in. I'm a bit of a collector, I guess. Speaker_3: And a bit of a hoarder, if you ask me. (Receives a stern look from Speaker_4) Just joking, just joking! Though, honestly, all those plastic bags under the sink… Speaker_2: Oh, don't even get me started on plastic bags! It's a terrible habit, I know. I try to remember my reusable ones, but… Speaker_1: Yeah, I'm trying to be better about that too. It’s just…convenient. And the shops always give them out automatically. Speaker_4: It is a terrible waste, though. Honestly. And speaking of terrible habits, have you been to the doctor about your cholesterol, Reginald

Anyway, have you been following this whole… political mess? It's just endlessly depressing. Speaker_2: Honestly, I try to avoid it as much as possible. It's just a constant stream of negativity. Plus, it makes my head hurt. I did see something about house prices going up again though. Absolutely mental. Speaker_1: Mental is an understatement. You’d need to win the lottery to afford a shoebox in Cambridge these days. I'm seriously considering moving back north. At least up in Sunderland, you can get an actual house for your money.
